title: Surface-muon production for ultraslow-muon sources of $μ^+$-based colliders
summary: Anti-muon colliders based on ultraslow muons, such as $μ$TRISTAN and the $μ^+p$ collider LH$μ$C, need muon intensities well beyond those of present facilities. We study surface-\mup\ production by 3~GeV protons in graphite, molybdenum and tungsten targets with Geant4, for single, tilted and multi-layer target geometries. As single targets, molybdenum and tungsten give comparable yields, more than twice that of graphite, because a larger fraction of the beam interacts. Tilting a target with respect to a narrow beam and splitting it into several layers both raise the yield substantially: five-layer Mo and W targets give 6--8 times the surface-muon yield quoted for the J-PARC MLF graphite target, counted at the production target before capture and transport.

AI.tldr: A Geant4 simulation study shows that 3 GeV proton bombardment of tilted, multi-layer molybdenum or tungsten targets can substantially increase surface-muon yields relative to graphite, supporting future ultraslow-muon-based muon colliders.
AI.motivation: Future anti-muon colliders based on ultraslow muons, including μTRISTAN and the μ+p collider LHμC, require muon intensities far beyond those available at present facilities.
AI.method: Surface-μ+ production by 3 GeV protons was simulated with Geant4 using graphite, molybdenum, and tungsten targets in single, tilted, and multi-layer geometries.
AI.result: For single targets, Mo and W give comparable yields and more than twice that of graphite because a larger fraction of the proton beam interacts. Tilting the target relative to a narrow beam and splitting it into layers both increase the yield substantially; five-layer Mo and W targets provide 6–8 times the surface-muon yield quoted for the J-PARC MLF graphite target, counted at the production target before capture and transport.
AI.conclusion: Tilted and multi-layer Mo or W targets are predicted to offer significantly higher surface-muon production than the reference graphite target, indicating a promising route toward the intensities needed for ultraslow-muon sources and μ+‑based colliders.

title: Muon Collider: Towards the Energy Frontier
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures; submitted to the Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science
summary: A muon collider has emerged as a compelling candidate for the next energy-frontier particle accelerator, combining the discovery potential of multi-TeV lepton collisions with a footprint and power consumption far smaller than existing or proposed hadron and electron-positron colliders. Advances over the past two decades in high-power targets, muon production and capture, ionization cooling, rapid acceleration, high-field magnets, collider ring design, and machine-detector integration have transformed the concept from a long-term vision into a credible path toward a future flagship facility. This review summarizes the physics opportunities, the accelerator complex's design and status, the unique experimental environment, recent technical achievements, ongoing international R&D, and remaining steps toward realizing a high-energy muon collider by the middle of the century.

AI.tldr: This review argues that a muon collider is a credible candidate for the next energy-frontier particle accelerator, offering multi-TeV lepton collisions with a smaller footprint and lower power consumption than hadron or electron-positron colliders. It summarizes physics opportunities, accelerator design and status, the experimental environment, recent technical advances, international R&D, and remaining steps toward a mid-century facility.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the need for a next-generation energy-frontier particle accelerator that combines the discovery potential of multi-TeV lepton collisions with a much smaller footprint and lower power consumption than existing or proposed hadron and electron-positron colliders.
AI.method: This is a review, not a report of a single new experiment. It summarizes the physics opportunities of a muon collider, the design and status of the accelerator complex, the unique experimental environment, recent technical achievements, ongoing international R&D, and remaining steps toward realization.
AI.result: Advances over the past two decades in high-power targets, muon production and capture, ionization cooling, rapid acceleration, high-field magnets, collider ring design, and machine-detector integration have transformed the muon collider from a long-term vision into a credible path toward a future flagship facility.
AI.conclusion: A high-energy muon collider is presented as a credible energy-frontier facility, with ongoing international R&D and remaining technical and implementation steps needed to realize it by the middle of the century.

title: Surrogate-assisted beam distribution shaping at the CERN Proton Synchrotron and Super Proton Synchrotron
summary: The Super Proton Synchrotron at CERN delivers protons to the North Area experimental facility at 400 GeV/c. The extracted beam is split twice vertically in the transfer line with Lambertson septa to serve three fixed-target experiments simultaneously. A significant fraction of the beam is lost during these splitting processes, driving radioactive activation of the Lambertson septa. This contribution investigates reducing the splitting losses by optimising the vertical beam distribution before extraction. The developed method relies on resonant excitation with the transverse damper, reshaping the Gaussian vertical profile into a uniform and ultimately bimodal distribution, with the excitation amplitude acting as a single continuous control knob. A loss reduction of up to 23.5 % was measured. In simulations, the vertical amplitude detuning is established as a second knob that reduces the resulting beam envelope. This technique was verified with measurements at the CERN Proton Synchrotron. Surrogate models based on generative deep learning were developed for efficient real-time validation and Bayesian system identification.

AI.tldr: The paper studies reducing beam losses from vertical beam splitting at CERN’s SPS by reshaping the extracted vertical beam distribution using resonant excitation with the transverse damper, supported by generative deep-learning surrogate models and measurements at the PS.
AI.motivation: The SPS delivers 400 GeV/c protons to the North Area, where Lambertson septa split the beam twice vertically to serve three fixed-target experiments simultaneously. A significant fraction of the beam is lost during splitting, causing radioactive activation of the septa, so the work aims to reduce these splitting losses by optimising the vertical beam distribution before extraction.
AI.method: The method uses resonant excitation with the transverse damper to reshape the Gaussian vertical profile into a uniform and ultimately bimodal distribution, with excitation amplitude as a single continuous control knob. Simulations identify vertical amplitude detuning as a second knob reducing the resulting beam envelope. Generative deep-learning surrogate models were developed for efficient real-time validation and Bayesian system identification, and the technique was verified with measurements at the CERN Proton Synchrotron.
AI.result: A loss reduction of up to 23.5% was measured. In simulations, vertical amplitude detuning reduced the resulting beam envelope, and the technique was verified experimentally at the CERN Proton Synchrotron.
AI.conclusion: Optimising the vertical beam distribution before extraction via transverse-damper resonant excitation can reduce splitting losses, with vertical amplitude detuning providing an additional simulated control and surrogate models supporting real-time validation and Bayesian system identification.

title: Multi-Gaussian Model for Intrabeam Scattering
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, submitted to Nuclear Inst. and Methods in Physics Research, A
summary: Conventional analytical models of intrabeam scattering (IBS), such as the Piwinski model and Bjorken-Mtingwa model, generally rely on the assumption of a Gaussian beam distribution, limiting their applicability to non-Gaussian cases. In this work, we develop a multi-Gaussian model to extend analytical IBS calculations to a broader class of non-Gaussian phase-space distributions. The proposed approach represents a non-Gaussian distribution as a superposition of Gaussian components sharing a common covariance matrix but having different mean values. We derived a generalized model for evaluating the momentum second-moment evolution rate and the IBS growth rate. Furthermore, for equally spaced Gaussian components, we developed an infinite bunch train model and introduce a practical truncation rule to reduce computational costs. The model is applied to a representative steady-state microbunching (SSMB) storage ring, where longitudinal overlap between neighboring microbunches is shown to enhance IBS growth rates in all three directions. The proposed framework provides a practical approach to evaluating IBS in non-Gaussian beam distributions and offers a basis for further development toward a more general non-Gaussian IBS theory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multi-Gaussian model that extends analytical intrabeam scattering (IBS) calculations from Gaussian to non-Gaussian beam distributions by representing the distribution as a superposition of Gaussian components with a shared covariance matrix and different means. It derives generalized momentum second-moment and IBS growth-rate expressions, develops an infinite bunch train model with a truncation rule for equally spaced components, and applies the framework to an SSMB storage ring, finding enhanced IBS growth rates in all three directions due to longitudinal overlap between neighboring microbunches.
AI.motivation: Conventional analytical IBS models, including the Piwinski and Bjorken-Mtingwa models, assume a Gaussian beam distribution, which limits their applicability to non-Gaussian phase-space distributions. The authors aim to extend analytical IBS evaluation to a broader class of non-Gaussian beams.
AI.method: A non-Gaussian distribution is represented as a superposition of Gaussian components that share a common covariance matrix but have different mean values. The authors derive a generalized model for the momentum second-moment evolution rate and the IBS growth rate. For equally spaced Gaussian components, they develop an infinite bunch train model and introduce a practical truncation rule to reduce computational cost. The model is applied to a representative steady-state microbunching (SSMB) storage ring.
AI.result: In the representative SSMB storage ring application, longitudinal overlap between neighboring microbunches is shown to enhance IBS growth rates in all three directions. The paper does not provide experimental validation or quantitative growth-rate values in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-Gaussian framework provides a practical approach for evaluating IBS in non-Gaussian beam distributions and offers a basis for further development toward a more general non-Gaussian IBS theory.

title: Conformal Uncertainty Quantification of a Normalizing Flow Surrogate for the FACET-II Two-Bunch Beam
summary: Fast surrogate models of the beam can be used for tuning, diagnostics, and control where end-to-end simulation is too slow. At FACET-II, a normalizing flow surrogate predicts the 6D high peak current two-bunch beam used for plasma wakefield acceleration (PWFA) in less than a second, from 37 injector and linac machine parameters (such as the RF phases controlling the bunch compression). However, a surrogate can predict an incorrect beam that seems plausible, so operators and controllers need to know when to trust its predictions. We use conformal prediction to generate a prediction-specific uncertainty with guaranteed coverage. That is, if we sample new machine parameters from the same distribution as our calibration data, the uncertainty will cover the simulation output at least 90% of the time. We provide two implementations: prediction intervals for beam parameters with fixed and adaptive widths, and a region in the full 6D phase space covering 95% of the electrons, 90% of the time. The median size of this region is 5 (drive) and 2 (witness) times smaller than a Gaussian ellipsoid with the same coverage. Across 1,000 independent test simulations, our prediction intervals identify failure cases for the surrogate, specifically the slice peak current of highly compressed bunches.

AI.tldr: A normalizing-flow surrogate predicts the FACET-II 6D high-peak-current two-bunch beam from 37 injector and linac parameters in under one second; conformal prediction adds prediction-specific uncertainty with guaranteed coverage, produces compact 6D phase-space regions, and identifies surrogate failure cases for the slice peak current of highly compressed bunches.
AI.motivation: End-to-end simulation is too slow for tuning, diagnostics, and control, so fast beam surrogates are needed. However, a surrogate can predict an incorrect beam that appears plausible, so operators and controllers need prediction-specific uncertainty indicating when its outputs can be trusted.
AI.method: The paper uses a normalizing flow surrogate that maps 37 injector and linac machine parameters, including RF phases controlling bunch compression, to the 6D high-peak-current two-bunch beam used for plasma wakefield acceleration. Conformal prediction is applied to generate prediction-specific uncertainty with guaranteed coverage. Two implementations are provided: prediction intervals for beam parameters with fixed and adaptive widths, and a region in the full 6D phase space covering 95% of electrons 90% of the time. The approach is evaluated across 1,000 independent test simulations.
AI.result: For new machine parameters sampled from the same distribution as the calibration data, the conformal uncertainty covers the simulation output at least 90% of the time. The median 6D region size is 5 times smaller for the drive bunch and 2 times smaller for the witness bunch than a Gaussian ellipsoid with the same coverage. The prediction intervals identify surrogate failure cases, specifically the slice peak current of highly compressed bunches.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction provides calibrated, prediction-specific uncertainty for the normalizing-flow beam surrogate, enabling compact phase-space coverage regions and detection of important failure cases. The abstract does not provide conclusions about online deployment, controller performance, or generalization beyond the stated calibration distribution.

title: Narrowband active noise control for continuous wave operation of TESLA cavities
summary: TESLA 9-cell elliptical cavities are used in the accelerators of the European XFEL and LCLS-II. The high duty cycle upgrade study for EuXFEL and the LCLS-II-HE program target loaded quality factors of 6.10^7 and beyond, leading to RF cavity half bandwidths below 11 Hz. Stable operation in these conditions heavily relies on active RF resonance control, since the RF drive power required to maintain amplitude and phase lock would surpass amplifier max ratings if detuning is not compensated. To counteract mechanical vibrations, e.g. introduced by rotational machines in the proximity of the accelerating modules, a dedicated narrowband active noise control algorithm was introduced in previous work. This proceeding presents CPU based implementations and latest test results obtained at the Cryomodule Test Bench (CMTB) at DESY and LCLS-II at SLAC, where the stable operation gradient of a cavity could be increased from 9 to 15 MV/m without violating RF control limits.

AI.tldr: CPU-based narrowband active noise control was implemented and tested for TESLA 9-cell cavities, increasing stable cavity operation from 9 to 15 MV/m without exceeding RF control limits at CMTB/DESY and LCLS-II/SLAC.
AI.motivation: High-duty-cycle upgrades for EuXFEL and LCLS-II-HE target loaded quality factors of 6×10^7 and beyond, corresponding to RF cavity half-bandwidths below 11 Hz. Under these conditions, mechanical vibration-induced detuning must be actively compensated because otherwise the RF drive power needed for amplitude and phase lock would exceed amplifier ratings.
AI.method: The paper presents CPU-based implementations of a dedicated narrowband active noise control algorithm, introduced in previous work, and reports latest test results obtained at the Cryomodule Test Bench at DESY and at LCLS-II at SLAC.
AI.result: The stable operating gradient of a cavity was increased from 9 to 15 MV/m without violating RF control limits.
AI.conclusion: Narrowband active noise control supports stable operation of high-Q TESLA cavities under tight RF bandwidth constraints; the abstract does not provide further algorithm details or broader quantitative conclusions.

title: Quantum Startup, Recoil Statistics and Collective Gain in Free-Electron Lasers
summary: We examine the conditions under which quantum signatures can be distinguished from classical dynamics and statistical fluctuations in a free-electron laser. Starting from minimal coupling and the Bambini--Renieri frame, we derive the momentum-photon exchange Hamiltonian and its Raman-Nath ladder. An interaction-picture expansion retains detuning exactly and organizes recoil corrections through the mismatch between neighboring orders. Its validity depends on the accumulated recoil phase over the populated ladder, rather than on elementary recoil alone. Numerical checks and Gaussian entrance packets illustrate the effects of preparation and resonance averaging. We distinguish number-state exchange amplitudes from predictions for a coherent optical seed, and joint electron-field coherence from reduced radiation coherence. The Wigner representation connects finite recoil translations with classical transport and identifies the information required for bunching. A cavity channel then provides the basis for comparison with the recoil-resolved oscillator proposed by Kling and Giese, including the optical-undulator preparation, stimulated back-action and narrow resonance acceptance. Space charge, spontaneous diffusion and FEL-induced energy spread are compared with recoil and high-gain bandwidth scales. The coherent undulator pump is essential to exclude artificial zero-recoil antibunching from a number-state preparation. Startup and excess photon variance alone do not establish a quantum signature: the specified observable must remain distinguishable from a classical stochastic baseline under compatible preparation, propagation and detection conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a quantum treatment of free-electron-laser dynamics in the Bambini–Renieri frame to determine when quantum recoil and photon-exchange effects can be distinguished from classical transport and stochastic fluctuations. It derives a momentum–photon exchange Hamiltonian, organizes recoil corrections through an interaction-picture expansion, and uses Wigner and cavity analyses to specify conditions under which a claimed quantum signature remains distinguishable from a classical stochastic baseline.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to clarify the conditions under which quantum signatures in a free-electron laser can be separated from classical dynamics and statistical fluctuations, rather than inferred from startup behavior or excess photon variance alone.
AI.method: Starting from minimal coupling and the Bambini–Renieri frame, the authors derive the momentum–photon exchange Hamiltonian and its Raman–Nath ladder. An interaction-picture expansion retains detuning exactly and organizes recoil corrections via mismatch between neighboring orders, with validity governed by the accumulated recoil phase over the populated ladder. Numerical checks and Gaussian entrance packets examine preparation and resonance-averaging effects. The work distinguishes number-state exchange amplitudes from coherent-seed predictions and joint electron–field coherence from reduced radiation coherence, and uses a Wigner representation to connect finite recoil translations with classical transport. A cavity channel enables comparison with the recoil-resolved oscillator of Kling and Giese, including optical-undulator preparation, stimulated back-action, and narrow resonance acceptance; space charge, spontaneous diffusion, and FEL-induced energy spread are compared with recoil and high-gain bandwidth scales.
AI.result: The analysis finds that validity depends on the accumulated recoil phase over the populated ladder, not on elementary recoil alone. A coherent undulator pump is essential to exclude artificial zero-recoil antibunching from a number-state preparation. Startup and excess photon variance alone do not establish a quantum signature; the specified observable must remain distinguishable from a classical stochastic baseline under compatible preparation, propagation, and detection conditions. No quantitative numerical values are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Quantum signatures in free-electron lasers require a specified observable that is distinguishable from a classical stochastic baseline under compatible preparation, propagation, and detection conditions. Recoil-phase accumulation, coherent undulator pumping, and careful separation of quantum coherence from reduced radiation coherence are central to such claims, while startup statistics or excess photon variance alone are insufficient.

title: Equivalent-circuit analysis of the transverse resonant beam coupling impedance due to ceramic-chamber RF shields in the J-PARC Main Ring spill-feedback quadrupoles
summary: Ceramic vacuum chambers in fast-ramping or fast-response magnets are equipped with RF shields of conducting strips closed through lumped capacitors, which form a resonant circuit coupled to the transverse dipole moment of the beam. We evaluate the transverse beam coupling impedance due to the RF shields of the ceramic chambers in the spill-feedback quadrupole magnets of the J-PARC Main Ring. The RF shield is modelled by a magneto-quasi-static partial element equivalent circuit, and the laminated yoke of the magnet by a two-dimensional field solution with a complex permeability. The analysis shows a low-$Q$ resonant coupling impedance. The yoke lowers the resonance frequency and raises the shunt impedance per quality factor, and its effect cannot be neglected. The quality factor is determined mainly by the losses in the capacitors and in the laminations. The predicted peak impedance of the three chambers exceeds the resistive-wall impedance of the whole ring. The model can be applied to other machines and to the design of future rapid-cycling synchrotrons.

AI.tldr: The transverse beam coupling impedance due to RF shields in ceramic chambers of the J-PARC Main Ring spill-feedback quadrupoles is analyzed using an equivalent-circuit and magnetic-field model, revealing a low-Q resonance whose predicted peak exceeds the resistive-wall impedance of the entire ring.
AI.motivation: Ceramic vacuum chambers in fast-ramping or fast-response magnets use conducting-strip RF shields closed by lumped capacitors, forming a resonant circuit coupled to the beam transverse dipole moment. The paper evaluates this impedance for the J-PARC Main Ring spill-feedback quadrupoles.
AI.method: The RF shield is modeled with a magneto-quasi-static partial element equivalent circuit, while the laminated magnet yoke is represented by a two-dimensional field solution using a complex permeability.
AI.result: The analysis predicts a low-Q resonant coupling impedance. The yoke lowers the resonance frequency and raises the shunt impedance per quality factor, with its effect found to be non-negligible. The quality factor is determined mainly by losses in the capacitors and laminations. The predicted peak impedance of the three chambers exceeds the resistive-wall impedance of the whole ring. No numerical impedance values are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The laminated-yoke effect cannot be neglected in this impedance analysis, and the model can be applied to other machines and to the design of future rapid-cycling synchrotrons.

title: Powering the Space Elevator
summary: Powering the Space Elevator is a report on the work of an International Space Elevator Consortium study group tasked with determining the technology options for delivering power to the climbers on the space elevator at any altitude above Earth. The book covers options such as laser power beaming, microwave beaming, a solar-powered climber, and delivering power through the electrical conductivity of the tether. This report starts with the reference conceptual design of a climber from the 2023 study report, "The Climber/Tether Interface of the Space Elevator," and adds features to the climber that allow it to ascend or descend the elevator tether. The strengths and limitations of current technologies are identified, along with areas for future research.

AI.tldr: An International Space Elevator Consortium report reviews power-delivery options for space-elevator climbers—laser power beaming, microwave beaming, solar-powered climbers, and electrically conductive tethers—and identifies strengths, limitations, and future research needs.
AI.motivation: The study group was tasked with determining technology options for delivering power to space-elevator climbers at any altitude above Earth.
AI.method: The report is based on an International Space Elevator Consortium study group. It starts from the 2023 reference conceptual climber design in the study report on the climber/tether interface, adds features enabling ascent and descent, and assesses candidate power-delivery technologies. The abstract does not provide a quantitative modeling or experimental method.
AI.result: The report presents laser power beaming, microwave beaming, solar-powered climber, and tether-conductivity power options; identifies strengths and limitations of current technologies; and identifies areas for future research. No quantitative performance results or selected final architecture are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The abstract does not state an explicit final downselection or concluding technology choice. The reported outcome is an assessment of power-delivery options with identified strengths, limitations, and future research needs.

title: Cancellation of cryocooler-induced vibration in trapped-ion systems
summary: Mechanical cryocoolers offer numerous benefits for the operation of vacuum systems containing trapped atomic ions. However, the fidelity of laser-based gates can be degraded by phase noise induced by the cryocooler vibrations. We present a feed-forward vibration-cancellation system that directly measures inner shield displacement with an auxiliary interferometer and applies a compensating phase correction to the laser drive. The interferometer signal is demodulated, and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) system unwraps the displacement measurement signal, computes the required correction phase, and updates the RF drive of an in-line acousto-optic modulator (AOM) to correct for the vibration-induced dephasing. With cancellation active, the qubit coherence time improves from $3.0\pm0.4$ ms to $35\pm5$ ms, consistent with a simulation based on the measured vibration spectrum. We further validate the cancellation by artificially increasing the mechanical coupling of the cryocooler to the vacuum chamber. The vibration-induced decoherence rate is suppressed by a factor of approximately 70 at an RMS (root mean square) displacement of 0.65 $\mathrmμ$m.

AI.tldr: A feed-forward vibration-cancellation system uses an auxiliary interferometer, FPGA signal processing, and an in-line acousto-optic modulator to compensate cryocooler-induced phase noise in trapped-ion laser gates, improving qubit coherence from 3.0±0.4 ms to 35±5 ms and suppressing vibration-induced decoherence by about 70× at 0.65 μm RMS displacement.
AI.motivation: Mechanical cryocoolers are beneficial for trapped-ion vacuum systems, but their vibrations induce phase noise that can degrade the fidelity of laser-based gates.
AI.method: The authors measure inner shield displacement with an auxiliary interferometer, demodulate the signal, use an FPGA to unwrap the displacement measurement and compute a correction phase, and update the RF drive of an in-line acousto-optic modulator to compensate vibration-induced dephasing. They also validate the system by artificially increasing the cryocooler-to-vacuum-chamber mechanical coupling.
AI.result: With cancellation active, qubit coherence time improves from 3.0±0.4 ms to 35±5 ms, consistent with a simulation based on the measured vibration spectrum. The vibration-induced decoherence rate is suppressed by approximately a factor of 70 at an RMS displacement of 0.65 μm.
AI.conclusion: Feed-forward phase correction can effectively cancel cryocooler-induced vibration noise and improve coherence in trapped-ion systems; no intense-laser or laser–plasma connection is reported.

title: Giant and sign-tunable spin Hall effect of light in a nonlocal nonlinear Rydberg medium
summary: We demonstrate that long-range Rydberg atom interactions provide a tunable mechanism for generating the giant spin Hall effect of light (SHEL) in a cold atomic medium. For a coherently driven 87Rb medium with Rydberg S states, we derive the linear, local, and nonlocal Kerr susceptibilities for the two orthogonal probe polarization components and evaluate the resulting spatial and angular SHEL shifts. The nonlocal third-order susceptibility reshapes the complex birefringence of the medium, and drastically enhances the y-polarized SHEL shift by about one to two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, it can reverse the direction of both the spatial and angular shifts relative to the predictions of linear response. The effect is controllably tuned by the laser detuning, the quantization-axis orientation, the atomic density, and the principal quantum number of the Rydberg state. In the 87Rb medium, we find that the spatial and angular shifts reverse sign when the principal quantum number of the Rydberg state are around n=40 and 60, respectively. At high-lying excited Rydberg states, the spatial shift can be enhanced to several tens of micrometres-a magnitude that should be directly observable in experiment. These results demonstrate that Rydberg-mediated nonlocal optical nonlinearity is an efficient mechanism for spin-dependent light transport and for future photonic sensing applications.

AI.tldr: Long-range Rydberg interactions in a cold 87Rb medium produce giant, tunable, and sign-reversible spin Hall shifts of light through nonlocal Kerr nonlinearity.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to identify a controllable mechanism for generating and enhancing the spin Hall effect of light, using Rydberg-mediated optical nonlinearities to reshape the medium's birefringence and tune spin-dependent spatial and angular shifts.
AI.method: For a coherently driven 87Rb medium with Rydberg S states, the authors derive linear, local, and nonlocal Kerr susceptibilities for two orthogonal probe polarization components and evaluate the resulting spatial and angular SHEL shifts, including their dependence on laser detuning, quantization-axis orientation, atomic density, and Rydberg principal quantum number.
AI.result: The nonlocal third-order susceptibility strongly modifies the complex birefringence and enhances the y-polarized SHEL shift by about one to two orders of magnitude. It can also reverse both spatial and angular shift directions relative to linear-response predictions; in 87Rb, sign reversal occurs near principal quantum numbers n=40 for the spatial shift and n=60 for the angular shift. At high-lying Rydberg states, the spatial shift can reach several tens of micrometres, a magnitude expected to be directly observable experimentally.
AI.conclusion: Rydberg-mediated nonlocal optical nonlinearity is an efficient and tunable mechanism for spin-dependent light transport, with potential use in future photonic sensing applications.

title: Collisional lineshapes of an N$_2$-perturbed electronic transition in O$_2$ from first principles of quantum theory validated by accurate experimental spectra
comment: Submitted for consideration to Physical Review Letters
summary: We demonstrate the feasibility of predicting the lineshape of an electronic molecular transition collisionally perturbed by another molecule from first principles of quantum mechanics. We consider an N$_2$-perturbed O$_2$ $A$-band transition, which is relevant to spectroscopic observations in Earth's atmosphere. This approach simultaneously incorporates the electronic structure, quantum scattering and lineshape effects required to accurately predict pressure- and temperature-dependence of observed lineshapes. The $\textit{ab initio}$ lineshapes reproduce measurements to better than 0.6%. Theory also provides new physical constraints on beyond-Voigt lineshape parameters in fits of high-precision data, yielding fit residuals at the 0.08% level. This work motivates advances in molecular electronic structure calculations and demonstrates the potential to generate comprehensive spectroscopic reference data from first principles.

AI.tldr: First-principles quantum calculations predict N2-perturbed O2 A-band collisional lineshapes, reproducing experimental spectra to better than 0.6% and enabling 0.08%-level fits with beyond-Voigt constraints.
AI.motivation: The work aims to predict pressure- and temperature-dependent collisional lineshapes of an electronic molecular transition from first principles, motivated by spectroscopic observations of O2 in Earth's atmosphere and by the need for comprehensive spectroscopic reference data.
AI.method: The authors combine ab initio electronic structure, quantum scattering, and lineshape theory to model the N2-perturbed O2 A-band transition, validate the predicted lineshapes against accurate experimental spectra, and use the theory to constrain beyond-Voigt lineshape parameters in fits to high-precision data.
AI.result: The ab initio lineshapes reproduce measurements to better than 0.6%. Theory also provides new physical constraints on beyond-Voigt lineshape parameters, yielding fit residuals at the 0.08% level.
AI.conclusion: Predicting collisional lineshapes of an electronic molecular transition from first principles of quantum mechanics is demonstrated to be feasible. The approach motivates advances in molecular electronic structure calculations and shows potential for generating comprehensive spectroscopic reference data from first principles.

title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators
comment: 53 pages. English and Chinese versions in one PDF. Code: https://github.com/junelu0214/OpenPINN-PINO
summary: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.

AI.tldr: OpenPINN/PINO is an extensible open-source PyTorch framework that unifies specification, agent assistance, code generation, and evaluation for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators; three examples show that method choices and agent diagnostics can improve accuracy.
AI.motivation: Fragmented implementations in physics-informed learning hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison of methods.
AI.method: The framework uses two shared specifications: ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data; MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register problem templates and method components and combine or compare strategies. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, propose solver plans, and diagnose training logs and evaluation results. The framework validates specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code.
AI.result: For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative L2 error by about 75% from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative L2 error by about 68% across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization; after initial training failure, all three runs met the 10% target, with relative L2 displacement errors of 3.51%–6.31%.
AI.conclusion: OpenPINN/PINO provides an extensible, validated workflow for organizing, integrating, comparing, and diagnosing physics-informed methods. The reported examples indicate that selectable method components and agent diagnostics can materially improve accuracy; the abstract does not report a broader benchmark.

title: Spin-free potential-energy curves, spectroscopic constants, and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 CO states correlating with the first atomic asymptote
summary: We report ab initio potential-energy curves and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 spin-free adiabatic electronic states of $^{12}$C$^{16}$O correlating with the lowest dissociation limit, C($^3$P)+O($^3$P). Our state-averaged CASSCF/icMRCI(+Q) calculations with the aug-cc-pV5Z basis cover the complete set of singlet, triplet, and quintet manifolds. For the ground state, we examine basis-set convergence using the aug-cc-pV$n$Z series ($n=T,Q,5,6$) and extrapolate to the complete-basis-set limit. The resulting potential-energy curves reproduce the established topology of the low-lying CO states, including the double-minimum structure of the 2$^{1}Σ^{+}$ state and pronounced adiabatic mixing in several excited states. We determine rovibrational levels and spectroscopic constants for bound states and selected local minima, assess uncertainties, and compare our results with experiment and previous calculations. We find good agreement with experiment for the ground state and well-characterized low-lying singlet and triplet states. For the $1^1Σ^+$ ground state, $R_e=1.131~Å$ and $ω_e=2161.04$~cm$^{-1}$ are both within $0.5\%$ of experiment. The dissociation energy is $D_0=89473\pm141$~cm$^{-1}$. The most strongly bound quintet, $1^5Π$, has $D_e=6401$~cm$^{-1}$ and $ω_e=982~$cm$^{-1}$. The $1^5Σ^+$ state has a shallow long-range well with $D_e=849$cm$^{-1}$, while $2^5Σ^+$, $2^5Π$, and $1^5Δ$ are predominantly repulsive. Variations in the permanent dipole moments with bond length indicate changes in electronic character and charge redistribution, particularly where adiabatic states interact strongly. These data provide a basis for interpreting rovibrational spectra and for future studies of nonadiabatic effects, spin--orbit coupling, and collision dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper reports ab initio spin-free potential-energy curves, permanent dipole-moment functions, rovibrational levels, and spectroscopic constants for all 18 CO states correlating with C(3P)+O(3P), including singlet, triplet, and quintet manifolds.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state a broader motivation beyond the need for a complete set of CO potential-energy and dipole-moment data; it indicates that these data can support interpretation of rovibrational spectra and future studies of nonadiabatic effects, spin-orbit coupling, and collision dynamics.
AI.method: State-averaged CASSCF/icMRCI(+Q) calculations with the aug-cc-pV5Z basis cover all singlet, triplet, and quintet states correlating with the lowest dissociation limit. For the ground state, basis-set convergence is examined with aug-cc-pVnZ (n=T,Q,5,6) and extrapolated to the complete-basis-set limit. Rovibrational levels and spectroscopic constants are derived for bound states and selected local minima, with uncertainty assessment and comparison to experiment and previous calculations.
AI.result: The calculations reproduce established low-lying CO topology, including the double-minimum 2(1)Sigma+ state and strong adiabatic mixing in several excited states. For the 1(1)Sigma+ ground state, Re=1.131 Å and omega_e=2161.04 cm-1 are within 0.5% of experiment, and D0=89473±141 cm-1. The most strongly bound quintet, 1(5)Pi, has De=6401 cm-1 and omega_e=982 cm-1; 1(5)Sigma+ has a shallow long-range well with De=849 cm-1, while 2(5)Sigma+, 2(5)Pi, and 1(5)Delta are predominantly repulsive. Dipole-moment variations with bond length indicate electronic-character changes and charge redistribution, especially where adiabatic states interact strongly.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the computed data agree well with experiment for the ground state and well-characterized low-lying singlet and triplet states, and that the complete set of potential-energy curves and dipole-moment functions provides a basis for interpreting rovibrational spectra and for future studies of nonadiabatic effects, spin-orbit coupling, and collision dynamics.

title: Non-Intrusive Rubin Substructuring for Geometrically Nonlinear Structures via Nonlinear Manifolds
summary: Component mode synthesis enables modular reduction of large structural models, but its extension to geometrically nonlinear systems remains challenging. This work generalizes the Rubin method by introducing a cubic displacement manifold that statically condenses high-frequency free-interface modes onto the retained low-frequency modes and residual attachment modes. The reduced equations of motion, with cubic polynomial restoring forces, are derived by Galerkin projection onto the manifold tangent subspace. The consistency of the reduced forces is guaranteed by the cubic expansion of the component-level reduced manifold. We further present a non-intrusive procedure that combines elastic-force identification with finite-difference estimates of tangent-stiffness derivatives, which allows the reduced model to be constructed from the linear Rubin model and tangent-stiffness evaluations. In the proposed numerical tests, the reduced assembled models accurately reproduce the nonlinear responses of the full finite-element models, including internal resonance and modal coupling. Scalability and significant computational gains are demonstrated with an industrial scale model of a wing-box tip tank assembly, for which an online speed-up of about 24,666 was obtained.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Rubin component mode synthesis to geometrically nonlinear structures using a cubic displacement manifold, derives reduced equations via Galerkin projection, and develops a non-intrusive construction procedure. Numerical tests reproduce full finite-element nonlinear responses, including internal resonance and modal coupling, and demonstrate large computational gains.
AI.motivation: Component mode synthesis enables modular reduction of large structural models, but extending it to geometrically nonlinear systems remains challenging.
AI.method: A cubic displacement manifold is introduced to statically condense high-frequency free-interface modes onto retained low-frequency modes and residual attachment modes. Reduced equations with cubic polynomial restoring forces are derived by Galerkin projection onto the manifold tangent subspace, with reduced-force consistency ensured by the cubic expansion of the component-level reduced manifold. A non-intrusive procedure combines elastic-force identification with finite-difference estimates of tangent-stiffness derivatives, constructing the reduced model from the linear Rubin model and tangent-stiffness evaluations.
AI.result: The reduced assembled models accurately reproduce nonlinear responses of full finite-element models, including internal resonance and modal coupling. Scalability and significant computational gains are demonstrated on an industrial-scale wing-box tip tank assembly, with an online speed-up of about 24,666.
AI.conclusion: The proposed nonlinear manifold-based Rubin substructuring provides an accurate, scalable, and non-intrusive reduced-order modeling approach for geometrically nonlinear structures, achieving substantial online computational savings.

title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space
summary: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.

AI.tldr: This workshop proceedings summarizes how space-based quantum sensors—atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers—can probe dark matter, test general relativity, and detect gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.
AI.motivation: Quantum sensors can serve as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model, and space provides microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, varying gravitational potentials, and access to Solar System bodies that enhance such fundamental-physics investigations.
AI.method: The paper reports the proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors, summarizing the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts. No specific mission design, experimental implementation, or new data analysis is provided in the abstract.
AI.result: The proceedings identify and summarize opportunities to investigate dark matter, test general relativity, and detect gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from ground-based observatories using space-based quantum sensors.
AI.conclusion: Space-based quantum sensors offer a promising route to fundamental-physics tests, particularly for dark matter, general relativity, and gravitational-wave detection; the abstract does not provide quantitative performance estimates or mission-specific conclusions.

title: Coordinating integration of multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation codes with design structure matrices
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Fusion Engineering and Design
summary: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation design structure matrix methods to make coupling architectures in integrated fusion design codes more transparent and computationally efficient, demonstrating them on SIMSOPT stellarator optimisation and the PROCESS systems code.
AI.motivation: Integrated analysis and optimisation codes for nuclear fusion reactor design are becoming larger, more multidisciplinary, and more complex, yet the coupling structure that strongly affects computational efficiency is typically hidden within design-framework implementations. Because this issue extends beyond fusion, the authors frame it within the broader MDAO field.
AI.method: The authors present DSM and extended DSM methods from MDAO, originally developed for complex aerospace-system design, and apply them as a proof of concept to two fusion-related case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. They use automatically generated DSMs to reveal structural assumptions and feedback loops and then modify solver architecture accordingly.
AI.result: The case studies show that DSMs can identify structural assumptions in design codes and provide architectural insight for improving computational efficiency. Modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM produced a significant reduction in model evaluations; the abstract does not provide a quantitative value.
AI.conclusion: DSM methods can improve the transparency and efficiency of fusion design codes. Such architectural changes are expected to be especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher-fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.

title: Probing scalar-mediated Lorentz violation with hydrogen masers and spin-precession of molecules
comment: 43 pages, 10 figures, and 3 pages of appendices; comments are welcome
summary: We propose using hydrogen maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession experiments, traditionally employed in precision frequency measurements and searches for the electron electric dipole moment, as complementary probes of light scalar-mediated, spin-dependent fifth forces. We investigate their sensitivity to Lorentz-violating interactions mediated by scalars with masses ranging from $\mathcal{O}(10^{-4}~μ\mathrm{eV})$ to $\mathcal{O}(10~\mathrm{keV})$. While hydrogen maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession measurements probe different combinations of Lorentz-violating couplings, we find that the strongest projected sensitivities can be achieved using spin-precession of ultracold molecules, benefiting from their extended coherence times. These experimental approaches provide access to previously unexplored regions of parameter space, probing interaction ranges extending from centimeter to sub-angstrom scales. Our proposals highlight the potential of precision atomic and molecular experiments to search for new spin-dependent scalar-mediated interactions and violations of fundamental spacetime symmetries.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes hydrogen maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession experiments as complementary precision probes of light scalar-mediated, spin-dependent fifth forces and Lorentz-violating interactions. It projects sensitivity over scalar masses from O(10^-4 μeV) to O(10 keV), finding that ultracold-molecule spin precession offers the strongest projected reach because of long coherence times.
AI.motivation: Precision frequency measurements and electron-electric-dipole-moment searches using hydrogen masers and molecular spin precession can be repurposed to search for Lorentz-violating interactions mediated by light scalars and to test fundamental spacetime symmetries. The authors aim to identify complementary experimental probes of spin-dependent fifth forces across previously unexplored parameter space.
AI.method: The authors investigate the sensitivity of hydrogen maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession experiments to Lorentz-violating interactions mediated by scalars with masses from O(10^-4 μeV) to O(10 keV). They compare the combinations of Lorentz-violating couplings probed by the two approaches and evaluate projected sensitivities, including the advantage of extended coherence times in ultracold-molecule spin-precession experiments.
AI.result: Hydrogen maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession measurements probe different combinations of Lorentz-violating couplings. The strongest projected sensitivities are obtained with spin precession of ultracold molecules, enabled by their extended coherence times. These approaches access previously unexplored parameter space, corresponding to interaction ranges from centimeter to sub-angstrom scales. The abstract does not provide specific numerical sensitivity values.
AI.conclusion: Precision atomic and molecular experiments, particularly ultracold-molecule spin precession, show promise for searching for new spin-dependent scalar-mediated interactions and violations of fundamental spacetime symmetries.

title: Constitutive-fibre mechanics: mechanics-directed uncertainty in constitutive function space
summary: A structural prediction rests on constitutive functions that are known only through a finite number of tests. The tests fix the response along the states they visit; together with a declared regularity bound they leave a set of admissible constitutive functions, which we call the constitutive fibre. Constitutive-fibre mechanics (CFM) computes the range of a quantity of interest over this set. Adjoint solves of the mechanical problem represent the test observations and the quantity of interest as elements of the constitutive function space. The part of the sensitivity of the quantity of interest that is orthogonal to all observation sensitivities is hidden from the tests; for exact data it alone determines the half-width of the prediction, and for data with tolerance the half-width is a finite convex problem in the span of the adjoint representers. Comparing the two values shows whether a new type of test or a more precise test is needed, and a rank-one update ranks candidate tests before they are performed. A learned constitutive class can only under-represent the range; the deficit is computable. Beyond the linear range, an optimality system with state-dependent representers gives the extreme constitutive functions. The same set decides whether the prediction is defined for every admissible constitutive function, which is a different question from its precision. For a phase-field bar with unknown degradation function, 3% of the sensitivity of the stability eigenvalue is hidden and produces 70% of its uncertainty. For an open-hole composite lamina, the coupon that sharpens the compliance most is not the one that makes the prediction valid; validity is proved on a declared cell by a certificate accepted in exact arithmetic.

AI.tldr: Constitutive-fibre mechanics quantifies uncertainty in structural predictions by computing the range of a quantity of interest over admissible constitutive functions consistent with finite tests and a regularity bound. Adjoint sensitivities identify test-hidden uncertainty, support test ranking, extend to nonlinear constitutive laws, and distinguish prediction precision from validity.
AI.motivation: Structural predictions depend on constitutive functions that are known only through a finite number of tests, so there is a need to characterise the resulting uncertainty and determine which additional or more precise tests would be most informative.
AI.method: The admissible constitutive functions form a constitutive fibre defined by test observations and a declared regularity bound. Adjoint solves represent observations and the quantity of interest in constitutive function space; the component orthogonal to all observation sensitivities determines the prediction half-width for exact data, while tolerant data yield a finite convex problem over adjoint representers. Rank-one updates rank candidate tests, and an optimality system with state-dependent representers handles the nonlinear range.
AI.result: For a phase-field bar with an unknown degradation function, 3% of the stability-eigenvalue sensitivity is hidden and produces 70% of its uncertainty. For an open-hole composite lamina, the coupon that most sharpens compliance is not the one that establishes prediction validity; validity is certified on a declared cell in exact arithmetic.
AI.conclusion: Constitutive-fibre mechanics separates uncertainty quantification from validity, shows that learned constitutive classes can only under-represent the admissible range with a computable deficit, and provides a basis for selecting new tests or improving test precision.

title: A high-dimensional spatial-physical coupling operator for generalizable super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulent flows
summary: Accurate representation of turbulent flows requires simultaneously capturing multi-scale spatial structures and the complex, nonlinear coupling between distinct physical quantities (\textit{e.g.}, velocity components and density). In practice, however, turbulent data are often constrained by low spatial resolution due to hardware limitations and computational costs. While current data-driven super-resolution methods have shown promise by learning mappings via convolutional neural networks (CNNs), they typically treat physical variables as independent channels. This simplified approach neglects intrinsic cross-variable correlations, causing models to struggle with high-fidelity reconstruction, particularly under extremely sparse conditions or in out-of-distribution regimes. To bridge this gap, we propose an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends the standard convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension. Unlike conventional linear channel mixing, our framework constructs a unified spatial-physical representation within CNNs to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions. By lifting features into a higher-dimensional manifold, this operator significantly enhances the model's representation capacity. Experiments demonstrate that this approach enables strong reconstruction performance and zero-shot generalization, offering a physics-aware inductive bias for super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulence. More broadly, this work suggests that high-dimensional operators offer a promising avenue for modeling intricate multi-scale turbulent flows.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension to improve super-resolution and generalization for three-dimensional turbulent flows.
AI.motivation: Accurate turbulent-flow representation requires capturing multi-scale spatial structures and nonlinear coupling among physical variables, but turbulent data are often low-resolution due to hardware and computational limits. Existing CNN-based super-resolution methods treat physical variables as independent channels, neglect cross-variable correlations, and struggle under extremely sparse or out-of-distribution conditions.
AI.method: The authors introduce an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends standard convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension. Within CNNs, it constructs a unified spatial-physical representation to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions and lifts features into a higher-dimensional manifold to increase representation capacity.
AI.result: Experiments indicate strong reconstruction performance and zero-shot generalization, providing a physics-aware inductive bias for super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulence. Quantitative results and specific metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The work suggests that high-dimensional operators are a promising avenue for modeling intricate multi-scale turbulent flows.

title: On the Structure of the Nuclear-Clock Isotope $^{229}$Th Beyond Quadratic Order
summary: Precision measurements of the exceptionally low-energy nuclear transition of $^{229}$Th, offer an extraordinary sensitivity to a variety of new light fields. However, interpreting such measurements requires nuclear-structure information beyond what is currently constrained by spectroscopy. We develop a systematic description of the electric multipole interactions governing the hyperfine structure of ${}^{229}$Th, including the hexadecapole contribution, and perform a symmetry-based analysis of the resulting hyperfine splittings in crystalline environments. Hyperfine spectroscopy generally constrains combinations of nuclear moments and crystal-field gradients, leading to degeneracies when higher multipole interactions are allowed. We then combine experimental nuclear observables, particle-rotor relations, and a deformed-Fermi charge-density model to investigate the electromagnetic contribution to the nuclear clock's sensitivity to variations in the fine-structure constant. We find that higher-order nuclear deformation and state-dependent differences in the radial charge distribution of the clock states can substantially alter the predicted sensitivity, introducing large uncertainties that are not constrained by existing measurements. Our results highlight the importance of combining nuclear and solid-state theory with complementary measurements, including spectroscopy of higher-spin states, to constrain the nuclear structure and improve predictions of the clock's sensitivity to new physics. Our symmetry-based analysis also provides a framework for using hyperfine spectroscopy to investigate local defect symmetries in crystalline hosts.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a systematic multipole and symmetry-based description of $^{229}$Th hyperfine structure and shows that poorly constrained nuclear deformation and charge-density effects can substantially limit predictions of the nuclear clock's sensitivity to fine-structure-constant variation.
AI.motivation: Precision measurements of the exceptionally low-energy $^{229}$Th nuclear transition are highly sensitive to new light fields, but interpreting them requires nuclear-structure information beyond current spectroscopic constraints.
AI.method: The authors systematically describe electric multipole interactions governing $^{229}$Th hyperfine structure, including the hexadecapole contribution, perform a symmetry-based analysis of hyperfine splittings in crystalline environments, and combine experimental nuclear observables, particle-rotor relations, and a deformed-Fermi charge-density model to assess the electromagnetic contribution to clock sensitivity.
AI.result: Higher-order nuclear deformation and state-dependent differences in the radial charge distribution of the clock states can substantially alter the predicted sensitivity to fine-structure-constant variation, introducing large uncertainties not constrained by existing measurements; hyperfine spectroscopy generally constrains combinations of nuclear moments and crystal-field gradients, producing degeneracies when higher multipoles are included. No quantitative sensitivity values are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Constraining the nuclear structure of $^{229}$Th requires combining nuclear and solid-state theory with complementary measurements, including spectroscopy of higher-spin states, to improve predictions of the clock's sensitivity to new physics; the symmetry-based analysis also provides a framework for probing local defect symmetries in crystalline hosts.

title: A Riemann-invariant contact-capturing scheme with WENO reconstruction and RH-motivated dual-speed dissipation for compressible two-phase mixture flows
summary: This work develops and benchmarks centred (Riemann-solver-free) finite-volume fluxes for a hyperbolic two-phase mixture model with velocity non-equilibrium. The baseline method combines a Riemann-invariant contact-capturing algorithm (RICCA) with dual-speed dissipation and primitive-variable WENO3/WENO5 reconstruction, avoiding full eigen-decomposition while retaining a conservative update. An RH-motivated companion flux (RICCA--RH) is introduced, in which the acoustic weight in $α= |V_n| + Ba$ is controlled by a binary pressure/Rankine--Hugoniot switch. On one-dimensional gas--magma Riemann suite, RICCA--RH tracks legacy RICCA and is sharper than first-order FORCE/Lax--Friedrichs at material contacts; a linearised spectral study clarifies how its dual-speed dissipation differs from FORCE. With WENO5, RICCA, RICCA--RH and FORCE produce essentially identical smooth profiles, indicating that most differences are confined to first-order contact metrics. In two dimensions (gas--liquid benchmarks), the production flux implemented on CPU and Apple Metal reproduces expansion-tube, collision and forward-facing-step patterns and yields intermediate cut-based roughness between RICCA and FORCE. High order is obtained using an approximate face-normal acoustic characteristic reconstruction, a pragmatic multi-variable hybrid sensor, and a Zhang--Shu-style invariant-domain face limiter on $(ρ,α,c)$. An under-dissipative soft-switch variant that rings severely is also documented, and a resident 2D Metal kernel on Apple Silicon is reported to deliver up to $3.9\times$ wall-clock speedup on completed CPU/Metal comparisons (peak on the $101\times101$ expansion tube).

AI.tldr: The paper develops and benchmarks centred, Riemann-solver-free finite-volume fluxes for a hyperbolic compressible two-phase mixture model with velocity non-equilibrium. It combines RICCA with dual-speed dissipation and WENO reconstruction, introduces an RH-motivated variant, tests it on 1D gas–magma and 2D gas–liquid benchmarks, and reports CPU/Apple Metal implementations with up to 3.9× speedup.
AI.motivation: The work aims to provide and assess centred finite-volume fluxes for a hyperbolic two-phase mixture model with velocity non-equilibrium, avoiding full eigen-decomposition while retaining a conservative update and improving contact capturing relative to standard first-order centred fluxes.
AI.method: The baseline method combines a Riemann-invariant contact-capturing algorithm (RICCA), dual-speed dissipation, and primitive-variable WENO3/WENO5 reconstruction. A companion RICCA–RH flux controls the acoustic weight in α=|V_n|+Ba using a binary pressure/Rankine–Hugoniot switch. The study uses one-dimensional gas–magma Riemann tests, a linearised spectral analysis, and two-dimensional gas–liquid benchmarks. High order uses approximate face-normal acoustic characteristic reconstruction, a multi-variable hybrid sensor, and a Zhang–Shu-style invariant-domain face limiter on (ρ,α,c). CPU and Apple Metal implementations are compared, and an under-dissipative soft-switch variant is documented.
AI.result: RICCA–RH tracks legacy RICCA and is sharper than first-order FORCE/Lax–Friedrichs at material contacts in the 1D gas–magma Riemann suite. The linearised spectral study clarifies how its dual-speed dissipation differs from FORCE. With WENO5, RICCA, RICCA–RH, and FORCE produce essentially identical smooth profiles, indicating that most differences are confined to first-order contact metrics. In 2D gas–liquid benchmarks, the production flux reproduces expansion-tube, collision, and forward-facing-step patterns and yields intermediate cut-based roughness between RICCA and FORCE. A resident 2D Metal kernel on Apple Silicon delivers up to 3.9× wall-clock speedup on completed CPU/Metal comparisons, with the peak on the 101×101 expansion tube.
AI.conclusion: The proposed centred finite-volume framework is effective for compressible two-phase mixture flows, with RICCA–RH offering contact-capturing behaviour comparable to legacy RICCA and sharper than first-order FORCE/Lax–Friedrichs. High-order accuracy is achieved with reconstruction, sensing, and invariant-domain limiting, while the under-dissipative soft-switch variant is shown to ring severely. The Apple Metal implementation demonstrates substantial acceleration. No substantive intense-laser or laser–plasma connection is reported.

title: On the velocity range limitation of DBSCAN for event-based particle tracking and a proposed solution
summary: Event-based cameras offer new opportunities for particle tracking in fluid mechanics by providing asynchronous, sparse measurements with high temporal resolution and no fixed acquisition frequency. Processing such data requires algorithms capable of fully exploiting these distinctive features. A natural first approach to perform particle tracking on event-based data is to apply a clustering algorithm, in particular DBSCAN, as it does not require specifying the number of clusters a priori. In this paper, we show, using a simplified synthetic two-particle system, that this classical algorithm is severely limited in terms of the accessible velocity range vmax/vmin. To address this limitation, and to take advantage of the absence of a fixed acquisition frequency in event-based cameras, we propose a new two-dimensional, two-component (2D2C) particle-tracking algorithm based on clustering. The method relies on a recursive application of DBSCAN with multiple temporal normalizations, retaining only clusters that satisfy a set of validation criteria. A key feature of the proposed algorithm is that it does not assume any characteristic time scale or typical velocity. The algorithm is evaluated on realistic synthetic datasets generated from numerical simulations of turbulent flows, and the influence of key parameters is systematically investigated. Particular attention is given to the definition of evaluation metrics adapted to clusters of events for particle tracking.
