Three members reach observed maximum full-profile relative errors of $6.5\times10^{-3}$, $9.2\times10^{-4}$, and $7\times10^{-5}$ over $a\in[10^{-9},10^{9}]$ and $|v|\le10^{5}$. Extended-domain and randomized checks support these error levels. For the tested SIU, MOOG, and Humlicek w4 implementations, the relative error instead approaches 100% towards small values of the damping parameter. We compare synthesis-weighted costs on an Apple M1 and an AMD EPYC 9554 using gfortran 15, and propagate errors through solar-dwarf, red-supergiant, and M-dwarf syntheses. The least expensive member costs 0.98-1.05 times as much as the tabulated Synspec kernel on the M1 and 1.11-1.20 times as much on the EPYC, with a maximum flux error smaller by a factor of 3.6. The intermediate member costs less than every tested arithmetic kernel and holds the flux error below $10^{-3}$. The most accurate member costs 1.6-3.0 times less than w4 and gives 3.4-5.0 times smaller maximum flux errors in the tested syntheses.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces QLG, a family of branchless single-precision Voigt approximations for spectral synthesis, separable in the damping parameter and designed with controlled full-profile relative error. Three members achieve maximum relative errors of 6.5e-3, 9.2e-4, and 7e-5 over wide parameter ranges, with synthesis tests showing favorable accuracy-cost tradeoffs against common kernels.
AI.motivation: The Voigt function is evaluated repeatedly in spectral synthesis, and several widely used implementations have an absolute error floor. The authors aim to provide branchless, single-precision approximations that remain accurate across a wide damping-parameter range and are suitable for efficient spectral synthesis.
AI.method: The authors construct QLG, named for Lorentzian and Gaussian generators L and G plus an envelope q that multiplies every fitted correction and vanishes at both endpoints. The leading Lorentzian wing amplitude is fixed analytically. The approximation family is branchless, single-precision, and separable in the damping parameter a. Three members are evaluated with observed maximum full-profile relative errors, extended-domain checks, randomized checks, and synthesis-weighted cost comparisons on Apple M1 and AMD EPYC 9554 using gfortran 15. Errors are propagated through solar-dwarf, red-supergiant, and M-dwarf syntheses and compared with SIU, MOOG, Humlicek w4, and the tabulated Synspec kernel.
AI.result: Three QLG members reach observed maximum full-profile relative errors of 6.5e-3, 9.2e-4, and 7e-5 over a in [1e-9, 1e9] and |v| <= 1e5. Extended-domain and randomized checks support these error levels. For tested SIU, MOOG, and Humlicek w4 implementations, relative error instead approaches 100% toward small damping-parameter values. The least expensive member costs 0.98-1.05 times as much as the tabulated Synspec kernel on M1 and 1.11-1.20 times as much on EPYC, with maximum flux error smaller by a factor of 3.6. The intermediate member costs less than every tested arithmetic kernel and keeps flux error below 1e-3. The most accurate member costs 1.6-3.0 times less than w4 and gives 3.4-5.0 times smaller maximum flux errors in the tested syntheses.
AI.conclusion: QLG provides branchless single-precision Voigt approximations with explicitly controlled full-profile relative error over a very wide damping-parameter range. Its members offer competitive or improved synthesis-weighted cost and flux accuracy relative to tested kernels, enabling different accuracy-cost tradeoffs for spectral synthesis.

title: Stokes flow in a wedge with a moving contact point: well-posedness with a fixed contact angle and Navier slip
summary: We study 2D Stokes flow in a wedge-like region bounded by a solid substrate with Navier slip and by a free surface driven by surface tension. The two meet at a moving contact point with a fixed contact angle. This is the model of a moving contact line at scales below the slip length, in its simplest setting. The slip length is the only length scale, and nothing is prescribed at the contact point beyond the angle: no relaxation law for the angle, and no contact-point dissipation. Slip removes the paradox found by Huh and Scriven, the infinite dissipation at a contact line that moves without slip, but in this model a weaker singularity remains. We give, to our knowledge, the first rigorous characterisation of this singularity for solutions of the free-boundary problem near the stationary state. For small contact angles and small initial data satisfying two compatibility conditions, we prove local existence, uniqueness and Lipschitz dependence on the data. The compatibility conditions are the price of the fixed angle for solutions regular in time up to the initial time. Rather than hiding the singularity, the solution class carries it explicitly in corner expansions. The velocity is continuous up to the contact point. The pressure has a logarithmic singularity, the slip-regularised version of that of Huh and Scriven. Its coefficient is proportional to the contact-point velocity. The slope of the free boundary has a corresponding logarithmic correction, the slip-scale counterpart of the Cox-Voinov relation. The linearised problem combines terms of different scaling, which prevents a direct treatment by the Mellin transform. We solve it by a Lax-Milgram argument, and an auxiliary test function problem shows that the variational solution satisfies the equations. Explicit Mellin representations then yield the corner expansions, and the nonlinear problem is solved by a contraction argument.

AI.tldr: The paper proves local well-posedness for 2D Stokes flow in a wedge with Navier slip, surface tension, and a moving contact point at fixed contact angle, and rigorously characterizes the remaining logarithmic corner singularity.
AI.motivation: The model describes a moving contact line at scales below the slip length in its simplest setting. Navier slip removes the Huh-Scriven infinite-dissipation paradox of a moving contact line without slip, but a weaker singularity remains, and the paper aims to characterize it rigorously near the stationary state.
AI.method: The authors study 2D Stokes flow in a wedge bounded by a solid substrate with Navier slip and a free surface driven by surface tension, meeting at a moving contact point with fixed contact angle; the slip length is the only length scale, with no angle relaxation law or contact-point dissipation prescribed. For small contact angles and small initial data satisfying two compatibility conditions, they prove local existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz dependence. The linearized problem is solved by a Lax-Milgram argument with an auxiliary test-function problem, Mellin representations yield corner expansions, and the nonlinear problem is solved by a contraction argument.
AI.result: For small contact angles and small initial data satisfying two compatibility conditions, the paper obtains local existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz dependence on the data. The velocity is continuous up to the contact point; the pressure has a logarithmic singularity whose coefficient is proportional to the contact-point velocity; and the free-boundary slope has a corresponding logarithmic correction, the slip-scale counterpart of the Cox-Voinov relation. The compatibility conditions are required for solutions regular in time up to the initial time, and the singularity is carried explicitly in corner expansions.
AI.conclusion: Navier slip removes the Huh-Scriven infinite dissipation but leaves a weaker singularity, which the paper characterizes rigorously for the free-boundary problem near the stationary state. The solution class explicitly includes the corner singularity rather than hiding it, giving what the authors describe as the first rigorous characterization of this singularity for such solutions.

title: Generating Circularly Polarized and Chiral Cathodoluminescence from a Single Plasmonic Nanoantenna
summary: The generation and control of circularly polarized and chiral light is important for a wide range of applications, from sensing to optical communication and catalysis. Generally, the generation of chiral light emission from plasmonic nanostructures relies on the use of nanoantennas with predefined chiral shape, which requires complex nanofabrication. In this work, we show how localized electron excitation controls the generation of circularly polarized- and chiral cathodoluminescence from a single achiral plasmonic nanoantenna. We exploit the $π$/2 phase difference between the transverse and longitudinal components of the electric field that is carried by 30 keV electrons, to coherently excite degenerate dipolar modes of which the far-field radiation interferes in the far field, thereby creating a strong optical spin-Hall effect. Using angle-resolved cathodoluminescence polarimetry we measure the angle-resolved Stokes parameters for selected positions of the electron beam near the nanoparticle and show how the precise location of the electron beam controls the generation of the circularly polarized and chiral electric field components. Our findings represent an elemental form of generation of circularly polarized light, by synthesizing the circularly rotating electric fields characteristic for CPL from interference of orthogonal dipolar modes with controlled phase lag.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that localized electron-beam excitation of a single achiral plasmonic nanoantenna can generate circularly polarized and chiral cathodoluminescence, with the electron-beam position controlling the emitted polarization and chiral field components.
AI.motivation: Circularly polarized and chiral light is useful for applications including sensing, optical communication, and catalysis, but conventional plasmonic generation typically requires nanoantennas with predefined chiral shapes and complex nanofabrication.
AI.method: The authors use 30 keV electrons, whose transverse and longitudinal electric-field components carry a π/2 phase difference, to coherently excite degenerate dipolar modes of a single achiral plasmonic nanoantenna. Far-field interference of these modes produces an optical spin-Hall effect, and angle-resolved cathodoluminescence polarimetry measures angle-resolved Stokes parameters for selected electron-beam positions near the nanoparticle.
AI.result: Angle-resolved Stokes measurements show that the precise electron-beam location controls the generation of circularly polarized and chiral electric-field components from the single achiral nanoantenna. The abstract does not provide quantitative polarization values or efficiency metrics.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish an elemental approach to generating circularly polarized light by synthesizing circularly rotating electric fields through interference of orthogonal dipolar modes with a controlled phase lag, using localized electron excitation rather than a predefined chiral nanostructure.

title: Learning Similarity-Reduced Ion Kinetics across Scales and Regimes in Capacitively Coupled Plasmas
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to Applied Physics Letters
summary: Systematic kinetic investigations of discharge-mode and heating-mechanism transitions in low-pressure capacitively coupled plasmas (CCPs) are computationally expensive because particle-in-cell/Monte Carlo collision (PIC/MCC) simulations must resolve the inherently slow ion relaxation.In this Letter, we propose a similarity-reduced ion-kinetic representation and a machine learning (ML) reconstruction method for weakly ionized Boltzmann-Poisson discharge systems.Using discharge similarity, the three-dimensional control parameter space, comprising gas pressure p, gap distance d, and driving frequency f, is reduced into a two-dimensional similarity space (pd, fd).A dual-branch ML model predicts the ion density profile at the reference scale and the conditional ion velocity distribution.Taking a 1D3V argon discharge as the paradigm, we use the reconstructed ion kinetic state to initialize the PIC/MCC simulation, which then relaxes to a self-consistent periodic steady state after only a brief evolution.Compared to conventional uniform initializations, this approach achieves a maximum computational speedup of 56.8 times and a median speedup of 27.7 times.Furthermore, the physical regimes of complex nonlinear discharge transitions, including the alpha--gamma mode transition, local-to-nonlocal electron collisional heating mode transition and low-density jumps, are accurately mapped within the similarity space.Similarity transformations extend these boundaries across scales, opening a new avenue for rapid kinetic characterization and optimization of radio-frequency plasma sources.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a similarity-reduced ion-kinetic representation and a dual-branch machine learning reconstruction method to accelerate particle-in-cell/Monte Carlo collision simulations of low-pressure capacitively coupled plasmas and to map discharge-mode and heating transitions in a reduced similarity space.
AI.motivation: Systematic kinetic investigations of discharge-mode and heating-mechanism transitions in low-pressure capacitively coupled plasmas are computationally expensive because particle-in-cell/Monte Carlo collision simulations must resolve inherently slow ion relaxation.
AI.method: Using discharge similarity, the three-dimensional control-parameter space of gas pressure p, gap distance d, and driving frequency f is reduced to a two-dimensional similarity space (pd, fd). A dual-branch machine learning model predicts the ion density profile at the reference scale and the conditional ion velocity distribution. For a 1D3V argon discharge, the reconstructed ion kinetic state initializes the PIC/MCC simulation, which then relaxes to a self-consistent periodic steady state after a brief evolution.
AI.result: Compared with conventional uniform initialization, the approach achieves a maximum computational speedup of 56.8 times and a median speedup of 27.7 times. Complex nonlinear discharge transitions, including the alpha--gamma mode transition, the local-to-nonlocal electron collisional heating mode transition, and low-density jumps, are accurately mapped within the similarity space, and similarity transformations extend these boundaries across scales.
AI.conclusion: The similarity-reduced machine learning approach enables rapid kinetic characterization and optimization of radio-frequency plasma sources by accelerating PIC/MCC simulations and mapping complex discharge transitions across scales and regimes.

title: Parity nonconservation in hyperfine transitions of hydrogen-like muonic atoms
summary: We investigate parity nonconservation (PNC) in the $2s_{1/2}(F=0)\leftrightarrow 2s_{1/2}(F=1)$ hyperfine transition of hydrogenlike muonic $^{13}\mathrm{C}^{5+}$ and $^{15}\mathrm{N}^{6+}$. Finite-nuclear-size effects and the Uehling potential are incorporated directly into the Dirac equation, whereas the leading kinematic-recoil and Fermi--Breit hyperfine corrections to the energy levels are treated to first order in perturbation theory. The spin-independent PNC amplitude is evaluated using hyperfine-resolved energy denominators and is proportional to the weak charge $Q_W$. The spin-dependent amplitude is proportional to $κ=κ_a+κ_Z$, where $κ_a$ and $κ_Z$ denote the nuclear-anapole and direct neutral-current couplings, respectively. For absorption we obtain the PNC degree $\mathcal P_{\rm abs}(^{13}\mathrm{C})=-5.9\times10^{-8}Q_W +1.3\times10^{-5}κ$ and $\mathcal P_{\rm abs}(^{15}\mathrm{N})=-8.8\times10^{-9}Q_W -8.1\times10^{-6}κ$. Nuclear-structure calculations indicate that $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ has enhanced relative sensitivity to direct $Z^0$-boson exchange, whereas the spin-dependent interaction in $^{15}\mathrm{N}$ is expected to be dominated by the nuclear-anapole contribution. In an idealized cavity-polarimetry model, a column density of order $10^{15}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ is required; however, the production of metastable hydrogenlike muonic ions remains the principal experimental challenge.

AI.tldr: The paper calculates parity-nonconserving amplitudes in the 2s1/2(F=0)↔2s1/2(F=1) hyperfine transition of hydrogenlike muonic 13C5+ and 15N6+, separating weak-charge and spin-dependent contributions and assessing experimental feasibility.
AI.motivation: To investigate parity nonconservation in hyperfine transitions of hydrogenlike muonic ions as a probe of the weak charge and of spin-dependent nuclear-anapole and direct neutral-current couplings, including nuclear-structure-dependent sensitivities.
AI.method: Finite-nuclear-size effects and the Uehling potential are included directly in the Dirac equation; leading kinematic-recoil and Fermi–Breit hyperfine corrections are treated to first order in perturbation theory. The spin-independent and spin-dependent PNC amplitudes are evaluated with hyperfine-resolved energy denominators, and an idealized cavity-polarimetry model is used to estimate required column density.
AI.result: For absorption, the PNC degrees are P_abs(13C) = -5.9×10^-8 Q_W + 1.3×10^-5 κ and P_abs(15N) = -8.8×10^-9 Q_W - 8.1×10^-6 κ, with κ = κ_a + κ_Z. Nuclear-structure calculations indicate enhanced relative sensitivity of 13C to direct Z0-boson exchange and dominance of the nuclear-anapole contribution in 15N; an idealized cavity-polarimetry model requires a column density of order 10^15 cm^-2.
AI.conclusion: PNC in these hydrogenlike muonic hyperfine transitions provides distinct weak-charge and spin-dependent sensitivities, with 13C and 15N offering complementary sensitivity to direct neutral-current and nuclear-anapole effects. The principal experimental challenge remains producing metastable hydrogenlike muonic ions.

title: Orbital differentiation in a rare earth ion near half filling
summary: In the electronic structure of rare earth ions, details can be crucial for understanding the origin of correlated states. Currently, state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods (e.g. CASSCF) can capture single-ion properties of molecular magnets and some band insulating systems, but are expensive to perform, and cannot be applied to metallic systems. Here, we carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty. The calculated experimental observables from our model agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density also agrees with DFT predictions. By tuning the crystal field parameters, our full multiplet-derived wavefunctions reveal the presence of orbital differentiation of the ground $J=\frac{5}{2}$ manifold into two groups, which are distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness. This violation of Hund's rule, observed with a fast and inexpensive calculation tool, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may provide support for the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

AI.tldr: The paper performs full multiplet calculations for cubic rock-salt SmN using Quanty, reproduces magnetic susceptibility, inelastic neutron scattering, and DFT spin-density results, and finds crystal-field-tuned orbital differentiation within the ground J=5/2 manifold, interpreted as a violation of Hund's rule with possible relevance to proposed unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.
AI.motivation: Details of rare earth ion electronic structure are important for understanding correlated states, but state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods such as CASSCF are expensive and cannot be applied to metallic systems.
AI.method: The authors carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty and tune the crystal field parameters to examine the full multiplet-derived wavefunctions.
AI.result: The calculated observables agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density agrees with DFT predictions. Tuning the crystal field reveals orbital differentiation of the ground J=5/2 manifold into two distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness, a violation of Hund's rule.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that a fast and inexpensive full multiplet calculation tool can reveal orbital differentiation in a rare earth material, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may support the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

title: A conditional quadrature method of moments for populations of oblate spheroidal particles
summary: Non-spherical particle populations are encountered in numerous industrial processes, where particle size, shape, and velocity jointly influence transport, breakage, and classification dynamics. The resulting coupled distributions of geometric and kinematic particle properties evolve within a high-dimensional phase space whose accurate representation remains a significant challenge. We present a conditional quadrature method of moments (CQMOM) for oblate spheroidal particles described by a five-dimensional phase space that includes their size, aspect ratio, and velocity. The dimensionality of the problem is reduced by assuming that the particles continuously adopt their drag-maximizing orientation. In the solution algorithm, the resulting conditional quadrature representation of the particle phase space is combined with a Strang splitting of the continuous and discontinuous mathematical operators governing the moment transport. We verify this CQMOM framework against Monte Carlo simulations of the same particle model for representative test cases of increasing complexity, including drag, breakage, recoil, and attrition, at different Stokes numbers. With two nodes per coordinate, the particle number, the mean size, and the mean aspect ratio agree with the Monte Carlo solution within its statistical uncertainty, and the velocity statistics to within 7 %. Time-step and quadrature resolution studies identify the conditional velocity quadrature as the main source of the remaining deviations, for which we discuss potential remedies. Overall, the results demonstrate that the conditional quadrature representation preserves the geometric-kinematic correlations of the particle population in a five-dimensional phase space, at a cost more than 60 times lower than that of a single Monte Carlo realization.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a conditional quadrature method of moments (CQMOM) for oblate spheroidal particle populations in a five-dimensional phase space of size, aspect ratio, and velocity, using a drag-maximizing orientation assumption and Strang splitting. Benchmarked against Monte Carlo simulations for drag, breakage, recoil, and attrition, it reproduces key statistics and preserves geometric-kinematic correlations at over 60 times lower cost than a single Monte Carlo realization.
AI.motivation: Non-spherical particle populations are common in industrial processes, and their size, shape, and velocity jointly affect transport, breakage, and classification. Accurately representing the resulting coupled geometric and kinematic distributions in a high-dimensional phase space remains a significant challenge.
AI.method: The authors present a conditional quadrature method of moments for oblate spheroidal particles described by a five-dimensional phase space including size, aspect ratio, and velocity. They reduce dimensionality by assuming particles continuously adopt their drag-maximizing orientation, combine the conditional quadrature representation with Strang splitting of continuous and discontinuous moment-transport operators, and verify the framework against Monte Carlo simulations for drag, breakage, recoil, and attrition at different Stokes numbers.
AI.result: With two nodes per coordinate, particle number, mean size, and mean aspect ratio agree with the Monte Carlo solution within its statistical uncertainty, and velocity statistics agree within 7%. Time-step and quadrature resolution studies identify the conditional velocity quadrature as the main source of remaining deviations. The method costs more than 60 times less than a single Monte Carlo realization.
AI.conclusion: The conditional quadrature representation preserves the geometric-kinematic correlations of the particle population in a five-dimensional phase space at substantially lower computational cost than Monte Carlo, with potential remedies discussed for deviations attributed mainly to the conditional velocity quadrature.

title: Quantum differential interference contrast microscope
summary: Optical sensing and imaging of transparent unstained biological and material specimen makes use of optical interference to translate phase shifts into intensity measurements, that are readily available in the optical domain. This is the case of Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopes. However, environmental disturbances such as acoustic vibrations, air currents, temperature shifts, and mechanical drifts cause random phase noise that degrades the precision attainable in the estimation of the unknown phase shift. Although there are tools to compensate for these random phase drifts, such using common path interference techniques or phase stabilization systems, these are not always an option and its introduction is generally at the expense of device simplicity and robustness. Here we introduce a quantum version of Differential Interference Contrast microscopy (qDIC), that makes use of quantum interference for polarization analysis. When compared with standard schemes that make use of coherent light, our approach shows that the transfer of classical DIC microscopy into the quantum domain offers a route towards quantum-enhanced resilience to environmental disturbances, allowing the enhancement of phase sensitivity without sacrificing the simplicity and robustness of the optical setup.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum version of differential interference contrast microscopy that uses quantum interference for polarization analysis to improve phase sensitivity and resilience to environmental phase noise while retaining optical setup simplicity and robustness.
AI.motivation: Classical DIC microscopy converts phase shifts into intensity measurements but is degraded by random phase noise from acoustic vibrations, air currents, temperature shifts, and mechanical drifts. Existing compensation and stabilization methods are not always available and typically reduce device simplicity and robustness.
AI.method: The authors propose quantum differential interference contrast microscopy (qDIC), which employs quantum interference for polarization analysis instead of the coherent-light schemes used in standard DIC microscopy.
AI.result: Compared with standard coherent-light schemes, qDIC is reported to provide quantum-enhanced resilience to environmental disturbances and enhanced phase sensitivity without sacrificing the simplicity and robustness of the optical setup. Quantitative performance metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Transferring classical DIC microscopy into the quantum domain offers a route toward quantum-enhanced resistance to environmental phase noise and improved phase sensitivity while preserving a simple and robust optical configuration.

title: Energy partition in resonant instabilities in multi-component plasmas
summary: Space and astrophysical plasmas are often collisionless and exhibit non-equilibrium velocity distributions. When these departures from equilibrium are sufficiently large, the plasma becomes unstable to various kinetic micro-instabilities, which provide a mechanism for transferring energy from the particles to the electromagnetic (EM) fields. In multi-component plasmas, different species interact with the generated EM waves in distinct ways, acting as sources or sinks of wave energy through resonant wave--particle interactions. Consequently, the nonlinear evolution of kinetic instabilities is governed not only by the species driving the instability but also by the resonant response of other plasma populations. In this work, considering proton-$α$-particle plasmas with parameters representative of the solar wind, we investigate the generation, saturation, and energy partition of kinetic micro-instabilities, such as Alfvén/ion-cyclotron and fast-magnetosonic/whistler wave instabilities. We combine linear Vlasov--Maxwell theory and hybrid particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations to analyze these instabilities and to quantify the exchange of energy and momentum between ion populations during the instability evolution. Our results demonstrate that minor ions play a fundamental role in regulating the nonlinear saturation of kinetic instabilities and the transfer of energy among plasma populations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies kinetic micro-instabilities in multi-component proton–α-particle plasmas with solar-wind-like parameters, using linear Vlasov–Maxwell theory and hybrid PIC simulations to examine instability generation, saturation, and energy partition. It finds that minor ions are fundamental in regulating nonlinear saturation and energy transfer among plasma populations.
AI.motivation: Space and astrophysical plasmas are often collisionless and can have non-equilibrium velocity distributions that drive kinetic micro-instabilities, transferring energy from particles to electromagnetic fields. In multi-component plasmas, different species can act as wave-energy sources or sinks through resonant wave–particle interactions, so nonlinear evolution depends on both the driving species and the resonant response of other plasma populations.
AI.method: The authors consider proton–α-particle plasmas with parameters representative of the solar wind and investigate Alfvén/ion-cyclotron and fast-magnetosonic/whistler wave instabilities. They combine linear Vlasov–Maxwell theory with hybrid particle-in-cell simulations to analyze instability generation and saturation and to quantify energy and momentum exchange between ion populations during instability evolution.
AI.result: The abstract reports that minor ions play a fundamental role in regulating the nonlinear saturation of kinetic instabilities and the transfer of energy among plasma populations. No specific quantitative values or detailed saturation levels are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: In multi-component plasmas, the nonlinear saturation and energy partition of kinetic micro-instabilities are governed not only by the species driving the instability but also by the resonant response of other plasma populations, with minor ions playing a fundamental regulatory role.

title: Exposing and overcoming the polarizability pathology of the Fermi-Omont pseudopotential
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to Phys. Rev. A
summary: Any realistic electron-atom or ion-atom potential energy function contains a long-range contribution from the atomic polarizability which gives a $1/r^4$ long-range tail. This modifies the well-known Wigner threshold law for orbital momenta $L>0$, causing these $L\neq 0$ scattering phase shifts to vary linearly in energy instead of as $k^{2L+1}$. The $L>0$ Fermi-Omont zero-range pseudopotentials are erroneously divergent at zero energy due to this modification, a divergence deriving from very long-range physics that should not be incorporated into a Dirac delta function. Here, we investigate some alternative scenario for repairing this pathological behavior to obtain smooth and accurate potential energy curves calculated using the Fermi-Omont pseudopotential concept, with some systematic benchmarking tests for comparison.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why L>0 Fermi-Omont zero-range pseudopotentials diverge at zero energy when the realistic atomic 1/r^4 polarizability tail modifies the Wigner threshold law, and it benchmarks alternative repair strategies for producing smooth, accurate potential energy curves.
AI.motivation: Realistic electron-atom and ion-atom potential energy functions contain a long-range 1/r^4 tail from atomic polarizability. This changes the Wigner threshold law for L>0, making those phase shifts vary linearly in energy rather than as k^(2L+1), and causes L>0 Fermi-Omont zero-range pseudopotentials to diverge at zero energy. The divergence comes from very long-range physics that should not be absorbed into a Dirac delta function.
AI.method: The authors investigate alternative scenarios for repairing this pathological behavior so that smooth and accurate potential energy curves can be calculated using the Fermi-Omont pseudopotential concept. They also perform systematic benchmarking tests for comparison. The abstract does not identify the specific alternative scenarios or benchmarking systems.
AI.result: The abstract reports the diagnosis of the polarizability pathology: the 1/r^4 long-range tail modifies the Wigner threshold law for L>0 and makes the corresponding Fermi-Omont zero-range pseudopotentials erroneously divergent at zero energy. Alternative repair scenarios are investigated and systematically benchmarked, but specific quantitative results or a best-performing repair are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The polarizability-induced divergence of L>0 Fermi-Omont pseudopotentials must be addressed to obtain smooth and accurate potential energy curves within the Fermi-Omont pseudopotential framework. Systematic benchmarking is used to compare repair approaches, but the abstract does not state final comparative conclusions.

title: Development and Validation of a preCICE Based OpenMOC OpenFOAM Coupling Framework for Nuclear Reactor Analysis
summary: To address the long computation time required by stochastic solvers, which are applied in the coupled neutronics-thermal hydraulics (N-TH) calculations, a faster N-TH coupling framework is developed based on the multiphysics coupling library preCICE, which enables data exchange between OpenMOC and OpenFOAM. As an alternative to commonly used stochastic solvers, like OpenMC, OpenMOC is used as a neutronics solver providing much faster steady-state solution in a Picard iteration. To realize this coupling strategy, OpenMC is used for an initial one-time computation cost for multi-group cross sections data generation that is used throughout OpenMOC calculations. A preCICE library adapter for OpenMOC is also developed, allowing data exchange between neutronic power distributions and thermal hydraulic temperature fields. Our proposed coupling framework is validated through simulations of a simplified 2 times 2 fuel assembly, and a quartered geometry of 17 times 17 fuel assembly. The comparison shows good agreement with established referenced solutions, highlighting our proposed coupling framework for the steady-state N-TH coupling at a fraction of the time required by stochastic solver codes. This advantages could be extended for future applications where fast approximated solutions are required to address the change of N-TH coupling due to small parametric changes like in digital twin of nuclear reactor.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and validates a preCICE-based multiphysics coupling framework between OpenMOC and OpenFOAM for steady-state neutronics–thermal hydraulics analysis of nuclear reactors, using OpenMC only for one-time multi-group cross-section generation. It demonstrates good agreement with reference solutions for simplified fuel-assembly cases at substantially lower computational time than stochastic-solver-based coupling.
AI.motivation: Stochastic neutronics solvers used in coupled neutronics–thermal hydraulics calculations require long computation times. The authors therefore aim to develop a faster coupling framework suitable for steady-state N–TH analysis and potentially for applications requiring rapid approximate solutions, such as digital twins under small parametric changes.
AI.method: The framework uses the preCICE multiphysics coupling library to exchange data between OpenMOC and OpenFOAM. OpenMOC serves as a deterministic neutronics solver within a Picard iteration, while OpenMC is used once to generate multi-group cross-section data for subsequent OpenMOC calculations. A preCICE adapter for OpenMOC is developed to exchange neutronic power distributions and thermal-hydraulic temperature fields. Validation is performed using a simplified 2×2 fuel assembly and a quartered 17×17 fuel assembly.
AI.result: The coupled framework shows good agreement with established reference solutions for the two validation cases. It provides steady-state N–TH coupling at a fraction of the computation time required by stochastic-solver-based codes. The abstract does not report quantitative error metrics or specific speedup factors.
AI.conclusion: The preCICE-based OpenMOC–OpenFOAM coupling is a validated and faster alternative for steady-state neutronics–thermal hydraulics analysis. Its efficiency advantages may support future applications requiring fast approximate solutions, including digital twins of nuclear reactors subject to small parametric changes.

title: Direct Numerical Simulation of Vortex-Induced Instability Over a Semi-Infinite Flat Plate with Discrete Roughness
summary: The receptivity of flow over a semi-infinite flat plate to a combination of deterministic free stream excitation and surface roughness, is investigated by solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation (NSE). The free stream excitation is in the form of a convecting vortex with fixed strength and sign, while the roughness element is a Gaussian bump. Two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) direct numerical simulations (DNS) are performed to determine whether the nonmodal nonlinear nature of transition, previously established for the vortex-induced instability in [Sundaram et al., Effects of free stream excitation on the boundary layer over a semi-infinite flat plate, Phys. Fluids, 32, 094110 (2020))], holds in the presence of surface roughness. The study aims to capture the fundamental differences arising due to the addition of surface roughness using instantaneous flow features, vorticity dynamics and application of nonlinear theories of receptivity. Roughness accelerates the transition process significantly, while retaining the indicator of nonmodal response, i.e. the spatio-temporal wave front (STWF). The inherently 2D nature of the vortex-induced instability evolves to three-dimensionality much faster in the presence of roughness, necessitating a 3D framework to capture the effects of roughness accurately. The cumulative response to the surface bump and convecting vortex can be separated into four stages, viz. are (i) generation of vortical disturbances at the roughness, (ii) a spatio-temporal amplification of the disturbance field, (iii) emergence and amplification of the STWF marked by sequence of unsteady separation bubbles, and (iv) emergence of turbulent flow due to merging of the unsteady separation bubbles to turbulent spots.

AI.tldr: Two- and three-dimensional direct numerical simulations solve the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations for flow over a semi-infinite flat plate subjected to a convecting free-stream vortex and a Gaussian surface bump. Roughness accelerates transition while preserving the spatio-temporal wave front indicative of nonmodal vortex-induced instability, and the response proceeds through four stages from roughness-generated vortical disturbances to turbulent spots.
AI.motivation: The study investigates the receptivity of a semi-infinite flat-plate boundary layer to combined deterministic free-stream excitation and discrete surface roughness. It specifically asks whether the previously established nonmodal nonlinear character of vortex-induced instability persists when a Gaussian roughness bump is added, and aims to identify fundamental differences caused by roughness.
AI.method: The incompressible Navier–Stokes equations are solved using two-dimensional and three-dimensional direct numerical simulations. The free-stream excitation is a convecting vortex of fixed strength and sign, and the roughness is a Gaussian bump. The analysis uses instantaneous flow features, vorticity dynamics, and nonlinear theories of receptivity. Specific parameter values and quantitative transition metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.result: Roughness significantly accelerates the transition process while retaining the spatio-temporal wave front as an indicator of nonmodal response. The inherently two-dimensional vortex-induced instability develops three-dimensionality much faster with roughness, so a three-dimensional framework is needed to capture roughness effects accurately. The cumulative response is separated into four stages: generation of vortical disturbances at the roughness, spatio-temporal amplification of the disturbance field, emergence and amplification of the spatio-temporal wave front marked by unsteady separation bubbles, and emergence of turbulence through merging of these bubbles into turbulent spots.
AI.conclusion: Surface roughness accelerates and promotes three-dimensionalization of the vortex-induced transition, but the nonmodal nonlinear nature of the instability is retained, as evidenced by the spatio-temporal wave front. Accurate characterization of the roughness-affected transition requires three-dimensional simulation, and the combined roughness–vortex response follows a four-stage progression culminating in turbulent spots.

title: Topological Timing of Bound States by Spacetime Mass Windings
summary: Topology usually determines where a wave is trapped. Here we show that it can also determine when a trapped state brightens or dims. We consider a dimerized photonic lattice in which a real Dirac mass, varying in space, binds a Jackiw-Rebbi state, while staggered gain and loss, switched in time, act as an imaginary Dirac mass on that same state. Together, the two masses form a mass field in space and time whose isolated zeros carry an integer winding. Combining a continuum Dirac description with finite-lattice simulations, we show that the sign of this winding fixes whether the bound state reaches a maximum or a minimum at the switch, while the gain and loss remain below the bulk gap. The windings obey a conservation law: they are created and annihilated in pairs, and their sum along a boundary determines which extrema are protected. Full-wave simulations of a passive waveguide array, in which the propagation distance plays the role of time, reproduce these predictions with loss alone. These results provide a topological handle on the timing of localized optical responses, relevant to switching, gating, and pulse shaping of confined modes in integrated photonic circuits and topological lasers.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a spacetime mass field with integer winding can topologically control when a trapped Jackiw-Rebbi state reaches a maximum or minimum, with winding conservation protecting selected extrema; waveguide-array simulations reproduce the effect using loss alone.
AI.motivation: Topology is usually used to determine where a wave is trapped. The authors investigate whether topology can also determine when a trapped state brightens or dims, aiming for a topological handle on the timing of localized optical responses relevant to switching, gating, and pulse shaping in integrated photonic circuits and topological lasers.
AI.method: The authors consider a dimerized photonic lattice in which a real, spatially varying Dirac mass binds a Jackiw-Rebbi state, while staggered gain and loss switched in time act as an imaginary Dirac mass on the same state. The two masses form a spacetime mass field whose isolated zeros carry an integer winding. The analysis combines a continuum Dirac description with finite-lattice simulations, and full-wave simulations of a passive waveguide array use propagation distance as time.
AI.result: The sign of the winding fixes whether the bound state reaches a maximum or a minimum at the switch, while gain and loss remain below the bulk gap. The windings obey a conservation law: they are created and annihilated in pairs, and their sum along a boundary determines which extrema are protected. Full-wave simulations of a passive waveguide array reproduce these predictions with loss alone. Quantitative experimental metrics are not provided.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a topological handle on the timing of localized optical responses, with relevance to switching, gating, and pulse shaping of confined modes in integrated photonic circuits and topological lasers.

title: Kinetic-Ballooning and Resistive X-Point Dynamics in Quasicontinuous Exhaust Tokamak Plasmas
summary: We investigate quasicoherent modes (QCMs) and their interaction with scrape-off-layer (SOL) plasma blobs (filaments) in the type-I-ELM-free quasicontinuous exhaust (QCE) regime, extending the analysis in [K. Zhang et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 055102 (2026)]. Two-fluid electromagnetic turbulence simulations are compared for two self-consistent turbulence states with different separatrix densities. In both cases, a separatrix-spanning QCM resides within the radial-electric-field well, whereas blobs are observed only in the case with higher separatrix density. The QCM exhibits similar kinetic-ballooning-mode (KBM) signatures in both cases, with modest differences in coherence and harmonic content. The primary difference is the presence of an additional resistive X-point mode (RXM), which emerges as the near-X-point collisionality increases. The coexistence of the KBM and RXM shifts the potential--density cross-phase from its KBM-like value toward the interchange value in the SOL, allowing QCM perturbations to be ejected as blobs. These intermittent blobs account for over half of the net radial $E\times B$ transport in the far SOL. Neither QCM onset nor blob ejection requires an increase in upstream collisionality. The results distinguish the KBM-dominated mechanism that regulates the pedestal from the RXM-assisted blob-launching mechanism that enables intermittent SOL exhaust.

AI.tldr: Two-fluid electromagnetic turbulence simulations show that, in type-I-ELM-free quasicontinuous exhaust tokamak plasmas, a separatrix-spanning quasicontinuous mode with kinetic-ballooning-mode signatures regulates the pedestal, while an additional resistive X-point mode at higher near-X-point collisionality shifts the potential-density cross-phase toward the interchange value in the scrape-off layer and enables intermittent blob ejection that dominates far-SOL radial E×B transport.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to clarify quasicoherent modes and their interaction with scrape-off-layer plasma blobs in the type-I-ELM-free quasicontinuous exhaust regime, extending prior analysis and distinguishing the mechanism regulating the pedestal from that enabling intermittent scrape-off-layer exhaust.
AI.method: The authors compare two-fluid electromagnetic turbulence simulations of two self-consistent turbulence states with different separatrix densities. They analyze the radial location of the separatrix-spanning quasicontinuous mode, kinetic-ballooning-mode signatures, harmonic content and coherence, the emergence of a resistive X-point mode with increasing near-X-point collisionality, and the potential-density cross-phase in the scrape-off layer.
AI.result: In both cases, a separatrix-spanning quasicontinuous mode lies within the radial-electric-field well, with similar kinetic-ballooning-mode signatures and modest differences in coherence and harmonic content. Blobs appear only in the higher-separatrix-density case, where an additional resistive X-point mode emerges as near-X-point collisionality increases. Coexistence of the kinetic-ballooning and resistive X-point modes shifts the potential-density cross-phase from a kinetic-ballooning-like value toward the interchange value in the scrape-off layer, allowing quasicontinuous-mode perturbations to be ejected as blobs. These intermittent blobs account for over half of the net radial E×B transport in the far scrape-off layer, and neither quasicontinuous-mode onset nor blob ejection requires increased upstream collisionality.
AI.conclusion: The results distinguish a kinetic-ballooning-mode-dominated mechanism that regulates the pedestal from a resistive-X-point-mode-assisted blob-launching mechanism that enables intermittent scrape-off-layer exhaust in quasicontinuous exhaust tokamak plasmas.

title: Quantum adiabatic and diabatic optimization: A Hilbert space engineering strategy with Rydberg arrays
summary: Neutral-atom arrays provide a versatile platform for encoding combinatorial optimization problems with arbitrary graph connectivity [Nguyen et al., PRX Quantum 4, 010316 (2023)]. Although the dynamics of individual encoding gadgets has been studied [Bombieri et al., PRX Quantum 6, 020306 (2025)], understanding annealing bottlenecks in larger networks remains challenging. We investigate how engineering the Hilbert-space geometry controls quantum annealing in a family of blockaded-chain models motivated by these encodings. While boundary terms encode the target maximum independent set problem, the bulk geometry induces an auxiliary optimization problem associated with independent sets of cliques. Spectrally, the energetics of the quantum system can be approximated by physically derived clique weights. When the target problem and the auxiliary problems are consistent, the low-energy modes lie predominantly within the target subspace. This spectral structure motivates a diabatic annealing strategy that exploits target-compatible excited states, as tested on the diamond-chain graph family. These results provide a framework for predicting annealing bottlenecks, and demonstrate Hilbert-space engineering as a strategy for improving neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how engineering Hilbert-space geometry controls quantum annealing in blockaded Rydberg-atom chain models for maximum independent set, showing that auxiliary clique problems shape low-energy spectra and motivate a diabatic annealing strategy tested on diamond-chain graphs.
AI.motivation: Neutral-atom arrays can encode combinatorial optimization problems with arbitrary graph connectivity, but annealing bottlenecks in larger encoded networks remain difficult to understand despite studies of individual encoding gadgets.
AI.method: The authors investigate quantum annealing in blockaded-chain models motivated by neutral-atom encodings. Boundary terms encode the target maximum independent set problem, while bulk Hilbert-space geometry induces an auxiliary optimization problem over independent sets of cliques. They approximate the quantum system's energetics using physically derived clique weights and propose a diabatic annealing strategy exploiting target-compatible excited states, tested on the diamond-chain graph family.
AI.result: When the target and auxiliary problems are consistent, low-energy modes lie predominantly within the target subspace. The spectral structure enables a diabatic annealing strategy using target-compatible excited states, tested on diamond-chain graphs. No quantitative performance metrics are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a framework for predicting annealing bottlenecks and demonstrates Hilbert-space engineering as a strategy for improving neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols.

title: High-Order Regularization for Singular and Nearly Singular Laplace and Stokes Layer Potentials in Two Dimensions
comment: 36 pages, 11 figures; code and data available at https://github.com/han-zhou-math/high-order-reg-2d
summary: Layer potentials represent the solutions of many elliptic boundary value problems, but their kernels have the singularity of the fundamental solution, so standard quadrature loses accuracy at targets on or near the boundary. In two dimensions, Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel gives a smooth kernel involving the exponential integral $E_1$, but for the single layer its regularization error is only first order in the smoothing radius $δ$. We construct modified kernels for two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials that achieve regularization error $O(δ^p)$, $p=3,5,7$, uniformly for targets on and near the curve. The resulting method is both high-order accurate and easy to implement: the integrals are evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes for all targets. Choosing $δ=c h^q$ with $q<1$, where $h$ is the node spacing, keeps the discretization error smaller than the regularization error as $h\to0$, and numerical experiments confirm the predicted $O(h^{pq})$ convergence. Finally, we combine the near-curve evaluation with a fast Poisson solver to compute the potentials on the entire Cartesian grid.

AI.tldr: The paper develops modified kernels that regularize singular and nearly singular two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials to orders O(δ^3), O(δ^5), and O(δ^7), enabling high-order accurate evaluation with a fixed periodic trapezoidal rule and extension to Cartesian-grid evaluation via a fast Poisson solver.
AI.motivation: Standard quadrature for layer potentials loses accuracy at targets on or near the boundary because the kernels inherit the singularity of the fundamental solution. In two dimensions, Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel produces a smooth kernel involving the exponential integral E1, but for the single layer its regularization error is only first order in the smoothing radius δ.
AI.method: The authors construct modified kernels for two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials with regularization error O(δ^p) for p=3,5,7, uniformly for targets on and near the curve. Integrals are evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes for all targets. They choose δ=c h^q with q<1, where h is the node spacing, so that discretization error remains smaller than regularization error as h→0. Near-curve evaluation is combined with a fast Poisson solver to compute potentials on the entire Cartesian grid.
AI.result: The method is reported to be high-order accurate and easy to implement. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted O(h^{pq}) convergence, with regularization errors of order O(δ^p) for p=3,5,7. Specific quantitative error values or computational costs are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Modified-kernel regularization provides high-order, direct quadrature for singular and nearly singular two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes layer potentials, including targets on and near the boundary, and can be combined with a fast Poisson solver for Cartesian-grid potential evaluation. Further details on applications and performance are not provided in the abstract.

title: Fluid exchange and renewal in the left atrial appendage
summary: Fluid exchange through the opening of a cavity does not uniquely determine how the cavity is washed out. We investigate this phenomenon in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a deforming side cavity of the heart, using simulations of 17 patient-specific atria with wall motion reconstructed from time-resolved computed tomography. Fluid exchange through the LAA ostium is decomposed into a component driven by LAA volume change and a component due to simultaneous bidirectional flow, with no net volume transport. Washout of a scalar initially confined to the LAA is compared with predictions from two well-mixed washout models and assessed alongside residence-time distributions. Volume-driven transport accounts for approximately 24-78% of total exchange across the simulated atria. Relative washout efficiencies are approximately 26-53% with respect to the inflow-driven washout model that assumes scalar-free inflow. A scalar-balance decomposition identifies two contributions to this discrepancy: re-ingestion of previously expelled scalar and preferential export of scalar-poor fluid. Both effects reduce the effective washout rate in every configuration. Residence-time distributions reveal coexisting distinct younger and older fluid regions, and a regional analysis of one appendage localizes the older population predominantly in its distal region. These findings show that substantial exchange across the LAA ostium coexists with prolonged distal retention. Effective renewal depends on how much fluid crosses the ostium and which fluid is exchanged.

AI.tldr: Simulations of 17 patient-specific left atrial appendages show that fluid exchange through the ostium substantially overestimates washout because previously expelled scalar is re-ingested and scalar-poor fluid is preferentially exported, producing prolonged distal retention.
AI.motivation: Fluid exchange through a cavity opening does not by itself determine how thoroughly the cavity is washed out; the study investigates this mismatch in the deforming left atrial appendage.
AI.method: The authors simulated 17 patient-specific atria with wall motion reconstructed from time-resolved computed tomography. They decomposed ostial fluid exchange into volume-change-driven transport and simultaneous bidirectional flow with no net volume transport, compared scalar washout with two well-mixed washout models, assessed residence-time distributions, and used a scalar-balance decomposition to identify contributions to reduced washout efficiency.
AI.result: Volume-driven transport accounted for approximately 24-78% of total exchange. Relative washout efficiencies were approximately 26-53% versus an inflow-driven model assuming scalar-free inflow. Re-ingestion of previously expelled scalar and preferential export of scalar-poor fluid reduced the effective washout rate in every configuration. Residence-time distributions showed coexisting younger and older fluid regions, with older fluid predominantly distal in the regional analysis of one appendage.
AI.conclusion: Substantial exchange across the left atrial appendage ostium can coexist with prolonged distal retention; effective renewal depends both on how much fluid crosses the ostium and on which fluid is exchanged.

title: Dual-Comb Spectrometry Enabled by Gain-Assisted Electro-Optic Fiber Ring Resonators
summary: Broadband dual-comb spectroscopy (DCS) with widely tunable repetition rates and simplified frequency stabilization is desirable for diverse sensing applications. Here, we demonstrate DCS using two gain-assisted fiber ring resonators that share a continuous-wave (CW) laser and incorporate intracavity electro-optic (EO) phase modulation. Intracavity gain compensates for round-trip losses, sustaining repeated phase modulation and enabling flat-top comb spectra with a 20-dB bandwidth exceeding 1.8 THz. Harmonic-order selection provides widely tunable repetition rates from approximately 5 to 0.2 GHz without substantially compromising the spectral bandwidth. The comb phase noise closely follows that of the radio-frequency (RF) drive at low offset frequencies. Without active frequency stabilization, the two combs exhibit an instrument-limited beat-note linewidth of 2 Hz, indicating high mutual coherence. The generated dual combs enable high-speed DCS at the single-interferogram rate, providing a platform for dynamic spectroscopic measurements. This all-fiber architecture, together with its simplified operation, offers a promising route towards compact and readily integrable dual-comb instruments.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates dual-comb spectroscopy using two gain-assisted fiber ring resonators that share a continuous-wave laser and use intracavity electro-optic phase modulation, achieving broad flat-top spectra, widely tunable repetition rates, high mutual coherence, and single-interferogram-rate operation.
AI.motivation: Broadband dual-comb spectroscopy with widely tunable repetition rates and simplified frequency stabilization is desirable for diverse sensing applications.
AI.method: Two gain-assisted fiber ring resonators share a continuous-wave laser and incorporate intracavity electro-optic phase modulation. Intracavity gain compensates round-trip losses, sustaining repeated phase modulation; harmonic-order selection tunes the repetition rate.
AI.result: The combs provide flat-top spectra with a 20-dB bandwidth exceeding 1.8 THz and repetition rates tunable from approximately 5 to 0.2 GHz without substantially compromising spectral bandwidth. Low-offset comb phase noise closely follows the radio-frequency drive. Without active frequency stabilization, the two combs show a 2 Hz instrument-limited beat-note linewidth, indicating high mutual coherence, and enable high-speed dual-comb spectroscopy at the single-interferogram rate.
AI.conclusion: The all-fiber architecture and simplified operation offer a promising route toward compact, readily integrable dual-comb instruments for dynamic spectroscopic measurements.

title: Collisionality scaling of the tokamak density limit
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in Physical Review Letters
summary: The threshold at which density-limiting plasma instabilities occur in tokamak fusion reactors is not well understood. Here, we present the first large-scale empirical evidence of a common collisionality threshold present across multiple devices and confinement regimes. Machine-learning-guided analysis of a diverse experimental database identifies a scaling in edge effective collisionality ($ν_*$) that bears resemblance to the widely utilized Greenwald limit but yields a substantially lower false positive rate. This threshold decreases with dimensionless pressure ($β$), consistent with theoretical expectations for enhanced transport from electromagnetic effects on resistive ballooning mode turbulence. These results suggest that future burning plasma devices such as ITER and ARC could potentially achieve higher density, and thus fusion power, than previously expected.

AI.tldr: Machine-learning analysis of a multi-device tokamak database finds a common edge-effective-collisionality threshold for density-limiting instabilities that resembles the Greenwald limit with fewer false positives and decreases with dimensionless pressure.
AI.motivation: The threshold for density-limiting plasma instabilities in tokamak fusion reactors is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors perform machine-learning-guided analysis of a diverse experimental database spanning multiple devices and confinement regimes to identify a scaling in edge effective collisionality.
AI.result: A common collisionality threshold is identified across devices and regimes; its scaling resembles the Greenwald limit but has a substantially lower false positive rate and decreases with dimensionless pressure, consistent with enhanced transport from electromagnetic effects on resistive ballooning mode turbulence.
AI.conclusion: Future burning plasma devices such as ITER and ARC could potentially achieve higher density, and therefore higher fusion power, than previously expected.

title: High-order Crank-Nicolson method via diagonal Padé factorization
summary: We present a numerical method to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation at arbitrary order of accuracy in the time step, particularly well suited for tridiagonal Hamilton operators. The method is based on a factorization of the diagonal Padé approximants of the matrix exponential into products of linear factors, which preserves tridiagonal matrix structure at every time step and yields a propagator of order 2q in the time step at a cost of O(qN) operations. The propagator is exactly unitary by construction, and at lowest order q=1 it reduces to the standard Crank-Nicolson algorithm. We further extend the method to any Hamiltonian admitting a decomposition into a sum of tridiagonal or diagonal operators via high-order split-operator techniques (McLachlan, 2022), retaining O(qN) scaling at each time step. We also analytically show and numerically verify that the precision is dictated by the split-operator method. This covers a broad range of physically relevant cases, including higher-dimensional systems, higher-order spatial discretizations, and non-separable potentials.

AI.tldr: A high-order, exactly unitary numerical propagator for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation is constructed by factoring diagonal Padé approximants of the matrix exponential into linear factors, preserving tridiagonal structure and achieving order 2q with O(qN) cost; it is extended to decomposable Hamiltonians using high-order split-operator methods.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state the motivation beyond providing a numerical method for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation at arbitrary time-step accuracy that is particularly suited to tridiagonal Hamiltonians and retains efficiency.
AI.method: Diagonal Padé approximants of the matrix exponential are factorized into products of linear factors, preserving tridiagonal matrix structure at every time step. The resulting propagator is exactly unitary by construction, has order 2q in the time step, and costs O(qN) operations; at q=1 it reduces to standard Crank-Nicolson. The approach is extended via high-order split-operator techniques to Hamiltonians decomposable into sums of tridiagonal or diagonal operators.
AI.result: The method yields an exactly unitary propagator of order 2q at O(qN) cost, reduces to Crank-Nicolson at lowest order, and retains O(qN) scaling per time step after split-operator extension. Analytical and numerical verification show that precision is dictated by the split-operator method.
AI.conclusion: The method applies to a broad range of physically relevant cases, including higher-dimensional systems, higher-order spatial discretizations, and non-separable potentials.

title: Symmetry-reduced k-point sampling and Wannier analysis with localized Gaussian orbitals
summary: Brillouin-zone sampling with localized orbitals requires consistent transformations between sparse real-space matrices and complex Bloch states. Symmetry reduces the number of reciprocal-space problems, but scalar integration weights alone cannot reconstruct the matrices and wavefunctions needed for densities and orbital analysis. We develop a unified formulation of these transformations for nonorthogonal Gaussian bases and describe its implementation in CP2K. Atom permutations, local orbital rotations, and lattice phases connect irreducible-point solutions to full symmetry orbits while preserving the overlap metric. Direct and fast lattice transforms couple this construction to self-consistent calculations, including complex orbital optimization and finite-temperature occupations. Gauge-consistent full-mesh orbitals and directed inter-point overlaps support Wannier90 export, Wannier construction, and Hamiltonian interpolation. In silicon and aluminium tests, symmetry reduces a 64-point mesh to four representatives while retaining cell energies or electronic free energies within $1.5\times10^{-12}$ hartree of the unreduced calculation. Hybrid exchange and many-body applications illustrate the additional role of auxiliary bases and transfer momenta. The resulting framework connects symmetry-reduced integration to gauge-consistent analysis of periodic electronic states within a localized-orbital representation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified CP2K formulation for symmetry-reduced Brillouin-zone sampling and gauge-consistent Wannier analysis using nonorthogonal localized Gaussian orbitals, with silicon and aluminium tests showing near-exact energies from a reduced k-point mesh.
AI.motivation: Brillouin-zone sampling with localized orbitals requires consistent transformations between sparse real-space matrices and complex Bloch states. Symmetry reduces reciprocal-space problems, but scalar integration weights alone cannot reconstruct the matrices and wavefunctions needed for densities and orbital analysis.
AI.method: The authors develop a unified formulation for nonorthogonal Gaussian bases in CP2K, mapping irreducible-point solutions to full symmetry orbits via atom permutations, local orbital rotations, and lattice phases while preserving the overlap metric. Direct and fast lattice transforms couple this construction to self-consistent calculations, including complex orbital optimization and finite-temperature occupations. Gauge-consistent full-mesh orbitals and directed inter-point overlaps support Wannier90 export, Wannier construction, and Hamiltonian interpolation; auxiliary bases and transfer momenta are discussed for hybrid exchange and many-body applications.
AI.result: In silicon and aluminium tests, symmetry reduces a 64-point mesh to four representatives while retaining cell energies or electronic free energies within 1.5×10^-12 hartree of the unreduced calculation. Hybrid exchange and many-body applications illustrate the additional role of auxiliary bases and transfer momenta.
AI.conclusion: The resulting framework connects symmetry-reduced integration to gauge-consistent analysis of periodic electronic states within a localized-orbital representation.

title: Surrogate-Based Optimization of Tandem Twin-Rotor Wind Turbines Accounting for Wake Interactions
summary: Wake interaction in a tandem twin-rotor turbine couples power capture with thrust on the shared support. This study develops a time-resolved surrogate for upstream IEA Wind 22 MW and downstream NREL 5 MW rotors. It covers spacing ratios $0.01\leq L/D\leq0.20$ and tip-speed ratios $4\leqλ\leq11$. Vortex-method simulations of 160 configurations under turbulent inflow train per-time-node XGBoost models to predict 600 s power, thrust, and torque histories. A CNN-Attention-LSTM network extends these histories, and a genetic algorithm balances the system power and thrust coefficients. Ten-fold cross-validation gives median power-history $R^2$ values of 0.995 upstream and 0.958 downstream for unseen configurations, but the first stage cannot extrapolate in tip-speed ratio. With fixed pitch and prescribed rotor speed, the coefficients apply where both rotors reach the simulated tip-speed ratio below rated wind speed. Increasing spacing raises upstream power by up to 6% and lowers downstream power by up to 62%. System power changes by less than 4% at fixed $λ$. The high-power end of the Pareto front lies near $λ=10$. At $L/D=0.20$, the system power coefficient is highest. This configuration has the lowest peak thrust among the high-power candidates.

AI.tldr: A time-resolved surrogate trained on 160 vortex-method simulations of tandem IEA 22 MW and NREL 5 MW rotors is coupled with a genetic algorithm to optimize spacing and tip-speed ratio while balancing system power and thrust. Median power-history R² is 0.995 upstream and 0.958 downstream; spacing raises upstream power by up to 6% but lowers downstream power by up to 62%, and L/D=0.20 near λ=10 is the best simulated high-power configuration.
AI.motivation: Wake interaction in a tandem twin-rotor wind turbine couples power capture with thrust on the shared support, motivating optimization that accounts for wake interactions.
AI.method: The study develops a time-resolved surrogate for an upstream IEA Wind 22 MW rotor and a downstream NREL 5 MW rotor over spacing ratios 0.01≤L/D≤0.20 and tip-speed ratios 4≤λ≤11. Vortex-method simulations of 160 configurations under turbulent inflow train per-time-node XGBoost models to predict 600 s power, thrust, and torque histories; a CNN-Attention-LSTM network extends the histories, and a genetic algorithm balances system power and thrust coefficients. Ten-fold cross-validation is used.
AI.result: Median power-history R² values are 0.995 upstream and 0.958 downstream for unseen configurations, although the first stage cannot extrapolate in tip-speed ratio. With fixed pitch and prescribed rotor speed, the coefficients apply where both rotors reach the simulated tip-speed ratio below rated wind speed. Increasing spacing raises upstream power by up to 6% and lowers downstream power by up to 62%; system power changes by less than 4% at fixed λ. The high-power end of the Pareto front lies near λ=10, and at L/D=0.20 the system power coefficient is highest, with the lowest peak thrust among the high-power candidates.
AI.conclusion: The surrogate-based optimization framework enables rapid evaluation and genetic-algorithm balancing of power and thrust for tandem twin-rotor wind turbines under wake interactions. Among the simulated high-power candidates, L/D=0.20 near λ=10 provides the highest system power coefficient and lowest peak thrust, subject to the stated interpolation limits and fixed-pitch, prescribed-rotor-speed assumptions.

title: Zernike-efficient phase contrast with a scanned electron probe
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 1 table; supplementary material (12 pages) . Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24170512
summary: For weak-phase objects, scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) with a far-field detector transfers at most half of the phase information per electron that Zernike phase-contrast (ZPC) conventional transmission electron microscopy (CTEM) achieves. We propose APEX (Apex Phase-plate EXit-wave imaging), a scanned-probe mode that combines a defocused probe, a $π/2$ phase element in a magnified image of the probe crossover, and in-focus image-plane detection at each scan position. It applies the generalized Zernike framework of Dwyer and Paganin to a scanned probe. In a linear model of a thin weak-phase object with an ideal phase dot, APEX transfers nearly the full Zernike Fisher information over a wide band, substantially more than diffraction-plane four-dimensional STEM (4D-STEM). In idealized simulations of myoglobin in vitreous ice at a cryo-EM dose (elastic scattering only, no chromatic aberration, full coherence), ideal-dot APEX at a probe defocus of 1 $μ$m reconstructs the phase more accurately than defocused 4D-STEM ptychography with one untuned probe setting. At a defocus of about 25 $μ$m, a crossed laser phase plate (XLPP) acts as the $π/2$ element, and APEX of a periodic specimen cell comes close to CTEM with the same plate. In two dimensions, this mode is equivalent to laser phase-plate CTEM of a small, scanned area. A single simulated APEX scan with the XLPP also separates two myoglobin phase screens 150 nm apart in vacuum, at known depths, which is not possible with one ZPC CTEM exposure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes APEX, a scanned-probe phase-contrast STEM mode that uses a defocused probe, a π/2 phase element in a magnified probe-crossover image, and in-focus image-plane detection. In idealized linear models and simulations, APEX transfers nearly full Zernike Fisher information and reconstructs weak-phase objects better than defocused 4D-STEM ptychography; with a crossed laser phase plate it approaches CTEM performance and can separate two phase screens at different known depths.
AI.motivation: For weak-phase objects, conventional scanning transmission electron microscopy with a far-field detector transfers at most half of the phase information per electron that Zernike phase-contrast CTEM achieves, motivating a scanned-probe mode with improved Zernike phase-contrast efficiency.
AI.method: The authors propose APEX (Apex Phase-plate EXit-wave imaging), which combines a defocused probe, a π/2 phase element placed in a magnified image of the probe crossover, and in-focus image-plane detection at each scan position. They apply the generalized Zernike framework of Dwyer and Paganin to a scanned probe, analyze a linear thin weak-phase object model with an ideal phase dot, and perform idealized simulations of myoglobin in vitreous ice at cryo-EM dose with elastic scattering only, no chromatic aberration, and full coherence. They also use a crossed laser phase plate (XLPP) at about 25 μm defocus as the π/2 element for a periodic specimen cell and demonstrate two-dimensional equivalence to laser phase-plate CTEM of a small scanned area.
AI.result: In the linear model, APEX transfers nearly the full Zernike Fisher information over a wide band, substantially more than diffraction-plane 4D-STEM. Ideal-dot APEX at 1 μm probe defocus reconstructs the phase more accurately than defocused 4D-STEM ptychography with one untuned probe setting in idealized myoglobin simulations. At about 25 μm defocus, XLPP-based APEX of a periodic specimen cell comes close to CTEM with the same plate. A single simulated APEX scan with the XLPP also separates two myoglobin phase screens 150 nm apart in vacuum at known depths, which is not possible with one ZPC CTEM exposure.
AI.conclusion: APEX is a Zernike-efficient scanned-probe phase-contrast mode that can approach the phase information transfer of Zernike phase-contrast CTEM and outperform defocused 4D-STEM ptychography in idealized settings. With a crossed laser phase plate, it can approximate CTEM performance and provide depth separation of phase screens. The reported evidence is based on linear modeling and idealized simulations, not experimental validation.

title: An Efficient Method for Directly Integrating the Vlasov Equation in Collisionless and Weakly-Collisional Simulations
comment: 31 pages, 20 figures, submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics. Comments welcome. Implementation in the public GIZMO code available at http://www.tapir.caltech.edu/~phopkins/Site/GIZMO.html
summary: We describe and test a new numerical method to solve the Vlasov/Boltzmann equation in systems with arbitrary levels of collisionality. The method combines recent ideas to evolve the distribution function (DF) directly in 6+1 dimensional phase-space in a manner which is Lagrangian in both position+velocity. The 'particles' of traditional Monte-Carlo/Particle-In-Cell/N-body (MC/PIC/NB) methods become mesh-generating points defining a volume partition, each of which carries a set of momentum-Lagrangian basis functions representing a local anisotropic momentum DF. The DF is then integrated between cells and bases via a higher-order reconstruction and Godunov-type method, evolving a 10 or 13-moment representation of each basis to ensure manifest mass/momentum/energy conservation. The method allows one to represent arbitrary DFs, including multiple independent streams but also collisional or phase-mixed or thermal distributions (unlike traditional 'moments' or waterbag/tessellation methods), and the cost is bounded to a modest multiplier of MC/PIC/NB costs. We provide an example implementation which uses a spatially-Lagrangian volume partition, second-order reconstruction, and simple set of bases which ensure constant cell masses and couple directly to existing MC/PIC/NB machinery, made public in the code GIZMO. We validate in a series of test problems, demonstrating manifest conservation, Galilean and translation and rotation invariance, and ability to represent complex DFs without spurious dissipation or instability. We discuss applications where this method can have advantages compared to traditional algorithms for simulations of dark matter, stellar, weakly-collisional neutral gas, and particulate/dust dynamics; multiphase/polydisperse flows; cosmic ray and radiation transport/hydrodynamics; and plasma physics.

AI.tldr: The paper presents and validates a Lagrangian phase-space method that evolves the distribution function directly for collisionless and weakly collisional systems, combining particle-like mesh points with momentum basis functions and moment-based Godunov updates, and demonstrates conservation and robustness in tests.
