AI.motivation: Traditional Monte-Carlo, Particle-In-Cell, and N-body methods, as well as conventional moment or waterbag/tessellation approaches, have limitations in representing arbitrary distribution functions efficiently. The authors seek a method applicable across arbitrary collisionality that preserves conservation and remains computationally practical relative to existing particle methods.
AI.method: The method evolves the Vlasov/Boltzmann distribution function directly in 6+1-dimensional phase space using a formulation Lagrangian in both position and velocity. Traditional particles become mesh-generating points that define a volume partition; each carries momentum-Lagrangian basis functions describing a local anisotropic momentum distribution. The distribution is integrated between cells and bases using higher-order reconstruction and a Godunov-type method, evolving a 10- or 13-moment representation of each basis to enforce mass, momentum, and energy conservation. An example implementation uses a spatially Lagrangian volume partition, second-order reconstruction, and simple bases ensuring constant cell masses, and is released in GIZMO.
AI.result: The method is validated on a series of test problems, demonstrating manifest conservation, Galilean, translation, and rotation invariance, and the ability to represent complex distribution functions without spurious dissipation or instability. The authors state that its cost is bounded to a modest multiplier of Monte-Carlo/Particle-In-Cell/N-body costs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method can represent arbitrary distribution functions, including multiple independent streams, collisional, phase-mixed, and thermal distributions, unlike traditional moment or waterbag/tessellation methods. It couples directly to existing Monte-Carlo/Particle-In-Cell/N-body machinery and is proposed for applications including dark matter, stellar, weakly collisional neutral gas, particulate/dust dynamics, multiphase/polydisperse flows, cosmic ray and radiation transport/hydrodynamics, and plasma physics.

title: Quantum Sensor of Mechanical Vibrations
summary: We report the use of a single trapped-ion motional mode as a probe of mechanical vibrations of the Paul trap structure. By exciting vibrations of the trap using an ultrasonic transducer mounted outside the vacuum chamber and probing the ion motion through motional sideband interactions, we observe a clear resonance response of the axial mode. We further demonstrate detection of trap vibrations with amplitudes as low as 0.6 picometers. These measurements show direct coupling between macroscopic mechanical motion and trapped-ion dynamics, providing a route toward vibration sensing using quantum control of motional states.

AI.tldr: A single trapped-ion motional mode is used to sense ultrasonic mechanical vibrations of a Paul trap, with axial-mode resonance detection reaching 0.6 picometer amplitude and indicating a route to quantum-controlled vibration sensing.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to probe mechanical vibrations of the Paul trap structure using a single trapped-ion motional mode and to establish a route toward vibration sensing based on quantum control of motional states.
AI.method: An ultrasonic transducer mounted outside the vacuum chamber excites vibrations of the trap structure; the ion motion is probed through motional sideband interactions, and the axial motional mode is monitored for resonance response.
AI.result: A clear resonance response of the axial mode is observed, and trap vibrations with amplitudes as low as 0.6 picometers are detected, demonstrating direct coupling between macroscopic mechanical motion and trapped-ion dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The measurements demonstrate vibration sensing with a trapped-ion motional mode and provide a route toward vibration sensing using quantum control of motional states; further performance details are not provided in the abstract.

title: Multicomponent Adaptive Sampling Configuration Interaction method in openLOWDIN: positronic and quantum nuclear systems
summary: We present a multicomponent Selective Configuration Interaction (SCI) method based on the deterministic Adaptive Sampling CI (ASCI) algorithm for computing energies and wavefunction properties of molecular systems containing leptons of variable masses, or quantum nuclei. Near-FCI accuracy is achieved by incorporating second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory or by dressing the Hamiltonian via Davidson's and co-workers shifted-Bk method. We validate the approach through benchmark positronic (e$^+$LiH, e$^+$OH$^-$, e$^+$Mg) and quantum nuclear systems (HCN), establishing a novel protocol for accurate convergence, based on the iterative adaptation of natural orbitals starting from those obtained by considering only cross-particle CISD excitations, to those obtained from SCI variational space, surpassing the accuracy of previous SCI studies. Overall, we show that the present multi-component SCI framework offers a simple, systematically improvable, and cost-effective alternative to traditional CI approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multicomponent Adaptive Sampling Configuration Interaction method in openLOWDIN for positronic and quantum-nuclear molecular systems, using perturbative corrections or shifted-Bk Hamiltonian dressing and an iterative natural-orbital protocol to approach near-FCI accuracy.
AI.motivation: Accurate yet cost-effective configuration interaction methods are needed for molecular systems containing leptons of variable mass or quantum nuclei, where traditional CI approaches can be expensive or insufficiently converged. The work also aims to improve convergence and accuracy relative to previous SCI studies.
AI.method: A multicomponent Selective Configuration Interaction method based on the deterministic Adaptive Sampling CI algorithm is implemented in openLOWDIN. Near-FCI accuracy is pursued through second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory or Davidson and co-workers' shifted-Bk Hamiltonian dressing. Convergence is improved by iteratively adapting natural orbitals, starting from orbitals obtained with only cross-particle CISD excitations and progressing to those from the SCI variational space.
AI.result: The approach is benchmarked on positronic systems e+LiH, e+OH-, and e+Mg and on the quantum nuclear system HCN. It achieves near-FCI accuracy and surpasses the accuracy of previous SCI studies; specific numerical errors and computational costs are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The multicomponent SCI framework provides a simple, systematically improvable, and cost-effective alternative to traditional CI approaches for molecular systems with variable-mass leptons or quantum nuclei.

title: Experimental Evidence of Elastic Instability in Viscoelastic Kolmogorov Flow
summary: Inertialess elastic instabilities can profoundly affect transport in complex-fluid flows, from mixing in microfluidic devices and displacement through porous media to polymer processing. While such instabilities are well understood in flows with curved streamlines, their origin in rectilinear flows like the prototypical Kolmogorov flow remains unresolved. Here, we report the first experimental evidence of the center-mode elastic instability, at vanishing inertia, in a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow, driven by electromagnetic forcing. The instability is characterized by the emergence of "arrow-shaped" structures in the velocity field, which fluctuates chaotically as the forcing strength increases. We reproduce these observations in simulations of the Oldroyd-B model and trace the dynamics in the confined flow to the travelling arrowhead structures that emerge from the center-mode instability of unbounded Kolmogorov flow. Our work establishes a generic route to purely elastic instability in rectilinear flows, broadening the conditions under which elastic turbulence and enhanced mixing can arise.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the first experimental observation of a center-mode elastic instability in a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow at vanishing inertia, with arrow-shaped velocity structures and chaotic fluctuations reproduced by Oldroyd-B simulations.
AI.motivation: Inertialess elastic instabilities strongly influence transport in complex fluids, but their origin in rectilinear flows such as Kolmogorov flow was unresolved despite being understood in curved-streamline flows.
AI.method: The authors experimentally drive a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow using electromagnetic forcing and characterize its velocity field. They reproduce the observations with simulations of the Oldroyd-B model and relate the confined-flow dynamics to travelling arrowhead structures arising from the center-mode instability of unbounded Kolmogorov flow.
AI.result: The experiments provide the first experimental evidence of the center-mode elastic instability at vanishing inertia, marked by arrow-shaped velocity structures that fluctuate chaotically as forcing strength increases. Oldroyd-B simulations reproduce these observations and trace the confined-flow dynamics to travelling arrowhead structures from the unbounded-flow center-mode instability.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a generic route to purely elastic instability in rectilinear flows and broadens the conditions under which elastic turbulence and enhanced mixing can arise.

title: Intraband vs. interband optical nonlinearities of transparent conducting oxides
summary: We show that the intraband thermo-optical response to ultrashort intense infra-red illumination of transparent conducting oxides is much stronger than the nonlinear response associated with resonant and non-resonant interband transitions in typical experimental setups. This finding rules out several speculative explanations of recent measurements.

AI.tldr: For transparent conducting oxides under ultrashort intense infrared illumination, the intraband thermo-optical nonlinearity is shown to dominate over resonant and non-resonant interband nonlinearities in typical experimental setups.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to identify the dominant optical nonlinear mechanism in transparent conducting oxides and to test explanations proposed for recent measurements.
AI.method: The abstract does not provide methodological details; it reports a comparison of the intraband thermo-optical response with resonant and non-resonant interband nonlinear responses under ultrashort intense infrared illumination.
AI.result: The intraband thermo-optical response is much stronger than the nonlinear response associated with resonant and non-resonant interband transitions in typical experimental setups.
AI.conclusion: Intraband thermo-optical effects should dominate in such measurements, ruling out several speculative explanations of recent results.

title: Magnetic Flux Eruptions in Magnetically Arrested Disks: Magnetic Reconnection and Bubble Expansion
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ; 14 pages, 10 figures
summary: Using a high-resolution GRMHD simulation of a magnetically arrested disk, we investigate the physical mechanism driving magnetic-flux eruption. The horizon-threading magnetic flux declines mainly in off-equatorial regions, whereas localized hot spots associated with magnetic reconnection appear near the equatorial plane around the onset of flux decline. A non-axisymmetric, magnetically supported low-density structure, which we identify as a magnetic bubble, expands radially and azimuthally within a pre-existing low-density channel in the filamentary accretion flow. Based on these findings, we propose a physical picture linking reconnection, bubble expansion, and horizon magnetic flux decline. The reconnection occurs in the pre-existing low-density channel, and may reconfigure the field and promote bubble expansion. Magnetic-pressure gradients provide broadly distributed outward support for the expansion, while magnetic tension contributes a localized outward force near the equator. Bubble expansion may limit gas replenishment, helping to maintain the low-density region and reduce the total pressure near the equator. This pressure reduction may facilitate equatorward electromagnetic energy transport. In the simulation, the polar electromagnetic energy flux reverses from poleward to equatorward near the onset of the horizon-flux decline. The equatorward transport is concentrated in the bubble sector and carries electromagnetic energy from the off-equatorial magnetosphere to the equatorial region. This energy supply may sustain localized reconnection and plasma heating as the eruption develops.

AI.tldr: A high-resolution GRMHD simulation of a magnetically arrested disk links equatorial magnetic reconnection and the radial/azimuthal expansion of a magnetically supported low-density bubble to the decline of horizon-threading magnetic flux, with equatorward electromagnetic energy transport potentially sustaining reconnection and plasma heating.
AI.motivation: To investigate the physical mechanism driving magnetic-flux eruption in magnetically arrested disks.
AI.method: The authors analyze a high-resolution general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulation of a magnetically arrested disk, examining the spatial decline of horizon-threading magnetic flux, localized reconnection hot spots, a non-axisymmetric low-density magnetic bubble in a pre-existing low-density channel, magnetic-pressure and magnetic-tension forces, and the direction of electromagnetic energy flux.
AI.result: Horizon-threading magnetic flux declines mainly in off-equatorial regions, while reconnection-associated hot spots appear near the equatorial plane around the onset of flux decline. A magnetically supported low-density magnetic bubble expands radially and azimuthally within a pre-existing low-density channel. Magnetic-pressure gradients provide broadly distributed outward support, and magnetic tension contributes a localized outward force near the equator. Bubble expansion may limit gas replenishment, maintain the low-density region, and reduce total pressure near the equator. The polar electromagnetic energy flux reverses from poleward to equatorward near the onset of horizon-flux decline; this equatorward transport is concentrated in the bubble sector and carries energy from the off-equatorial magnetosphere to the equatorial region.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a physical picture linking magnetic reconnection, bubble expansion, and horizon magnetic flux decline: reconnection in a pre-existing low-density channel may reconfigure the field and promote bubble expansion; expansion may limit gas replenishment and lower equatorial pressure, facilitating equatorward electromagnetic energy transport that may sustain localized reconnection and plasma heating as the eruption develops.

title: Collective coupling of over 100 individually trapped atoms to a single cavity mode
summary: Coupling optical tweezer arrays to high-finesse cavities provides a shared optical interface for neutral-atom registers. Scaling this interface to large tweezer arrays requires placing many traps within the coupling region of a single cavity mode while maintaining uniform trapping and site-resolved detection. Here we match a two-dimensional array of 192 optical tweezers to the coupling profile of a millimeter-scale Fabry-Perot cavity. To improve trap uniformity in the array generated by crossed acousto-optic deflectors, we combine optimization with optical feedback and atomic fluorescence feedback, achieving a mean cesium loading probability of approximately 58%. In each trial, fluorescence imaging determines whether each individual tweezer site is occupied, allowing the cavity transmission spectra to be grouped by atom number. The grouped spectra exhibit resolved normal-mode doublets, and the group with 120 imaged atoms yields an effective collective coupling of $G_{\mathrm{eff}}/(2π) = 21.30 \pm 0.23$ MHz. A model based on the calculated coupling profile and measured site loading probabilities predicts that the mean squared coupling per occupied site changes little between 97 and 120 atoms. The fitted collective coupling is therefore consistent with square-root scaling with atom number despite the spatial variation in single-atom coupling. These results provide an experimental basis for studying photon-mediated many-body dynamics and developing cavity-assisted readout and optical links between neutral-atom registers.

AI.tldr: The paper couples a 192-site two-dimensional optical-tweezer array to a single millimeter-scale Fabry-Pérot cavity mode, uses site-resolved fluorescence to group cavity spectra by atom number, and measures an effective collective coupling of 21.30 ± 0.23 MHz for 120 atoms, consistent with square-root scaling despite spatially varying single-atom coupling.
AI.motivation: Scaling cavity interfaces to large neutral-atom registers requires many tweezers within one cavity mode while preserving uniform trapping and site-resolved detection; such a shared optical interface could support photon-mediated many-body dynamics, cavity-assisted readout, and optical links between neutral-atom registers.
AI.method: A 192-site two-dimensional optical-tweezer array generated by crossed acousto-optic deflectors was matched to the coupling profile of a millimeter-scale Fabry-Pérot cavity. Trap uniformity was improved by combining optimization with optical feedback and atomic fluorescence feedback. Fluorescence imaging determined occupation at each tweezer site, allowing cavity transmission spectra to be grouped by atom number.
AI.result: The mean cesium loading probability was approximately 58%. Grouped cavity transmission spectra showed resolved normal-mode doublets. For the group with 120 imaged atoms, the effective collective coupling was G_eff/(2π) = 21.30 ± 0.23 MHz. A model using the calculated coupling profile and measured loading probabilities predicted little change in mean squared coupling per occupied site between 97 and 120 atoms, making the fitted collective coupling consistent with square-root scaling with atom number despite spatial variation in single-atom coupling.
AI.conclusion: The experiment establishes a large, site-resolved cavity-coupled neutral-atom platform and provides an experimental basis for studying photon-mediated many-body dynamics and developing cavity-assisted readout and optical links between neutral-atom registers.

title: Full-horizon magnetic control of the Vlasov--Poisson system for plasma confinement
summary: We study the full-horizon control of a two-dimensional Vlasov--Poisson system through an externally imposed magnetic field. The control is represented by time-dependent coefficients associated with smooth, spatially localized basis functions, and is designed to steer selected position and velocity moments of the distribution function while limiting particle dispersion and the control effort. Starting from the kinetic constrained optimization problem, we derive the continuous first-order optimality conditions, including a backward Vlasov equation, an elliptic adjoint equation, and the variational inequality associated with bounded controls. We then project this system onto a particle--grid representation and identify the resulting particle adjoints and control gradient. The full-horizon field is then computed on a reduced particle ensemble, initialized by an instantaneous control, and subsequently applied to a larger set of particles. Numerical experiments indicate that the instantaneous control field already provides an effective baseline, while the full-horizon correction can further reduce the relative thermal energy near the boundaries and improve confinement over the prescribed time interval.

AI.tldr: The paper develops full-horizon magnetic control for a two-dimensional Vlasov--Poisson plasma confinement model, deriving continuous optimality conditions, a particle-grid discretization, and numerical evidence that full-horizon corrections improve confinement relative to instantaneous control.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to control selected position and velocity moments of the distribution function in a Vlasov--Poisson plasma system using an externally imposed magnetic field while limiting particle dispersion and control effort over a prescribed time horizon.
AI.method: The control is represented by time-dependent coefficients of smooth, spatially localized basis functions. Starting from a kinetic constrained optimization problem, the authors derive continuous first-order optimality conditions comprising a backward Vlasov equation, an elliptic adjoint equation, and a variational inequality for bounded controls. They then project the system onto a particle-grid representation, identify particle adjoints and the control gradient, compute the full-horizon field on a reduced particle ensemble initialized by instantaneous control, and apply it to a larger particle set.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that the instantaneous control field provides an effective baseline, while the full-horizon correction further reduces relative thermal energy near the boundaries and improves confinement over the prescribed time interval.
AI.conclusion: Full-horizon magnetic control of the Vlasov--Poisson system can improve plasma confinement beyond an instantaneous-control baseline within the studied numerical setting; the abstract does not report experimental validation or broader parameter studies.

title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
summary: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

AI.tldr: A deep-learning and compressed-sensing framework reconstructs the spatiotemporal surface elevation of highly nonlinear unidirectional water waves from a single measurement location and uses the reconstruction to forecast rogue waves, validated against controlled wave-tank measurements.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse observations is difficult, despite the theoretical possibility of state-space reconstruction from a single time series via delay-coordinate embedding. The work aims to enable forecasting of extreme wave events from remarkably sparse measurements.
AI.method: The authors combine deep learning, compressed sensing, and self-similarity properties of a unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation to reconstruct the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field from observations at a single measurement location. These reconstructions are then used to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics using point observations from controlled water wave tank experiments. Specific neural-network architectures, training details, and measurement sampling parameters are not provided in the abstract.
AI.result: The reconstructed wave fields enabled forecasting of rogue waves from point observations in controlled water wave tank experiments, with excellent agreement between forecasts and measurements of the fully evolved wave field.
AI.conclusion: Extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations, and the framework may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

title: Microwave hinge states in an all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal insulator
summary: Higher-order topological states are studied in a woodpile photonic crystal (PhC) having a large complete photonic bandgap. According to theoretical predictions, we fabricate a three-dimensional all-dielectric PhC with a millimeter-scale lattice period. The structure consists of two distinct lattice types that coincide through a structural displacement, where their interface intersection gives rise to hinge states. Microwave transmission measurements reveal transmission peaks and spatial localization at the intersection, demonstrating the hinge states. Furthermore, we confirm the absence of hinge states at a specific intersection. As theoretically predicted, hinge states emerge at intersections where the localized boundary polarizations are topologically different, whereas they are absent at intersections where the boundary polarizations are equivalent.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally studies higher-order topological hinge states in a three-dimensional all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal with a large complete photonic bandgap, using microwave transmission measurements to demonstrate hinge-state localization and its dependence on boundary-polarization topology.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by theoretical predictions of higher-order topological states in a woodpile photonic crystal possessing a large complete photonic bandgap, and by the need to demonstrate hinge states in such a three-dimensional all-dielectric structure.
AI.method: The authors fabricate a three-dimensional all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal with a millimeter-scale lattice period. The structure contains two distinct lattice types that coincide through a structural displacement, and their interface intersection is designed to support hinge states. Microwave transmission measurements are used to probe transmission and spatial localization at the intersection.
AI.result: Microwave transmission measurements reveal transmission peaks and spatial localization at the intersection, demonstrating hinge states. The authors also confirm the absence of hinge states at a specific intersection. Hinge states emerge where the localized boundary polarizations are topologically different, whereas they are absent where the boundary polarizations are equivalent.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an experimental demonstration of higher-order topological hinge states in an all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal and confirms that hinge-state existence depends on whether the intersecting boundary polarizations are topologically different or equivalent.

title: Micro-Macro Tensor Neural Surrogates for Uncertainty Quantification in Collisional Plasma
summary: Plasma kinetic equations exhibit pronounced sensitivity to microscopic perturbations in model parameters and data, making reliable and efficient uncertainty quantification (UQ) essential for predictive simulations. However, the cost of uncertainty sampling, the high-dimensional phase space, and multiscale stiffness pose severe challenges to both computational efficiency and error control in traditional numerical methods. These aspects are further emphasized in presence of collisions where the high-dimensional nonlocal collision integrations and conservation properties pose severe constraints. To overcome this, we present a variance-reduced Monte Carlo framework for UQ in the Vlasov--Poisson--Landau (VPL) system, in which neural network surrogates replace the multiple costly evaluations of the Landau collision term. The method couples a high-fidelity, asymptotic-preserving VPL solver with inexpensive, strongly correlated surrogates based on the Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck (VPFP) and Euler--Poisson (EP) equations. For the surrogate models, we introduce a generalization of the separable physics-informed neural network (SPINN), developing a class of tensor neural networks based on an anisotropic micro-macro decomposition, to reduce velocity-moment costs, model complexity, and the curse of dimensionality. To further increase correlation with VPL, we calibrate the VPFP model and design an asymptotic-preserving SPINN whose small- and large-Knudsen limits recover the EP and VP systems, respectively. Numerical experiments show substantial variance reduction over standard Monte Carlo, accurate statistics with far fewer high-fidelity samples, and lower wall-clock time, while maintaining robustness to stochastic dimension.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a variance-reduced Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification framework for the collisional Vlasov--Poisson--Landau plasma system, using calibrated Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck and Euler--Poisson tensor neural network surrogates to replace costly Landau collision-term evaluations.
AI.motivation: Plasma kinetic equations are highly sensitive to microscopic perturbations in model parameters and data, so reliable and efficient uncertainty quantification is needed for predictive simulations. Uncertainty sampling, high-dimensional phase space, multiscale stiffness, nonlocal collision integrations, and conservation constraints make traditional numerical UQ computationally expensive and difficult to control.
AI.method: The authors couple a high-fidelity asymptotic-preserving Vlasov--Poisson--Landau solver with inexpensive, strongly correlated surrogates based on the Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck and Euler--Poisson equations. They generalize separable physics-informed neural networks into tensor neural networks using an anisotropic micro-macro decomposition, calibrate the VPFP model, and design an asymptotic-preserving SPINN whose small- and large-Knudsen limits recover the Euler--Poisson and Vlasov--Poisson systems, respectively.
AI.result: Numerical experiments report substantial variance reduction over standard Monte Carlo, accurate statistics with far fewer high-fidelity samples, and lower wall-clock time, while maintaining robustness to stochastic dimension.
AI.conclusion: The proposed micro-macro tensor neural surrogate framework supports efficient and reliable uncertainty quantification for collisional plasma kinetic equations by reducing surrogate complexity, velocity-moment costs, and the number of expensive high-fidelity VPL evaluations while preserving asymptotic consistency.

title: Absence of binding for the helium anion
summary: We study the helium anion in the nonrelativistic Coulomb model with an infinitely massive nucleus and spin-$\frac12$ electrons. We prove the absence of binding, with $E^{\mathrm{F}}(3,2)=E^{\mathrm{F}}(2,2)$ and no three-electron ground state. A decomposition relative to the helium ground state and completion of the square reduce the problem to a one-dimensional variational inequality.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the helium anion is unbound in the nonrelativistic Coulomb model with an infinitely massive nucleus and spin-1/2 electrons, showing E^F(3,2)=E^F(2,2) and no three-electron ground state.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not specify a broader motivation; the work addresses the question of whether the helium anion is bound in the stated nonrelativistic Coulomb model.
AI.method: The authors decompose relative to the helium ground state and complete the square, reducing the problem to a one-dimensional variational inequality.
AI.result: They prove the absence of binding for the helium anion, with E^F(3,2)=E^F(2,2) and no three-electron ground state.
AI.conclusion: Within the nonrelativistic Coulomb model with an infinitely massive nucleus and spin-1/2 electrons, the helium anion has no bound three-electron ground state.

title: Control strategies for magnetized plasma: a polar coordinates framework
summary: In this work, we provide an overview of various control strategies aimed at steering plasma toward desired configurations using an external magnetic field. From a modeling perspective, we focus on the Vlasov equation in a two-dimensional bounded domain, accounting for both a self-induced electric field and a strong external magnetic field. The results are presented in a polar coordinate framework, which is particularly well-suited for simulating toroidal devices such as Tokamaks and Stellarators. A key feature of the proposed control strategies is their feedback mechanism, which is based on an instantaneous prediction of the discretized system. Finally, different numerical experiments in the two-dimensional polar coordinate setting demonstrate the effectiveness of the approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews feedback-based control strategies for steering magnetized plasma toward desired configurations, modeled by the Vlasov equation in a two-dimensional bounded domain with self-induced electric and strong external magnetic fields, formulated in polar coordinates and validated through numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: The work aims to steer plasma toward desired configurations using an external magnetic field, with a polar-coordinate framework suited to simulating toroidal devices such as Tokamaks and Stellarators.
AI.method: The authors consider the Vlasov equation in a two-dimensional bounded domain with a self-induced electric field and a strong external magnetic field. They present control strategies with feedback based on instantaneous prediction of the discretized system and evaluate them in two-dimensional polar-coordinate numerical experiments.
AI.result: Different numerical experiments in the two-dimensional polar-coordinate setting demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed control approaches. No quantitative performance results are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed feedback control strategies are effective for steering magnetized plasma in the reported two-dimensional polar-coordinate setting, which is relevant to toroidal confinement devices.

title: Will it bend? Modelling hydrogel box hinges with a gel Lattice Spring Method
summary: Hydrogels are biocompatible smart materials comprised of a hydrophilic polymer network which can absorb a large volume of water (swelling). The changes in shape the gel undergoes as it swells or de-swells can be utilised in the design of actuators. This is of particular interest for many applications whereby hydrogel actuators would be combined into a complex origami-inspired structure which can fold and unfold according to application needs. In this paper, we therefore focus on one such actuator design, the bilayer hinge, which can induce bending (for potential use in a fold/unfold mechanism). We develop a model using the gel lattice spring method (gLSM) which can be used to simulate composite structures comprised of hydrogel and elastomer and compute the equilibrium bending angle of bilayer hinges for a range of geometries and material properties.

AI.tldr: The paper models hydrogel–elastomer bilayer hinges using a gel Lattice Spring Method to predict equilibrium bending angles for swelling-driven fold/unfold actuators across varied geometries and material properties.
AI.motivation: Hydrogels are biocompatible smart materials that swell and change shape, making them useful for actuators, particularly when integrated into origami-inspired foldable structures. The bilayer hinge is a key actuator design for inducing bending, motivating a simulation approach for composite hydrogel–elastomer structures.
AI.method: The authors develop a gel Lattice Spring Method (gLSM) model to simulate composite structures composed of hydrogel and elastomer and to compute the equilibrium bending angle of bilayer hinges over a range of geometries and material properties.
AI.result: A gLSM-based model is developed and applied to compute equilibrium bending angles of bilayer hinges for varied geometries and material properties. The abstract does not provide quantitative bending-angle results, experimental validation details, or specific parameter ranges.
AI.conclusion: The gLSM is presented as a suitable modelling approach for hydrogel–elastomer composite structures and for predicting the equilibrium bending of bilayer hinges, with potential utility in designing fold/unfold hydrogel actuators and origami-inspired structures. Specific quantitative conclusions and validation are not provided in the abstract.

title: Active Contrast-Dissipation All-Optical Encryption
summary: Optical encryption is meant to place secrecy in physical structure, yet adversaries can readily construct imperfect physical keys to probe the encryption system via trial-and-error iterations. Such systems inevitably leak target plaintext information and preserve invertible residual structural features, rendering the entire encryption scheme vulnerable to adversarial inversion attacks. Here, we report an active contrast-dissipation all-optical encryption architecture, which partitions wavefront modulation into M wavelength-private encryption layers and N shared decoding layers. Security rests on multi-dimensional physical keys that must match simultaneously, including illumination wavelength, precise spatial alignment and layer stacking sequence. With every key matched and authorized readout is preserved: the composite plaintext is reconstructed at a full-detector Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.997. We further impose active contrast dissipation as a core security constraint. Under physical perturbation it suppresses the foreground-background intensity contrast, so that the slightest key mismatch collapses the target features and dissipates the plaintext into randomized, diffuse speckle within chaotic background noise, leaving no residual semantic leakage to invert. Under nanoscale wavelength detuning, a 1 degree in-plane rotation, a single-pixel lateral displacement or layer-stacking tampering, the plaintext vanishes and the PCC approaches zero, whereas conventional diffractive encryptors retain identifiable contours. This work provide a feasible and reliable solution for high-security information encryption, with great application potential in communication security, information anti-counterfeiting, and confidential data storage.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an active contrast-dissipation all-optical encryption architecture using M wavelength-private encryption layers and N shared decoding layers, with security dependent on simultaneous matching of wavelength, spatial alignment, and layer-stacking sequence; authorized reconstruction reaches PCC 0.997, while slight key mismatches dissipate the plaintext into diffuse speckle and drive PCC toward zero.
AI.motivation: Optical encryption aims to embed secrecy in physical structure, but adversaries can construct imperfect physical keys and probe the system iteratively, leaking plaintext and leaving invertible residual structural features that enable adversarial inversion attacks.
AI.method: The architecture partitions wavefront modulation into M wavelength-private encryption layers and N shared decoding layers. Security relies on multi-dimensional physical keys that must match simultaneously: illumination wavelength, precise spatial alignment, and layer stacking sequence. Active contrast dissipation is imposed as a core security constraint to suppress foreground-background intensity contrast under physical perturbation.
AI.result: With all keys matched, the composite plaintext is reconstructed at a full-detector Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.997. Under nanoscale wavelength detuning, 1 degree in-plane rotation, single-pixel lateral displacement, or layer-stacking tampering, the plaintext vanishes and PCC approaches zero, whereas conventional diffractive encryptors retain identifiable contours.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a feasible and reliable solution for high-security information encryption, with potential applications in communication security, information anti-counterfeiting, and confidential data storage.

title: Structure and asymptotic preserving deep neural surrogates for uncertainty quantification in multiscale kinetic equations
summary: The high dimensionality of kinetic equations with stochastic parameters poses major computational challenges for uncertainty quantification (UQ). Traditional Monte Carlo (MC) sampling methods, while widely used, suffer from slow convergence and high variance, which become increasingly severe as the dimensionality of the parameter space grows. To accelerate MC sampling, we adopt a multiscale control variates strategy that leverages low-fidelity solutions from simplified kinetic models to reduce variance. To further improve sampling efficiency and preserve the underlying physics, we introduce surrogate models based on structure and asymptotic preserving neural networks (SAPNNs). These deep neural networks are specifically designed to satisfy key physical properties, including positivity, conservation laws, entropy dissipation, and asymptotic limits. By training the SAPNNs on low-fidelity models and enriching them with selected high-fidelity samples from the full Boltzmann equation, our method achieves significant variance reduction while maintaining physical consistency and asymptotic accuracy. The proposed methodology enables efficient large-scale prediction in kinetic UQ and is validated across both homogeneous and nonhomogeneous multiscale regimes. Numerical results demonstrate improved accuracy and computational efficiency compared to standard MC techniques.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes structure and asymptotic preserving neural network (SAPNN) surrogates combined with multiscale control variates to accelerate Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification for stochastic multiscale kinetic equations while preserving key physical properties.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional kinetic equations with stochastic parameters make uncertainty quantification computationally expensive. Standard Monte Carlo sampling suffers from slow convergence and high variance, which worsen as the parameter-space dimensionality increases.
AI.method: The authors use a multiscale control variates strategy based on low-fidelity simplified kinetic models to reduce variance, then introduce SAPNN surrogates designed to satisfy positivity, conservation laws, entropy dissipation, and asymptotic limits. The networks are trained on low-fidelity models and enriched with selected high-fidelity samples from the full Boltzmann equation.
AI.result: The method achieves significant variance reduction while maintaining physical consistency and asymptotic accuracy. Numerical results across homogeneous and nonhomogeneous multiscale regimes show improved accuracy and computational efficiency compared with standard Monte Carlo techniques; specific quantitative metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed combination of multiscale control variates and SAPNN surrogates enables efficient large-scale prediction for kinetic uncertainty quantification and outperforms standard Monte Carlo in the reported regimes.

title: Robust feedback control of collisional plasma dynamics in presence of uncertainties
summary: Magnetic fusion aims to confine high-temperature plasma within a device, enabling the fusion of deuterium and tritium nuclei to release energy. Due to the very large temperatures involved, it is essential to isolate the plasma from the device walls to prevent structural damage and the external magnetic fields play a fundamental role in achieving this confinement. In realistic settings, the physical mechanisms governing plasma behavior are highly complex, involving numerous uncertain parameters and intricate particle interactions, such as collisions, that significantly affect both confinement efficiency and overall stability. In this work, we address particularly these challenges by proposing a robust feedback control strategy designed to steer the plasma towards a desired spatial region, despite the presence of uncertainties. From a modeling perspective, we consider a collisional plasma described by a Vlasov-Poisson-BGK system, which accounts for a self-consistent electric field and a strong external magnetic field, while incorporating uncertainty in the model. A key feature of the proposed control strategy is its independence from the random parameter, making it particularly suitable for practical applications. A series of numerical simulations confirms the effectiveness of our approach and demonstrates the ability of external magnetic fields to successfully confine plasma away from the device boundaries, even in the presence of uncertain conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a robust feedback control strategy, independent of the random model parameter, to steer a collisional plasma modeled by a Vlasov-Poisson-BGK system with a self-consistent electric field and strong external magnetic field toward a desired spatial region under uncertainties. Numerical simulations indicate effective confinement away from device boundaries.
AI.motivation: Magnetic fusion requires confining high-temperature plasma and isolating it from device walls to prevent structural damage. Realistic plasma behavior is complex, with numerous uncertain parameters and collisional particle interactions that affect confinement efficiency and stability, motivating robust control under uncertainty.
AI.method: The plasma is modeled as a collisional Vlasov-Poisson-BGK system incorporating a self-consistent electric field, a strong external magnetic field, and model uncertainty. A robust feedback control strategy is designed to steer the plasma toward a desired spatial region, with the key feature that the controller is independent of the random parameter. Numerical simulations are used to assess the approach.
AI.result: Numerical simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy and show that external magnetic fields can confine the plasma away from device boundaries even under uncertain conditions. No quantitative performance metrics are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: A parameter-independent robust feedback control strategy can, in simulation, support magnetic confinement of collisional plasma away from device walls despite uncertainties, suggesting suitability for practical applications.

title: The 1/4-power law for bounded variation of wall turbulence from the Kármán-Howarth equation
summary: By applying the Kármán-Howarth (KH) equation to turbulent channel flows, we derive the $1/4$-power bounded laws for the peak dissipation and the normalized mean-square streamwise velocity fluctuation. The analysis requires two additional inputs, both standard in the study of turbulent wall flows: the logarithmic mean velocity profile and the near-isotropy of the spatial velocity derivatives. Self-similarity of KH equation yields, for the profile of the mean-square streamwise velocity, the form $c_1 - c_2 (y/δ)^{1/4}$ in the overlap region (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2023), where $δ$ is the half-channel height; it also provides the basis for constructing self-similar profiles for high-order moments of streamwise velocity (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2025). Furthermore, the analysis yields the form $c_1' - c_2' Re^{-1/4}_τ$ for the inner peak of the streamwise mean-square velocity (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2022), and a similar bounded relation for a characteristic wall dissipation (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2021).

AI.tldr: Applying the Kármán–Howarth equation to turbulent channel flow, with a logarithmic mean velocity profile and near-isotropy of spatial velocity derivatives as inputs, yields 1/4-power bounded laws for peak dissipation and normalized mean-square streamwise velocity fluctuation, plus self-similar profile forms for streamwise-velocity moments.
AI.motivation: The abstract aims to derive 1/4-power bounded laws for the peak dissipation and the normalized mean-square streamwise velocity fluctuation in turbulent channel flows from the Kármán–Howarth equation.
AI.method: The Kármán–Howarth equation is applied to turbulent channel flows using two standard inputs: the logarithmic mean velocity profile and near-isotropy of the spatial velocity derivatives. Self-similarity of the Kármán–Howarth equation is used to obtain profile forms and to construct self-similar profiles for high-order moments of streamwise velocity.
AI.result: The analysis yields a mean-square streamwise velocity profile of the form c1 - c2(y/δ)^(1/4) in the overlap region, where δ is the half-channel height; an inner-peak form c1' - c2' Re_τ^(-1/4) for the streamwise mean-square velocity; and a similar bounded relation for a characteristic wall dissipation. It also provides a basis for self-similar profiles of high-order streamwise-velocity moments.
AI.conclusion: The Kármán–Howarth-based analysis produces bounded 1/4-power laws and self-similar profile forms for wall turbulence under the stated standard inputs. The abstract does not provide quantitative validation, experimental comparisons, or details of the derivation.

title: Backward-scattering photoelectron holography of a polar molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser pulse
summary: We investigate photoelectron holographic interference in the polar CO molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser pulse using time-dependent Schrödinger equation simulations and a classical-trajectory-based analysis. The sub-cycle temporal confinement of the driving field enables the forward-scattering holographic (FSH) and backward-scattering holographic (BSH) interference structures in the photoelectron momentum distributions (PMDs) to be clearly distinguished. The FSH fringes exhibit a strong dependence on molecular orientation, which is associated with the orientation-dependent transverse displacement of the ionizing electron wave packet (EWP). Furthermore, the heteronuclear nature of CO results in different FSH fringe shifts for ionization occurring predominantly from the C and O sides of the molecule. In contrast, the curved interference structures in the negative parallel-momentum region are identified as BSH interference arising from the coherent superposition of direct and backward-scattered EWPs. The BSH fringe positions show weak dependence on molecular orientation and remain clearly visible after orientation averaging. We further show that BSH visibility depends on the carrier-envelope phase (CEP) and that the fringes remain discernible after CEP averaging. Moreover, the BSH interference pattern exhibits a systematic dependence on the internuclear separation, demonstrating its sensitivity to molecular geometry. These results highlight the potential of sub-cycle pulse enabled backward-scattering photoelectron holography for probing molecular structure and demonstrate its robustness against molecularorientation and CEP averaging

AI.tldr: The paper uses time-dependent Schrödinger equation simulations and classical-trajectory analysis to distinguish forward- and backward-scattering photoelectron holography in a polar CO molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser pulse, showing that backward-scattering fringes are robust to molecular-orientation and carrier-envelope-phase averaging and sensitive to internuclear separation.
AI.motivation: The work aims to clarify photoelectron holographic interference in a polar molecule under a sub-cycle laser field, where temporal confinement can separate forward-scattering and backward-scattering contributions, and to assess backward-scattering holography as a robust probe of molecular structure.
AI.method: The authors perform time-dependent Schrödinger equation simulations for the polar CO molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser pulse and analyze the resulting photoelectron momentum distributions using a classical-trajectory-based interpretation.
AI.result: Forward-scattering holographic fringes depend strongly on molecular orientation and on whether ionization occurs predominantly from the C or O side, reflecting orientation-dependent transverse displacement of the ionizing electron wave packet. Curved structures in the negative parallel-momentum region are identified as backward-scattering holography from coherent superposition of direct and backward-scattered wave packets; these fringes depend weakly on orientation, remain visible after orientation averaging, depend on carrier-envelope phase and remain discernible after CEP averaging, and show systematic dependence on internuclear separation.
AI.conclusion: Sub-cycle-pulse-enabled backward-scattering photoelectron holography is shown to be a potentially useful and robust approach for probing molecular structure and geometry, with resilience against molecular-orientation and carrier-envelope-phase averaging.

title: A spherical body in plasma simulated with adaptive mesh and algorithm refinement
summary: An absorbing sphere in a weakly ionized plasma is the oldest kinetic problem of probe theory. It presents key difficulties in plasma simulation: disparate velocity scales, orbital motion, phase-space regions that no characteristic of the plasma reaches, a boundary set by a kinetic flux balance, and collisions that qualitatively change the answer. We use this problem to demonstrate the Plasma Adaptive Mesh and Algorithm Refinement (PAMAR) framework introduced in a companion paper. Electrons and ions have separate solvers on their own adaptive $(r,v,μ)$ octrees, or on reduced phase spaces at the angular-moment level (Fokker-Planck and two-stream models), coupled through a radial Poisson field solver. Two exact references, a method of characteristics for the collisionless problem and integration along the orbits for elastic scattering, audit the solvers. We compute the current-voltage characteristic of the probe on both electron and ion branches, and the profiles of the potential and of the moments of both species agree with the exact solution. Far from the sphere, the potential follows the Coulomb law in neither limit: it falls as $r^{-2}$ without collisions and as $r^{-1}$ only beyond the ion mean free path. With elastic electron scattering, the kinetic solver follows the exact dependence of the collected current on the mean free path, from free flight toward diffusion, to 1 percent. Finally, we demonstrate the ion model selection cell by cell, using a fluid model coupled to the kinetic solver, with the interface set by the pressure anisotropy; with charge exchange, a sensor of ion trapping is also needed. According to exact solutions, the ion anisotropy extends to several probe radii, much farther than the electron loss cone.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates the Plasma Adaptive Mesh and Algorithm Refinement (PAMAR) framework on the classical absorbing-sphere probe problem in a weakly ionized plasma. Separate adaptive kinetic electron and ion solvers, reduced angular models, and a radial Poisson solver are validated against exact collisionless and elastic-scattering solutions, including probe current-voltage characteristics, potential and moment profiles, mean-free-path dependence, and cell-by-cell ion model selection.
AI.motivation: The absorbing sphere is the oldest kinetic probe problem and embodies central plasma-simulation difficulties: disparate velocity scales, orbital motion, phase-space regions unreachable by plasma characteristics, a boundary determined by kinetic flux balance, and collisions that qualitatively change the result. The authors use it to demonstrate and audit the PAMAR framework introduced in a companion paper.
AI.method: Electrons and ions are solved separately on adaptive $(r,v,\mu)$ octrees or on reduced phase spaces at the angular-moment level, including Fokker-Planck and two-stream models, and are coupled through a radial Poisson field solver. Exact references—a method of characteristics for the collisionless problem and integration along orbits for elastic scattering—are used to audit the solvers. The probe current-voltage characteristic is computed on both electron and ion branches, along with potential and species-moment profiles. Elastic electron scattering is included, and ion model selection is demonstrated cell by cell using a fluid model coupled to the kinetic solver, with the interface set by pressure anisotropy and, with charge exchange, a sensor of ion trapping.
AI.result: Potential and moment profiles for both species agree with the exact solution, and the current-voltage characteristic is computed on both electron and ion branches. Far from the sphere, the potential follows neither Coulomb limit: it falls as $r^{-2}$ without collisions and as $r^{-1}$ only beyond the ion mean free path. With elastic electron scattering, the kinetic solver follows the exact dependence of collected current on mean free path, from free flight toward diffusion, to 1 percent. Ion anisotropy extends to several probe radii, much farther than the electron loss cone, and cell-by-cell ion model selection is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: PAMAR successfully treats this multiscale kinetic probe problem and is validated against exact collisionless and elastic-scattering solutions. The results show correct probe characteristics and profiles, non-Coulomb far-field potential scaling, accurate mean-free-path-dependent electron current, and practical cell-by-cell selection of fluid versus kinetic ion models.

title: Local topology hallucinations in universal machine-learned interatomic potentials
summary: Predicting metastable states with universal machine-learned interatomic potentials requires that they preserve the minima and saddles of the reference potential-energy surface. Here we identify local topology hallucination, in which distinct model minima relax into the same reference basin. This failure arises from mode-selective curvature-sign errors shared by MACE, CHGNet and M3GNet. Curvature signs predicted by two of the three models agreed with density-functional calculations in 55 of 57 positive but only 5 of 56 negative cases. In LiGe$_2$S, two MACE minima connected by a verified saddle relaxed into one density-functional basin. Reference relaxation likewise returned nine of ten selected model minima to their reference basins. A directional test with two displaced reference calculations rejected 9 of 12 prospectively tested model instabilities. Model agreement alone therefore cannot establish that predicted minima are distinct metastable states.

AI.tldr: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials can exhibit local topology hallucinations, in which distinct predicted minima relax into the same reference basin because of mode-selective curvature-sign errors, so agreement among models does not prove that predicted minima are distinct metastable states.
AI.motivation: Predicting metastable states with universal machine-learned interatomic potentials requires preserving the minima and saddles of the reference potential-energy surface.
AI.method: The authors identify local topology hallucination and trace it to mode-selective curvature-sign errors shared by MACE, CHGNet, and M3GNet. They compare predicted curvature signs with density-functional calculations, examine a LiGe2S case with two MACE minima connected by a verified saddle, perform reference relaxation of selected model minima, and apply a directional test using two displaced reference calculations.
AI.result: Curvature signs from two of the three models agreed with density-functional calculations in 55 of 57 positive but only 5 of 56 negative cases. In LiGe2S, two MACE minima connected by a verified saddle relaxed into one density-functional basin, and reference relaxation returned nine of ten selected model minima to their reference basins. The directional test rejected 9 of 12 prospectively tested model instabilities.
AI.conclusion: Model agreement alone cannot establish that predicted minima are distinct metastable states; local topology hallucinations from curvature-sign errors can collapse distinct model minima into the same reference basin.

title: Scale-aware composite forcing enhances forward energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence
summary: In forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence (FHIT), conventional large-scale forcing sustains statistical stationarity but offers limited control over energy at intermediate scales. We propose a scale-aware composite forcing strategy for the lattice Boltzmann method, combining large-scale random forcing with feedback aligned with an intermediate-scale velocity field extracted by composite filtering. The magnitude of the cross-power spectrum between feedback and filtered velocity is concentrated in the target band, with a time-averaged fraction of 72.26%-74.56%. Feedback increases energy in both target and high-wavenumber bands, with larger relative gains at high wavenumbers. At feedback strengths $α$ = 1%, 3%, 5%, and 7%, the target-band energy fraction increases by 6.29%, 11.65%, 18.99%, and 19.89% relative to the baseline. The mean forward nonlinear energy flux across K = 12 rises to 1.18, 1.54, 2.32, and 3.06 times its baseline value, with larger relative increases than across K = 4. As $α$ increases from 0% to 7%, the mean Taylor-microscale Reynolds number rises from 73.94 to 97.86 and enstrophy increases by 181.98%, while longitudinal velocity-gradient skewness shifts toward zero and standardized velocity and normalized Q'-R' distributions largely retain their shapes. Mean $k_{\max}η$ values of 1.01 and 0.90 at 5% and 7% feedback indicate an approaching resolution limit and a risk of under-resolution, respectively. At approximately matched dissipation rates, 5% feedback gives a target-band energy fraction of 32.36%, versus 27.55% under enhanced large-scale forcing, and a post-transient forward flux across K = 12 generally 2.17-2.39 times larger. The strategy thus enables targeted control of energy distribution and nonlinear transfer, with feedback strength constrained by small-scale resolution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces scale-aware composite forcing for lattice Boltzmann simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, combining conventional large-scale random forcing with filtered intermediate-scale velocity feedback. It reports enhanced target-band energy and forward nonlinear energy transfer, with gains increasing with feedback strength but small-scale resolution imposing an upper limit.
AI.motivation: Conventional large-scale forcing in forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence maintains statistical stationarity but provides limited control over energy at intermediate scales. The authors seek a strategy that enables targeted control of energy distribution and nonlinear energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann simulations.
AI.method: A scale-aware composite forcing strategy is proposed for the lattice Boltzmann method. It combines large-scale random forcing with feedback aligned with an intermediate-scale velocity field extracted by composite filtering. The feedback strength is varied at alpha = 1%, 3%, 5%, and 7%, and the effects are assessed using cross-power spectra, target-band energy fractions, forward nonlinear energy flux, Taylor-microscale Reynolds number, enstrophy, velocity-gradient skewness, standardized velocity and normalized Q'-R' distributions, and resolution indicators including k_max eta. Comparisons are also made with enhanced large-scale forcing at approximately matched dissipation rates.
AI.result: The cross-power spectrum magnitude between feedback and filtered velocity is concentrated in the target band, with a time-averaged fraction of 72.26%-74.56%. Feedback increases energy in both target and high-wavenumber bands, with larger relative gains at high wavenumbers. At alpha = 1%, 3%, 5%, and 7%, the target-band energy fraction increases by 6.29%, 11.65%, 18.99%, and 19.89% relative to the baseline. Mean forward nonlinear energy flux across K = 12 rises to 1.18, 1.54, 2.32, and 3.06 times the baseline value, with larger relative increases than across K = 4. As alpha increases from 0% to 7%, the mean Taylor-microscale Reynolds number rises from 73.94 to 97.86 and enstrophy increases by 181.98%, while longitudinal velocity-gradient skewness shifts toward zero and standardized velocity and normalized Q'-R' distributions largely retain their shapes. Mean k_max eta values are 1.01 and 0.90 at 5% and 7% feedback, indicating an approaching resolution limit and a risk of under-resolution, respectively. At approximately matched dissipation rates, 5% feedback gives a target-band energy fraction of 32.36% versus 27.55% under enhanced large-scale forcing, and post-transient forward flux across K = 12 is generally 2.17-2.39 times larger.
AI.conclusion: Scale-aware composite forcing enables targeted control of energy distribution and nonlinear energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence. The achievable feedback strength is constrained by small-scale resolution, with stronger feedback approaching or exceeding adequate resolution conditions.

title: Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource
summary: We propose a new realization of Maxwells demon for photons and its use as an energy resource. The starting point is a multilayer dielectric mirror that transmits photons within a certain wavelength band but reflects photons at longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts the wavelength. A 3D box constructed from these one-way mirrors is a self-acting Maxwells demon for photons. The first case considered is a one-way mirror for visible photons, converting blue to red as an example. The next case is a one-way mirror that transmits visible light but reflects infrared light, followed by a perfect blackbody. We analyze a 3D box with such mirrors as walls to accumulate and store blackbody radiation. Applications include solar-powered thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics. The latter case would combine the 3D box with an ultra-low bandgap semiconductor photovoltaic cell inside. In the ideal optical limit, radiation can enter the box but cannot return through the entrance channel after conversion, allowing repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization. This can in principle move the conversion efficiency toward the thermodynamic limit for solar-energy conversion, the Landsberg limit of 93.3%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a photonic Maxwell's demon using wavelength-selective multilayer dielectric mirrors followed by irreversible wavelength conversion, forming a 3D box that admits photons but prevents their return after conversion. It analyzes visible-to-red and visible-to-infrared/blackbody configurations for solar thermal storage and thermophotovoltaics, suggesting that repeated photon recycling could approach the Landsberg solar-conversion limit of 93.3% in the ideal optical limit.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to realize Maxwell's demon for photons and exploit its one-way photon-handling capability as an energy resource, particularly to improve solar-energy conversion and storage.
AI.method: A multilayer dielectric mirror transmits photons in a selected wavelength band and reflects longer wavelengths; a following material irreversibly converts the transmitted photons to longer wavelengths. A 3D box with such one-way mirrors acts as a self-acting photonic Maxwell's demon. The paper considers a visible one-way mirror converting blue to red, and a mirror transmitting visible light while reflecting infrared light followed by a perfect blackbody. It analyzes a 3D box with these walls for accumulating and storing blackbody radiation, including solar thermal and thermophotovoltaic applications with an ultra-low-bandgap photovoltaic cell inside.
AI.result: The proposed configurations are analyzed conceptually rather than experimentally. In the ideal optical limit, radiation can enter the box but cannot return through the entrance after wavelength conversion, enabling repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization. The authors state that this can in principle move solar-energy conversion efficiency toward the thermodynamic Landsberg limit of 93.3%. No measured efficiencies or experimental demonstrations are reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: A self-acting photonic Maxwell's demon based on wavelength-selective one-way mirrors is proposed as a potential energy resource for solar thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics. Idealized operation could enable extensive photon recycling and approach the Landsberg limit, but practical implementation and performance details are not provided.

title: Experimental observation of higher-harmonic generation of whistler waves in magnetized plasma of Large Volume Plasma Device
summary: We report the higher-harmonic generation of whistler waves using a loop antenna in the Large Volume Plasma Device (LVPD). The antenna is energized using a pulse-forming network (PFN), and the excited magnetic fluctuations are measured using a three-axis B-dot probe. Experiments are performed in a moderate-density ($n_e \sim 1-2 \times 10^{17}\ \text{m}^{-3}$), low-temperature ($T_e \sim 2-5\ \text{eV}$) argon plasma in a uniform axial magnetic field ($B_z \sim 6.2\ \text{G}$). A Helmholtz coil is employed to investigate the dependence of the wave response and propagation on the local magnetic-field configuration. A clear distinction between wave characteristics is observed in the absence and presence of plasma: in plasma, the excited wave shows a significant $δB_y$ component along with $δB_x$, indicating polarization. In addition to the fundamental frequency, distinct spectral peaks are observed at $300\ \text{kHz}$, $450\ \text{kHz}$, and $600\ \text{kHz}$. These harmonics indicate nonlinear wave-plasma interactions, and bicoherence analysis further provides evidence of nonlinear coupling between the observed frequency components. The spatial propagation of the wave was systematically diagnosed using a linear array of five identical B-dot probes. Spatial cross-correlation analysis reveals strong structural coherence during wave propagation, allowing the explicit experimental determination of the wave phase velocity ($V_{ph}$) and parallel wave number ($k_{\parallel}$) for the generated higher harmonics. The measured propagation is oblique at an angle of approximately $48^\circ$ with respect to the background magnetic field, and the experimental dispersion relation agrees with the cold-plasma oblique whistler dispersion relation within experimental uncertainty.

AI.tldr: In the Large Volume Plasma Device, a loop antenna excited whistler waves in magnetized argon plasma, producing spectral peaks at 300, 450, and 600 kHz in addition to the fundamental. Bicoherence indicated nonlinear coupling, and multi-probe cross-correlation showed coherent oblique propagation at about 48° with dispersion consistent with cold-plasma oblique whistler theory.
AI.motivation: To experimentally demonstrate higher-harmonic generation of whistler waves in magnetized plasma and to determine whether the harmonics arise from nonlinear wave-plasma interactions and how they propagate and disperse.
AI.method: A loop antenna energized by a pulse-forming network was used in LVPD argon plasma with electron density about 1–2×10^17 m^-3, electron temperature about 2–5 eV, and a uniform axial magnetic field of about 6.2 G. Magnetic fluctuations were measured with a three-axis B-dot probe; a Helmholtz coil was used to investigate dependence on the local magnetic-field configuration. Spectral analysis and bicoherence analysis assessed harmonic content and nonlinear coupling, while a linear array of five identical B-dot probes and spatial cross-correlation determined phase velocity, parallel wave number, propagation angle, and dispersion.
AI.result: Distinct spectral peaks appeared at 300 kHz, 450 kHz, and 600 kHz in addition to the fundamental frequency. In plasma, the excited wave had a significant δB_y component along with δB_x, indicating polarization. Bicoherence provided evidence of nonlinear coupling among frequency components. Cross-correlation showed strong structural coherence during propagation, enabling experimental determination of phase velocity and parallel wave number for the higher harmonics. Propagation was oblique at approximately 48° to the background magnetic field, and the measured dispersion agreed with the cold-plasma oblique whistler dispersion relation within experimental uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence for higher-harmonic whistler-wave generation through nonlinear wave-plasma interactions in LVPD magnetized plasma and show that the generated harmonics propagate obliquely and follow cold-plasma oblique whistler dispersion within experimental uncertainty.

title: Parametrised-Quadratic Interface Reconstruction and Geometric Velocity Extension in the Volume-of-Fluid Framework
summary:
A conservative Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) framework using local parametric-curve interface reconstruction (PI-VOF) is developed for geometric interface propagation on fixed Cartesian grids. While VOF methods achieve conservative and second-order accurate interface advection under prescribed velocity fields, normal-velocity-driven interface propagation requires the interfacial velocity to be extended to neighbouring staggered-grid locations.
  Existing studies on interface evolution employ auxiliary distance functions, kernel smoothers, or high-resolution VOF in multiple grids to compute propagation velocities and address first-order-accuracy limitations. In contrast, PI-VOF directly employs higher-order parametric interface geometry for local normal-velocity extension, aiming to achieve second-order accurate interface evolution on fixed Cartesian grids. The resulting velocity field is employed in conservative geometric advection using a directionally split Eulerian-implicit and Lagrangian-explicit (EI-LE) scheme, while the reconstructed interface provides the geometric information required for curvature evaluation and the ghost-fluid finite-difference discretisation of sharp interfacial Dirichlet conditions. Static reconstruction and reversible-vortex advection tests demonstrate higher-order interface geometry and approximately second-order transport convergence, with mass conservation to the chosen tolerance on refined grids. Prescribed normal-velocity and curvature-dependent propagation tests establish near second-order convergence. Coupled Stefan benchmarks involving capillarity and attachment kinetics demonstrate approximately second-order thermal convergence and decreasing interface errors under mesh refinement. The results establish a geometric formulation connecting conservative VOF transport, local normal-velocity extension, and sharp Stefan conditions for evolving interfaces.

AI.tldr: A conservative PI-VOF framework reconstructs interfaces with local parametric curves, extends normal velocities geometrically to staggered-grid locations, and advects interfaces with a directionally split EI-LE scheme, yielding near second-order interface evolution, mass conservation to tolerance, and sharp Stefan interfacial conditions on fixed Cartesian grids.
AI.motivation: Existing interface-propagation approaches rely on auxiliary distance functions, kernel smoothers, or high-resolution VOF on multiple grids and are limited to first-order accuracy. The work aims to use higher-order local parametric interface geometry to achieve second-order accurate interface evolution on fixed Cartesian grids.
AI.method: PI-VOF employs local parametric-curve interface reconstruction and directly uses the reconstructed higher-order geometry for local normal-velocity extension to neighbouring staggered-grid locations. The extended velocity field is used in conservative geometric advection with a directionally split Eulerian-implicit and Lagrangian-explicit (EI-LE) scheme; the reconstructed interface supplies geometry for curvature evaluation and ghost-fluid finite-difference discretisation of sharp interfacial Dirichlet conditions.
AI.result: Static reconstruction and reversible-vortex advection tests show higher-order interface geometry, approximately second-order transport convergence, and mass conservation to the chosen tolerance on refined grids. Prescribed normal-velocity and curvature-dependent propagation tests establish near second-order convergence. Coupled Stefan benchmarks with capillarity and attachment kinetics show approximately second-order thermal convergence and decreasing interface errors under mesh refinement.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a geometric formulation linking conservative VOF transport, local normal-velocity extension, and sharp Stefan conditions for evolving interfaces.

title: Wake-Powered Spreading of Encapsulated Drops Impacting Under Liquid
summary: A drop impacting a wall in air spreads by converting its own kinetic energy into surface energy. We show that this picture fails when the wall is submerged in liquid. Millimetric perfluoropolyether drops, bare or encapsulated in an ultrathin silicone-oil shell, impacting a glass wall in water are flattened by the squeeze flow in the draining gap and shed most of their kinetic energy before impact. Nevertheless, they spread to more than twice their diameter on a water lubrication film that never ruptures, creating more surface energy than their entire kinetic and gravitational energy could supply. A two-stage energy scaling resolves this deficit. The liquid set in motion in the drop's wake supplies more than 90\% of the energy for spreading, so that the maximum spreading is governed by the Weber number of the ambient liquid rather than that of the drop. The shell acts mainly through its interfacial tension, while its biaxial-extension dissipation, negligible before impact, becomes appreciable during spreading.

AI.tldr: Millimetric perfluoropolyether drops, bare or encapsulated in an ultrathin silicone-oil shell, impact a glass wall under water. Although squeeze flow in the draining gap removes most of their kinetic energy before impact, the drops spread to more than twice their diameter on a persistent water lubrication film. A two-stage energy scaling shows that liquid set in motion in the drop wake supplies over 90% of the spreading energy, so maximum spreading depends on the ambient liquid Weber number rather than the drop Weber number.
AI.motivation: The conventional picture that an impacting drop spreads by converting its own kinetic energy into surface energy fails for a wall submerged in liquid. The study aims to explain the observed spreading and energy deficit, and to determine how an ultrathin encapsulating shell affects the process.
AI.method: The authors perform impact experiments with millimetric perfluoropolyether drops, either bare or encapsulated in an ultrathin silicone-oil shell, impacting a glass wall in water. They analyze the squeeze flow in the draining gap and develop a two-stage energy scaling to account for spreading and the role of the shell.
AI.result: The drops are flattened by squeeze flow in the draining gap and shed most of their kinetic energy before impact, yet they spread to more than twice their diameter on a water lubrication film that never ruptures, creating more surface energy than their entire kinetic and gravitational energy could supply. The liquid set in motion in the drop wake supplies more than 90% of the spreading energy, making the maximum spreading governed by the Weber number of the ambient liquid rather than that of the drop.
