The shell acts mainly through its interfacial tension; its biaxial-extension dissipation is negligible before impact but becomes appreciable during spreading.
AI.conclusion: Spreading of drops impacting a submerged wall is wake-powered and cannot be explained by the drop’s own kinetic and gravitational energy alone. The ambient liquid Weber number, rather than the drop Weber number, controls maximum spreading, and the encapsulating shell contributes through interfacial tension and non-negligible biaxial-extension dissipation during spreading.

title: Bandwidth-tunable thermal emitter via dynamic resonator coupling and loss
summary: We demonstrate a dynamically tunable omnidirectional thermal emitter that can be switched from a narrowband emission state to a broadband state. The structure is a metal-backed multilayer with subwavelength thickness across the mid-infrared, which forms an angle-insensitive (up to 60°) optical cavity with one input port. We used an ultrathin VO2 layer to dynamically switch the coupling and loss coefficients of this optical cavity, resulting in narrowband emission from the vibrational mode of a polar dielectric layer that is part of the multilayer stack when the VO2 is in its insulating phase, and broadband emission from a nearly impedance-matched cavity when the VO2 is switched to its lossy metallic phase. We fabricated the structure around a free-standing silicon membrane and integrated it onto a printed circuit board (PCB), which enabled electrical switching of the emitter at the ten-to-hundred millisecond scale, and can be used for free-space identification, tagging, or communication.

AI.tldr: A metal-backed subwavelength mid-infrared multilayer forms an angle-insensitive optical cavity whose coupling and loss are switched by an ultrathin VO2 layer, enabling electrical switching between narrowband and broadband thermal emission on ten-to-hundred millisecond timescales.
AI.motivation: The work aims to realize a dynamically tunable omnidirectional thermal emitter that can be switched between narrowband and broadband emission states, with potential use in free-space identification, tagging, or communication.
AI.method: The emitter uses a metal-backed multilayer with subwavelength thickness across the mid-infrared, forming a one-input-port optical cavity that remains angle-insensitive up to 60°. An ultrathin VO2 layer dynamically changes the cavity coupling and loss coefficients: in the insulating phase, narrowband emission arises from a vibrational mode of a polar dielectric layer in the stack; in the lossy metallic phase, broadband emission arises from a nearly impedance-matched cavity. The structure was fabricated around a free-standing silicon membrane and integrated onto a printed circuit board for electrical switching.
AI.result: The emitter switches from narrowband to broadband emission through the VO2 phase transition. It is angle-insensitive up to 60° and electrically switchable at the ten-to-hundred millisecond scale. Other performance metrics, such as emission efficiency and spectral bandwidth values, are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The demonstrated dynamically tunable omnidirectional thermal emitter can be electrically switched between narrowband and broadband states and is suitable for free-space identification, tagging, or communication applications.

title: Embedded Trigger Control System for Wave--Plasma Interaction Experiments in Large Volume Plasma Device
summary: {Magnetic-field control and synchronization are essential requirements in laboratory plasma experiments investigating wave propagation and plasma instabilities. In this work, an Embedded Trigger Control System (ETCS) has been designed and implemented for synchronized operation of a pulsed Helmholtz coil system and a broadband whistler-wave exciter in the Large Volume Plasma Device--Upgrade (LVPD-U). The experimental configuration employs an electrostatically shielded loop antenna driven by a thyratron-switched pulse-forming network to launch broadband whistler waves in the frequency range of approximately 150~kHz to 5~MHz. Simultaneously, a pulsed Helmholtz coil capable of generating magnetic fields up to $\pm150$~G is used to modify the local magnetic topology and create transient magnetic-null configurations. The developed ETCS utilizes the controlled evolution of the Helmholtz circuit $L/R$ time constant through the introduction of a lumped series inductor, enabling precise magnetic-field ramping and dynamic timing control. A microcontroller-based trigger architecture determines the desired firing instant from the calibrated current evolution of the Helmholtz circuit and synchronizes wave excitation with a prescribed magnetic-field amplitude. The system extends the effective circuit time constant by more than an order of magnitude, allowing accurate and repeatable wave launching during controlled magnetic-field evolution. The implemented approach provides a simple, reliable, and versatile synchronization platform for wave--plasma interaction studies requiring precise temporal coordination between pulsed magnetic-field generation and wave excitation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and implements an Embedded Trigger Control System (ETCS) to synchronize a pulsed Helmholtz coil with a broadband whistler-wave exciter in the Large Volume Plasma Device--Upgrade. The ETCS uses a lumped series inductor and microcontroller-based triggering to extend the coil circuit time constant and coordinate wave launching with a prescribed magnetic-field amplitude.
AI.motivation: Wave--plasma interaction experiments require precise synchronization between pulsed magnetic-field generation and wave excitation. The work aims to provide repeatable timing control for synchronized operation of a pulsed Helmholtz coil and a broadband whistler-wave source in LVPD-U.
AI.method: An ETCS was designed and implemented with a microcontroller-based trigger architecture. It determines the firing instant from the calibrated current evolution of the Helmholtz circuit and synchronizes excitation of an electrostatically shielded loop antenna, driven by a thyratron-switched pulse-forming network, with the magnetic field produced by a pulsed Helmholtz coil. A lumped series inductor is introduced to control the Helmholtz circuit L/R time constant and enable magnetic-field ramping and dynamic timing control.
AI.result: The system synchronizes broadband whistler-wave excitation over approximately 150 kHz to 5 MHz with pulsed magnetic fields up to ±150 G, including transient magnetic-null configurations. It extends the effective circuit time constant by more than an order of magnitude and supports accurate, repeatable wave launching during controlled magnetic-field evolution.
AI.conclusion: The ETCS provides a simple, reliable, and versatile synchronization platform for wave--plasma interaction studies requiring precise temporal coordination between pulsed magnetic-field generation and wave excitation. The abstract reports no substantive connection to intense lasers or laser--plasma interactions.

title: GranularGPT: Natural-Language-Driven End-to-End Discrete Element Method Simulations
summary: Discrete element method (DEM) simulations are widely used to investigate granular and particulate systems, but their application often requires specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and simulation post-processing. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to simplify these workflows by enabling users to interact with simulation tools through natural language. This study offers GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, from natural-language problem descriptions to simulation execution and automated post-processing. The framework enables users to generate DEM simulation cases, execute and monitor simulations, and automatically extract and report physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation across 60 normal-condition cases covering 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations achieve a simulation success rate of 91.7%. In the error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors are detected and 9 are successfully resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases are correctly identified and reported. The framework automatically extracts a range of DEM-relevant metrics, including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities. GranularGPT provides a foundation for improving the accessibility and efficiency of DEM simulation workflows while reducing the specialized expertise required for their operation.

AI.tldr: GranularGPT is an LLM-assisted agentic framework that converts natural-language problem descriptions into end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, including case generation, execution, monitoring, and automated extraction of granular and process metrics. It achieved a 91.7% simulation success rate across 60 normal-condition cases and resolved 9 of 10 repairable errors.
AI.motivation: DEM simulations are powerful for granular and particulate systems but require specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and post-processing. The authors aim to lower this barrier by letting users interact with DEM tools through natural language.
AI.method: The paper proposes GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM workflows. It generates simulation cases from natural-language descriptions, executes and monitors simulations, and automatically extracts and reports physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation covered 60 normal-condition cases across 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations, plus error-handling tests.
AI.result: GranularGPT achieved a 91.7% simulation success rate on 60 normal-condition cases. In error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors were detected and 9 were resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases were correctly identified and reported. It automatically extracted metrics including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities.
AI.conclusion: GranularGPT provides a foundation for making DEM simulation workflows more accessible and efficient while reducing the specialized expertise required to operate them.

title: Resolvent-based modeling of turbulent flow over multilayer compliant surfaces
summary: Compliant coatings offer a passive approach to modifying near-wall turbulence and potentially reducing skin-friction drag, but high-fidelity exploration of the coupled parameter space is costly. We develop a two-way coupled resolvent-Galerkin framework for turbulent channel flow over finite-thickness, layered viscoelastic coatings. The fluid is modeled using the Navier-Stokes equations linearized about a turbulent mean state, while the solid is represented by a through-thickness Galerkin discretization of the elastodynamic equations. The solid response is condensed into a spectral surface-impedance operator at the fluid-solid interface. At $Re_τ= 180$, stiff panels approach the rigid-wall response, whereas more compliant panels modify the low-rank response associated with the near-wall cycle. A Reynolds-number study shows that panels with fixed nondimensional material stiffness can produce different responses depending on whether their thickness scales with inner or outer flow length scales. The influence of viscoelastic damping is examined across low- and high-frequency regimes, where stiffness-proportional damping alters the high-frequency fractional-energy distribution, while the low-frequency distribution remains relatively insensitive to damping. For multilayer panels, the fluid-facing material determines the interfacial wave speed, while the subsurface stiffness distribution modifies the panel's effective thickness. Temporal stability analysis identifies regions of parameter space where a steady harmonic response is relevant and regions where instabilities grow. Finally, a leading-order, covariance-based drag-estimation framework relates the coupled response to changes in the mean flow and to the estimated skin-friction drag. Together, these tools provide a basis for screening coating designs and selecting candidates for high-fidelity simulations and experiments.

AI.tldr: A two-way coupled resolvent–Galerkin framework models turbulent channel flow over finite-thickness layered viscoelastic coatings, showing how compliance, Reynolds-number scaling, viscoelastic damping, multilayer stiffness, and stability affect near-wall flow response and estimated skin-friction drag.
AI.motivation: Compliant coatings are a passive route to modifying near-wall turbulence and potentially reducing skin-friction drag, but high-fidelity exploration of the coupled coating parameter space is costly; a lower-cost predictive modeling framework is needed for screening designs.
AI.method: The fluid is modeled with Navier–Stokes equations linearized about a turbulent mean state and coupled to a through-thickness Galerkin discretization of the elastodynamic equations for finite-thickness layered viscoelastic coatings. The solid response is condensed into a spectral surface-impedance operator at the fluid–solid interface. The study examines Re_tau=180, Reynolds-number scaling, viscoelastic damping, multilayer panels, temporal stability, and a leading-order covariance-based drag-estimation framework.
AI.result: Stiff panels approach the rigid-wall response, while more compliant panels modify the low-rank response associated with the near-wall cycle. For fixed nondimensional material stiffness, panel response depends on whether thickness scales with inner or outer flow length scales. Stiffness-proportional damping alters the high-frequency fractional-energy distribution, whereas the low-frequency distribution is relatively insensitive. In multilayer panels, the fluid-facing material determines interfacial wave speed and subsurface stiffness modifies effective thickness. Temporal stability analysis identifies steady harmonic-response and growing-instability regions. The drag-estimation framework relates the coupled response to mean-flow changes and estimated skin-friction drag; quantitative drag-reduction values are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The coupled resolvent–Galerkin tools provide a basis for screening compliant-coating designs and selecting candidates for high-fidelity simulations and experiments.

title: A microscopic revision of the rate equations of a heavily erbium-doped fiber laser
summary: Heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers can exhibit self-pulsing induced by interacting ion pairs, which was found in numerous experiments and supported by modeling. However, conventional rate-equation models rely on phenomenological parameters with an unclear microscopic origin. We derive a rate-equation model using a Lindblad master equation describing isolated erbium ions and interacting ion pairs coupled to a single cavity mode, with cooperative upconversion represented by an effective dissipative process. In the strong-dephasing limit, adiabatic elimination of coherences and ensemble averaging yield a closed system of equations for the cavity photon number, isolated-ion inversion, and pair populations. We show that in the same limit the pair-cavity coupling constant reduces to that of two independent ions, without superradiant or subradiant contributions. The resulting equations retain spontaneous emission, which provides a photon-number floor between pulses and substantially affects the laser pulsing dynamics. Numerical analysis reveals self-pulsing within finite pump-rate intervals and identifies the region of self-pulsing as a function of the upconversion rate and pair fraction. The model thus establishes a microscopic basis for analyzing self-pulsing in heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers.

AI.tldr: A microscopic rate-equation model for a heavily erbium-doped fiber laser is derived from a Lindblad master equation including isolated erbium ions, interacting ion pairs, a single cavity mode, and cooperative upconversion as an effective dissipative process. In the strong-dephasing limit, the model yields closed equations for cavity photon number, isolated-ion inversion, and pair populations, and predicts self-pulsing over finite pump-rate intervals depending on upconversion rate and pair fraction.
AI.motivation: Conventional rate-equation models of self-pulsing in heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers rely on phenomenological parameters whose microscopic origin is unclear. The paper aims to establish a microscopic basis for such modeling.
AI.method: The authors use a Lindblad master equation describing isolated erbium ions and interacting ion pairs coupled to a single cavity mode, with cooperative upconversion represented by an effective dissipative process. In the strong-dephasing limit, adiabatic elimination of coherences and ensemble averaging produce a closed system of equations for cavity photon number, isolated-ion inversion, and pair populations. The pair-cavity coupling constant is shown to reduce to that of two independent ions, without superradiant or subradiant contributions.
AI.result: The resulting equations retain spontaneous emission, which provides a photon-number floor between pulses and substantially affects the laser pulsing dynamics. Numerical analysis reveals self-pulsing within finite pump-rate intervals and identifies the self-pulsing region as a function of the upconversion rate and pair fraction.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a microscopic foundation for analyzing self-pulsing in heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers.

title: Cold stellarator coils that outlast power plant lifetime
summary: We show that a two order-of-magnitude reduction in stellarator coil peak neutron flux and heating can be achieved by moving coils much farther from the plasma if the plasma shape may change slightly and the vessel shielding is increased. Alternating coil and plasma optimizations move the closest coils of our main design over 25 cm out, without substantial degradation in key engineering and physics requirements. The field error decreases and the plasma boundary moves about 1 cm on average. Such coils would be at 4.2 K, use only one third to half the superconducting tape of the original, and require no replacement during the plant's lifetime. This reduced coil flux and heating could significantly enhance the viability of stellarator power plants.

AI.tldr: Moving stellarator coils farther from the plasma and increasing vessel shielding can reduce peak coil neutron flux and heating by two orders of magnitude, allowing cold superconducting coils to last the power plant lifetime with less tape and minimal physics degradation.
AI.motivation: Stellarator power plants require coils that can survive their lifetime, but close coils experience high neutron flux and heating. The paper aims to reduce this burden while preserving key engineering and physics requirements and improving plant viability.
AI.method: The authors use alternating coil and plasma optimizations to move the closest coils of the main design more than 25 cm farther from the plasma, permit slight plasma shape changes, and increase vessel shielding.
AI.result: The design achieves a two-order-of-magnitude reduction in stellarator coil peak neutron flux and heating. Field error decreases, the plasma boundary moves about 1 cm on average, coils operate at 4.2 K, use one third to half the superconducting tape of the original, and require no replacement during the plant lifetime.
AI.conclusion: Reduced coil neutron flux and heating could significantly enhance the viability of stellarator power plants by enabling lifetime cold superconducting coils with lower tape usage and acceptable physics performance.

title: FiuMD: Heterogeneous Batching for Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics with Neural Network Potentials
summary: FiuMD is a GPU molecular dynamics engine that advances many independent biomolecular simulations as a single batch, even when the systems differ in size, topology, force-field parameters, periodic box, timestep, or thermostat parameters. All systems are concatenated into global tensors, so the classical interaction terms and a shared TorchMD-Net neural network potential are evaluated for the whole batch at once, while each system keeps its own integration and thermostat. FiuMD started as a fork of TorchMD and reworks its system representation, force evaluation, and integration to handle such heterogeneous batches. We test it with coarse-grained C$α$ models of chignolin, Trp-cage, BBL, and $λ$-repressor. In double precision, forces within a heterogeneous batch agree with isolated FiuMD and TorchMD evaluations to within the precision of repeated evaluations, with a maximum relative difference of $7\times10^{-16}$ across 60 systems. Over 1000 steps without a thermostat, batched trajectories deviate by at most $2.5\times10^{-11}$ Angstrom from isolated ones, even when periodic images lie within the neural network cutoff. With a different target temperature for each system of the ensemble, the mean and width of each system's kinetic temperature match the values expected from its own thermostat. We show that when individual simulations are too small to fill the GPU, batching can improve throughput several-fold over TorchMD. On a single GPU, batching four different protein systems achieves a 4.6-7.8-fold speedup per step compared with sequential TorchMD simulations. Compared with sequential homogeneous FiuMD batches, heterogeneous batching provides up to a 4-fold speedup for smaller batches while maintaining comparable performance for larger ones.

AI.tldr: FiuMD is a GPU molecular dynamics engine that batches heterogeneous biomolecular simulations into global tensors so classical interactions and a shared TorchMD-Net neural network potential are evaluated once for the whole batch, while each system retains its own integration and thermostat. Tests on coarse-grained Cα models show numerical agreement with isolated simulations and several-fold throughput gains over TorchMD and homogeneous FiuMD batching.
AI.motivation: Individual biomolecular simulations can be too small to fill a GPU efficiently. FiuMD aims to improve throughput by advancing many independent simulations as one batch even when they differ in size, topology, force-field parameters, periodic box, timestep, or thermostat parameters.
AI.method: FiuMD, developed as a fork of TorchMD, reworks system representation, force evaluation, and integration for heterogeneous batches. It concatenates all systems into global tensors, evaluates classical interaction terms and a shared TorchMD-Net neural network potential for the whole batch at once, and preserves each system’s own integration and thermostat. It is tested with coarse-grained Cα models of chignolin, Trp-cage, BBL, and λ-repressor.
AI.result: In double precision, forces within a heterogeneous batch agree with isolated FiuMD and TorchMD evaluations to within repeated-evaluation precision, with a maximum relative difference of 7×10−16 across 60 systems. Over 1000 steps without a thermostat, batched trajectories deviate by at most 2.5×10−11 Å from isolated ones, including when periodic images lie within the neural network cutoff. With different target temperatures per system, each system’s kinetic-temperature mean and width match its own thermostat. On one GPU, batching four different protein systems gives a 4.6–7.8-fold speedup per step versus sequential TorchMD, and heterogeneous batching gives up to a 4-fold speedup over sequential homogeneous FiuMD batches for smaller batches while maintaining comparable performance for larger ones.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous batching in FiuMD enables numerically consistent and substantially faster GPU molecular dynamics for multiple independent biomolecular systems with differing properties, particularly when individual simulations underutilize the GPU.

title: On the relation of secondary motions to large- and very-large-scale motions
summary: The coexistence of secondary motions with large-scale and very-large-scale motions (LSMs/VLSMs) is investigated by direct numerical simulations of turbulent open-channel flow over streamwise-aligned Gaussian ridges, varying the ridge spacing $S$ and height $h$. First, the ridge height controls the secondary-motion strength and thereby the coexistence with VLSMs. VLSMs are suppressed for $h \geqslant 0.05δ$, with $δ$ the open-channel height, and re-emerge at $h = 0.025δ$, where the mean secondary motions are comparable in strength to those over strip-type surfaces. Previously reported differences between strip- and ridge-type surfaces thus reflect secondary-motion strength rather than surface type. Second, proper orthogonal decomposition and conditional averaging reveal instantaneous secondary motions that span approximately $2δ$, fill the channel height irrespective of $S$ and $h$, and are stronger than their mean. These are identified as LSMs spatially locked and amplified by the ridges. Over dense ridges, their alternation between neighbouring ridges yields weak, near-wall confined mean secondary motions, although VLSMs are suppressed over the full channel height. The ridge height thus sets the strength of the locked LSMs, whereas the ridge spacing sets where and for how long they persist. For weak locked LSMs, ridges spaced at their natural spanwise extent increase the VLSM energy, indicating that persistent locked LSMs concatenate into VLSMs. Third, large-scale instantaneous secondary motions persist over dense ridges in the absence of long streaks. This suggests that secondary motions are driven by intermittent cross-sectional motions rather than by long streaks, similar to the streak-less bursts in near-wall turbulence.

AI.tldr: Direct numerical simulations of turbulent open-channel flow over streamwise-aligned Gaussian ridges show that ridge height controls secondary-motion strength and thereby the suppression or emergence of very-large-scale motions, while ridge spacing controls the persistence of ridge-locked large-scale motions that can concatenate into very-large-scale motions.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates how secondary motions coexist with large-scale and very-large-scale motions (LSMs/VLSMs), and whether previously reported differences between strip-type and ridge-type surfaces arise from secondary-motion strength rather than surface type.
AI.method: The study uses direct numerical simulations of turbulent open-channel flow over streamwise-aligned Gaussian ridges, varying ridge spacing S and ridge height h. Proper orthogonal decomposition and conditional averaging are used to identify instantaneous secondary motions and their relation to LSMs/VLSMs.
AI.result: Ridge height controls secondary-motion strength and VLSM coexistence: VLSMs are suppressed for h ≥ 0.05δ and re-emerge at h = 0.025δ, where mean secondary motions are comparable to those over strip-type surfaces. Instantaneous secondary motions span about 2δ, fill the channel height irrespective of S and h, and are stronger than their mean; they are identified as LSMs spatially locked and amplified by ridges. Over dense ridges, their alternation between neighbouring ridges produces weak, near-wall confined mean secondary motions even though VLSMs are suppressed over the full channel height. Ridge height sets locked-LSM strength, whereas ridge spacing sets where and for how long they persist. For weak locked LSMs, ridges spaced at their natural spanwise extent increase VLSM energy, indicating that persistent locked LSMs concatenate into VLSMs. Large-scale instantaneous secondary motions persist over dense ridges without long streaks, suggesting that secondary motions are driven by intermittent cross-sectional motions rather than by long streaks.
AI.conclusion: The relation between secondary motions and LSMs/VLSMs is governed primarily by ridge height and spacing, with surface type differences reflecting secondary-motion strength. Persistent ridge-locked LSMs can concatenate into VLSMs, and secondary motions appear to be driven by intermittent cross-sectional motions rather than long streaks.

title: Inverse Design for Nonplanar Conformal Layers
summary: Conformal layering, where a deposited layer follows the nonplanar topography beneath it, arises from both deliberate passivation overlays and imperfect planarization between depositions. However, inverse design methods typically model planar, vertically extruded layers, resulting in geometric discrepancies between the modeled and fabricated structure. To address these discrepancies, we present differentiable mapping functions that incorporate both uniform conformal overlays and partially conformal interlayer dips into a standard inverse design paradigm, requiring no additional design parameters over planar structures. Using these mappings, we design (1) mode-selective GaAs grating reflectors with uniform conformal SiN passivation for high-aspect-ratio VCSELs, reaching differential modal reflectivities of 33.1% (single-etch) and 63.4% (dual-etch), and (2) a dual-layer silicon grating coupler whose upper layer dips up to 40 nm into the lower layer, reaching -0.75 dB coupling efficiency. Modeling conformal layering during optimization, rather than treating it as post-hoc fabrication error, permits direct exploitation of the conformal layering, yielding inherently fabricable and performant designs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces differentiable mapping functions that model nonplanar conformal layers within inverse design, enabling mode-selective GaAs grating reflectors with conformal SiN passivation and a dual-layer silicon grating coupler with interlayer dips, improving modeled-to-fabricated consistency and device performance.
AI.motivation: Standard inverse design assumes planar, vertically extruded layers, which creates geometric discrepancies when fabricated layers conform to nonplanar topography, whether from deliberate passivation overlays or imperfect planarization. The authors aim to include conformal layering during optimization rather than treating it as post-hoc fabrication error.
AI.method: The authors present differentiable mapping functions that incorporate uniform conformal overlays and partially conformal interlayer dips into a standard inverse design paradigm without adding design parameters relative to planar structures. They apply these mappings to design mode-selective GaAs grating reflectors with uniform conformal SiN passivation for high-aspect-ratio VCSELs and a dual-layer silicon grating coupler with partial conformality.
AI.result: The designed GaAs grating reflectors achieve differential modal reflectivities of 33.1% for the single-etch case and 63.4% for the dual-etch case. The dual-layer silicon grating coupler, whose upper layer dips up to 40 nm into the lower layer, reaches -0.75 dB coupling efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Modeling conformal layering during optimization, instead of treating it as a post-hoc fabrication error, allows direct exploitation of conformal topography and yields inherently fabricable, performant designs.

title: Analytic Model for Transient Plateau Filling in Vibrational Distributions of Periodically Driven Plasmas
summary: In periodically driven molecular plasmas, the vibrational distribution function is governed by the competition between vibration--vibration (V-V) up-pumping along the anharmonic ladder and vibration--translation (V-T) relaxation, producing the Treanor--Gordiets distribution. When vibrational energy accumulates across cycles faster than V-V exchange can populate the upper levels, the Gordiets plateau remains transiently depleted. Existing algebraic models assume a quasi-steady plateau, whereas exact transient solutions of the nonlinear V-V diffusion equation require the elapsed time since excitation and the source strength, which are unavailable in multidimensional simulations that track only local macroscopic variables. Here, elapsed time is replaced by a local vibrational energy timescale formed from the vibrational energy per molecule and its period-averaged rate of change. This reduces the diffusion equation in level space to an ordinary differential equation solved in closed form without linearization, yielding a level-dependent correction to the steady plateau governed by a single dimensionless group: the number of V-V collisions per energy timescale weighted by the plateau amplitude at the Treanor minimum. The distribution front advances as the square root of this group, and the steady distribution is recovered as the group grows large. Compared with state-to-state master-equation calculations for N$_2$ under nanosecond pulse trains spanning 300-1500 K, 0.041-1 atm, and 1-100 kHz (1440 sampled states), the model reduces the 90th-percentile error in level populations from 1.88 decades for the steady model and 1.32 decades for an adapted self-similar solution to 0.53 decades, at essentially the evaluation cost of the steady model.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a closed-form analytic model for transient filling of the vibrational-distribution plateau in periodically driven molecular plasmas. It replaces unavailable elapsed time with a local vibrational-energy timescale and achieves substantially lower population errors than steady or adapted self-similar models at nearly steady-model cost.
AI.motivation: Existing algebraic models assume a quasi-steady Gordiets plateau, but exact transient solutions of the nonlinear vibration-vibration diffusion equation require elapsed time since excitation and source strength, which are unavailable in multidimensional simulations tracking only local macroscopic variables.
AI.method: The elapsed time is replaced by a local vibrational energy timescale constructed from vibrational energy per molecule and its period-averaged rate of change. This reduces the level-space diffusion equation to an ordinary differential equation solved in closed form without linearization, giving a level-dependent correction to the steady plateau controlled by one dimensionless group: the number of vibration-vibration collisions per energy timescale weighted by the plateau amplitude at the Treanor minimum.
AI.result: The distribution front advances as the square root of the dimensionless group, and the steady distribution is recovered when the group is large. Against state-to-state master-equation calculations for N2 under nanosecond pulse trains over 300-1500 K, 0.041-1 atm, and 1-100 kHz (1440 sampled states), the model reduces the 90th-percentile error in level populations from 1.88 decades for the steady model and 1.32 decades for an adapted self-similar solution to 0.53 decades, at essentially the steady model's evaluation cost.
AI.conclusion: A closed-form, level-dependent transient correction captures plateau depletion and significantly improves vibrational-population predictions while remaining computationally comparable to the steady model. The abstract does not explicitly establish a connection to intense lasers or laser-plasma interactions.

title: Efficient scheduling of particle annihilation for long-time Wigner simulations
summary: Particle annihilation (PA) plays an indispensable role in alleviating the numerical sign problem in long-time simulations with the Wigner branching random walk (WBRW) method. However, the effect of PA frequency on long-time accuracy remains poorly understood, leaving its choice largely empirical. To provide systematic guidance for PA scheduling, we establish an overall error estimate for PA through a uniform mesh, separating WBRW variance, resampling variance and squared bias. The analysis shows that, beyond merely controlling particle growth, PA replaces the exponential-in-time variance bound with a linear-in-time bound, thereby alleviating the numerical sign problem. It also reveals bias-variance trade-off induced by PA frequency: frequent PA limits variance but can increase accumulated bias. More importantly, building on the newfound error structure, we propose a variance-constrained cost optimization strategy for adaptive PA scheduling across several PA methods. An intrinsic-time reparameterization provides a common clock for variance control, PA scheduling, and branching dynamics under time-dependent potentials. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical variance behavior and bias-variance trade-off, and results of our schedule populate the low-cost regime of the empirical Pareto frontier objecting to balance accuracy and efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how particle annihilation (PA) frequency affects long-time accuracy in Wigner branching random walk simulations, derives an error decomposition, and proposes adaptive PA scheduling to balance variance, bias, and cost.
AI.motivation: Particle annihilation is essential for mitigating the numerical sign problem in long-time Wigner branching random walk simulations, but the effect of PA frequency on long-time accuracy is poorly understood and its choice is largely empirical. The authors aim to provide systematic guidance for PA scheduling.
AI.method: The authors establish an overall error estimate for PA using a uniform mesh, separating WBRW variance, resampling variance, and squared bias. They analyze the bias-variance trade-off induced by PA frequency and propose a variance-constrained cost optimization strategy for adaptive PA scheduling across several PA methods, using intrinsic-time reparameterization as a common clock for variance control, PA scheduling, and branching dynamics under time-dependent potentials.
AI.result: The analysis shows that PA not only controls particle growth but also replaces an exponential-in-time variance bound with a linear-in-time bound, alleviating the numerical sign problem. It reveals that frequent PA limits variance but can increase accumulated bias. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical variance behavior and bias-variance trade-off, and the proposed schedule populates the low-cost regime of the empirical Pareto frontier balancing accuracy and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: PA scheduling can be guided systematically through error decomposition and variance-constrained cost optimization, enabling adaptive PA schedules that balance accuracy and efficiency in long-time Wigner simulations.

title: Solver-consistent learned curvature for algebraic volume-of-fluid simulations of rising bubbles: symmetry-preserving networks, closed-loop data aggregation and a posteriori benchmarks
summary: Curvature reconstructed from compressed volume fractions exhibits a persistent force-weighted bias in the tested algebraic volume-of-fluid formulation. In OpenFOAM interFoam, face curvature is underestimated by 11-22% for radii of 2.5-40 cells, explaining the 14-17% static Laplace-pressure deficit. This bias is consistent with approximately 2% rise-velocity underprediction in the first Hysing benchmark. We estimate curvature from 5 x 5 volume-fraction stencils using a two-hidden-layer perceptron with exact phase-exchange antisymmetry and invariance under all eight square-grid symmetries. Training uses solver-generated profiles of periodic translating bubbles, droplets, and flat films with exact analytical curvature labels. Iterative data aggregation incorporates model-solver feedback and resolves deployment instabilities found in 15 of 76 periodic cases with the initial model. Band-weighted face interpolation supplies the same capillary force to momentum prediction and pressure correction. Independent tests show static pressure-jump errors of 2-6% and reductions in time-averaged maximum capillary numbers by factors of 2.8-16. Across three grids, time-integrated rise-velocity errors decrease from 2.06-2.76% to 0.65-1.04% in the first Hysing benchmark and from 5.64-8.72% to 4.72-7.61% in the second. Tuned curvature smoothing gives smaller static pressure-jump errors, but its first-benchmark accuracy deteriorates with refinement and second-benchmark gains remain marginal. A separate interface-gated dissipative momentum closure achieves a held-out coefficient of determination of 0.47 on Favre-filtered targets but changes rise velocity by less than 0.03% of its peak. Capillary-force discretisation is therefore the more influential correction target for the tested laminar bubbles.

AI.tldr: A symmetry-preserving neural network learns solver-consistent curvature from volume-fraction stencils and, when coupled through band-weighted face interpolation, reduces capillary-force errors and rise-velocity errors in algebraic volume-of-fluid simulations of rising bubbles.
AI.motivation: The tested algebraic volume-of-fluid formulation shows a persistent force-weighted curvature bias: face curvature is underestimated by 11-22% for radii of 2.5-40 cells, explaining a 14-17% static Laplace-pressure deficit and consistent with about 2% rise-velocity underprediction in the first Hysing benchmark.
AI.method: Curvature is estimated from 5 x 5 volume-fraction stencils using a two-hidden-layer perceptron with exact phase-exchange antisymmetry and invariance under all eight square-grid symmetries. Training uses solver-generated profiles of periodic translating bubbles, droplets, and flat films with exact analytical curvature labels, plus iterative data aggregation incorporating model-solver feedback. Band-weighted face interpolation supplies the same capillary force to momentum prediction and pressure correction; the approach is evaluated with a posteriori benchmarks, including the Hysing cases.
AI.result: Iterative data aggregation resolves deployment instabilities found in 15 of 76 periodic cases with the initial model. Independent tests show static pressure-jump errors of 2-6% and reductions in time-averaged maximum capillary numbers by factors of 2.8-16. Across three grids, time-integrated rise-velocity errors decrease from 2.06-2.76% to 0.65-1.04% in the first Hysing benchmark and from 5.64-8.72% to 4.72-7.61% in the second. Tuned curvature smoothing gives smaller static pressure-jump errors, but first-benchmark accuracy deteriorates with refinement and second-benchmark gains remain marginal. A separate interface-gated dissipative momentum closure achieves a held-out coefficient of determination of 0.47 on Favre-filtered targets but changes rise velocity by less than 0.03% of its peak.
AI.conclusion: Capillary-force discretisation is the more influential correction target for the tested laminar bubbles.

title: Frequency Multiplexing of Purcell-Enhanced Optically Coherent NV Centers
summary: Integrating optically coherent quantum emitters into nanophotonic structures is key to scalable quantum networks. Realizing them with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is hindered by the degradation of optical coherence accompanying nanofabrication. Here, we overcome this challenge by integrating multiple NV centers into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity while preserving near-lifetime-limited optical coherence. We observe linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz, enabling the frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode, while maintaining charge-state stability over several minutes under resonant excitation. Tuning the cavity into resonance with the NV zero-phonon line enhances the optical emission, consistent with Purcell enhancement predicted by finite-element simulations. Additionally, individual cavities can be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines on the same chip. These results combine bulk-like optical coherence with frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.

AI.tldr: The paper integrates multiple optically coherent nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity, achieving near-lifetime-limited linewidths, frequency multiplexing within a common cavity mode, and Purcell-enhanced emission for scalable quantum network nodes.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum networks require optically coherent quantum emitters integrated into nanophotonic structures, but NV centers in diamond have been hindered by optical-coherence degradation during nanofabrication.
AI.method: Multiple NV centers were integrated into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity. The work used resonant excitation, optical linewidth measurements, charge-state stability monitoring, tuning of the cavity to the NV zero-phonon line, finite-element simulations of Purcell enhancement, and independent tuning of individual cavities on the same chip.
AI.result: Linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz were observed, enabling frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode while maintaining charge-state stability over several minutes under resonant excitation. Cavity resonance with the NV zero-phonon line enhanced optical emission, consistent with simulated Purcell enhancement, and individual cavities could be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines on the same chip.
AI.conclusion: The results combine bulk-like optical coherence, frequency multiplexing, and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.

title: Gas expansion in global models of nanosecond pulsed discharges: a reduced gas-dynamic model coupled to plasma kinetics
comment: 54 pages, 14 figures, plus 7 pages of supplementary material
summary: Global (zero-dimensional) kinetic models of nanosecond pulsed discharges describe the expansion of the heated gas channel (kernel) with simplified gas-dynamic closures. We show that these closures can lead to errors of tens of percent in the calculated gas density, temperature and species densities, especially in the first microseconds after every pulse. Here, we propose a fast, reduced gas-dynamic model of Lagrangian shells, closed by an approximate cylindrical acoustic radiation condition, with no fitted physical coefficient. The reduced model reproduces the axis density obtained by verified one- dimensional compressible computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations within 2.4% for smooth deposition profiles and axis pressures up to six times ambient, typically a thousand times faster than CFD. We couple it with our in-house global plasma-kinetics solver (SoPlasma-0D), whose energy partition after the pulse agrees well with that derived from measurements and with an independent calculation. Two microseconds after a single pulse in air, and compared with the proposed coupled model, the existing closures overestimate the axis density by up to a factor of 2.8, the atomic oxygen density by up to 2.7 and the temperature by up to 680 K. For repetitive pulses 200 or 430 ns apart, of equal energy per unit volume, no existing closure follows the coupled model at both intervals, in the gas density met by each later pulse and in the energy per molecule deposited by late pulses, which sets how strongly they dissociate and heat the gas. The proposed reduced model should therefore be used to describe the gas evolution during the expansion phase after every nanosecond pulse, and for repetitive pulses above about 100 kHz in kernels of radius up to about a millimetre.

AI.tldr: Global zero-dimensional models of nanosecond pulsed discharges use simplified gas-dynamic closures that can cause large errors in gas density, temperature, and species densities. The paper proposes a fast reduced Lagrangian-shell gas-dynamic model with an approximate cylindrical acoustic radiation condition, coupled to the SoPlasma-0D plasma-kinetics solver, and shows improved agreement with CFD and measurements for single and repetitive pulses.
AI.motivation: Global zero-dimensional kinetic models need to describe expansion of the heated gas channel after each nanosecond pulse, but existing simplified gas-dynamic closures can produce errors of tens of percent, especially in the first microseconds after a pulse. A fast reduced model without fitted physical coefficients is needed for single and repetitive discharges.
AI.method: The authors develop a reduced gas-dynamic model of Lagrangian shells closed by an approximate cylindrical acoustic radiation condition, with no fitted physical coefficient. They benchmark it against verified one-dimensional compressible CFD simulations and couple it with the in-house global plasma-kinetics solver SoPlasma-0D; the post-pulse energy partition is compared with measurements and an independent calculation.
AI.result: The reduced model reproduces the CFD axis density within 2.4% for smooth deposition profiles and axis pressures up to six times ambient, typically about a thousand times faster than CFD. Two microseconds after a single pulse in air, existing closures overestimate axis density by up to a factor of 2.8, atomic oxygen density by up to 2.7, and temperature by up to 680 K. For repetitive pulses 200 or 430 ns apart with equal energy per unit volume, no existing closure follows the coupled model at both intervals for the gas density met by later pulses or the energy per molecule deposited by late pulses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reduced model should be used to describe gas evolution during the expansion phase after every nanosecond pulse and for repetitive pulses above about 100 kHz in kernels with radius up to about one millimetre.

title: Solving the Discretised Shallow Water Equations on Distorted Structured Grids with Neural Physics
summary:
This paper presents a method for solving the shallow water equations on highly distorted structured grids using convolution-based operators following the Neural Physics approach. By mapping distorted physical grids to a uniform computational domain with Jacobian transformations, the governing advection and diffusion operators are reformulated in a structured convolutional form. This enables the use of efficient stencil-based operations and, following the Neural Physics concept, we do this through convolutional layers whose weights are determined by the chosen numerical methods rather than by training.
  The method introduces consistent mass-lumped formulations, conservative and non-conservative advection forms, and a diffusion operator, all expressed as convolutions. A nonlinear Petrov-Galerkin stabilisation is incorporated to control numerical oscillations on distorted meshes. Two approximations for the Laplacian operator are also proposed to accelerate pressure and diffusion solves. The framework is validated using the Carlisle 2005 flood event, demonstrating accurate predictions of water depth and velocity on distorted meshes for both linear and quadratic discretisations.
  The results show that distorted structured grids can retain conservation, stability and accuracy, whilst adapting the mesh statically. The convolutional formulation makes the method well suited to Neural Physics implementations and GPU acceleration, offering a scalable approach for flood modelling and large-scale geophysical simulations.

AI.tldr: A convolution-based Neural Physics method solves the shallow water equations on highly distorted structured grids by mapping them to a uniform computational domain, reformulating advection and diffusion as stencil operations, and adding stabilisation and Laplacian approximations. It is validated on the Carlisle 2005 flood event and supports GPU-oriented, scalable flood and geophysical modelling.
AI.motivation: The abstract frames the aim as solving the shallow water equations on highly distorted structured grids while retaining conservation, stability, and accuracy, and expressing the operators as convolutions so the method is suited to Neural Physics implementations and GPU acceleration for scalable flood modelling and large-scale geophysical simulations.
AI.method: Distorted physical grids are mapped to a uniform computational domain using Jacobian transformations, and the advection and diffusion operators are reformulated as structured convolutions. The convolutional layers use weights determined by the chosen numerical methods rather than by training, following the Neural Physics approach. The formulation includes consistent mass-lumped forms, conservative and non-conservative advection forms, and a diffusion operator. A nonlinear Petrov-Galerkin stabilisation controls oscillations on distorted meshes, and two Laplacian approximations are proposed to accelerate pressure and diffusion solves.
AI.result: The framework is validated using the Carlisle 2005 flood event, with accurate predictions of water depth and velocity on distorted meshes for both linear and quadratic discretisations. The results indicate that distorted structured grids can retain conservation, stability, and accuracy while adapting the mesh statically. The abstract does not provide quantitative error metrics or performance figures.
AI.conclusion: The convolutional formulation makes the method well suited to Neural Physics implementations and GPU acceleration, offering a scalable approach for flood modelling and large-scale geophysical simulations. Distorted structured grids are shown to be viable for this solver within the reported validation.

title: The role of turbulent jet dynamics on contrail formation from conventional and sustainable aviation fuels
summary: Large-eddy simulations (LES) coupled with a discretised population balance equation (PBE) are used to quantify the effect of turbulence on the early stages of contrail formation (jet regime) for both conventional (soot-rich) and sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs). SAFs typically have low aromatic content which causes a shift in the dominant nucleation pathway. The contribution from soot (non-volatile particulate matter, nvPM) is reduced, while the contribution from volatile particulate matter (vPM) is increased. The computational domain reproduces an experimental jet configuration that replicates the thermodynamic conditions encountered in the upper troposphere. The LES-PBE simulations capture well the jet-core cooling and bracket the experimental values of ice-crystal characteristics (number concentration, mean diameter and mass density) if a range of judicious values for parameters not specified in the experiments are employed. With the aid of one-dimensional, one-way coupled PBE approach, it is shown that soot particle activation can be reliably captured using steady aerosol-jet models. On the other hand, volatile particle activation is significantly affected by large fluctuations in temperature and humidity (and thereby supersaturation). Further downstream, non-linear dynamic coupling between the gas and aerosol phases becomes increasingly important for ice-crystal growth as well. Overall, the results demonstrate that for SAFs, turbulence is an important driver of particle activation and subsequent ice crystal growth and cannot be neglected. This finding motivates more fundamental studies to assess how turbulent jet dynamics modulates contrail formation in realistic engine configurations.

AI.tldr: Large-eddy simulations coupled with a discretised population balance equation quantify turbulent jet effects on early contrail formation for conventional soot-rich and sustainable aviation fuels; turbulence strongly affects volatile particle activation and ice-crystal growth, especially for SAFs.
AI.motivation: Sustainable aviation fuels typically have low aromatic content, shifting the dominant nucleation pathway from soot/non-volatile particulate matter toward volatile particulate matter, so the role of turbulent jet dynamics in early contrail formation under upper-tropospheric conditions needs quantification.
AI.method: Large-eddy simulations coupled with a discretised population balance equation reproduce an experimental jet configuration under upper-tropospheric thermodynamic conditions, are compared with experimental ice-crystal characteristics, and are analyzed with a one-dimensional, one-way coupled PBE approach.
AI.result: The LES-PBE simulations capture jet-core cooling and bracket experimental ice-crystal number concentration, mean diameter, and mass density when judicious values are used for parameters not specified in the experiments. Soot particle activation is reliably captured by steady aerosol-jet models, whereas volatile particle activation is significantly affected by large temperature and humidity fluctuations and thus supersaturation; downstream, nonlinear gas-aerosol coupling becomes increasingly important for ice-crystal growth.
AI.conclusion: For SAFs, turbulence is an important driver of particle activation and subsequent ice-crystal growth and cannot be neglected, motivating further fundamental studies of how turbulent jet dynamics modulate contrail formation in realistic engine configurations.

title: Variable-length MDI QKD under source imperfections and local randomization over horizontal links
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides security guarantees that hold despite device imperfections and finite-size effects. We address these challenges in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, combining its intrinsic untrusted detection with an imperfection model for Alice's and Bob's sources via fidelity bounds. We establish variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT), estimating the relevant Rényi entropies through conic optimization. We evaluate our model under a horizontal channel link, reporting secret keys for blocks as small as n~3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions, and show that compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric configurations, enabling communication distances beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops variable-length, composable security for measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution when Alice's and Bob's sources deviate from ideal, modeling source imperfections with fidelity bounds and computing finite-size key rates via conic optimization over a horizontal atmospheric link.
AI.motivation: QKD security proofs must remain valid under real device imperfections and finite-size, variable-length operating conditions. The authors aim to combine the untrusted-detection advantage of MDI QKD with a rigorous characterization of source imperfections, and to assess feasibility for horizontal free-space links relevant to satellite-based commercial systems.
AI.method: The authors apply the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT) to establish variable-length general security, bounding the sources of Alice and Bob through fidelity constraints and estimating the required Rényi entropies by conic optimization. They then evaluate the resulting key-rate model numerically for a horizontal channel link, including asymmetric configurations in which channel attenuations differ and are compensated by suitably chosen transmitted amplitudes.
AI.result: Secret keys are reported for blocks as small as n ~ 3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions. Compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes is shown to improve performance in asymmetric configurations, and communication distances beyond 80 km are enabled for commercial satellite systems.
AI.conclusion: Variable-length MDI QKD with bounded source imperfections and local randomization is shown to be security-provable via MEAT and conic entropy estimation, and to yield positive finite-size key rates over horizontal links, with amplitude-based attenuation compensation extending reach beyond 80 km in asymmetric settings.

title: A generic route to chaos in self-excited plasma oscillations
summary: We propose a generic autonomous route to chaos in self-excited plasma oscillations through nonlinear feedback from a finite-rate charging variable. Near the threshold of an oscillatory ion-acoustic instability, a multiple-scale reduction yields a Stuart-Landau amplitude equation, represented by a van der Pol-type modal surrogate and coupled to debris-charge evolution in a prototype case of plasma-debris interaction scenario. For a debris-induced ion-ion counter-streaming instability, charge-dependent forcing and frequency modulation, finite charging relaxation, phase-lagged modal response, mixed nonlinear feedback, and saturation form a closed dynamical system without an externally imposed periodic driver. Numerical bifurcation and Lyapunov analyses reveal multistability and a bounded chaotic branch reached through period doubling bifurcation and band formation. We test the proposed mechanism using a one-dimensional open-boundary \emph{hybrid} particle-in-cell-Monte Carlo collision simulation incorporating particle collection, photoemission, secondary-electron emission, and surface regulation. Weak-form sparse regression identifies finite intervals whose projected dynamics reproduce the sign structure of the reduced model, while independent $0$-$1$ chaos test, nonlinear predicatbility, surrogate-data, and Lyapunov diagnostics provide localized evidence of deterministic chaotic organization in the subsonic case. The combined results establish a proof-of-principle route by which a self-excited plasma mode can become chaotic through internally generated charging feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and tests a generic autonomous mechanism by which self-excited plasma oscillations can become chaotic through finite-rate charging feedback, without an externally imposed periodic driver.
AI.motivation: To identify a generic route to chaos in self-excited plasma oscillations and to test whether internally generated charging feedback, rather than an imposed periodic drive, can produce deterministic chaotic organization in a plasma-debris interaction prototype.
AI.method: Near the threshold of an oscillatory ion-acoustic instability, a multiple-scale reduction yields a Stuart-Landau amplitude equation represented by a van der Pol-type modal surrogate coupled to debris-charge evolution. The closed dynamical system includes charge-dependent forcing and frequency modulation, finite charging relaxation, phase-lagged modal response, mixed nonlinear feedback, and saturation. The authors use numerical bifurcation and Lyapunov analyses and test the mechanism with a one-dimensional open-boundary hybrid particle-in-cell-Monte Carlo collision simulation incorporating particle collection, photoemission, secondary-electron emission, and surface regulation. Weak-form sparse regression and independent 0-1 chaos, nonlinear predictability, surrogate-data, and Lyapunov diagnostics are also applied.
AI.result: The reduced system shows multistability and a bounded chaotic branch reached through period-doubling bifurcation and band formation. The hybrid simulation provides localized evidence of deterministic chaotic organization in the subsonic case, and weak-form sparse regression identifies finite intervals whose projected dynamics reproduce the sign structure of the reduced model. The abstract does not quantify chaos thresholds or parameter ranges beyond the subsonic case.
AI.conclusion: The combined results establish a proof-of-principle route by which a self-excited plasma mode can become chaotic through internally generated charging feedback. The abstract does not establish generality beyond the prototype or provide predictive scaling to other systems.

title: Physics-Spawned Neural Integration of Rotating Shallow-Water Dynamics
summary: Equation-derived neural integration can execute prescribed dynamics without training, while informative ensemble learning can estimate uncertain parameters and identify governing interactions without requiring differentiability. Together, these approaches motivate Physics-Spawned Informative Networks ($Φ$SpIN), a framework for prescribed and adaptive hybrid dynamical systems. As a first step toward flood modeling applications, we present $Φ$SpIN-SW, its prescribed-physics realization for the rotating shallow-water equations. Compatible C-grid operators on spherical Voronoi meshes define a computational graph that retains non-polynomial operations and advances the state through recurrent neural integration compiled with JAX. Analytical benchmarks characterize numerical errors, and global and coastal experiments closely reproduce reference solutions generated using the Model Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) model. At approximately 14~km global resolution, A100, H200 and B200 GPUs attain 9-, 19- and 34-fold higher timestep throughput than a 96-core MPAS-SW CPU reference under matched workloads. These results extend training-free neural integration beyond polynomial dynamics to complex geophysical simulation, establishing a computational foundation for subsequent adjoint-free ensemble estimation of physical and neural parameters and informative adaptation of operator structure.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ΦSpIN-SW, a training-free prescribed-physics neural integration framework for the rotating shallow-water equations on spherical Voronoi meshes; it reproduces MPAS reference solutions and achieves up to 34-fold higher timestep throughput on GPUs.
AI.motivation: Equation-derived neural integration can execute prescribed dynamics without training, while informative ensemble learning can estimate uncertain parameters and identify governing interactions without requiring differentiability. These capabilities motivate ΦSpIN, a framework for prescribed and adaptive hybrid dynamical systems, with ΦSpIN-SW serving as a first step toward flood modeling applications.
AI.method: ΦSpIN-SW defines a computational graph using compatible C-grid operators on spherical Voronoi meshes, retains non-polynomial operations, and advances the state through recurrent neural integration compiled with JAX. The authors evaluate numerical errors with analytical benchmarks and compare global and coastal experiments against reference solutions from the Model Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) model.
AI.result: Analytical benchmarks characterize numerical errors, and global and coastal experiments closely reproduce MPAS reference solutions. At approximately 14 km global resolution, A100, H200, and B200 GPUs achieve 9-, 19-, and 34-fold higher timestep throughput, respectively, than a 96-core MPAS-SW CPU reference under matched workloads.
AI.conclusion: The results extend training-free neural integration beyond polynomial dynamics to complex geophysical simulation and establish a computational foundation for subsequent adjoint-free ensemble estimation of physical and neural parameters and informative adaptation of operator structure.

title: Dynamics and stability of volatile thin liquid films on a heated vertical cylinder
summary: Volatile thin liquid films flowing down heated vertical cylinders are central to many heat transfer applications, including evaporative condensers, cooling of electronics, and solar thermal systems. Despite their importance, the coupled dynamics of evaporation, thermocapillarity, and interfacial instabilities on cylindrical geometries remain poorly understood. In this work, a lubrication-based model is developed to capture the nonlinear evolution of a volatile thin film under gravity, surface tension, van der Waals forces, and non-conservative evaporative flux. The model incorporates hydrodynamic pressure contributions to evaporation, enabling a unified description of phase-change effects on curved substrates. A linear stability analysis of the model equation is performed with a non-constant base film thickness. The linear growth rate is first obtained for a spatially uniform film. Then, for a spatially nonuniform film, a coupled system of linearized equations is solved using the finite element method. Further, the full liquid-vapor interface is numerically simulated to demonstrate liquid evaporation. Results reveal that evaporation accelerates film thinning, condensation promotes thickening, and van der Waals forces stabilize ultra-thin films by preventing rupture. The influence of Bond number, wavenumber, and pressure-dependent flux laws on droplet formation and collision dynamics is quantified. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into phase-change driven instabilities in cylindrical thin films and have direct implications for the design of efficient thermal management systems, evaporative cooling devices, and surface-engineered heat exchangers.

AI.tldr: A lubrication-based model is developed and analyzed to explain how evaporation, thermocapillarity, gravity, surface tension, van der Waals forces, and pressure-dependent evaporative flux govern the dynamics and stability of volatile thin liquid films on heated vertical cylinders.
AI.motivation: Volatile thin liquid films flowing down heated vertical cylinders are important in evaporative condensers, electronics cooling, and solar thermal systems, but the coupled effects of evaporation, thermocapillarity, and interfacial instabilities on cylindrical geometries are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors formulate a lubrication-based model for nonlinear film evolution including gravity, surface tension, van der Waals forces, and non-conservative evaporative flux, with hydrodynamic pressure contributions to evaporation. They perform linear stability analysis for uniform and nonuniform base film thickness, solving the coupled linearized equations for the nonuniform case using the finite element method, and numerically simulate the full liquid-vapor interface to demonstrate evaporation.
AI.result: Evaporation accelerates film thinning, condensation promotes thickening, and van der Waals forces stabilize ultra-thin films by preventing rupture. The study quantifies how Bond number, wavenumber, and pressure-dependent flux laws influence droplet formation and collision dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide mechanistic insights into phase-change-driven instabilities in cylindrical thin films and have implications for thermal management systems, evaporative cooling devices, and surface-engineered heat exchangers.

title: Axion electrodynamics and the advection-diffusion structure of TEM modes in hollow-conductor waveguides
summary: We present a systematic investigation of transverse electromagnetic (TEM) modes in hollow-conductor waveguides filled with a dielectric medium described by axion electrodynamics. While such modes do not propagate in conventional single-conductor waveguides, the coupling of the axion field to an external magnetic field enables their propagation. We show that the resulting TEM modes are governed by an advection-diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential, establishing a direct mathematical connection between axion electrodynamics and advection-diffusion phenomena. We illustrate this connection through explicit solutions and field profiles for cylindrical waveguides, considering uniform and rigid rotational drift fields, both individually and in combination, as well as different values of the parameter controlling the advection-to-diffusion ratio (Péclet number). These results establish a transport-based framework for understanding how spatial variations of the axion-electrodynamics background shape the transverse electromagnetic fields in hollow-conductor waveguides.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically studies TEM modes in hollow-conductor waveguides filled with a dielectric medium governed by axion electrodynamics. Coupling between the axion field and an external magnetic field permits TEM propagation, and the modes are shown to obey an advection-diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential. Explicit cylindrical-waveguide solutions illustrate the role of uniform and rotational drift fields and the Péclet number.
AI.motivation: TEM modes do not propagate in conventional single-conductor waveguides, but coupling of the axion field to an external magnetic field can enable their propagation. The paper aims to systematically investigate these modes and establish a transport-based framework connecting axion electrodynamics with advection-diffusion phenomena.
AI.method: The authors perform a theoretical investigation of TEM modes in hollow-conductor waveguides filled with a dielectric medium described by axion electrodynamics. They derive an advection-diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential and obtain explicit solutions and field profiles for cylindrical waveguides, considering uniform and rigid rotational drift fields separately and in combination, and varying the Péclet number.
AI.result: The resulting TEM modes are governed by an advection-diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential, establishing a direct mathematical connection between axion electrodynamics and advection-diffusion phenomena. Explicit solutions and field profiles are presented for cylindrical waveguides under different drift-field configurations and Péclet numbers.
AI.conclusion: Coupling of the axion field to an external magnetic field enables TEM propagation in hollow-conductor waveguides. Spatial variations of the axion-electrodynamics background shape the transverse electromagnetic fields, and the proposed transport-based framework provides a way to understand this behavior.

title: Simulations of turbulent heat and particle transport in stellarator plasmas
comment: PhD thesis, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (2025). Advisors: J. M. García-Regaña and I. Calvo. 152 pages, 59 figures, 11 tables
summary:
Achieving sustained energy production in magnetic confinement fusion reactors requires a deep understanding of turbulent transport of heat and particles. This thesis investigates turbulent transport with a particular emphasis on stellarators, using simulations with the $δf$ gyrokinetic code stella for the W7-X, LHD, TJ-II and NCSX stellarators, the ASDEX Upgrade (AUG) tokamak and the Cyclone Base Case (CBC). It addresses two questions: how do density gradients affect turbulent heat transport, and can turbulence help retain particles in the plasma core?
  In the first part, an inter-machine study shows a strong reduction of the ion heat flux in NCSX and W7-X with increasing density gradients, attributed to the stabilization of ion-temperature-gradient-driven modes without significantly destabilizing trapped-electron modes or universal instabilities. This beneficial effect is absent in tokamaks, where the heat flux increases with the density gradient, highlighting the role of magnetic geometry. The ion heat flux in stellarators does not follow the growth rate of the fastest-growing linear mode, underscoring the importance of nonlinear effects. Trapped-electron modes dominate in CBC, AUG, TJ-II, LHD and NCSX, while passing-particle-driven universal instabilities contribute significantly in W7-X.
  The second part addresses the long-standing discrepancy between the strongly hollow density profiles predicted by neoclassical theory in large stellarators and the flat or weakly peaked profiles measured in W7-X. Nonlinear simulations and a particle balance analysis show that turbulence provides a robust inward particle flux, driven by finite ion and electron temperature gradients, that can account for the observed profiles: the sign of the turbulent particle flux matches the sign of the discrepancy between the experimental and neoclassical fluxes across the entire plasma radius of W7-X.

AI.tldr: This thesis uses δf gyrokinetic stella simulations across several stellarators and tokamaks to show that magnetic geometry and nonlinear effects govern turbulent heat transport under density gradients, and that turbulence-driven inward particle flux can explain the flat or weakly peaked density profiles observed in W7-X despite neoclassical predictions of strong hollowness.
AI.motivation: Sustained energy production in magnetic confinement fusion reactors requires a deep understanding of turbulent transport of heat and particles. The thesis focuses on stellarators and addresses how density gradients affect turbulent heat transport and whether turbulence can help retain particles in the plasma core.
AI.method: The study uses simulations with the δf gyrokinetic code stella for the W7-X, LHD, TJ-II and NCSX stellarators, the ASDEX Upgrade tokamak and the Cyclone Base Case. It performs an inter-machine study of density-gradient effects on turbulent heat transport and combines nonlinear simulations with a particle balance analysis to investigate turbulent particle transport and experimental density profiles.
AI.result: Increasing density gradients strongly reduce the ion heat flux in NCSX and W7-X, attributed to stabilization of ion-temperature-gradient-driven modes without significantly destabilizing trapped-electron modes or universal instabilities; this beneficial effect is absent in tokamaks, where heat flux increases with density gradient. The ion heat flux in stellarators does not follow the growth rate of the fastest-growing linear mode, indicating important nonlinear effects. Trapped-electron modes dominate in CBC, AUG, TJ-II, LHD and NCSX, while passing-particle-driven universal instabilities contribute significantly in W7-X. Turbulence provides a robust inward particle flux driven by finite ion and electron temperature gradients, and the sign of the turbulent particle flux matches the sign of the discrepancy between experimental and neoclassical fluxes across the entire W7-X plasma radius.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic geometry strongly influences turbulent heat transport, nonlinear effects are essential in stellarators, and turbulence-driven inward particle transport can account for the observed flat or weakly peaked density profiles in W7-X rather than the strongly hollow profiles predicted by neoclassical theory.

title: U-HamGNN: a universal model for magnetic Hamiltonians conditioned on spin and Hubbard U
summary: The electronic structure of a magnetic crystal depends jointly on its spin configuration and the on-site Hubbard correction U, requiring a separate DFT+U calculation for each combination. We introduce U-HamGNN, an equivariant network that takes these two inputs directly and predicts spin-resolved Hamiltonians across diverse crystal chemistries. A spectral-hybrid optimizer that weights each update direction by how consistently the gradient points along it reaches 8% lower Hamiltonian error than Muon and 26% lower than AdamW in a ten-epoch benchmark. The predicted bands reproduce U-dependent gap opening and altermagnetic spin splitting within the trained window and beyond it; exchange couplings and magnetic-order calls derived from the Hamiltonian agree with DFT+U on a calibration set. This universal model provides a new tool for magnetic research.

AI.tldr: U-HamGNN is an equivariant neural model that directly predicts spin-resolved magnetic Hamiltonians from spin configuration and Hubbard U, avoiding separate DFT+U runs for each combination. It uses a spectral-hybrid optimizer, reproduces U-dependent gaps and altermagnetic splitting, and yields exchange couplings and magnetic-order calls consistent with DFT+U on a calibration set.
AI.motivation: Magnetic crystal electronic structure depends jointly on spin configuration and on-site Hubbard U, so conventional DFT+U requires a separate calculation for every combination. The paper aims to provide a universal model that takes these two inputs directly and predicts magnetic Hamiltonians across diverse crystal chemistries.
AI.method: The authors introduce U-HamGNN, an equivariant network conditioned on spin and Hubbard U that predicts spin-resolved Hamiltonians.
