They also propose a spectral-hybrid optimizer that weights each update direction by how consistently the gradient points along it, benchmarked against Muon and AdamW over ten epochs.
AI.result: The spectral-hybrid optimizer reaches 8% lower Hamiltonian error than Muon and 26% lower than AdamW in a ten-epoch benchmark. Predicted bands reproduce U-dependent gap opening and altermagnetic spin splitting within and beyond the trained window. Exchange couplings and magnetic-order calls derived from the Hamiltonian agree with DFT+U on a calibration set.
AI.conclusion: U-HamGNN provides a universal tool for magnetic research by predicting spin- and U-conditioned magnetic Hamiltonians and supporting downstream band, exchange-coupling, and magnetic-order analyses consistent with DFT+U in the reported tests.

title: Motion of a cylinder between parallel plates: complete Stokes resistance and pressure response
summary: A circular cylinder moving between two parallel plates is the canonical confined problem of two-dimensional Stokes flow. Rotation and translation of the cylinder along the channel become coupled and generate a pressure difference along the channel under zero-net-flux conditions. Existing results use different methods. We develop a completed double-layer boundary integral formulation based on the channel Green function to resolve narrow gaps at arbitrary transverse positions. The channel Green kernels are derived from a Fourier-transformed biharmonic problem, permitting explicit treatment of the free-space singularity, the slowly decaying nearest-wall contribution, and the small-wavenumber limit for accurate kernel evaluation under strong confinement. The boundary integral equation is discretised by a spectrally accurate Nyström scheme on a graded parametrisation, and the pressure jump follows from the zero-wavenumber limit of the streamwise momentum balance. A single linear system yields the full resistance matrix and pressure-jump coefficients for an eccentric cylinder; an additional right-hand side treats imposed net flux. For nonzero coefficients, comparisons with independent COMSOL finite-element simulations show relative differences below \(0.1\%\) for the resistance coefficients and at most \(0.0122\%\) for the pressure-response coefficients and excess hydraulic resistance. Reciprocity, symmetry constraints, and lubrication asymptotics provide additional checks on the numerical results. We track the coupling between rotation and translation and the pressure generated by the cylinder from the channel scale into the lubrication regime, and determine the pressure--flow relation, driving torque and efficiency of the rotating-cylinder pump for asymmetric clearances.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a completed double-layer boundary integral method using channel Green functions and a spectrally accurate Nyström discretization to compute the full Stokes resistance matrix and pressure response of an eccentric cylinder moving between parallel plates, including strong confinement and lubrication regimes.
AI.motivation: The motion of a circular cylinder between parallel plates is a canonical confined two-dimensional Stokes-flow problem in which rotation and translation couple and produce a pressure difference under zero-net-flux conditions; existing results rely on different methods, motivating a unified accurate formulation valid for narrow gaps at arbitrary transverse positions.
AI.method: A completed double-layer boundary integral formulation based on the channel Green function is developed. The channel Green kernels are derived from a Fourier-transformed biharmonic problem, with explicit treatment of the free-space singularity, the slowly decaying nearest-wall contribution, and the small-wavenumber limit. The boundary integral equation is discretized by a spectrally accurate Nyström scheme on a graded parametrization, and the pressure jump is obtained from the zero-wavenumber limit of the streamwise momentum balance. One linear system gives the full resistance matrix and pressure-jump coefficients for an eccentric cylinder, with an additional right-hand side for imposed net flux.
AI.result: Comparisons with independent COMSOL finite-element simulations show relative differences below 0.1% for nonzero resistance coefficients and at most 0.0122% for pressure-response coefficients and excess hydraulic resistance. Reciprocity, symmetry constraints, and lubrication asymptotics provide additional checks. The coupling between rotation and translation and the cylinder-generated pressure are tracked from the channel scale into the lubrication regime, and the pressure–flow relation, driving torque, and efficiency of the rotating-cylinder pump are determined for asymmetric clearances.
AI.conclusion: The proposed boundary integral formulation provides accurate resistance and pressure-response coefficients for a confined eccentric cylinder across confinement regimes, including lubrication asymptotics, and enables characterization of the pressure–flow relation, driving torque, and pumping efficiency for asymmetric clearances.

title: Altermagnetism-induced magneto-optical effects
summary: Altermagnets break time-reversal symmetry despite their zero net magnetization, enabling time-reversal-odd responses while retaining the advantages of antiferromagnets. However, magneto-optical (MO) effects are not universal among altermagnets because MO effects typically arise from magnetic dipole order (ferromagnetism), which is generally absent in altermagnets. In this work, we address this limitation by establishing octupolar MO effects, which arise from magnetic octupole order through spatial dispersion. Owing to this distinct origin, octupolar MO effects do not necessarily require spin-orbit coupling even in collinear magnets and can arise without an external magnetic field in antiferromagnets where conventional MO effects are symmetry-forbidden. Such antiferromagnets include $d$-wave altermagnets such as RuO$_2$ and KV$_2$Se$_2$O, certain $g$- and $i$-wave altermagnets, including CrSb, as well as noncoplanar antiferromagnets such as MnTe$_2$ and pyrochlore iridates with all-in-all-out magnetic order. From an experimental perspective, octupolar MO effects can reach detectable magnitudes and offer potential for magnetic-domain imaging, as supported by numerical calculations showing $μ$rad-scale Faraday rotation for a 100-nm-thick sample in the visible-light range and a sign reversal between opposite domains. Furthermore, octupolar MO effects are linked to an $f$-sum rule, enabling a quantitative estimate of the spin magnetic octupole moment from optical measurements. These results extend the scope of MO effects to a broad class of antiferromagnets, including altermagnets, and open a field-free optical route to exploring magnetic octupole order.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes octupolar magneto-optical effects originating from magnetic octupole order via spatial dispersion, extending magneto-optics to altermagnets and other antiferromagnets. It predicts detectable domain-dependent Faraday rotation and an f-sum rule for quantifying the spin magnetic octupole moment.
AI.motivation: Magneto-optical effects are not universal among altermagnets because they usually arise from magnetic dipole order, i.e., ferromagnetism, which is generally absent in altermagnets. The authors aim to overcome this limitation and describe magneto-optical responses in a broader class of antiferromagnets.
AI.method: The authors theoretically establish octupolar magneto-optical effects arising from magnetic octupole order through spatial dispersion. They analyze symmetry properties, including cases without spin-orbit coupling and without an external magnetic field, identify candidate altermagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials, perform numerical calculations of Faraday rotation, and derive an f-sum rule.
AI.result: Octupolar magneto-optical effects do not necessarily require spin-orbit coupling in collinear magnets and can occur without an external magnetic field where conventional magneto-optical effects are symmetry-forbidden. Candidates include d-wave altermagnets such as RuO$_2$ and KV$_2$Se$_2$O, certain g- and i-wave altermagnets including CrSb, and noncoplanar antiferromagnets such as MnTe$_2$ and pyrochlore iridates. Numerical calculations give μrad-scale Faraday rotation for a 100-nm-thick sample in the visible range, with sign reversal between opposite domains, and the f-sum rule enables quantitative estimation of the spin magnetic octupole moment from optical measurements.
AI.conclusion: Octupolar magneto-optical effects extend the scope of magneto-optics to a broad class of antiferromagnets, including altermagnets, and provide a field-free optical route to exploring magnetic octupole order.

title: A full-wave ICRH solver with full kinetic accuracy using only first order differential equations
summary: Accurate full-wave computation of ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) typically requires solving the computationally demanding integro-differential dielectric tensor of the hot plasma. Based on the method in [Phys. Plasmas 32, 082110 (2025)], we develop BO-FW1D, a 1D frequency domain finite difference full-wave solver which generates full kinetic, accurate and efficient simulations utilizing a fluid plasma model. To accurately convert the conductivity tensor in phase space into a first-order differential equation, we introduce a mathematically rigorous framework using pseudodifferential operator theory based on Kohn-Nirenberg ordering. Benchmarks with an all-orders 1D full-wave solver show high consistency in critical kinetic effects and electric-field distributions, while substantial computational acceleration is achieved. This work could lay the foundation for developing full-wave solvers that combine full kinetic accuracy with high computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BO-FW1D, a one-dimensional frequency-domain finite-difference full-wave solver for ion cyclotron resonance heating that uses a fluid plasma model yet retains full kinetic accuracy by reformulating the phase-space conductivity tensor as first-order differential equations via pseudodifferential operator theory with Kohn-Nirenberg ordering. Benchmarks against an all-orders solver show consistent kinetic effects and electric-field profiles with substantial computational acceleration.
AI.motivation: Accurate full-wave ICRH computation normally requires the computationally demanding integro-differential dielectric tensor of a hot plasma, creating a need for methods that preserve full kinetic accuracy while reducing computational cost.
AI.method: Based on the method in Phys. Plasmas 32, 082110 (2025), the authors develop BO-FW1D, a 1D frequency-domain finite-difference full-wave solver using a fluid plasma model. A mathematically rigorous pseudodifferential operator framework with Kohn-Nirenberg ordering converts the conductivity tensor in phase space into a first-order differential equation.
AI.result: Benchmarks against an all-orders 1D full-wave solver show high consistency in critical kinetic effects and electric-field distributions, while achieving substantial computational acceleration; the specific speedup factor is not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The approach can provide a foundation for full-wave solvers that combine full kinetic accuracy with high computational efficiency.

title: An implicit high-order flux reconstruction method with logarithmic variables for hypersonic flows in thermochemical nonequilibrium
summary: Simulating hypersonic flows in thermochemical nonequilibrium requires solving the Navier-Stokes equations for reacting, possibly ionised mixtures. Compact high-order computations of viscous two-temperature air flows on unstructured grids have not gone beyond P = 2. We present an implicit Flux Reconstruction (FR) method for such flows, built on three ingredients. First, the solver stores and updates the logarithms of the partial densities and temperatures, making every state admissible without a positivity limiter and, for ionised mixtures, imposing charge neutrality consistently with the implicit update. Second, shocks are captured by subcell order blending, extended to steady implicit computations on curved Gauss-Legendre meshes, with second-order subcell blending in subsonic regions and an automatic freeze of the blending near convergence. Third, a pseudo-transient Newton method with a physicality-limited update and automatic CFL control reaches steady state from the free stream with the same settings at every order. The design order is verified up to sixth order on a manufactured solution for five-species air with finite-rate chemistry and vibrational relaxation. Steady viscous solutions up to sixth order are obtained for five- and eleven-species air on the High Enthalpy shock tunnel Göttingen (HEG) cylinder and for eleven-species air on the RAM-C II vehicle. To our knowledge, this work gives the first design-order verification of a high-order method with finite-rate air chemistry and vibrational relaxation, and the first high-order finite-element-type computations of viscous eleven-species, two-temperature air. On the HEG cylinder, the stagnation-point heat flux is within 2% of finite-volume references and within 6% of the measurements, with a comparable number of degrees of freedom to second-order finite-volume computations but on meshes with 20 to 40 times fewer elements.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an implicit high-order Flux Reconstruction solver for hypersonic thermochemical-nonequilibrium air flows, using logarithmic variables for admissibility and charge neutrality, subcell order blending for shocks, and a pseudo-transient Newton method with automatic CFL control; it verifies design order up to sixth order and computes steady viscous five- and eleven-species air solutions.
AI.motivation: Compact high-order computations of viscous two-temperature air flows in thermochemical nonequilibrium on unstructured grids had not progressed beyond polynomial degree P = 2, motivating a robust implicit high-order method for reacting, possibly ionised mixtures.
AI.method: An implicit Flux Reconstruction method stores and updates logarithms of partial densities and temperatures to ensure admissible states without a positivity limiter and to impose charge neutrality for ionised mixtures. Shock capturing uses subcell order blending extended to steady implicit computations on curved Gauss-Legendre meshes, with second-order subcell blending in subsonic regions and automatic freezing near convergence. A pseudo-transient Newton method with a physicality-limited update and automatic CFL control reaches steady state from the free stream at every order.
AI.result: Design order is verified up to sixth order on a manufactured solution for five-species air with finite-rate chemistry and vibrational relaxation. Steady viscous solutions up to sixth order are obtained for five- and eleven-species air on the HEG cylinder and eleven-species air on the RAM-C II vehicle. The work reports the first design-order verification of a high-order method with finite-rate air chemistry and vibrational relaxation and the first high-order finite-element-type computations of viscous eleven-species, two-temperature air. On the HEG cylinder, stagnation-point heat flux is within 2% of finite-volume references and within 6% of measurements, with comparable degrees of freedom to second-order finite-volume computations but meshes with 20 to 40 times fewer elements.
AI.conclusion: The proposed implicit high-order Flux Reconstruction framework is capable of robust, design-order-accurate steady computations of hypersonic thermochemical-nonequilibrium flows, including viscous eleven-species two-temperature air, while achieving accuracy comparable to finite-volume references with substantially coarser meshes.

title: Darcy plume oscillations at low injection velocities
summary: We numerically investigate miscible buoyancy-driven Darcy plumes at low injection velocities. Below a critical injection velocity, the steady plume becomes unstable and develops periodic oscillations. Approaching the critical velocity, the oscillation amplitude vanishes while the frequency remains finite at the critical point, consistent with a supercritical Hopf bifurcation, whereas at lower injection velocities increasingly complex dynamics emerge. Unsteadiness also strongly enhances lateral mixing, increasing the mixing-layer thickness by a factor of approximately 2-3 compared with a steady plume. These findings reveal a previously unexplored dynamical regime of Darcy plumes with important consequences for subsurface transport and leakage.

AI.tldr: Numerical study of miscible buoyancy-driven Darcy plumes shows that below a critical injection velocity the steady plume undergoes a supercritical Hopf bifurcation to periodic oscillations, with more complex dynamics at lower velocities and 2–3-fold enhanced lateral mixing.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to characterize a previously unexplored dynamical regime of Darcy plumes at low injection velocities, motivated by consequences for subsurface transport and leakage.
AI.method: The authors numerically investigate miscible buoyancy-driven Darcy plumes at low injection velocities, examining plume stability, oscillation amplitude and frequency near the critical velocity, and mixing-layer thickness relative to a steady plume. The abstract does not specify the numerical scheme or governing parameter values.
AI.result: Below a critical injection velocity, the steady plume becomes unstable and develops periodic oscillations. The oscillation amplitude vanishes while the frequency remains finite at the critical point, consistent with a supercritical Hopf bifurcation. At lower injection velocities, increasingly complex dynamics emerge. Unsteadiness enhances lateral mixing, increasing mixing-layer thickness by approximately a factor of 2–3 compared with a steady plume.
AI.conclusion: Low-injection-velocity Darcy plumes can exhibit a distinct oscillatory dynamical regime that strongly enhances lateral mixing, with important implications for subsurface transport and leakage.

title: A regime dependent parameterization of the refractive-index structure parameter $C_n^2$
summary: Vertical profiles of the refractive-index (RI) structure parameter, $C_n^2$, are required in atmospheric-optics calculations. The Hufnagel--Valley (HV) model is a useful reference profile and it is widely used however, it is difficult to say that it produces consistent results at the observed altitude, magnitude, and thickness of all turbulent layers and it can diverge from realistic measurements in particular height ranges, sites, and stability regimes. This study develops a regime-dependent RI structure parameter considering meteorological conditions and, more importantly, it provides a structure that can be calibrated against measured $C_n^2$ throughout the surface layer (SL), atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and free atmosphere. The formulation combines SL including distinct unstable, near-neutral, and stable limits; convective ABL; and free-atmospheric turbulence when kinetic-energy and temperature-variance dissipation rates are available. The $C_n^2$ is formed by weighting the contribution of different layers. We use representative, physically plausible meteorological profiles to examine the model's limiting behavior, transitions between atmospheric regimes, continuity, sensitivity to its parameters, and propagation-related differences from the HV 5/7 model. The intended outcome is a measurement-calibrated model that remains physically interpretable across meteorological regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a regime-dependent parameterization of the atmospheric refractive-index structure parameter C_n^2 that combines surface-layer, convective boundary-layer, and free-atmosphere turbulence and is intended to be calibrated against measurements while remaining physically interpretable.
AI.motivation: Vertical C_n^2 profiles are needed for atmospheric-optics calculations. The widely used Hufnagel-Valley reference profile may not consistently reproduce the observed altitude, magnitude, and thickness of all turbulent layers and can diverge from measurements for particular height ranges, sites, and stability regimes.
AI.method: The authors formulate C_n^2 by weighting contributions from the surface layer, including distinct unstable, near-neutral, and stable limits; the convective atmospheric boundary layer; and free-atmospheric turbulence when kinetic-energy and temperature-variance dissipation rates are available. Representative, physically plausible meteorological profiles are used to examine limiting behavior, regime transitions, continuity, parameter sensitivity, and propagation-related differences from the HV 5/7 model.
AI.result: The abstract reports examinations of the model's limiting behavior, transitions between atmospheric regimes, continuity, sensitivity to parameters, and differences from HV 5/7 using representative meteorological profiles. No quantitative validation results or measurement-calibration outcomes are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The intended outcome is a measurement-calibrated C_n^2 model that remains physically interpretable across meteorological regimes and can be calibrated against measured C_n^2 throughout the surface layer, atmospheric boundary layer, and free atmosphere. Actual calibration and validation against measurements are not reported in the abstract.

title: Scaling of the Radial Motion and Size of Filamentary Structures in the Scrape-Off Layer Inferred from 100 kHz Visible Imaging on 294 MAST Discharges
summary: Filaments are important carriers of cross-field transport in the scrape-off layer of a tokamak. Analytic models predict that their radial velocity varies with their size. We measured the radial velocity and size of a large population of filaments on MAST, using data recorded from a 100 kHz, 48 x 256 pixel camera in the outboard midplane in the FAIR-MAST archive. Computer vision techniques were used to automate the identification of filaments and tracking of their trajectories, which yielded 86,042 filament tracks over 294 discharges in 4 campaigns. The archive does not contain spatial calibration, so we have obtained a pixel scale by regression of the plasma limb column in the image on the EFIT outboard LCFS radius, with bootstrap intervals. The scale is 2.7-5.2 millimetres per pixel. We find a median velocity of 424 m/s, and median radial width of 3.6 cm. The dependence of velocity on size is mild, with a log-log slope of +0.05 (95% interval +0.03 to +0.07) when the effects of exposure blurring are corrected for. This is because filaments are not in either velocity regime; they span the range $\hat{a}$ = 0.13-1.97 in two-region units, which straddles the maximum velocity predicted by the two-region model, but the normalized velocity $\hat{v}$ is much smaller than the scale of the model, at $\hat{v} \approx 0.06$.

AI.tldr: Computer-vision analysis of 100 kHz visible imaging from 294 MAST discharges identifies 86,042 scrape-off-layer filament tracks and finds a median radial velocity of 424 m/s, median radial width of 3.6 cm, and only mild size–velocity scaling.
AI.motivation: Filaments are important carriers of cross-field transport in the tokamak scrape-off layer, and analytic models predict that their radial velocity depends on their size; a large-population measurement was needed to test this scaling.
AI.method: The authors used a 100 kHz, 48 x 256 pixel camera viewing the outboard midplane in the FAIR-MAST archive and applied computer vision to automate filament identification and trajectory tracking, yielding 86,042 tracks over 294 discharges in four campaigns. Because the archive lacked spatial calibration, they regressed the plasma limb column against the EFIT outboard LCFS radius with bootstrap intervals, obtaining a pixel scale of 2.7–5.2 mm/pixel.
AI.result: The median filament radial velocity was 424 m/s and the median radial width was 3.6 cm. After correcting for exposure blurring, the log-log slope of velocity versus size was +0.05 (95% interval +0.03 to +0.07). Filaments spanned a_hat = 0.13–1.97 in two-region units, straddling the maximum velocity predicted by the two-region model, while the normalized velocity was much smaller than the model scale at v_hat approximately 0.06.
AI.conclusion: The dependence of filament radial velocity on size is mild because the filaments do not lie in either velocity regime of the two-region model; their normalized velocity is much lower than the model scale despite spanning sizes around the predicted velocity maximum.

title: Accelerating Atomistic-Continuum Simulations of Multilayer 2D Materials with Functional Principal Component Analysis-Based Machine Learning
summary: Atomistic-continuum simulations of complex wrinkling deformations in large-area multilayer two-dimensional (2D) materials are computationally expensive. To accelerate these simulations, this work presents a machine-learning (ML) framework that first constructs a low-dimensional representation of the deformation field, then learns the deformation in this reduced space. Dimensionality reduction of deformed 2D membranes is challenging because of the extremely high dimensionality of discretized deformation fields, the need to preserve surface continuity and prescribed geometric constraints, the stochastic nature of wrinkling patterns, and the limited availability of training data. We address these challenges using two-dimensional functional principal component analysis (FPCA). The proposed FPCA representation reduces deformation fields containing millions of degrees of freedom to latent spaces with only tens of dimensions while preserving the continuity of the deformed surface. In addition, prescribed homogeneous boundary constraints are satisfied exactly through an appropriate choice of basis functions in the FPCA representation. A neural network is then trained to predict the principal components from the system and loading parameters. The resulting ML-predicted deformation fields are used as high-quality initial configurations for the atomistic-continuum solver, which subsequently performs energy minimization to obtain equilibrium solutions. The framework is demonstrated for multilayer graphene subjected to uniaxial compression, biaxial compression, and combined biaxial compression and simple shear. For the most computationally intensive large-strain cases, the proposed approach achieves speedups of at least 6.8 times while converging to final energies comparable to, and in some cases lower than, those obtained using conventional atomistic-continuum initialization.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a functional principal component analysis (FPCA)-based machine-learning framework to accelerate atomistic-continuum simulations of wrinkling in large-area multilayer 2D materials by learning deformations in a low-dimensional latent space and using predictions as solver initializations.
AI.motivation: Atomistic-continuum simulations of complex wrinkling deformations in large-area multilayer two-dimensional materials are computationally expensive, motivating a reduced-order machine-learning approach that can accelerate these simulations while respecting geometric constraints and limited training data.
AI.method: The framework uses two-dimensional functional principal component analysis to reduce discretized deformation fields with millions of degrees of freedom to latent spaces with tens of dimensions, preserving surface continuity and exactly satisfying prescribed homogeneous boundary constraints through the choice of basis functions. A neural network is trained to predict the principal components from system and loading parameters, and the resulting deformation fields are used as high-quality initial configurations for the atomistic-continuum solver, followed by energy minimization.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated for multilayer graphene under uniaxial compression, biaxial compression, and combined biaxial compression and simple shear. For the most computationally intensive large-strain cases, it achieves speedups of at least 6.8 times while converging to final energies comparable to, and in some cases lower than, those from conventional atomistic-continuum initialization.
AI.conclusion: FPCA-based reduced-order machine learning can accelerate atomistic-continuum simulations of multilayer 2D material wrinkling while maintaining final energy quality; broader generalization beyond the demonstrated graphene loading cases is not provided in the abstract.

title: Magnetic control of hydrodynamic spin coupling between rotors: Ferrohydrodynamic effects in the two-rotor problem
comment: 51 pages, 18 figures, 8 tables. The following article has been submitted to Physics of Fluids
summary: The hydrodynamic spin coupling between two rotors ("fluid gears") is investigated numerically for a magnetic fluid in non-uniform magnetic fields. An active cylinder drives a torque-free passive one inside a circular corral, with one rotor heated. The model combines magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and ferrohydrodynamics (FHD), with the full Kelvin force and temperature-dependent Langevin magnetisation. For the oil-based ferrofluid EFH1 the Lorentz force is negligible, and the Kelvin force drives thermomagnetic convection from the heated rotor. Steady torque-free states are computed with Taylor-Hood finite elements, the gear ratio $Γ$ being an additional unknown. Without a field the results agree within 1-8% with published planar simulations up to $\mathrm{Re}\approx 50$. About 17,000 steady states cover 34 arrangements of wires, NdFeB rods and magnet cores, gaps $G=0.1$-$0.7$, $\mathrm{Re}=10$-$40$ and heating of 5-20 K. Because the coupling is weak, fields of 1-2 mT change $Γ$ by an amount comparable to $Γ$ itself. At 2 mT it is reversed, strengthened or weakened in nine cases out of ten. The outcome is set by the source position: at the experimental gap and $\mathrm{Re}=20$ a source below the corral or behind the active rotor strengthens the gear-like counter-rotation up to 2.7-fold, and a source above the corral reverses it into belt-like corotation. Several sources do not act additively, and a magnet core inside the active rotor raises $|Γ|$ at small gaps to seven times the largest hydrodynamic value. At fixed geometry and Reynolds number, field strength and heating act approximately through a single thermomagnetic source parameter.

AI.tldr: A numerical study shows that non-uniform magnetic fields can strongly modify, weaken, or reverse the hydrodynamic gear coupling between an active and a passive rotor in a ferrofluid, with the field-source position and thermomagnetic effects controlling the gear ratio.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates how magnetic fields can control the hydrodynamic spin coupling, or ``fluid gearing,'' between two rotors in a magnetic fluid, motivated by the weak coupling regime in which modest fields may substantially alter or reverse the gear ratio.
AI.method: The authors combine magnetohydrodynamics and ferrohydrodynamics with the full Kelvin force and temperature-dependent Langevin magnetisation for the oil-based ferrofluid EFH1, in which the Lorentz force is negligible. Steady torque-free states are computed with Taylor-Hood finite elements, treating the gear ratio Γ as an additional unknown. About 17,000 steady states are calculated across 34 arrangements of wires, NdFeB rods, and magnet cores, with gaps G=0.1–0.7, Re=10–40, and heating of 5–20 K.
AI.result: Without a field, the results agree within 1–8% with published planar simulations up to Re≈50. Fields of 1–2 mT change Γ by an amount comparable to Γ itself, and at 2 mT Γ is reversed, strengthened, or weakened in nine out of ten cases. At the experimental gap and Re=20, a source below the corral or behind the active rotor strengthens gear-like counter-rotation up to 2.7-fold, while a source above the corral reverses it into belt-like corotation. Several sources are non-additive, and a magnet core inside the active rotor raises |Γ| at small gaps to seven times the largest hydrodynamic value. At fixed geometry and Reynolds number, field strength and heating act approximately through a single thermomagnetic source parameter.
AI.conclusion: The hydrodynamic gear coupling is weak enough to be strongly tuned by millitesla-scale non-uniform fields, with the source position determining whether counter-rotation is enhanced or reversed. Magnet-core placement can produce much larger gear ratios, and field strength and heating can be approximately collapsed into one thermomagnetic source parameter at fixed geometry and Reynolds number.

title: Targeted material doping to enable the formation and coherent propagation of Laser Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LIPSS): the ZnO paradigm
summary: This work explores how the initial free carrier density governs the formation and coherent propagation of Low Spatial Frequency Laser-Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LSF-LIPSS). As a paradigm we have analyzed the behavior of ad-hoc-doped ZnO films. ZnO is a multifunctional Transparent Conducting Oxide (TCO) with many scientific and technologic uses including applications in biomedicine, photonics, sensing or photocatalysis. Many of them would benefit from the use of large area, electrically anisotropic surfaces. By introducing small amounts of Yb3+ as donor dopant in ZnO films grown by Pulse Laser Deposition (PLD), we have substantially improved its carrier density at room temperature (RT) and its electrical conductivity while preserving the functional properties of pure ZnO. For RT carrier densities ne > 1019 cm-3, coherent propagation of LSF-LIPSS has been successfully achieved upon irradiation with 350 fs laser pulses at 1030 nm at high repetition rate (500 kHz) and for laser scanning speeds well above 1 m/s. However, the ablation mechanism (ZnO sublimation at the LIPSS valleys) and the large melting temperature of ZnO, make the thermal conductivity of the substrate, the film thickness and the irradiation pulse duration to play a crucial role in determining the morphology of the LSF-LIPPS propagated over large areas, especially in avoiding film cracking. The results achieved upon optimization fully confirm the role of free carrier density in the large-scale propagation of high quality LSF-LIPSS in doped ZnO and enable using these structures to easily generate large electrical anisotropies over macroscopic regions with conductivities along the LIPSS several times larger than transversally.

AI.tldr: Yb3+-doped ZnO films with room-temperature carrier densities above 10^19 cm^-3 enable coherent propagation of low-spatial-frequency laser-induced periodic surface structures under 350 fs, 1030 nm, 500 kHz irradiation at scanning speeds above 1 m/s, producing large-area electrically anisotropic surfaces; morphology and cracking depend on substrate thermal conductivity, film thickness, and pulse duration.
AI.motivation: ZnO is a multifunctional transparent conducting oxide whose applications could benefit from large-area, electrically anisotropic surfaces. The work aims to understand how the initial free carrier density governs the formation and coherent propagation of low-spatial-frequency LIPSS and to enable high-quality structures over macroscopic areas.
AI.method: Small amounts of Yb3+ were introduced as a donor dopant into ZnO films grown by pulsed laser deposition, increasing room-temperature carrier density and electrical conductivity while preserving pure-ZnO functional properties. The films were irradiated with 350 fs pulses at 1030 nm and 500 kHz at laser scanning speeds above 1 m/s. The ablation mechanism, ZnO sublimation at LIPSS valleys, and the high melting temperature of ZnO were considered while optimizing substrate thermal conductivity, film thickness, and pulse duration to control morphology and avoid film cracking.
AI.result: For room-temperature carrier densities ne > 10^19 cm^-3, coherent propagation of low-spatial-frequency LIPSS was achieved. Optimized structures were formed over large areas without film cracking and generated large electrical anisotropies over macroscopic regions, with conductivity along the LIPSS several times larger than transversally. Substrate thermal conductivity, film thickness, and irradiation pulse duration were crucial for the propagated morphology.
AI.conclusion: The initial free carrier density plays a decisive role in the large-scale coherent propagation of high-quality low-spatial-frequency LIPSS in doped ZnO. Targeted Yb3+ doping of ZnO enables these structures to produce large-area electrical anisotropy, providing a practical route to macroscopically anisotropic transparent conducting oxide surfaces.

title: Linear Electrostatic Instabilities Driven by Relativistic Non-Maxwellian Pair Beams
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in Plasma
summary: We investigate how non-Maxwellian momentum distributions affect the linear growth of electrostatic instabilities driven by relativistic pair beams, motivated by the lack of a universally accepted analytical description of blazar-induced pair beams. Different beam distributions are used to describe relativistic pair beams in analytical studies and particle-in-cell simulations. A systematic comparison is therefore needed to determine how the beam distribution influences the instability growth rates. We formulate the relativistic electrostatic response in the weak-beam limit for an anisotropic $κ$-type distribution and compare the resulting growth rates with those obtained for Gaussian and Maxwell--Jüttner distributions. We require $κ>3/2$ for a finite root-mean-square momentum spread. For the parameters considered, the $κ$-type distributions yield higher maximum growth rates than the Gaussian distribution, even when their mean momenta and momentum spreads are the same. The fastest-growing modes correspond to parallel propagation for the $κ$ and Gaussian distributions, whereas the Maxwell--Jüttner distribution exhibits its maximum for oblique propagation for a mildly relativistic beam. An additional calculation for a highly relativistic pair beam with $κ=2$ finds an oblique maximum of the electrostatic growth rate. The beam momentum distribution influences the linear growth of electrostatic instabilities under the conditions investigated.

AI.tldr: The paper compares linear electrostatic instability growth for relativistic pair beams with anisotropic kappa-type, Gaussian, and Maxwell-Jüttner momentum distributions. Kappa distributions can produce higher maximum growth rates than Gaussian distributions with the same mean momentum and spread; propagation direction of the fastest mode depends on distribution and beam relativity.
AI.motivation: There is no universally accepted analytical description of blazar-induced pair beams, and different beam momentum distributions are used in analytical studies and particle-in-cell simulations, so a systematic comparison is needed to determine how the beam distribution affects instability growth rates.
AI.method: The authors formulate the relativistic electrostatic response in the weak-beam limit for an anisotropic kappa-type distribution, requiring kappa > 3/2 for a finite root-mean-square momentum spread, and compare the resulting linear growth rates with those for Gaussian and Maxwell-Jüttner distributions.
AI.result: For the parameters considered, kappa-type distributions yield higher maximum growth rates than the Gaussian distribution even at equal mean momenta and momentum spreads. The fastest-growing modes are parallel-propagating for the kappa and Gaussian distributions, while the Maxwell-Jüttner distribution has an oblique maximum for a mildly relativistic beam. A highly relativistic pair beam with kappa = 2 also has an oblique maximum electrostatic growth rate.
AI.conclusion: The beam momentum distribution influences the linear growth of electrostatic instabilities under the conditions investigated.

title: An Analytic Two-Dimensional Benchmark for Integrated Autocorrelation Times in Branching Monte Carlo Part II: Operator Estimation from Functional Expansion Tallies
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to M&C 2027, the International Conference on Mathematics and Computational Methods Applied to Nuclear Science and Engineering (American Nuclear Society). Part II of two; the companion paper is Part I, submitted separately
summary: Functional expansion tallies can represent transport operators for Monte Carlo correlation prediction without first constructing a fine cell transition matrix. title: Where the Error Lives: Separating Lid-Edge and Body-Induced Error in Neural Pressure Prediction for 3D Cavity Flow
summary: Can a pressure surrogate score much better globally without better resolving the pressure around immersed bodies? We test this in a three-dimensional lid-driven cavity with an unregularized lid and centered pressure at native $128^3$ resolution. On 60 cases from 12 unseen geometries, with predictions sealed before the CFD truth existed, adding a body-free, Reynolds-conditioned reference correction to the same frozen $64^3$ surrogate lifted to $128^3$ lowers the mean full-volume relative $L_2$ error from 20.6% to 7.5%. In the post hoc regional analysis, the lid-edge junction occupies 1.5% of the fluid but holds 69% of the truth pressure energy and 95% of the uncorrected surrogate's squared error. Interior error changes by just +0.16% relative, and object-local peak error and recall change little on average. Retrospective ablations locate the learned term's contribution in the interior and near the bodies; rebasing on the reference lowers global error further with little change in cohort-mean near-body metrics. Reference-relative body-response error remains about 25% in the interior near-body band. Grid-refinement, lid-regularization and convergence checks delimit the numerical scope. In this benchmark, a large global gain chiefly reflects correction of a shared boundary field, not better resolution of the body response. We recommend reporting regional truth-energy and model-error shares alongside near-body and reference-relative body-response errors.

title: Observation of temporal routing of topological edge states
comment: To be published in Phys. Lett. A
summary: The switching or routing of topological edge states is crucial for disorder-immune state transfer. Previous experimental observations have primarily relied on optical waveguide arrays that treat the spatial coordinate as an equivalent temporal dimension. However, direct experimental observation of the routing dynamics of topological edge states in physical time remains challenging. Here, we report the experimental observation of temporal routing of topological edge states. By constructing a lattice composed of two coupled nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chains, the topological edge states exhibit temporal routing behavior controlled by nonlinearity. As the excitation voltage increases from the linear regime, we observe that the voltage intensity distribution transitions from periodic interchain exchange to slowed interchain exchange and ultimately to localization with strongly suppressed interchain exchange, thereby validating the phenomenon of temporal routing. These dynamics are experimentally observed within a finite time window limited by circuit dissipation. Our findings provide valuable insights into the temporal manipulation of topological edge states.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates temporal routing of topological edge states in a lattice of two coupled nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains, where increasing excitation voltage changes interchain dynamics from periodic exchange to slowed exchange and then to strongly suppressed exchange/localization within a dissipation-limited time window.
AI.motivation: Routing and switching of topological edge states are important for disorder-immune state transfer, but prior experimental observations have mainly used optical waveguide arrays that map spatial coordinates onto an effective temporal dimension; direct observation of topological edge-state routing dynamics in physical time remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors construct a lattice composed of two coupled nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains and use the excitation voltage as a control parameter, experimentally observing the voltage intensity distribution and its interchain exchange dynamics in physical time.
AI.result: As the excitation voltage increases from the linear regime, the voltage intensity distribution transitions from periodic interchain exchange to slowed interchain exchange and finally to localization with strongly suppressed interchain exchange, validating temporal routing. These dynamics are observed within a finite time window limited by circuit dissipation.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide experimental insight into temporal manipulation of topological edge states and support nonlinear control of their routing dynamics, while the observation window is constrained by circuit dissipation.

title: Stability of Plasma Echo Growth and the Sharp Sobolev Stability Threshold for the Vlasov--Poisson--Landau Equation
comment: 162 pages. The roadmap of the proof can be found in Appendix C
summary: We establish stability of growing plasma echo cascades for the Vlasov--Poisson--Landau equation with Coulomb collisions near a global Maxwellian. The occurrence of plasma echoes, or even a growing cascade in a reduced model, does not by itself establish this stability. We prove that the amplification persists under changes in the linearized operator, including collisions and the exact evolving background coefficients, and under nonlinear perturbations. This yields optimality of the exponent $1/3$ obtained by Chaturvedi, Luk, and Nguyen in the Sobolev stability threshold. Specifically, we construct solutions with initial Sobolev perturbations of size $ν^{1/3}[\log(1/ν)]^p$ whose transport profiles exhibit norm inflation before the enhanced-dissipation time scale $ν^{-1/3}$. Since collisions preclude the backward Sobolev construction used in collisionless echo arguments, we prepare the initial data at physical time zero and control the entire forward evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper proves stability of growing plasma echo cascades for the Vlasov-Poisson-Landau equation with Coulomb collisions near a global Maxwellian, showing that echo amplification persists under collisions, exact evolving background coefficients, and nonlinear perturbations. It constructs Sobolev perturbations of size ν^{1/3}[log(1/ν)]^p whose transport profiles inflate before the enhanced-dissipation time ν^{-1/3}, establishing optimality of the exponent 1/3 in the Sobolev stability threshold of Chaturvedi, Luk, and Nguyen.
AI.motivation: The occurrence of plasma echoes, or even a growing cascade in a reduced model, does not by itself establish stability. The authors aim to show that echo amplification survives changes in the linearized operator, including Coulomb collisions and the exact evolving background coefficients, as well as nonlinear perturbations, and thereby determine the sharp Sobolev stability threshold.
AI.method: The analysis establishes stability of growing plasma echo cascades for the Vlasov-Poisson-Landau equation with Coulomb collisions near a global Maxwellian. Because collisions preclude the backward Sobolev construction used in collisionless echo arguments, the authors prepare initial data at physical time zero and control the entire forward evolution, including the full linearized operator with collisions, exact evolving background coefficients, and nonlinear perturbations.

title: An Analytic Two-Dimensional Benchmark for Integrated Autocorrelation Times in Branching Monte Carlo Part I: Transport Spectra and Branching Theory
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 0 tables. Submitted to M&C 2027, the International Conference on Mathematics and Computational Methods Applied to Nuclear Science and Engineering (American Nuclear Society). Part I of two; the companion paper is Part II, submitted separately
summary: Predicting correlations between source generations can support uncertainty estimation and variance reduction in Monte Carlo transport. We derive a two-dimensional benchmark for planar isotropic exponential flights in a reflecting square. An image construction gives the exact collision and absorption spectra. Critical branching preserves the mean transport operator but changes mode covariances through the offspring second moment. These covariances give tally autocorrelations and integrated autocorrelation times, with a large-population, finite-window approximation for normalized source tallies. Direct Monte Carlo measurements test the predictions for absorption/rebirth and two-offspring fission. The benchmark provides a reference for assessing reduced correlation models, for correcting reported tally uncertainties, and for checking the tallies of a production code for correlation bias.

AI.method: The authors derive a two-dimensional benchmark for planar isotropic exponential flights in a reflecting square. An image construction provides exact collision and absorption spectra. title: The Akhmediev breather for the Dysthe equation and the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave
summary: In this article we define and compute the breather of the Dysthe equation for deep water waves, the analogue of the Akhmediev breather of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS). When a single pair of modes is unstable, the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave consists of the Stokes wave and the translates and time shifts of a single solution, the breather. The construction uses only gauge and translation invariance, not integrability or a Hamiltonian structure. We use the parameterisation method to find the breather as a power series whose coefficients follow recursively from linear equations. This is not an asymptotic expansion: the series is the Taylor series of the breather itself. For deep water waves we map the envelope amplification over steepness and group length and give a simple formula, based on the linear stability analysis, that summarises it to within a few per cent. Our results agree well with Euler simulations: the edge of the instability band of the Dysthe equation lies much closer to the onset of growth than that of the NLS, and, away from the onset and below breaking, the crest and height amplifications lie less than 5% below the Euler ones.

AI.tldr: The paper defines and computes the Akhmediev-type breather for the Dysthe equation for deep-water waves, shows that it organizes the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave when one mode pair is unstable, and validates its amplification predictions against Euler simulations.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to define and compute the Dysthe-equation analogue of the Akhmediev breather of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation and to characterize the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave for deep-water waves when a single pair of modes is unstable.
AI.method: The breather is constructed using gauge and translation invariance rather than integrability or a Hamiltonian structure. A parameterisation method yields the breather as a power series whose coefficients follow recursively from linear equations; this is the Taylor series of the breather itself, not an asymptotic expansion. Envelope amplification is mapped over steepness and group length, and a simple formula based on linear stability analysis is given.

title: Magnon-Phonon-Polariton Optomechanics in a van der Waals Magnet
summary: The layered anti-ferromagnet CrSBr hosts self-hybridized exciton-polaritons that couple parametrically to coherent magnons and phonons. In this work, we explore the tripartite optomechanical interaction between these quasiparticles in suspended CrSBr membranes supporting high-$Q$ breathing-type acoustic phonon modes. Using resonant pump-probe spectroscopy on the polariton state, we resolve the coupled dynamics in the $\simeq 20$ GHz range while sweeping the magnon mode across the phonon resonance with an external magnetic field. We observe an attractive magnon-phonon interaction of strength $V/2π= -43$ MHz, which primarily leads to phonon amplification. At the magnon-phonon resonance, we find predominantly unidirectional energy flow from magnons to phonons while the possible back-action is limited by kinetic losses of coherent magnons. Our study enables direct interfacing of collective magnetic excitations with sound and light in layered van der Waals materials, paving the way for quantum-coherent transduction in the GHz range with optical readout.

AI.tldr: Resonant pump-probe spectroscopy of self-hybridized exciton-polaritons in suspended CrSBr membranes reveals coupled magnon-phonon-polariton dynamics near 20 GHz; a magnetic field tunes magnons through the phonon resonance, producing an attractive -43 MHz magnon-phonon coupling and predominantly unidirectional magnon-to-phonon energy flow.
AI.motivation: To understand and control tripartite optomechanical interactions among exciton-polaritons, coherent magnons, and acoustic phonons in layered van der Waals magnets, enabling direct light-sound-magnetism interfacing and GHz quantum-coherent transduction with optical readout.
AI.method: The study uses suspended CrSBr membranes supporting high-Q breathing-type acoustic phonon modes and resonant pump-probe spectroscopy on the polariton state. An external magnetic field sweeps the magnon mode across the phonon resonance, resolving coupled dynamics in the approximately 20 GHz range and determining the magnon-phonon interaction strength and energy-flow directionality.
AI.result: An attractive magnon-phonon interaction of strength V/2π = -43 MHz is observed, primarily leading to phonon amplification. At the magnon-phonon resonance, energy flow is predominantly unidirectional from magnons to phonons, while possible back-action is limited by kinetic losses of coherent magnons.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates magnon-phonon-polariton optomechanics in a van der Waals magnet and enables direct interfacing of collective magnetic excitations with sound and light, paving the way for quantum-coherent transduction in the GHz range with optical readout.

title: Radial Evolution of a Corotating Interaction Region from a High-Resolution MHD Simulation
summary: Corotating interaction regions (CIRs) are large-scale structures formed by fast--slow solar wind interaction, playing a crucial role in heliospheric dynamics and space weather. However, the evolution of individual CIRs and their full three-dimensional morphology remain poorly understood. We investigate the radial evolution of a single CIR using a high-resolution simulation combined with a backmapping method. The simulation reproduces the major plasma and magnetic signatures observed by Wind at 1~AU and by MAVEN and Tianwen-1 at $\sim$1.6~AU. The CIR exhibits a warped, shell-like spiral structure tilted relative to the heliospheric current sheet, consistent with theoretical predictions. During its developing stage, geometric changes are modest, and the radial scalings of velocity ($V_r \propto r^{0.02}$), density ($N \propto r^{-2.00}$), magnetic field ($B_{\rm total} \propto r^{-1.74}$), and temperature ($T \propto r^{-0.97}$) are comparable to those of the background solar wind. In the mature stage, the CIR drifts in longitude and expands toward high latitudes, while its longitudinal and latitudinal widths decrease with distance. The full-domain scalings change markedly to $V_r \propto r^{0.13}$, $N \propto r^{-1.91}$, $B_{\rm total} \propto r^{0.35}$, and $T \propto r^{-0.52}$, differing from both the background wind and the ecliptic-plane CIR. This study quantifies the radial evolution of a CIR from formation to maturity and highlights the importance of its three-dimensional structure in characterizing its morphology and dynamics.

AI.tldr: A high-resolution MHD simulation with backmapping tracks a single corotating interaction region from formation to maturity, reproducing multi-spacecraft observations and revealing its warped three-dimensional spiral structure and distance-dependent radial scalings.
AI.motivation: Corotating interaction regions are important for heliospheric dynamics and space weather, but the evolution of individual CIRs and their full three-dimensional morphology remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors use a high-resolution MHD simulation combined with a backmapping method to investigate the radial evolution of a single CIR and compare the simulated plasma and magnetic signatures with observations from Wind at 1 AU and MAVEN and Tianwen-1 at about 1.6 AU.
AI.result: The simulation reproduces the major observed plasma and magnetic signatures. The CIR forms a warped, shell-like spiral structure tilted relative to the heliospheric current sheet. In its developing stage, radial scalings are V_r proportional to r^0.02, N proportional to r^-2.00, B_total proportional to r^-1.74, and T proportional to r^-0.97. title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
summary: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating 95% confidence; their intervals contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, versus 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort, failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes versus 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss. Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. At maximum effort, Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but uses 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. title: A Five-Dimensional Geometric Formulation of Geophysical Fluid Dynamics
summary: We apply a geometric formulation of Newtonian dynamics to inviscid compressible geophysical flow, with gravity and the effects of rotating or moving coordinates incorporated in the metric tensor. This construction relies on the introduction of an auxiliary fifth coordinate, which allows mass and momentum transport, internal energy, and pressure work to be combined into a single mass--momentum tensor. The covariant divergence of this tensor leads to the continuity equation for mass density, the three momentum equations, and the thermodynamic equation, with the system closed by an equation of state. A time-independent metric also yields conservation of total energy. We recover familiar forms of the equations and illustrate the construction in rotating spherical and terrain-following coordinates. The thin-shell and spherical-geopotential approximations, with constant effective gravity, simplify the metric while retaining vertical gravity and the traditional Coriolis terms. Emphasis is placed on the connection between the geometric structure of the formulation and the equations commonly used in atmospheric dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a five-dimensional geometric formulation of inviscid compressible geophysical fluid dynamics in which gravity and rotating or moving coordinates are encoded in the metric tensor. A single mass-momentum tensor combines mass and momentum transport, internal energy, and pressure work; its covariant divergence yields the continuity, momentum, and thermodynamic equations, closed by an equation of state. A time-independent metric gives total energy conservation, and the construction is illustrated in rotating spherical and terrain-following coordinates, including thin-shell and spherical-geopotential approximations.
AI.motivation: To connect the geometric structure of Newtonian dynamics with the equations commonly used in atmospheric dynamics and to unify mass and momentum transport, internal energy, and pressure work within a single geometric framework that incorporates gravity and rotating or moving coordinates.
AI.method: The authors apply a geometric formulation of Newtonian dynamics to inviscid compressible geophysical flow, introducing an auxiliary fifth coordinate and incorporating gravity and coordinate rotation or motion in the metric tensor. They form a mass-momentum tensor whose covariant divergence produces the mass continuity equation, three momentum equations, and the thermodynamic equation, with closure by an equation of state. They also examine conservation properties for a time-independent metric and illustrate the formulation in rotating spherical and terrain-following coordinates, including thin-shell and spherical-geopotential approximations with constant effective gravity.

Simplified metrics retain vertical gravity and traditional Coriolis terms under thin-shell and spherical-geopotential approximations. AI.conclusion: The five-dimensional geometric construction provides a unified representation of inviscid compressible geophysical flow and clarifies the connection between geometric structure and equations commonly used in atmospheric dynamics. title: Probing Phase Fluctuations in Cuprates by Multidimensional Josephson Spectroscopy
summary: The normal state of cuprate superconductors is believed to host precursor electron pairing above the superconducting transition temperature. These pre-formed pairs, which extend over an unknown temperature range, are expected to lack long-range phase coherence. Because spectroscopic evidence for this hypothesis is only indirect, new methods to probe these physics are needed. Nonlinear terahertz spectroscopy allows one to probe high-order time correlation functions and is therefore sensitive to fluctuations. Measurements of third-harmonic generation along the superconducting planes have revealed responses persisting above Tc, but a clear relation between these optical responses and specific properties of the fluctuating state has not yet been established. Here, we apply angle-resolved multidimensional terahertz spectroscopy to probe the optical nonlinearity of the Josephson tunneling resonance in La1.83Sr0.17CuO4 across the superconducting to normal state transition. We find that among all third-order nonlinear responses, the non-rephasing multidimensional signal is especially sensitive to non-mean field fluctuations of the order parameter. We measure a crossover occurring at T ~ Tc between a mean-field optical nonlinearity that dominates at low temperatures and one that is mediated by short-range superconducting fluctuations. We present a theoretical framework that connects the out-of-plane optical response in both regimes to the fluctuating in-plane superconducting state, and contrast the sensitivity of different types of terahertz nonlinearities to fluctuating order.

AI.tldr: Angle-resolved multidimensional terahertz spectroscopy probes the Josephson tunneling resonance in La1.83Sr0.17CuO4, showing that the non-rephasing third-order nonlinear response is especially sensitive to non-mean-field order-parameter fluctuations and revealing a crossover near Tc from mean-field-dominated nonlinearity to short-range superconducting-fluctuation-mediated nonlinearity.
AI.motivation: The normal state of cuprate superconductors is thought to contain precursor electron pairing above Tc, but evidence is indirect and the temperature range of pre-formed pairs is unknown. Existing third-harmonic-generation measurements show responses above Tc, yet their relation to the fluctuating state is unclear, motivating methods sensitive to high-order time correlations and fluctuations.
AI.method: The authors apply angle-resolved multidimensional terahertz spectroscopy to measure third-order optical nonlinearities of the Josephson tunneling resonance in La1.83Sr0.17CuO4 across the superconducting-to-normal transition. They identify the non-rephasing multidimensional signal as especially sensitive to non-mean-field order-parameter fluctuations and develop a theoretical framework linking the out-of-plane optical response to the fluctuating in-plane superconducting state.
AI.result: Among the third-order nonlinear responses, the non-rephasing multidimensional signal is especially sensitive to non-mean-field fluctuations of the order parameter. A crossover occurs at T ~ Tc between a mean-field optical nonlinearity dominant at low temperatures and a nonlinearity mediated by short-range superconducting fluctuations. The theoretical framework connects the out-of-plane optical response in both regimes to the fluctuating in-plane superconducting state and contrasts the sensitivity of different terahertz nonlinearities to fluctuating order.
AI.conclusion: Multidimensional Josephson spectroscopy provides a sensitive probe of phase fluctuations and fluctuating order in cuprates, establishing a link between terahertz nonlinear optical responses and the fluctuating in-plane superconducting state across the superconducting-to-normal transition. The abstract does not provide further quantitative details or a specified temperature range for precursor pairing.

title: Drift of a Charged Particle in a Black Hole Magnetosphere: the Effect of Black Hole Spin
summary: Sparse plasma immersed in a strong magnetic field is common in astrophysical scenarios, for which a collisionless description is more appropriate. The guiding-center approximation serves as an effective tool for describing the motion of charged particles in a strong magnetic field, revealing the drift, a sub-leading order motion that causes particles to deviate from the magnetic field lines. It is widely accepted that the charged particles drift under the induction of gravity in Newtonian framework. However, a covariant formulation of the guiding-center approximation, as well as the drift of a charged particle induced by strong gravitational field, has yet to be fully explored. As a preliminary study, we aim to analyze the drift of a single charged particle in a black hole magnetosphere via a covariant approach. Particularly, we focus on the effects of black hole spin. We first examine the drift caused by the rotation of a massive object in the Newtonian regime using the language of gravitoelectromagnetism. A covariant formula of drift is derived, which is confirmed to reduce to the Newtonian results in the weak gravitational field and low speed limit. The impact of BH spin on the drift is analyzed in detail in Kerr spacetime specifically, for which we define the drift rate whose value quantifies the significance of the drift. Our results indicate that the impact of BH spin on the drift of a charged particle in a BH magnetosphere can be comparable to that of other factors in some extreme cases.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a covariant guiding-center treatment of charged-particle drift in a black hole magnetosphere, derives a drift formula that reduces to Newtonian gravitoelectromagnetic results, and shows in Kerr spacetime that black hole spin can significantly affect the drift in extreme cases.
AI.motivation: Sparse strongly magnetized astrophysical plasmas require collisionless descriptions, and the guiding-center approximation is useful for charged-particle motion. Although gravitational drift is known in Newtonian theory, a covariant guiding-center formulation and the drift induced by strong gravity remain insufficiently explored; this preliminary study focuses on black hole spin effects.
AI.method: The authors analyze a single charged particle in a black hole magnetosphere using a covariant approach. They first study drift due to rotation of a massive object in the Newtonian regime via gravitoelectromagnetism, derive a covariant drift formula, verify its reduction to Newtonian results in the weak-field and low-speed limit, and then analyze Kerr spacetime in detail, defining a drift rate to quantify drift significance.
AI.result: The derived covariant drift formula reduces to the Newtonian results in the weak-gravitational-field and low-speed limit. In Kerr spacetime, the impact of black hole spin on the drift of a charged particle in a black hole magnetosphere can be comparable to that of other factors in some extreme cases.
AI.conclusion: Black hole spin can be an important influence on charged-particle drift in black hole magnetospheres in extreme regimes. The work provides a preliminary covariant guiding-center framework, but further details beyond those in the abstract are not provided.

title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
comment: Accepted for NeurIPS 2026. The first two authors contributed equally. 41 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Code is available at https://github.com/MinchanJeong/NestedLoRA-VMC
summary: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NestedLoRA-VMC, a neural-network variational Monte Carlo method for quantum excited states that uses a low-rank reparameterization of a rank-K variational objective, MCMC-based stochastic gradients, and sequential nesting to recover the lowest K eigenstates. On Li–Ne at K=10, its accuracy is comparable to NES-VMC and a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.
AI.motivation: Solving the electronic Schrödinger equation scales exponentially with electron number, and extending neural-network VMC from ground states to excited states is limited by existing paradigms: penalty-based methods require tuning overlap-penalty weights against unknown energy gaps, while NES-VMC avoids penalties but requires K^2 Laplacians per step. The work aims to resolve this trade-off.
AI.method: The authors apply a low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization to the rank-K variational excited-state objective. The reparameterized objective supports a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator using MCMC sampling from per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest K eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm is NestedLoRA-VMC and inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle.
AI.result: On the first-row atoms Li through Ne with K=10, NestedLoRA-VMC achieves accuracy comparable to NES-VMC and to a state-of-the-art penalty-based method. The abstract does not provide numerical energy errors, computational timings, or scaling measurements.
AI.conclusion: NestedLoRA-VMC provides a penalty-free, LoRA-based variational Monte Carlo approach for excited states with a global optimality guarantee and competitive accuracy on Li–Ne. The abstract does not establish a measured computational-cost advantage over the compared methods.

title: A quantitative measure of predictability for surface gravity waves
summary: We introduce a Bayesian inference framework to characterize the predictability of a one dimensional ocean surface wave field given surface elevation measurements from a sensor. Unlike the classical theories that only sketch the boundary of a predictable zone based on group velocity, we use the Bayesian posterior uncertainty of surface elevation to quantify the local predictability at every spatiotemporal location. Our approach first constructs a prior distribution to encode existing knowledge of the wave field such as the spectrum and propagation direction. By conditioning on the (possibly noisy) measurement data, we infer the posterior distribution of the wave field, from which a spatiotemporal uncertainty map is extracted. This map agrees well with the group-velocity-based classical predictable zone theory when the frequency spectrum has bounded support. Meanwhile, it also demonstrates predictability even for a spectrum with unbounded frequency support where the classical predictable zone degenerates. A refined analysis of posterior uncertainty using observability Gramian matrix reveals a `data-informed' part and an `un-informed' part of the wave field, with the latter being fundamentally un-predictable. Furthermore, nonlinear effects can be naturally introduced into the Bayesian framework by incorporating the nonlinear ocean surface wave equations. This is the first time that nonlinearity is rigorously treated in the predictable zone problem. We perform numerical tests using both bounded, piecewise constant spectrum and unbounded JONSWAP spectrum. The numerical results confirm the proposed advantages of our method for linear waves and reveal how wave steepness affects the predictability of nonlinear waves. Nonlinear modal interactions redistribute uncertainty between the inside and the outside of the predictable zone with an amount proportional to the wave steepness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Bayesian inference framework that quantifies local spatiotemporal predictability of a one-dimensional ocean surface gravity wave field from surface elevation measurements, including nonlinear effects.
AI.motivation: Classical predictable-zone theories use group velocity only to sketch the boundary of a predictable region and do not provide a local quantitative predictability measure. Nonlinearity had not been rigorously treated in the predictable-zone problem.
AI.method: A prior distribution encodes wave-field knowledge such as spectrum and propagation direction. Conditioning on possibly noisy surface elevation measurements yields a posterior distribution and a spatiotemporal uncertainty map. Posterior uncertainty is analyzed with an observability Gramian matrix, and nonlinear ocean surface wave equations are incorporated into the Bayesian framework.
AI.result: The uncertainty map agrees with group-velocity-based predictable-zone theory for bounded frequency spectra and indicates predictability for an unbounded JONSWAP spectrum where the classical predictable zone degenerates. The Gramian analysis identifies data-informed and fundamentally uninformed wave-field components. Numerical tests with bounded piecewise-constant and unbounded JONSWAP spectra confirm advantages for linear waves and show that wave steepness affects nonlinear predictability; nonlinear modal interactions redistribute uncertainty across the predictable-zone boundary in proportion to wave steepness.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian posterior-uncertainty approach provides a quantitative local measure of surface gravity wave predictability and is claimed to be the first rigorous treatment of nonlinearity in the predictable-zone problem.

title: Quantitative Theory for the Amplitude of Fluorescence Quantum Beats from Geminate Triplet-Pair Fusion
summary: We derive the amplitude of fluorescence quantum beats caused by geminate triplet-exciton fusion from the full set of parameters that characterize singlet fission and triplet exciton dynamics. We apply the theory to tetracene and rubrene single crystals. We find that the amplitude depends on the fission time in tetracene, but does not do so in rubrene, where it is determined by the dimensionality of triplet transport. Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the experimental data in both materials, for a fission time of the order of 200 ps and isotropic triplet transport in tetracene, and for a triplet hopping time along the herringbone axis of 200-300 ps and anisotropic transport in rubrene.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a quantitative theory for fluorescence quantum-beat amplitudes arising from geminate triplet-pair fusion and tests it against tetracene and rubrene single-crystal data using kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively relate fluorescence quantum-beat amplitudes to the full set of singlet-fission and triplet-exciton dynamical parameters.
AI.method: The authors derive the quantum-beat amplitude from singlet-fission and triplet-exciton parameters, apply the theory to tetracene and rubrene single crystals, and compare it with kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of triplet transport and fusion.
AI.result: The beat amplitude depends on fission time in tetracene but not in rubrene, where it is governed by the dimensionality of triplet transport. The data are reproduced with a fission time of order 200 ps and isotropic triplet transport in tetracene, and with a 200–300 ps triplet hopping time along the herringbone axis and anisotropic transport in rubrene.
