AI.conclusion: The derived theory and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations quantitatively reproduce the experimental fluorescence quantum-beat data in both tetracene and rubrene, linking beat amplitudes to material-specific singlet-fission and triplet-transport dynamics.

title: Control variates with neural surrogates for uncertainty quantification in kinetic equations
summary: Efficient uncertainty quantification for kinetic equations with random inputs is challenging because it requires repeated simulations of high-dimensional models, such as the Boltzmann, Landau, and related collisional equations, whose computational cost can quickly become prohibitive. Multifidelity control variates address this difficulty by coupling a small number of high-fidelity simulations with many evaluations of lower-complexity reduced models. In this work, we analyze the case in which the reduced model is replaced by a neural surrogate rather than evaluated through a classical numerical scheme. We show that the resulting estimator remains unbiased and that the change in the optimal variance induced by the neural approximation is controlled by the error between the exact low-fidelity observable and its neural approximation. This estimate is then combined with residual stability estimates for inhomogeneous Fokker--Planck and Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook surrogates. We also extend the analysis to several control variates and to an asymptotic-preserving (AP) hierarchy containing the limiting Euler observable. In the fluid limit, the optimal hierarchical variance converges to the variance associated with the limiting Euler control, while the contribution of the intermediate kinetic correction vanishes. Numerical tests based on micro--macro neural surrogates illustrate the predicted variance stability and the behavior of the AP hierarchy.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes multifidelity control-variate estimators for uncertainty quantification in kinetic equations when the low-fidelity reduced model is replaced by a neural surrogate. It establishes unbiasedness and bounds the induced change in optimal variance by the surrogate approximation error, extends the analysis to multiple control variates and an asymptotic-preserving hierarchy with an Euler fluid limit, and illustrates the theory with micro–macro neural surrogate tests.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification for kinetic equations with random inputs is computationally demanding because it requires repeated simulations of high-dimensional collisional models such as the Boltzmann, Landau, and related equations. Multifidelity control variates reduce this cost by combining a few high-fidelity simulations with many evaluations of cheaper reduced models; the paper addresses the theoretical gap when such reduced models are neural surrogates rather than classical numerical approximations.
AI.method: The authors analyze a multifidelity control-variate estimator in which the low-fidelity model is a neural surrogate. They prove unbiasedness and derive a bound showing that the change in optimal variance caused by the neural approximation is controlled by the error between the exact low-fidelity observable and its neural approximation. This estimate is combined with residual stability estimates for inhomogeneous Fokker–Planck and Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook surrogates. The analysis is extended to several control variates and to an asymptotic-preserving hierarchy containing the limiting Euler observable. Numerical tests use micro–macro neural surrogates.
AI.result: The estimator remains unbiased when the reduced model is replaced by a neural surrogate. The change in optimal variance is controlled by the neural surrogate approximation error. Residual stability estimates are obtained for inhomogeneous Fokker–Planck and Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook surrogates. For multiple control variates and the asymptotic-preserving hierarchy, the fluid-limit analysis shows that the optimal hierarchical variance converges to the variance associated with the limiting Euler control, while the contribution of the intermediate kinetic correction vanishes. Numerical tests illustrate the predicted variance stability and the behavior of the asymptotic-preserving hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: Neural surrogates can be incorporated into multifidelity control variates for kinetic uncertainty quantification while preserving unbiasedness and keeping the variance degradation controlled by surrogate error. The theory covers multiple control variates and an asymptotic-preserving hierarchy whose fluid limit recovers the Euler-control variance. The abstract does not provide specific quantitative numerical error or speedup values.

title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
comment: 115 pages, many figures. Based on lectures given at Queen Mary University of London
summary:
These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly.
  The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students.
  The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

AI.tldr: Introductory lecture notes that teach modern machine learning and deep learning to physics and mathematics students using physical intuition, progressing from linear regression and gradient descent to neural networks, Transformers, and large language models.
AI.motivation: The author, a physicist, wanted to provide a self-contained and intuitive route into modern machine learning for readers with physics or mathematics backgrounds, and the notes respond to student requests for greater emphasis on large language models.
AI.method: The paper is a set of pedagogical lecture notes rather than a novel research study. It explains concepts from scratch using physical intuition, beginning with maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression, and stochastic gradient descent, then covering neural networks, backpropagation, vanishing gradients, normalization, regularization, adversarial examples, kernel methods, word embeddings, recurrent networks, LSTMs, attention, Transformers, and large language models.
AI.result: The notes provide broad introductory coverage of deep learning and natural language processing, including scaling laws, GPT history, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning, and test-time scaling. No empirical results or originality are claimed.
AI.conclusion: The notes are intended as a coherent, accessible introduction for third- and fourth-year students and readers from other departments, with basic material explained from scratch. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, although the emphasized basic ideas are expected to remain relevant.

title: Ship-as-a-buoy for Phase-resolved Reconstruction of Surface Waves
summary: We develop a data assimilation framework to address the ``ship-as-a-buoy'' problem, i.e., estimation of the wave field from time series of ship motion. Unlike previous algorithms which only provide information of wave spectrum, our approach reconstructs the instantaneous phase-resolved wave field. The full framework includes two steps: the first step to generate an initial (rough) estimation of the wave field using the response-amplitude-operators (RAOs), and the second step to refine the reconstruction using an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) to incorporate the measured motion time series. Together with EnKF in the second step, we model the coupled wave-ship dynamics by a high-order spectral (HOS) method for waves and a Cummins equation for ship motion (although higher-fidelity ship model can be applied). We conduct extensive tests of our method for the case with one ship, and the naturally extended cases with multiple ships or with uncertain parameters in the ship motion model. For all test cases we demonstrate favorable reconstruction of the wave field, which in general further improves with the number of ships available and with uncertain parameters properly estimated. We also provide insights on the successful reconstruction in terms of ensemble correlations between the motion time series and features of the wave field.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a two-step data assimilation framework for the 'ship-as-a-buoy' problem, reconstructing the instantaneous phase-resolved wave field from ship motion time series rather than only wave spectra. It first uses response-amplitude operators (RAOs) for a rough estimate, then refines it with an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) using measured motions and coupled wave-ship dynamics modeled by a high-order spectral (HOS) method and the Cummins equation. Tests with one ship, multiple ships, and uncertain ship-motion parameters show favorable reconstruction, generally improving with more ships and with proper parameter estimation.
AI.motivation: Previous algorithms for estimating waves from ship motion provide only wave-spectrum information. This work aims to reconstruct the instantaneous phase-resolved wave field from time series of ship motion, addressing the 'ship-as-a-buoy' problem.
AI.method: The framework has two steps: (1) generate an initial rough wave-field estimate using response-amplitude operators (RAOs); (2) refine the reconstruction with an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) incorporating measured motion time series. Coupled wave-ship dynamics are modeled using a high-order spectral (HOS) method for waves and the Cummins equation for ship motion, though a higher-fidelity ship model can be applied. Tests cover one ship, multiple ships, and uncertain parameters in the ship motion model.
AI.result: For all test cases, the method demonstrates favorable reconstruction of the wave field. Reconstruction generally improves as the number of ships increases and when uncertain parameters are properly estimated. The paper also provides insights into successful reconstruction through ensemble correlations between motion time series and wave-field features.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data assimilation framework successfully addresses the ship-as-a-buoy problem by reconstructing a phase-resolved wave field from ship motion. It supports naturally extended cases with multiple ships and uncertain ship-motion parameters, and the modeling approach can accommodate higher-fidelity ship models.

title: Modular Programmable Photonics with Unitary Tiles
summary: Programmable photonics provides a versatile platform for optical information processing, but extending programmable transformations to large numbers of optical modes remains challenging. We investigate a modular architecture composed of unitary tiles arranged in alternating and staggered columns. Each physical tile interlaces fixed multiport mixers with programmable phase shifts, confining individual mixing operations to small groups of modes while connecting them across a larger processor. We analyze the relationship between circuit depth, intertile connectivity, and attainable transformations, distinguishing ideal programmable tiles from their physical phase-stack implementations. Numerical target-fitting results show a transition in the reconstruction errors at $R = 2K$, where $K$ and $R$ are the number of tile rows and columns, respectively. This design ultimately aims to enable large and reliable port-count optical photonic processors.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a modular programmable photonic architecture made of unitary tiles with fixed multiport mixers and programmable phase shifts, analyzing how circuit depth and intertile connectivity affect attainable transformations and finding a reconstruction-error transition at R = 2K.
AI.motivation: Programmable photonics is a versatile platform for optical information processing, but scaling programmable transformations to large numbers of optical modes remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors investigate unitary tiles arranged in alternating and staggered columns. Each tile interlaces fixed multiport mixers with programmable phase shifts, confining mixing operations to small mode groups while connecting them across a larger processor. They analyze circuit depth, intertile connectivity, and attainable transformations, distinguishing ideal programmable tiles from physical phase-stack implementations, and perform numerical target fitting.
AI.result: Numerical target-fitting results show a transition in reconstruction errors at R = 2K, where K is the number of tile rows and R is the number of tile columns.
AI.conclusion: The modular unitary-tile design ultimately aims to enable large and reliable port-count optical photonic processors.

title: Interaction Landscapes of Structurally Distorted Toroidal Classical Spin Textures
comment: to appear in Adv. Theory Simul
summary: We develop a classical discrete magnetostatic model of localized magnetic moments arranged in a toroidal texture, where the moments are represented by static current loops and study the behavior of the magnetic dipole-dipole interaction under several types of structural deformations. The purpose is to disentangle effects due to geometric and magnetic deformations, including elliptical, lopsided, alternating, and tilted configurations. In particular, we investigate how distortions modify the toroidal moment and the interaction energy between pairs of toroidal structures. The resulting interaction landscapes exhibit characteristic symmetry patterns and anisotropies that are highly sensitive to the underlying deformation. As a separate proof-of-concept comparison, first-principles calculations on a molecular spin-toroidal system reveal qualitatively similar orientation-dependent behavior. The calculated interaction is microscopically the conventional pairwise magnetic dipole-dipole interaction between localized moments arranged in a spin-toroidal texture; the toroidal moment characterizes the collective texture and should not be interpreted as introducing an additional elementary interaction term. Our results provide a platform for exploring orientation-dependent interactions of spin-toroidal textures in molecular magnets and related nanoscale magnetic systems that are essential to understand the role of toroidal order.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a classical discrete magnetostatic model of toroidal magnetic textures built from static current loops and maps how elliptical, lopsided, alternating, and tilted structural deformations reshape the toroidal moment and pairwise magnetic dipole-dipole interaction landscapes. A first-principles molecular spin-toroidal comparison shows qualitatively similar orientation-dependent behavior.
AI.motivation: The study aims to disentangle geometric and magnetic deformation effects and to understand orientation-dependent interactions of spin-toroidal textures relevant to molecular magnets and related nanoscale magnetic systems.
AI.method: Localized magnetic moments in a toroidal texture are represented by static current loops in a classical discrete magnetostatic model. The magnetic dipole-dipole interaction is evaluated for several structural deformations, including elliptical, lopsided, alternating, and tilted configurations, and compared with first-principles calculations on a molecular spin-toroidal system as a proof of concept.
AI.result: Distortions modify the toroidal moment and the interaction energy between toroidal structures, producing characteristic symmetry patterns and anisotropies that are highly sensitive to the underlying deformation. The first-principles molecular calculations reveal qualitatively similar orientation-dependent behavior. The interaction remains microscopically the conventional pairwise magnetic dipole-dipole interaction, with the toroidal moment characterizing the collective texture rather than adding an elementary interaction term.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a platform for exploring orientation-dependent interactions of spin-toroidal textures in molecular magnets and related nanoscale magnetic systems, supporting understanding of the role of toroidal order.

title: Self-similarity of axisymmetric Marangoni flows on a deep viscous subphase
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: Local gradients of surface tension caused by inhomogeneous distributions of surfactant molecules are known to generate Marangoni flows, the mechanics of which have important consequences in various areas of science and engineering. In this paper, we investigate the deposition of insoluble surfactants on the surface of a deep, viscous subphase, which propagate axisymmetrically without diffusing. We study these flows from the perspective of self-similarity, i.e., seeking solutions which show universal features on appropriate length and time scales. We first present a closed form, self-similar solution of the first kind for the axisymmetric spreading of surfactants, which is globally valid at long times. We then numerically study `filling' flows of surfactant, where the surfactant distribution is locally depleted such that inward flows are generated to `fill' the surfactant-free area. These flows have the special feature of forming cusp-like structure in finite time, which have been studied extensively in the literature of self-similarity of the second kind. We show that these flows admit a countably infinite number of stable similarity solutions based on the local behavior of the initial surfactant concentration profile. We remark on a few unique features of these results in contrast to filling flows in other physical limits.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes axisymmetric Marangoni flows produced by insoluble surfactant deposition on a deep viscous subphase, deriving a closed-form first-kind self-similar spreading solution and numerically showing that surfactant-filling flows form finite-time cusps and admit a countably infinite family of stable similarity solutions determined by the local initial surfactant profile.
AI.motivation: Surface-tension gradients from inhomogeneous surfactant distributions generate Marangoni flows with important scientific and engineering consequences. The authors aim to characterize axisymmetric, non-diffusing surfactant spreading on a deep viscous subphase through self-similarity and universal length- and time-scale features.
AI.method: The authors seek self-similar solutions for axisymmetric surfactant spreading. They derive a closed-form first-kind similarity solution valid globally at long times, then numerically study filling flows in which local surfactant depletion drives inward flow. They analyze finite-time cusp formation and the stability and multiplicity of second-kind similarity solutions as functions of the local initial surfactant concentration profile, contrasting the results with filling flows in other physical limits.
AI.result: A closed-form first-kind self-similar solution is obtained for axisymmetric surfactant spreading and is globally valid at long times. Filling flows develop cusp-like structures in finite time and admit a countably infinite number of stable similarity solutions based on the local behavior of the initial surfactant concentration profile. The authors identify distinctive features relative to filling flows in other physical limits.
AI.conclusion: Self-similarity provides a framework for describing axisymmetric Marangoni spreading and filling flows on a deep viscous subphase. The filling regime exhibits finite-time cusp formation and a countably infinite set of stable similarity solutions, with features that differ from related filling flows in other physical limits. The abstract does not establish a connection to intense lasers or laser–plasma physics.

title: Spectral integral method for reflection and transmission by one-dimensional periodic arrays of penetrable cylinders
summary: The spectral integral method (SIM) is extended from a single cylinder to an infinite one-dimensional (1-D) periodic array (a grating) of identical, homogeneous, arbitrarily shaped smooth cylinders. The cylinders may be dielectric or metallic with complex electrical permittivity. Interactions among all members of the array are carried exactly by the 1-D quasi-periodic Green's function, Gp, in the exterior boundary integral equation, so only the boundary of one reference cylinder is discretized. Gp is written as the free-space Green's function plus a regular part that is infinitely differentiable on the reference cylinder whenever the cylinders do not touch. The regular part and its gradient are evaluated with Ewald's method. Floquet reflection and transmission amplitudes, as well as reflectance, transmittance, and absorptance, are obtained from the boundary data. For the analytic boundaries and numerical examples considered here, the SIM exhibits root-exponential convergence in N for glass and gold gratings, where N is the number of samples on the boundary, for both polarizations, at oblique incidence and with several diffraction orders. Several numerical examples are provided.

AI.tldr: The spectral integral method is extended to infinite one-dimensional periodic arrays of penetrable cylinders, using a quasi-periodic Green's function evaluated by Ewald's method to compute Floquet reflection, transmission, and absorption with root-exponential convergence in boundary samples for the tested glass and gold gratings.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state a separate motivation; the work extends the spectral integral method from a single cylinder to an infinite one-dimensional grating of identical, homogeneous, arbitrarily shaped smooth dielectric or metallic cylinders, treating all inter-cylinder interactions exactly while discretizing only one reference cylinder.
AI.method: The spectral integral method is extended to a one-dimensional periodic array of identical homogeneous smooth cylinders with arbitrary shape and complex permittivity. A one-dimensional quasi-periodic Green's function, written as the free-space Green's function plus a regular part and evaluated with Ewald's method, is used in the exterior boundary integral equation. Only the boundary of one reference cylinder is discretized. Floquet reflection and transmission amplitudes, reflectance, transmittance, and absorptance are obtained from the boundary data.
AI.result: For the analytic boundaries and numerical examples considered, the spectral integral method exhibits root-exponential convergence in N, the number of boundary samples, for glass and gold gratings, for both polarizations, at oblique incidence, and with several diffraction orders. Several numerical examples are provided.
AI.conclusion: The spectral integral method is applicable to reflection and transmission by one-dimensional periodic arrays of penetrable cylinders in the studied cases, with exact inter-cylinder interactions carried by the quasi-periodic Green's function and discretization limited to one reference cylinder. The reported convergence is root-exponential in N for the analytic boundaries and examples considered; broader claims are not provided in the abstract.

title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS
summary: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

AI.tldr: A hybrid MPI/OpenMP implementation enables large-scale Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion machine-learning potentials in LAMMPS, demonstrated on Hf–Ti free energies and Zr segregation in nanocrystalline Cu.
AI.motivation: MCMD simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because machine-learning interatomic potentials are impractical at this scale in existing implementations; the work aims to make ACE-potential MCMD practical at microstructure length scales.
AI.method: The paper introduces a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with ACE potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and distributed over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized with OpenMP threads. It is demonstrated by HCP/BCC free-energy calculations in strongly anharmonic Hf–Ti and by simulating Zr segregation in a 670,000-atom nanocrystalline Cu sample, including comparison of ACE and empirical Cu–Zr potentials.
AI.result: At a fixed number of CPUs, Monte Carlo wall time decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks; larger simulation cells reduce free-energy statistical errors because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. The Hf–Ti free energies are calculated, and for Cu–Zr the ACE and empirical potentials predict similar grain-boundary compositions but different amounts of Zr dissolved in the grains. Absolute runtimes are not provided.
AI.conclusion: The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at microstructure length scales, enabled by the hybrid parallelization and demonstrated on anharmonic free-energy and nanocrystalline segregation problems.

title: Graph Neural Network based non-local models: Toward application to RANS turbulence modeling
summary: Most machine-learning closures for the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations are local, predicting the closure quantities at each point solely from local flow features, despite the non-local nature of turbulent interactions. We propose a non-local closure framework based on Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) that exploits the mesh connectivity. Each finite-volume cell becomes a graph node, and cells sharing a face are connected by an edge. Through message passing, each layer aggregates information from neighboring nodes, so that after $k$ layers the prediction at a cell depends on its $k$-hop neighborhood, which naturally accounts for non-local effects. To make training feasible when each simulation yields a single large graph, we also introduce a breadth-first-search $k$-hop subgraph sampling strategy, which acts as data augmentation and cuts the cost per processed graph during training. We compare GCNs with feed-forward networks (FNNs) of equal size on two periodic-hills benchmarks: a laminar advection-diffusion transport problem that mimics the non-local character of RANS closures, and the turbulent eddy-viscosity prediction of the Closure Challenge dataset at $Re = 5600$. In the laminar case, FNNs are accurate only within the training regime and with sufficiently informative inputs, whereas GCNs generalize better to unseen geometries, including out-of-distribution flows, and partly compensate for missing input features. In the turbulent proof-of-concept case, the graph-based models achieve modest but consistent improvements compared to FNNs, supporting GCNs as a promising route to non-local RANS closures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a graph-convolutional, non-local closure framework for RANS turbulence modeling, using mesh-based message passing and breadth-first-search k-hop subgraph sampling. It compares GCNs with equal-size feed-forward networks on laminar and turbulent periodic-hills benchmarks, finding better generalization in the laminar case and modest consistent gains in turbulent eddy-viscosity prediction.
AI.motivation: Most machine-learning closures for the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations are local, predicting closure quantities at each point only from local flow features, even though turbulent interactions are non-local. The work aims to build a closure framework that naturally represents and exploits non-local spatial dependence.
AI.method: Each finite-volume cell is represented as a graph node, and cells sharing a face are connected by an edge. Graph Convolutional Networks perform message passing so that after k layers a cell prediction depends on its k-hop neighborhood. To train on simulations that each produce one large graph, the authors introduce a breadth-first-search k-hop subgraph sampling strategy that serves as data augmentation and reduces per-graph training cost. Equal-size GCNs and feed-forward networks are compared on two periodic-hills benchmarks: a laminar advection-diffusion transport problem and turbulent eddy-viscosity prediction using the Closure Challenge dataset at Re = 5600.
AI.result: In the laminar case, feed-forward networks are accurate only within the training regime and with sufficiently informative inputs, whereas GCNs generalize better to unseen geometries, including out-of-distribution flows, and partly compensate for missing input features. In the turbulent proof-of-concept case, graph-based models achieve modest but consistent improvements over feed-forward networks.
AI.conclusion: The results support GCN-based non-local closures as a promising route toward RANS turbulence modeling, with the turbulent evidence described as a proof of concept rather than a comprehensive validation.

title: Windowed Singularity Subtraction for the Spectral Integral Method
summary: In 2004, the spectral integral method (SIM) was proposed to solve TM$_z$ scattering by homogeneous two-dimensional dielectric objects and perfect electrical conductors with smooth boundaries. Its error decreases exponentially as the number of boundary points increases linearly. Plasmonic resonances, however, require TE$_z$ polarization and permittivities with a negative real part. The extension of SIM to this case shows that the original global singularity subtraction suffers catastrophic cancellation, with a round-off floor that grows exponentially with the attenuation accumulated across the object. To resolve this issue, this work introduces a windowed singularity subtraction that limits this cancellation amplification to an exponential factor that the user can set independently of the object size, provided the window is adequately resolved. Numerical results verify the accuracy of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the spectral integral method (SIM) from TM$_z$ scattering to TE$_z$ plasmonic-resonance problems, where the original global singularity subtraction suffers catastrophic cancellation. It proposes windowed singularity subtraction that bounds cancellation amplification by a user-selected exponential factor independent of object size, provided the window is adequately resolved, and numerical results verify the method's accuracy.
AI.motivation: SIM was originally proposed for TM$_z$ scattering by homogeneous two-dimensional dielectric objects and perfect electrical conductors with smooth boundaries, with exponential error reduction as boundary points increase linearly. Plasmonic resonances require TE$_z$ polarization and permittivities with a negative real part; extending SIM to this case reveals catastrophic cancellation in the original global singularity subtraction, with a round-off floor growing exponentially with attenuation across the object.
AI.method: The work introduces a windowed singularity subtraction for the spectral integral method. It limits cancellation amplification to an exponential factor that the user can set independently of the object size, provided the window is adequately resolved.
AI.result: Numerical results verify the accuracy of the proposed windowed singularity subtraction method. The abstract does not provide quantitative error levels, convergence rates, or specific test geometries.
AI.conclusion: Windowed singularity subtraction addresses the catastrophic cancellation and exponentially growing round-off floor encountered when extending SIM to TE$_z$ plasmonic-resonance problems. The abstract reports numerical verification of accuracy but gives no further performance or applicability details.

title: A Hierarchically Compressed Immittance Operator Formulation for Fast Statics-to-Full-Wave Electromagnetic Simulation with the Boundary Element Method
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation
summary: The boundary element method allows the electromagnetic simulation of three-dimensional problems with a two-dimensional discretization, using a surface integral representation of Maxwell's equations. For applications involving broadband simulations or multiscale geometries, the well-known low-frequency breakdown of conventional integral equation formulations must be addressed, while ensuring that dielectric, semiconducting, and lossy metallic regions are modeled rigorously, including the skin effect. In this work, a new boundary element formulation based on an immittance operator is proposed, where the underlying integral equations are inherently valid from statics to the full-wave regime. To enable efficient matrix assembly and solution, a hierarchical matrix compression strategy is devised, leveraging fast direct factorization as an intermediate step, and fast matrix-vector products for the iterative solution of the final system of equations. The proposed formulation is capable of electrostatic, magnetostatic, quasistatic, and full-wave simulations of dielectrics, semiconductors, and lossy metals. Representative numerical examples drawn from a variety of applications demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a boundary element method formulation using an immittance operator that remains valid from statics to the full-wave regime, combined with hierarchical matrix compression, fast direct factorization, and fast matrix-vector products to enable efficient electromagnetic simulation of dielectric, semiconducting, and lossy metallic structures.
AI.motivation: Conventional boundary element integral equation formulations suffer from low-frequency breakdown in broadband or multiscale electromagnetic simulations. A formulation is needed that remains valid from statics to full-wave while rigorously modeling dielectric, semiconducting, and lossy metallic regions, including the skin effect.
AI.method: A new boundary element formulation based on an immittance operator is introduced, with underlying integral equations inherently valid from statics to the full-wave regime. For efficient matrix assembly and solution, the authors devise a hierarchical matrix compression strategy, use fast direct factorization as an intermediate step, and employ fast matrix-vector products for iterative solution of the final system.
AI.result: The formulation supports electrostatic, magnetostatic, quasistatic, and full-wave simulations of dielectrics, semiconductors, and lossy metals. Representative numerical examples from various applications demonstrate accuracy and efficiency. Specific quantitative performance metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchically compressed immittance operator boundary element formulation enables rigorous statics-to-full-wave electromagnetic simulation and efficient matrix assembly and solution. The abstract reports demonstrated accuracy and efficiency but does not provide detailed numerical comparisons or complexity figures.

title: What explainable deep learning reveals about wall-bounded turbulence: insights from conditional surprisal
summary: Explainable deep learning (XDL) has identified regions of wall turbulence important for prediction that are only partly captured by classical coherent-structure criteria. We examine turbulent channel flow at friction Reynolds numbers $Re_τ\simeq125$ and $550$ by comparing SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) with conditional surprisal, which quantifies how unexpected an observed velocity transition is given its initial state. Although SHAP selection favours energetic fluid and largely overlaps classical masks, selected fluid outside these masks is less energetic but exhibits higher surprisal. Near the wall, at comparable fluctuation energy and wall distance, high-surprisal voxels outside classical masks are approximately 11 and 5 times more likely to be selected by SHAP than low-surprisal voxels, respectively. Within classical masks, the factor is about 1.3. SHAP-selected structures containing paired high- and low-speed regions exhibit surprisal maxima near their internal $u=0$ interfaces, where transverse velocity fluctuations remain nonzero. These interfaces contain vortical and SHAP-only regions, with the latter accounting for more than half of their reconstructed area. In part of the buffer layer, the SHAP-only portions have higher mean surprisal than the vortical portions. However, comparison with generic $u=0$ surfaces indicates that much of the raw interfacial surprisal excess is associated with surrounding fluctuation energy; after energy matching, the equally weighted surface comparison is statistically compatible with unity on the retained common support. Together, these results show how state-conditioned velocity transitions complement instantaneous structure-identification criteria in characterizing SHAP-selected flow.

AI.tldr: Explainable deep learning (SHAP) and conditional surprisal are compared in turbulent channel flow at Re_tau ~125 and 550. SHAP-selected wall-turbulence regions include high-surprisal, lower-energy fluid outside classical coherent-structure masks, especially near internal u=0 interfaces; after energy matching, much of the raw interfacial surprisal excess is linked to surrounding fluctuation energy. State-conditioned velocity transitions therefore complement instantaneous structure-identification criteria.
AI.motivation: Explainable deep learning has identified regions of wall turbulence important for prediction that are only partly captured by classical coherent-structure criteria. The paper examines how SHAP-selected flow relates to conditional surprisal, which quantifies how unexpected an observed velocity transition is given its initial state.
AI.method: The study examines turbulent channel flow at friction Reynolds numbers Re_tau ~125 and 550, comparing SHAP with conditional surprisal. It analyzes overlap with classical masks, fluctuation energy and wall-distance matching, paired high- and low-speed structures, internal u=0 interfaces, vortical versus SHAP-only regions, and comparisons with generic u=0 surfaces under energy matching.
AI.result: SHAP selection favours energetic fluid and largely overlaps classical masks, but selected fluid outside those masks is less energetic and has higher surprisal. Near the wall, at comparable fluctuation energy and wall distance, high-surprisal voxels outside classical masks are approximately 11 and 5 times more likely to be selected by SHAP than low-surprisal voxels, respectively; within classical masks the factor is about 1.3. SHAP-selected structures with paired high- and low-speed regions show surprisal maxima near internal u=0 interfaces, where transverse velocity fluctuations remain nonzero. These interfaces contain vortical and SHAP-only regions, with SHAP-only regions accounting for more than half of their reconstructed area. In part of the buffer layer, SHAP-only portions have higher mean surprisal than vortical portions. Comparison with generic u=0 surfaces indicates that much of the raw interfacial surprisal excess is associated with surrounding fluctuation energy; after energy matching, the equally weighted surface comparison is statistically compatible with unity on the retained common support.
AI.conclusion: Conditional surprisal shows that state-conditioned velocity transitions complement instantaneous structure-identification criteria in characterizing SHAP-selected wall-bounded turbulent flow.

title: Controlling Mode-Locking in Liquid Light
summary: Mode-locking is the process by which the phases of many cavity modes organize collectively into a stationary state. In lasers, mode-locking originates from the interplay of gain, loss, dispersion and nonlinearities, most commonly resulting in the emission of short pulses. However, pulse formation is prevented when the gain recovery is fast enough to suppress amplitude fluctuations. Mode-locking then produces an extended state of nearly constant intensity, whose dynamics is governed by the phase. Yet, a general framework for designing the phase of such extended photonic states remains lacking. Here we introduce a hydrodynamic approach to designing extended photonic states, in which the phase dynamics are understood and controlled as a flow of liquid-like light. The intensity, clamped by fast gain, plays the role of a constant density, the instantaneous frequency that of a flow velocity, and the programmable radio-frequency modulation applied to the laser acts as a potential landscape that controls the flow. We derive analytical solutions connecting the applied modulation to the instantaneous frequency and hence to the spectrum emitted by the laser. We further provide experimental evidence for the liquid light shaping framework by measuring the frequency comb spectra emitted by a fast-gain semiconductor laser around 1.6 micron under the control of a programmed modulation, and comparing them to the ones predicted by the analytical solution. The hydrodynamic picture of mode-locking provides a predictive design principle for frequency combs, pointing toward a programmable synthesizer of light, and establishes fast-gain lasers as an accessible, electrically driven platform for nonequilibrium fluids of light.

AI.tldr: Introduces a hydrodynamic framework for controlling the phase of extended, fast-gain mode-locked photonic states, derives analytical modulation-to-spectrum relations, and tests them using frequency-comb spectra from a 1.6-micron semiconductor laser.
AI.motivation: Fast gain recovery can suppress amplitude fluctuations and prevent short-pulse formation, producing an extended nearly constant-intensity mode-locked state whose dynamics are governed by phase. A general framework for designing the phase of such extended photonic states was lacking.
AI.method: The authors model the phase dynamics as flow of liquid-like light: gain-clamped intensity acts as constant density, instantaneous frequency as flow velocity, and programmable radio-frequency modulation as a potential landscape. They derive analytical solutions linking applied modulation to instantaneous frequency and emitted spectrum, then compare predicted frequency-comb spectra with measurements from a fast-gain semiconductor laser around 1.6 micron under programmed modulation.
AI.result: Analytical solutions connect the applied modulation to the instantaneous frequency and hence the laser spectrum. Experimental frequency-comb spectra from the fast-gain semiconductor laser around 1.6 micron under programmed modulation are compared with predictions from the analytical solution; quantitative agreement metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The hydrodynamic picture of mode-locking provides a predictive design principle for frequency combs, points toward a programmable light synthesizer, and establishes fast-gain lasers as an accessible, electrically driven platform for nonequilibrium fluids of light.

title: Transferable neural-network preconditioners for Wilson--Clover propagator inversions
summary: We investigate two single--layer neural-network architectures for accelerating four-dimensional Wilson--Clover propagator inversions on lattice ensembles in practical use; both transfer directly without retraining. The first is a gauge-covariant parallel transport convolution (PTC) network that directly reduces the number of generalized conjugate residual (GCR) solver iterations. The second is a CNN-like network used together with a multigrid-inspired algorithm. The two approaches can be combined to further reduce GCR iterations. PTC transfers without retraining across lattice volumes, lattice spacings, and pion masses while maintaining comparable acceleration, whereas the CNN-like network transfers directly from small- to large-volume ensembles with strong acceleration. A cost comparison accounting for both basis construction and solves shows that the proposed scheme is more advantageous for large-volume ensembles than for small-volume ones.

AI.tldr: The paper studies two single-layer neural-network preconditioners to accelerate four-dimensional Wilson--Clover propagator inversions on lattice ensembles, showing direct transfer without retraining and greater cost benefit on large-volume ensembles.
AI.motivation: The work aims to accelerate practical four-dimensional Wilson--Clover propagator inversions on lattice ensembles using neural-network preconditioners that transfer directly without retraining.
AI.method: The authors investigate a gauge-covariant parallel transport convolution (PTC) network that reduces generalized conjugate residual (GCR) solver iterations, and a CNN-like network used with a multigrid-inspired algorithm; the two approaches can be combined to further reduce GCR iterations.
AI.result: PTC transfers without retraining across lattice volumes, lattice spacings, and pion masses while maintaining comparable acceleration, whereas the CNN-like network transfers directly from small- to large-volume ensembles with strong acceleration. A cost comparison including basis construction and solves shows the proposed scheme is more advantageous for large-volume than small-volume ensembles.
AI.conclusion: The proposed neural-network preconditioning scheme can accelerate Wilson--Clover propagator inversions with transferability without retraining, and its cost advantage is greater for large-volume lattice ensembles; specific numerical speedups and ensemble details are not provided in the abstract.

title: An LLM-assisted theoretical model for aeroengine installation noise scattering
summary: A theoretical model is developed for the canonical problem of aeroengine fan noise impinging on, and scattering from, a nearby semi-infinite rigid plate. The model chains two Wiener--Hopf problems in different coordinate systems. The first stage solves the duct-radiation problem analytically in axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates. The second stage expands the field incident on the plate into a double angular spectrum of plane waves: the axial spectrum is inherited from the first stage, while the spanwise spectrum is generated by a Weyl--Sommerfeld expansion of the cylindrical harmonics. Each spectral component is then scattered by the plate. The mathematical crux is the coordinate transformation between the axisymmetric duct frame and the Cartesian plate frame. The core physical insight--that the Weyl--Sommerfeld identity provides an exact spectral bridge between these systems--originates entirely with the authors. The heavy algebra of translating between the two spectral representations, together with the associated numerical verification, was carried out with the assistance of a large language model (LLM), under strict human oversight and independent numerical cross-checking. This division of labour enables the LLM to handle tedious symbolic manipulation without compromising rigour. Results are presented for spinning modes radiating from a cylindrical duct with a subsonic jet into a quiescent ambient. The case study demonstrates that, under systematic verification, LLMs can accelerate tedious algebra in theoretical fluid mechanics, contributing a concrete empirical example to the broader discussion on AI's role in theoretical research.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a two-stage Wiener--Hopf theoretical model for aeroengine fan noise radiating from a cylindrical duct and scattering from a nearby semi-infinite rigid plate, with an LLM used under human oversight to perform tedious spectral-algebra transformations and numerical verification.
AI.motivation: The work addresses the canonical problem of aeroengine fan noise impinging on and scattering from a nearby semi-infinite rigid plate, while also examining whether LLMs can safely accelerate tedious algebra in theoretical fluid mechanics.
AI.method: The model chains two Wiener--Hopf problems in different coordinate systems. The first stage solves duct radiation analytically in axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates. The second expands the field incident on the plate into a double angular spectrum of plane waves, inheriting the axial spectrum from the first stage and generating the spanwise spectrum through a Weyl--Sommerfeld expansion of cylindrical harmonics; each spectral component is then scattered by the plate. The key step is the coordinate transformation between the axisymmetric duct frame and the Cartesian plate frame. Heavy algebraic translation between spectral representations and associated numerical verification were performed with LLM assistance under strict human oversight and independent numerical cross-checking.
AI.result: Results are presented for spinning modes radiating from a cylindrical duct with a subsonic jet into a quiescent ambient. The case study indicates that, under systematic verification, LLMs can accelerate tedious algebra in theoretical fluid mechanics and provides a concrete empirical example for discussions of AI in theoretical research.
AI.conclusion: The authors identify the Weyl--Sommerfeld identity as providing an exact spectral bridge between the duct and plate systems, with this core physical insight originating entirely with them. Their division of labour allows the LLM to handle tedious symbolic manipulation without compromising rigour, supporting LLM assistance in theoretical research when paired with human oversight and independent checks.

title: Subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic waves for enhancing Brillouin gain in a planar waveguide structure
summary: We propose a planar waveguide structure consisting of two layers separated by a gap that provides subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic modes and a large overlap integral between them. This, in turn, leads to an increase in Brillouin gain. Using the structure of two Si$_3$N$_4$ layers with a subwavelength gap from SiO$_2$ as an example, we demonstrate that a hybridized transverse-magnetic (TM) optical mode exhibits strong field confinement in the SiO$_2$ gap. Simultaneously, a high-frequency acoustic mode can be confined in the same gap, providing a high spatial overlap between the optical and acoustic fields. This provides a high opto-acoustic interaction with a Brillouin gain up to $5$ W$^{-1}$m$^{-1}$. The proposed structure is compatible with planar photonic integration and offers a promising platform for compact, low-threshold Brillouin lasers and coherent phonon generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a planar waveguide with a subwavelength gap between two Si3N4 layers that confines both optical and acoustic modes, increases their spatial overlap, and enhances Brillouin gain to up to 5 W^-1 m^-1.
AI.motivation: The work aims to enhance Brillouin gain in a planar photonic platform by using subwavelength confinement and strong overlap between optical and acoustic modes.
AI.method: A planar waveguide structure with two layers separated by a subwavelength SiO2 gap is proposed. In the example, two Si3N4 layers form the structure; a hybridized transverse-magnetic optical mode is confined in the SiO2 gap, and a high-frequency acoustic mode is confined in the same gap, producing high opto-acoustic spatial overlap.
AI.result: The structure provides strong opto-acoustic interaction with a Brillouin gain up to 5 W^-1 m^-1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed structure is compatible with planar photonic integration and is promising for compact, low-threshold Brillouin lasers and coherent phonon generation.

title: Detecting False Self-Consistency in Density-Functional Calculations
comment: 31 pages main text + 65 pages Supplementary Information, 3 figures
summary: Density-functional calculations feed materials databases and machine-learning models, and are declared converged when energy changes and residuals fall below thresholds. We show that these criteria, and even the agreement of independent optimizers, can accept a state from which the energy still descends or whose Hamiltonian is inconsistent with the energy. A variational formulation of self-consistency in the space of Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians yields a descent probe that exposes lower states accessible from a returned solution, and a frozen-orbital Janak test detects such an inconsistency. Both apply to any code without modification. In VASP, a UO$_2$ PBE+$U$ calculation converges 1.46 eV above a lower state, and CoO and FeO converge as metals 0.8-0.9 eV above insulating states. In a census of 339 converged calculations on tungsten-free Materials Project structures, recomputed with a modified static protocol, 57 (16.8%) show energy decreases above the threshold, 49 without an initial energy rise exceeding the tolerance.

AI.tldr: Standard density-functional convergence checks based on energy/residual thresholds and optimizer agreement can certify false self-consistency. A variational Kohn-Sham-Hamiltonian descent probe and a frozen-orbital Janak test detect lower accessible states or Hamiltonian-energy inconsistency, revealing failures in VASP and in 16.8% of a 339-calculation Materials Project census.
AI.motivation: Materials databases and machine-learning models rely on density-functional calculations that are declared converged using energy-change and residual thresholds, but these criteria may accept states that are not truly self-consistent or variationally stable.
AI.method: The authors formulate self-consistency variationally in the space of Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians, yielding a descent probe that exposes lower states accessible from a returned solution, and introduce a frozen-orbital Janak test to detect Hamiltonian-energy inconsistency. Both are code-independent and are applied to VASP calculations and a 339-calculation Materials Project census recomputed with a modified static protocol.
AI.result: In VASP, a UO2 PBE+U calculation converges 1.46 eV above a lower state, and CoO and FeO converge as metals 0.8–0.9 eV above insulating states. In the census of 339 converged tungsten-free Materials Project calculations, 57 (16.8%) show energy decreases above the threshold, including 49 without an initial energy rise exceeding the tolerance.
AI.conclusion: Conventional convergence criteria and independent-optimizer agreement are insufficient to establish true self-consistency. The proposed probes can detect false convergence without code modification and expose substantial hidden errors in density-functional workflows and materials databases.

title: Relativistic and quantum fluid dynamics: nonlinear momentum evolution
summary: We present an alternative framework for nonlinear momentum evolution in fluid dynamics, in which relativistic effects are proposed as an underlying mechanism for nonlinear behavior, even in the low-velocity regime. By interpreting the second-order velocity diffusion equation from a quantum-mechanical perspective, we establish a connection between higher-order viscous transport and the reduced Planck constant, identifying the second-order viscosity coefficient with \(\hbar\). Furthermore, we show that the coupling of second-order velocity diffusion and nonlinear momentum evolution leads to a Dirac-type equation for quantum fluids. These findings reveal a potential connection among relativistic effects, higher-order fluid transport, and quantum wave dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework linking nonlinear momentum evolution in fluids to relativistic effects, higher-order viscous transport, and quantum wave dynamics, including a Dirac-type equation for quantum fluids.
AI.motivation: The authors seek an alternative explanation for nonlinear momentum behavior in fluid dynamics, proposing relativistic effects as an underlying mechanism even in the low-velocity regime and exploring connections among relativity, higher-order fluid transport, and quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The second-order velocity diffusion equation is interpreted from a quantum-mechanical perspective; the second-order viscosity coefficient is identified with the reduced Planck constant, and second-order velocity diffusion is coupled with nonlinear momentum evolution to derive a Dirac-type equation for quantum fluids.
AI.result: The framework establishes a connection between higher-order viscous transport and the reduced Planck constant and shows that coupling second-order velocity diffusion with nonlinear momentum evolution leads to a Dirac-type equation for quantum fluids. The abstract reports no quantitative validation or experimental comparison.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest a potential connection among relativistic effects, higher-order fluid transport, and quantum wave dynamics, but specific validation and implications beyond this proposed connection are not provided in the abstract.

title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
comment: 62 pages, 23 figures, preprint including the final bibliographic reference
summary: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews laser processing across energy applications, including laser-driven inertial confinement fusion, solar-energy harvesting and recycling, laser surface texturing for electrochemical performance, and lithium-ion battery materials and manufacturing. It emphasizes precise, efficient, scalable laser solutions and outlines future prospects for sustainable energy.
AI.motivation: Laser processing is presented as a transformative technology for energy generation, storage, and sustainability, motivating a broad review of its precise, efficient, and scalable applications across the energy sector.
AI.method: The chapter provides a qualitative overview of laser applications: it examines laser-driven inertial confinement fusion facilities and key laser parameters, solar-energy harvesting and module recycling, laser-based surface texturing for electrochemical performance, and laser techniques for lithium-ion battery materials and manufacturing. No specific experimental or systematic-review methodology is provided.
AI.result: The abstract reports a review of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, photovoltaic and concentrated-solar applications, laser-assisted solar-module recycling, surface texturing for electrochemical enhancement, and lithium-ion battery advances in materials, manufacturing, performance, safety, and scalability. No quantitative results or specific performance metrics are provided.
AI.conclusion: Laser processing is concluded to offer significant promise for sustainable energy solutions, with future prospects discussed. Detailed conclusions and quantitative assessments are not provided in the abstract.

title: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs
summary: Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/fycAIwj/Newton-PINet.

AI.tldr: Newton-PINet is a physics-informed meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs that combines a skip-connected multilayer network, least-squares output-layer solving, two-stage gradient-based/gradient-free training, and Newton linearization; it substantially outperforms recent neural solvers on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark while using fewer training tasks and less time.
AI.motivation: Solving parameterized PDEs and generalizing to unseen instances is important, but data-driven operator learning typically needs large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.method: The proposed Newton-PINet uses a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections whose output-layer weights are solved by least squares. It adopts a two-stage strategy: gradient-based training to learn robust representations from available tasks, followed by gradient-free fine-tuning of the output layer for fast task-specific generalization. A Newton linearization method accelerates the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems.
AI.result: On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours).
AI.conclusion: Newton-PINet advances meta-learning of physics-informed neural networks toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers for nonlinear PDEs; code and datasets are publicly available.

title: A multi-fidelity dataset of two-dimensional steady laminar channel flow around obstacles
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Data: https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/11554 and https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/11553 . Code: https://github.com/ASaydam/ms-cofd-2dsl and https://github.com/ASaydam/ms-cofd-2dsl-bench
summary: Surrogates that correct inexpensive flow simulations need the same flows solved at several fidelities and an estimate of the numerical error of the reference solutions. This dataset contains 4,500 two-dimensional, steady, laminar channel flows past a single obstacle. Each is solved in five numerical configurations: second-order convection on meshes with cell sizes of 2, 1, 0.5 and 0.25 mm, and first-order convection on the 1 mm mesh. A seeded generator draws the obstacles from five shape families in three size classes. All 22,500 OpenFOAM runs were iterated to initial residuals of $10^{-6}$, and each run's residuals, iterations and provenance are recorded. Every run provides the velocity and pressure on a regular grid with geometry channels, and the pressure and wall shear along the obstacle. Its 20 flow attributes, computed on the simulation mesh, include drag and lift split into pressure and friction parts. The four second-order levels give an estimate of the discretisation uncertainty of 19 attributes of every case. Fixed splits include three out-of-distribution test sets.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a 22,500-run OpenFOAM dataset of 4,500 two-dimensional steady laminar channel flows past a single obstacle, solved at five numerical fidelities and accompanied by flow attributes, provenance, and discretisation-uncertainty estimates for surrogate modelling.
AI.motivation: Surrogates that correct inexpensive flow simulations require the same flows solved at several fidelities and an estimate of the numerical error of the reference solutions.
AI.method: A seeded generator draws obstacles from five shape families and three size classes. Each of 4,500 cases is solved in five configurations: second-order convection on 2, 1, 0.5 and 0.25 mm meshes and first-order convection on the 1 mm mesh. All 22,500 OpenFOAM runs are iterated to initial residuals of 10^-6, with residuals, iterations and provenance recorded. Outputs include velocity and pressure on a regular grid with geometry channels, pressure and wall shear along the obstacle, and 20 flow attributes on the simulation mesh, including pressure and friction contributions to drag and lift. The four second-order levels provide discretisation-uncertainty estimates for 19 attributes per case, and fixed splits include three out-of-distribution test sets.
AI.result: The dataset contains 4,500 two-dimensional steady laminar channel-flow cases and 22,500 simulation runs across five numerical configurations, with recorded convergence data, provenance, flow fields, wall quantities and derived flow attributes. Discretisation uncertainty is estimated for 19 attributes using the four second-order mesh levels, and three out-of-distribution test sets are included in fixed splits.
AI.conclusion: The dataset is intended to support multi-fidelity surrogate development and numerical-error estimation for inexpensive flow simulations. The abstract does not report surrogate performance or additional conclusions.

title: Intrinsic Berry Curvature on the Higher-order Poincare Sphere
summary: Higer-order geometric phase enable versatile spin-orbit manipulation of structured light . Con ventional theories describe this phase via a total-angular-momentum dependent Berry curvature . We develop an intrinsic theory restricted to the effective two-dimensional subspace, where the Berry curvature is independent of the topological charge of the light field . In our framework, the total-angular-momentum difference does not alter the effective monopole strength, whereas it controls the solid angle enclosed by the trajectory of the state evolution, insteadly. Our theory provides a different topological interpretation of geometric phase of the structured light, which unifies the underlying structures of generalized Poincare Spheres. Furthermore, it does not impose any specific form on the physical operation of the optical element, naturally encomoassing the case of previously reported experiment, and can be applied in arbitrary state evolutions in both classical structured light and quantum spin-orbit systems .

AI.tldr: The paper develops an intrinsic Berry-curvature theory for the higher-order geometric phase of structured light in an effective two-dimensional subspace, making the curvature independent of topological charge and unifying generalized Poincaré sphere structures.
AI.motivation: Conventional descriptions treat the higher-order geometric phase through a total-angular-momentum-dependent Berry curvature. The authors seek an intrinsic formulation restricted to the effective two-dimensional subspace.
AI.method: They formulate an intrinsic theory in which the Berry curvature is independent of the light field's topological charge. In this framework, the total-angular-momentum difference does not change the effective monopole strength but instead controls the solid angle enclosed by the state-evolution trajectory. The theory does not impose a specific form on the physical operation of the optical element.
AI.result: The framework provides a different topological interpretation of the geometric phase of structured light and unifies the underlying structures of generalized Poincaré spheres. It naturally encompasses previously reported experimental cases and is applicable to arbitrary state evolutions in classical structured light and quantum spin-orbit systems.
AI.conclusion: An intrinsic Berry-curvature description on the higher-order Poincaré sphere is established, offering a topological interpretation independent of topological charge and broad applicability to classical and quantum spin-orbit state evolutions.

title: GPRidge: Gaussian-process Accelerated Calculations of Minimum Energy Paths and First-order Saddle Points
comment: Supporting Information included as an appendix. Prepared for submission to the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling. Reproducibility archive, including the GPRidge 0.5.0 source snapshot and run records: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23776354
summary: GPRidge, a Gaussian-process (GP) library for accelerating calculations of minimum energy paths and first-order saddle points with compiled-language and Python bindings, is presented. An evaluation controller uses GP predictions to iteratively adjust the Cartesian coordinates of the atoms. The fitted GP energy surface and measured energies and forces pass from the path calculation to local refinement of the saddle point. New evaluations improve the surrogate and check the candidate geometry. For the molecular calculations, acceptance requires measured-force convergence and an independent Hessian with only one negative eigenvalue. A second negative eigenvalue triggers an escape and renewed refinement. The controller supports a joint inverse-distance GP for molecules and local GP residuals on periodic systems. Applications to the 24 Baker-Chan and 20 Birkholz-Schlegel molecular reactions using the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA-S-1.1), and to 72 Pt heptamer and island rearrangements on Pt(111) using a Morse potential, are presented. On matched Baker-Chan reactions, GPRidge uses 7.8- and 7.0-fold fewer energy-and-force evaluations than climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) and off-path climbing-image nudged elastic band (OCI-NEB), respectively, reducing validation-inclusive CI-NEB time by 41%. All 20 Birkholz-Schlegel saddle points pass the independent index-one check, compared with 17 for the classical dimer method started from the same path maxima; on those 17 reactions, the GP dimer stage uses 6.4-fold fewer evaluations. All 72 Pt(111) paths meet the OptBench force criterion, with median evaluation counts of 30 and 23 for the heptamer and island problems, against 778 and 443 for CI-NEB.

AI.tldr: GPRidge is a Gaussian-process library for accelerating minimum-energy-path and first-order saddle-point calculations. It iteratively updates atomic coordinates using GP predictions, refines saddle candidates locally, validates them with measured forces and an independent Hessian, and reports large evaluation savings over CI-NEB, OCI-NEB, and dimer benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state the motivation beyond the stated aim of accelerating calculations of minimum energy paths and first-order saddle points.
AI.method: GPRidge provides a Gaussian-process library with compiled-language and Python bindings. An evaluation controller uses GP predictions to iteratively adjust Cartesian atomic coordinates. The fitted GP energy surface and measured energies and forces are passed from the path calculation to local saddle-point refinement; new evaluations improve the surrogate and check the candidate geometry. Molecular acceptance requires measured-force convergence and an independent Hessian with only one negative eigenvalue, while a second negative eigenvalue triggers an escape and renewed refinement. The controller supports a joint inverse-distance GP for molecules and local GP residuals for periodic systems. Applications used the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA-S-1.1) on 24 Baker-Chan and 20 Birkholz-Schlegel molecular reactions, and a Morse potential on 72 Pt heptamer and island rearrangements on Pt(111).
AI.result: On matched Baker-Chan reactions, GPRidge used 7.8-fold and 7.0-fold fewer energy-and-force evaluations than CI-NEB and OCI-NEB, respectively, and reduced validation-inclusive CI-NEB time by 41%. All 20 Birkholz-Schlegel saddle points passed the independent index-one check, versus 17 for the classical dimer method started from the same path maxima; on those 17 reactions, the GP dimer stage used 6.4-fold fewer evaluations. All 72 Pt(111) paths met the OptBench force criterion, with median evaluation counts of 30 and 23 for the heptamer and island problems, versus 778 and 443 for CI-NEB.
AI.conclusion: GPRidge provides an evaluation-efficient framework for molecular and periodic minimum-energy-path and saddle-point calculations, with reported improvements in evaluation cost and saddle-point validation success over the compared methods. The abstract reports performance results rather than a broader formal conclusion.

title: Terahertz and infrared links in controlled non-Kolmogorov turbulence
summary: Hybrid terahertz/infrared (THz/IR) links are usually modeled with Kolmogorov turbulence, but whether the turbulence spectral type matters equally for both bands has not been investigated. We transmit co-propagating 625 GHz and 1550 nm links through laboratory-controlled turbulence while a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and thermistors independently measure its spectral exponent and structure parameter on the shared path. Inlet-air temperature, not airflow speed, drives the exponent from Kolmogorov-like to non-Kolmogorov. At comparable structure parameters, this change reverses which model better reproduces the IR attenuation at the nominal inner scale, whereas the THz attenuation is insensitive to it. With type-matched models, predicted and measured bit-error-rate trends agree within 0.14 (IR) and 0.06 (THz) decades. IR predictions therefore require the spectral shape and inner scale, not turbulence strength alone.

AI.tldr: Co-propagating 625 GHz and 1550 nm links were tested through laboratory-controlled non-Kolmogorov turbulence; inlet-air temperature drove the spectral exponent, and type-matched models reproduced bit-error-rate trends, with infrared attenuation depending on spectral shape and inner scale while terahertz attenuation was insensitive.
AI.motivation: Hybrid terahertz/infrared links are usually modeled with Kolmogorov turbulence, but whether the turbulence spectral type matters equally for both bands had not been investigated.
AI.method: The authors transmitted co-propagating 625 GHz and 1550 nm links through controlled turbulence while a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and thermistors independently measured the spectral exponent and structure parameter on the shared path; they compared attenuation and bit-error-rate trends using type-matched models.
AI.result: Inlet-air temperature, not airflow speed, drove the exponent from Kolmogorov-like to non-Kolmogorov. At comparable structure parameters, this change reversed which model better reproduced infrared attenuation at the nominal inner scale, whereas terahertz attenuation was insensitive. Type-matched models agreed with measured bit-error-rate trends within 0.14 decades for infrared and 0.06 decades for terahertz.
AI.conclusion: Infrared link predictions require the turbulence spectral shape and inner scale, not turbulence strength alone, while terahertz attenuation is less sensitive to spectral type under the reported conditions.

title: Recovery of accidental bound states in the continuum in vertically asymmetric photonic lattices through radiation-source parity restoration
summary: Vertical asymmetry generally precludes accidental bound states in the continuum (BICs) in planar photonic lattices, yet the underlying physical mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we show that accidental-BIC formation is governed by the definite parity of the transverse radiation-source profile rather than by geometric vertical mirror symmetry. A semianalytical coupled-mode analysis shows that an accidental BIC occurs when the radiation overlap integral of a leaky Bloch mode vanishes. We decompose the overlap into contributions from the even- and odd-parity components of the transverse radiation-source profile. Complete radiation suppression requires both contributions to vanish simultaneously. In vertically symmetric lattices, the source profile has definite even or odd parity, causing one contribution to vanish identically.
