Thickness tuning can null the remaining contribution and produce an accidental BIC. In vertically asymmetric lattices, by contrast, both parity components are generally present. The waveguide dispersion forbids their simultaneous vanishing, thereby precluding an accidental BIC. Introducing a parity-restoring layer into a vertically asymmetric lattice restores definite parity to the transverse radiation-source profile, thereby enabling the formation of an accidental BIC. Finite-element simulations confirm the analytically predicted recovery of accidental BICs for both TE$_0$ and TE$_1$ Bloch modes.

AI.tldr: The paper explains accidental bound states in the continuum (BICs) in planar photonic lattices through the parity of the transverse radiation-source profile, rather than vertical geometric mirror symmetry, and shows that adding a parity-restoring layer enables accidental BICs in vertically asymmetric lattices.
AI.motivation: Vertical asymmetry generally prevents accidental BICs in planar photonic lattices, but the physical mechanism responsible was unclear. The authors aim to identify the governing mechanism and a route to recover accidental BICs in asymmetric structures.
AI.method: A semianalytical coupled-mode analysis decomposes the radiation overlap integral of a leaky Bloch mode into even- and odd-parity contributions from the transverse radiation-source profile. The conditions for simultaneous vanishing are analyzed for vertically symmetric and asymmetric lattices, and a parity-restoring layer is introduced. Finite-element simulations test the predicted recovery for TE0 and TE1 Bloch modes.
AI.result: Accidental BICs require both even- and odd-parity radiation-overlap contributions to vanish. In vertically symmetric lattices, definite source parity eliminates one contribution and thickness tuning can null the other. In vertically asymmetric lattices, both components are generally present and waveguide dispersion forbids their simultaneous vanishing, precluding accidental BICs. A parity-restoring layer restores definite parity and enables accidental BICs, as confirmed by finite-element simulations for TE0 and TE1 Bloch modes.
AI.conclusion: Accidental-BIC formation is governed by the definite parity of the transverse radiation-source profile rather than by geometric vertical mirror symmetry. Parity restoration provides a mechanism for recovering accidental BICs in vertically asymmetric photonic lattices.

title: Ternary-Valued FDTD Method for Nonlinear Optics: Third-Harmonic Generation on a Multiplier-Free Solver
summary: I show that a finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) solver with field variables restricted to the ternary alphabet $\{-1,0,+1\}$ can reproduce nonlinear optical physics quantitatively on both CPUs and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Building on the general ternary-valued FDTD algorithm, in which each Yee cell stores an integer state that accumulates the discrete curl of neighbouring symbols without being drained, I extend the scheme to inhomogeneous and Kerr media and to Mur absorbing boundaries, without performing any multiplication operations. Dielectric contrast is implemented as a multiplexer, since the difference between ternary symbols takes only a few values, the instantaneous Kerr nonlinearity as a coefficient look-up table and the Mur boundary coefficients as canonical signed-digit shift--add chains. The scheme reproduces the third-harmonic conversion efficiency of a floating-point reference to within $1.4\%$. A symmetry of the governing physics, expressed through the even harmonics forbidden by centrosymmetric $χ^{(3)}$, provides a reference-free self-check for both ternary and floating-point models. The complete solver fits on a small, low-cost FPGA and contains no multiplier anywhere in its datapath, placing nonlinear optical modelling within reach of embedded and autonomous platforms rather than of high-performance computers.

AI.tldr: A multiplier-free ternary-valued FDTD solver is extended to inhomogeneous and Kerr media with Mur absorbing boundaries and reproduces floating-point third-harmonic conversion efficiency within 1.4%, fitting on a small low-cost FPGA.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to bring quantitative nonlinear optical modelling to embedded and autonomous platforms by using a low-cost, multiplier-free FPGA-compatible FDTD scheme instead of relying on high-performance computers.
AI.method: The solver restricts field variables to {-1,0,+1}; each Yee cell stores an integer state that accumulates the discrete curl of neighbouring symbols without being drained. The scheme is extended to inhomogeneous and Kerr media and Mur absorbing boundaries without multiplication: dielectric contrast uses a multiplexer, instantaneous Kerr nonlinearity uses a coefficient look-up table, and Mur boundary coefficients use canonical signed-digit shift-add chains. A symmetry involving even harmonics forbidden by centrosymmetric chi(3) provides a reference-free self-check.
AI.result: The ternary scheme reproduces the third-harmonic conversion efficiency of a floating-point reference to within 1.4%. The complete solver fits on a small, low-cost FPGA and contains no multiplier anywhere in its datapath.
AI.conclusion: Quantitative nonlinear optical modelling, specifically third-harmonic generation, is feasible with a multiplier-free ternary-valued FDTD solver on low-cost FPGA hardware, making it suitable for embedded and autonomous platforms rather than only high-performance computers.

title: Population structure of the velocity distribution in normal shock waves: Gaussian representations, Mach-number similarity, and prediction
summary: Normal shock waves are commonly described as mixtures of upstream and downstream Maxwellians. Discrete-velocity solutions of three relaxation models up to Mach 12 and direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) of hard-sphere and variable-hard-sphere gases up to Mach 25 are used to examine the population structure, Mach-number similarity and upstream precursor of their velocity distributions. Three anisotropic Gaussian populations reproduce the streamwise reduced distributions of the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) model and of DSMC to within 4\% up to Mach 12, and of DSMC to within 6\% at Mach 25, whereas two Maxwellians incur errors up to 50\% (BGK) and 37\% (DSMC). Collision histories identify the hard-sphere beam with unscattered stream molecules, which carry half of the peak viscous stress; the other populations are effective descriptions, not collision classes. Above Mach 5, Rankine--Hugoniot-scaled distributions are nearly Mach-independent, with corrections linear in $1/M^2$, consistent with the scaled kinetic equation. At equal normalised density, Mach 8 and 12 give the heat flux and stress at Mach 25 within 1\%, comparable to the accuracy of the reference; with one moment equation for position, physical-space profiles follow within 5\%. Comparing three prediction methods shows that the accuracy comes from the scaling; the Gaussian form adds compactness. Ahead of the shock, the mass of upstream-moving molecules decays as a stretched exponential with effective exponent 0.68--0.87. Collisions regenerate upstream-moving molecules, which explains a decay slower than free-flight survival; a linear cascade model with a downstream-Maxwellian source and no input from the shock interior reproduces the decay rates within 1.2\%.

AI.tldr: Three anisotropic Gaussian populations accurately describe normal-shock velocity distributions, and Rankine–Hugoniot scaling yields near-Mach-independent shock structure and predictive profiles above Mach 5.
AI.motivation: Normal shock waves are commonly modeled as mixtures of upstream and downstream Maxwellians, but the paper examines whether this bimodal picture captures the population structure, Mach-number similarity, and upstream precursor of the velocity distribution.
AI.method: The study uses discrete-velocity solutions of three relaxation models up to Mach 12 and direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) of hard-sphere and variable-hard-sphere gases up to Mach 25. It compares three anisotropic Gaussian populations with two Maxwellians, uses collision histories, applies Rankine–Hugoniot scaling, tests a one-moment position equation and three prediction methods, and models the upstream precursor with a linear cascade model.
AI.result: Three anisotropic Gaussian populations reproduce streamwise reduced distributions within 4% up to Mach 12 for the Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK) model and DSMC, and within 6% for DSMC at Mach 25; two Maxwellians incur errors up to 50% for BGK and 37% for DSMC. Collision histories identify the hard-sphere beam with unscattered stream molecules carrying half the peak viscous stress, while other populations are effective descriptions rather than collision classes. Above Mach 5, scaled distributions are nearly Mach-independent with corrections linear in 1/M^2. At equal normalized density, Mach 8 and 12 reproduce Mach 25 heat flux and stress within 1%, and one moment equation gives physical-space profiles within 5%. Ahead of the shock, upstream-moving molecule mass decays as a stretched exponential with effective exponent 0.68–0.87, and a linear cascade model reproduces decay rates within 1.2%.
AI.conclusion: The bimodal Maxwellian description is inadequate, whereas three anisotropic Gaussian populations provide a compact and accurate representation. Predictive accuracy above Mach 5 comes mainly from Rankine–Hugoniot scaling, with the Gaussian form adding compactness. The upstream precursor decays more slowly than free-flight survival because collisions regenerate upstream-moving molecules, and this behavior is captured by a downstream-Maxwellian-source cascade model.

title: Cavity Control of Emission Dynamics from Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
summary: Optically addressable negatively charged boron vacancy ($\mathrm{V_B^-}$) defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising for quantum sensing at room temperature. The two-dimensional structure of hBN allows direct access to the local environment, enabling proximal sensing of target materials. However, its broadband emission and low quantum yield hinder efficient light-matter interaction, and the coupling of $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ optical dipoles to confined cavity fields remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrate $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defects with a tunable plano-concave microcavity, achieving three-dimensional optical confinement. This approach yields photoluminescence (PL) enhancement and cavity-modified optical decay dynamics, providing insights into the orientation of the $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect dipole. Time-resolved PL measurements identify a distinct fast decay component, suggesting a complex dipole geometry for the defects. Therefore, a tilted optical dipole model is considered to attribute the fast and slow decay components to in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, respectively. Additionally, optically detected magnetic resonance and excitation-polarisation-dependent PL measurements provide further insights into local symmetry breaking and potential optical dipole configurations. These results highlight the role of optical dipole orientation in $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect-cavity coupling.

AI.tldr: The paper couples negatively charged boron vacancy defects in hexagonal boron nitride to a tunable plano-concave microcavity to study cavity-controlled emission dynamics and optical dipole orientation.
AI.motivation: VB- defects in hBN are promising room-temperature quantum sensors and the two-dimensional host enables proximal sensing, but broadband emission, low quantum yield, and limited understanding of dipole coupling to confined cavity fields restrict efficient light-matter interaction.
AI.method: The authors integrate VB- defects with a tunable plano-concave microcavity for three-dimensional optical confinement and use photoluminescence, time-resolved photoluminescence, optically detected magnetic resonance, and excitation-polarization-dependent photoluminescence measurements, interpreted with a tilted optical dipole model.
AI.result: The approach produces photoluminescence enhancement and cavity-modified optical decay dynamics. Time-resolved measurements reveal distinct fast and slow decay components, attributed respectively to in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, while magnetic resonance and polarization-dependent measurements provide insight into local symmetry breaking and possible dipole configurations.
AI.conclusion: Optical dipole orientation plays an important role in VB- defect-cavity coupling, and the results provide insight into the defect dipole geometry relevant to cavity-controlled emission.

title: Machine Learning the $GW$ Self-Energy Operator for Real Materials
summary: Machine learning of $GW$ in solids has largely focused on prediction of scalar quasiparticle energy corrections. Here, we introduce a phase-aware many-body transformer that predicts the full $\mathbf{k}$-resolved complex self-energy matrix. As a proof of principle, we apply the model to predict quasiparticle energies before and after diagonalization of the quasiparticle Hamiltonian, obtaining a test set mean absolute error (MAE) of 29 meV for a dataset of 1745 2D materials in the static COHSEX approximation and 60 meV for a more limited dataset of 433 materials calculated within a plasmon-pole model. COHSEX pretraining followed by finetuning reduces this MAE to 42 meV. The predicted matrices also accurately reproduce QP wavefunctions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a phase-aware many-body transformer that predicts the full k-resolved complex GW self-energy matrix for real materials, rather than only scalar quasiparticle energy corrections. It predicts quasiparticle energies and wavefunctions, with test MAEs of 29 meV in static COHSEX for 1745 2D materials, 60 meV in a plasmon-pole model for 433 materials, and 42 meV after COHSEX pretraining and finetuning.
AI.motivation: Prior machine learning of GW in solids has largely focused on predicting scalar quasiparticle energy corrections. The authors aim to predict the full k-resolved complex self-energy matrix and thereby also capture quasiparticle wavefunctions.
AI.method: The authors develop a phase-aware many-body transformer that predicts the full k-resolved complex self-energy matrix. As a proof of principle, they use it to predict quasiparticle energies before and after diagonalization of the quasiparticle Hamiltonian, with evaluation in the static COHSEX approximation and within a plasmon-pole model, including COHSEX pretraining followed by finetuning.
AI.result: The test set MAE is 29 meV for 1745 2D materials in the static COHSEX approximation and 60 meV for a more limited dataset of 433 materials calculated with a plasmon-pole model. COHSEX pretraining followed by finetuning reduces the MAE to 42 meV. The predicted matrices also accurately reproduce quasiparticle wavefunctions.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that a phase-aware many-body transformer can predict full GW self-energy matrices and quasiparticle energies and wavefunctions for real materials, with accuracy characterized by the reported MAE values across the studied datasets and approximations.

title: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds
summary: Autoregressive neural operators approximate time-dependent PDE solvers by repeatedly composing a learned transition, although the resulting states need not remain feasible under the discrete constraints of the numerical problem. We study this issue for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility together with prescribed boundary values. We formulate autoregressive operator learning as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets and introduce PCM-NO, a projected-residual realization of this feasible-transition principle. The neural backbone predicts a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection extracts its admissible component, and a metric retraction maps the advanced state to the prescribed feasible set. With exact affine constraint solves, the resulting transition is closed on the feasible set, while an affine identity separates admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure. With approximate solves, tangent-only residuals admit a cumulative upper bound, whereas per-step retraction resets feasibility to the residual achieved by the current solve. Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow demonstrate the superiority of PCM-NO in preserving solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics across both in-distribution and stress settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PCM-NO, a projected-residual autoregressive neural operator that keeps predicted states on solver-defined affine feasible sets for incompressible flow, improving long-rollout constraint satisfaction and accuracy.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive neural operators repeatedly compose learned transitions but can produce states that violate the discrete constraints of the numerical PDE problem. The paper studies this for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility and prescribed boundary values.
AI.method: Autoregressive operator learning is formulated as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets. PCM-NO uses a neural backbone to predict a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection to extract its admissible component, and a metric retraction to map the advanced state onto the prescribed feasible set. The paper also analyzes exact affine constraint solves, an affine identity separating admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure, and approximate solves with cumulative residual bounds and per-step feasibility reset.
AI.result: Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow show that PCM-NO better preserves solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics in both in-distribution and stress settings.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing solver-defined feasibility through tangent projection and metric retraction improves autoregressive neural operator rollout fidelity and constraint satisfaction for incompressible flow.

title: High-quality intrinsic circular dichroism in silicon-based bound states in the continuum metasurfaces via strong coupling
summary: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) can significantly enhance spin-selective light-matter interactions. However, current BIC metasurfaces generally rely on single or multiple chiral BIC modes to enhance circular dichroism (CD), limiting their application in functional integrated devices. This paper proposes a method that utilizes the strong coupling effect in BIC metasurfaces to achieve intrinsic CD with both a high quality factor (Q-factor) and high efficiency. The metasurface is designed as a silicon-based cross-shaped nanohole array, which can simultaneously support a TM-like BIC mode and a TE-like guided-mode resonance (GMR) mode. By introducing under-etching to break the out-of-plane symmetry and tuning the in-plane asymmetry parameter, strong coupling between the quasi-BIC (QBIC) mode and the GMR mode can be induced, thereby achieving near-perfect intrinsic CD with a high Q-factor. In the strong-coupling region, the resonant wavelengths of the QBIC and GMR modes exhibit anti-crossing behavior, while the imaginary parts of the eigenfrequency cross; the corresponding Rabi splitting energy reaches a minimum of 3.16 meV, and the induced intrinsic CD achieves a maximum of 0.995 at a wavelength of 1653.9 nm, with a high Q-factor of 1083. The evolution of far-field polarization singularities shows that, under strong coupling, the Γ point corresponds to a left-handed circular polarization singularity (C-point). Furthermore, the strong-coupling-induced CD exhibits good robustness. Even under considerable variations in structural parameters, the high-Q and high-efficiency CD response is maintained. This method offers a novel design strategy for integrated chiral photonic devices and holds promise for applications in areas such as chiral sensing, chiral lasers, and nonlinear chiral optics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes silicon-based cross-shaped nanohole BIC metasurfaces that exploit strong coupling between a quasi-BIC mode and a guided-mode resonance to achieve near-unity intrinsic circular dichroism with a high Q-factor and robustness.
AI.motivation: Current BIC metasurfaces generally rely on single or multiple chiral BIC modes to enhance circular dichroism, which limits their use in functional integrated devices. The authors aim to achieve intrinsic circular dichroism with both a high quality factor and high efficiency.
AI.method: A silicon-based cross-shaped nanohole metasurface is designed to simultaneously support a TM-like BIC mode and a TE-like guided-mode resonance. Under-etching breaks out-of-plane symmetry, and the in-plane asymmetry parameter is tuned to induce strong coupling between the quasi-BIC and guided-mode resonance modes. The coupling is analyzed through anti-crossing behavior, eigenfrequency imaginary parts, Rabi splitting, far-field polarization singularities, and robustness to structural parameter variations.
AI.result: The Rabi splitting energy reaches a minimum of 3.16 meV. The induced intrinsic circular dichroism reaches a maximum of 0.995 at 1653.9 nm with a high Q-factor of 1083. Under strong coupling, the Γ point corresponds to a left-handed circular polarization singularity, and the high-Q, high-efficiency circular dichroism response remains robust under considerable structural parameter variations.
AI.conclusion: Strong coupling in BIC metasurfaces provides a design strategy for high-Q, high-efficiency intrinsic circular dichroism and integrated chiral photonic devices, with potential applications in chiral sensing, chiral lasers, and nonlinear chiral optics.

title: Self-assembly of dipolar nanoclusters on an attractive substrate: A coarse-grained simulation approach
summary: Recently, Thomas et al. [Nanoscale 17, 18291 (2025)] showed that bismuth oxido nanoclusters (BiO-NCs) of the type [Bi$_{38}$ O$_{45}$ (Boc-L-Phe-O)$_{24}$] form chains when deposited onto gold or pyrolitic graphite substrates. This chain formation is significantly enhanced when the bismuth in the BiO-NCs is partially replaced by cerium through doping. In this work, we study a simplified, coarse-grained model of this process, namely (magnetic) Stockmayer particles in the presence of an attractive substrate. The model is investigated by means of molecular dynamics simulations. The deposition experiment is mimicked by a rapid quench from high temperature to a low temperature below the bulk coexistence curve. The results are found to be qualitatively similar to the experimental observations reported earlier. In our simulations, we find significant chain formation in the bulk even at rather low concentrations, which is in contrast to the BiO-NCs in ethanol for which dynamic light scattering reveals negligible aggregation in the absence of the substrate. This lends support to a scenario, conjectured in the work of Thomas at al., where the dipole moments are induced by the particle-substrate interaction and hence there is little dipole moment in the bulk. In a second part, we study the system in equilibrium. We consider the scaling of chains, the number of layers populated as a function of two-dimensional density, and we draw analogies to polymers on interfaces, which have been extensively studied over the past decades. Most notably, it is found that the chains behave as self-avoiding walks at low densities, which gives way to rod-like scaling at higher densities.

AI.tldr: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics of Stockmayer particles on an attractive substrate qualitatively reproduces substrate-assisted chain formation of bismuth oxido nanoclusters, supports substrate-induced dipole moments, and shows equilibrium chain scaling from self-avoiding walks at low density to rod-like behavior at higher density.
AI.motivation: Experiments by Thomas et al. reported that BiO nanoclusters form chains on gold or pyrolytic graphite, with enhanced chain formation after partial cerium doping. The authors seek a simplified model to test the proposed mechanism, particularly the conjecture that dipole moments are induced by particle-substrate interactions rather than being substantial in bulk.
AI.method: The paper uses a coarse-grained model of magnetic Stockmayer particles in the presence of an attractive substrate, investigated with molecular dynamics simulations. Deposition is mimicked by a rapid quench from high temperature to a low temperature below the bulk coexistence curve. Equilibrium simulations analyze chain scaling, the number of populated layers versus two-dimensional density, and analogies to polymers at interfaces.
AI.result: Simulations show chain formation qualitatively similar to the earlier experiments. Significant chain formation occurs in the bulk even at rather low concentrations, contrasting with BiO nanoclusters in ethanol, where dynamic light scattering shows negligible aggregation without substrate. This supports the scenario of substrate-induced dipole moments with little bulk dipole moment. In equilibrium, chains behave as self-avoiding walks at low densities and exhibit rod-like scaling at higher densities.
AI.conclusion: A simplified coarse-grained Stockmayer-particle model captures the qualitative chain assembly observed for BiO nanoclusters on attractive substrates and provides support for substrate-induced dipoles. Its equilibrium chain statistics connect dipolar cluster assembly to established descriptions of polymers on interfaces, although the abstract does not report quantitative matching to the experiments or realistic chemical specificity.

title: Score-Based Stochastic Closure Modeling via Offline Indirect Learning and Online Data Assimilation
summary: Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a score-based stochastic closure modeling framework that uses indirect offline training and online data assimilation without direct closure data, and demonstrates improved state prediction and generalization on two-dimensional turbulent flows.
AI.motivation: Reduced-order models of large complex systems inevitably lose information that classical deterministic closures cannot address, while learning stochastic closures is hindered by the difficulty or prohibitive cost of obtaining direct closure data from measurements or first-principles simulations.
AI.method: The framework builds on score-based diffusion models and combines indirect offline training with online data assimilation, avoiding the need for direct closure data. It also combines the learned stochastic closure with known physical dynamics and uses posterior-score assimilation, optionally with state-level data assimilation.
AI.result: In numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows, indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves system-state predictions. The learned closure combined with known physics generalizes better across regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Posterior-score assimilation represents non-Gaussian closure features better than standard Gaussian-assumption data assimilation, and combining it with state-level assimilation further improves state prediction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in complex dynamical systems where non-Gaussian model-form uncertainties are significant and true closure data are unavailable for both offline learning and online assimilation, supporting applications in mechanics and engineering.

title: Material Tailored Multispectral Magnetization via the Inverse Faraday Effect in Tunable Coaxial Nanoantenna
summary: All-optical control of magnetization via the Inverse Faraday Effect presents a transformative pathway for ultrafast high-density data storage and nanoscale spintronics. However, unlocking its full potential requires moving beyond traditional gold-centric, narrowband constraints. In this study, we present a comprehensive theoretical framework evaluating IFE-driven static magnetic field generation across a diverse library of plasmonic materials, including gold, silver, copper, aluminum, and titanium nitride. Using a dimensionally tunable coaxial nanoantenna, we map the optomagnetic response across the deep-ultraviolet to near-infrared spectrum. Our findings reveal highly distinct, material-dependent behaviors: aluminum uniquely sustains robust magnetization in the deep-UV, whereas silver, copper, and gold exhibit superior efficiency at longer wavelengths. Crucially, we demonstrate that shifting the excitation to the near-infrared regime amplifies the generated magnetic field by several orders of magnitude, establishing these frequencies as critical for helicity-dependent all-optical switching. Furthermore, by resolving the local optical spin density, we elucidate how extreme subwavelength confinement drives synchronized drift currents, enabling efficient multispectral magnetization through localized surface plasmon resonances and higher-order Fabry-Perot modes. Strikingly, comparing these distinct modes reveals that structural geometry tunes the resonant wavelength, while the maximum achievable optomagnetic amplitude is fundamentally governed by the metal's intrinsic properties.

AI.tldr: This theoretical study evaluates Inverse Faraday Effect-driven static magnetization in a dimensionally tunable coaxial plasmonic nanoantenna across gold, silver, copper, aluminum, and titanium nitride, mapping the optomagnetic response from the deep ultraviolet to the near infrared. It finds strongly material-dependent behavior, orders-of-magnitude magnetic-field enhancement in the near infrared, and explains multispectral magnetization through localized surface plasmon resonances and higher-order Fabry-Perot modes.
AI.motivation: All-optical magnetization control via the Inverse Faraday Effect is attractive for ultrafast high-density data storage and nanoscale spintronics, but existing approaches are constrained by gold-centric, narrowband plasmonic designs. The paper aims to move beyond these limitations by assessing a broader material library and a tunable geometry over a wide spectral range.
AI.method: The authors develop a comprehensive theoretical framework for IFE-driven static magnetic field generation using a dimensionally tunable coaxial nanoantenna. They compare plasmonic materials including gold, silver, copper, aluminum, and titanium nitride, map the optomagnetic response from the deep ultraviolet to the near infrared, and resolve the local optical spin density to analyze the role of localized surface plasmon resonances and higher-order Fabry-Perot modes.
AI.result: The calculations reveal distinct material-dependent optomagnetic behavior: aluminum sustains robust magnetization in the deep ultraviolet, while silver, copper, and gold are more efficient at longer wavelengths. Shifting excitation to the near infrared amplifies the generated magnetic field by several orders of magnitude. Extreme subwavelength confinement drives synchronized drift currents, enabling efficient multispectral magnetization through localized surface plasmon resonances and higher-order Fabry-Perot modes. Comparing modes shows that structural geometry tunes the resonant wavelength, whereas the maximum achievable optomagnetic amplitude is fundamentally governed by the metal's intrinsic properties.
AI.conclusion: Material choice and spectral regime strongly determine IFE-based optomagnetic performance in coaxial nanoantennas. Near-infrared excitation is identified as critical for helicity-dependent all-optical switching because of orders-of-magnitude field enhancement, while geometric tuning controls resonance and intrinsic material properties set the ultimate optomagnetic amplitude.

title: Metallic or insulating magnetic phases of transition-metal oxides in light of the Slater vs Mott controversy
summary: Magnetic d-electron oxides usually have a long-range-ordered ground state and an above-ground-state disordered para phase. The historical Slater-Mott controversy still reverberating to date pertains to understanding the origin of the insulating vs metallic nature of these two phases. Slater suggested that the insulating character evolved from the long-range order (LRO) antiferromagnetic (AFM) cell-doubling, leading to energy band repulsion and thus to forming a band gap. The reliance on LRO to explain gapping suggests that the absence of LRO in the spin-disordered para-phase would deprive the system from band repulsion, thus predicting a metallic paramagnetic (PM) phase. This, however, conflicts with numerous current observations. The alternative Mott-Peierls-Hubbard view abandons the mean-field-like band structure view emphasizing instead the local interelectronic repulsion U as a strong correlation signature of gapping both at the presence or absence of LRO. However, U is not an easily measured or calculated quantity in periodic systems, a situation often leading in practice to treating U as an adjustable parameter. The current work uses a parameter-free mean-field-like approach (Density Functional Theory, DFT), allowing energy-lowering symmetry breaking. This is done by considering local magnetic motifs as building blocks of the macroscopic AFM or PM phases. It is found that even when such motifs are isolated electronically from each other (i.e. vanishing LRO) by embedding them in quantum barriers (such as magnetic NiO6 octahedra surrounded locally by wide-gap MgO) they exhibit an intrinsic band gap. Thus, the origin of the band gaps in AFM or PM phases need not be LRO or strong correlation and can be understood within the mean-field-like band structure approach with symmetry breaking.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the Slater–Mott controversy over whether band gaps in magnetic transition-metal oxides require long-range antiferromagnetic order or strong electronic correlation. Using parameter-free DFT with local magnetic motifs as building blocks, it finds intrinsic gaps even when motifs are electronically isolated by wide-gap barriers, supporting a mean-field-like symmetry-breaking band-structure explanation.
AI.motivation: The historical Slater–Mott controversy concerns the origin of insulating versus metallic behavior in long-range-ordered and disordered para phases of magnetic d-electron oxides. Slater’s long-range-order-based gapping picture predicts a metallic paramagnetic phase when order is absent, conflicting with many observations, while the Mott–Peierls–Hubbard view relies on the local repulsion U, which is difficult to measure or calculate and is often treated as adjustable.
AI.method: The work uses a parameter-free mean-field-like Density Functional Theory approach that permits energy-lowering symmetry breaking. Local magnetic motifs are treated as building blocks of macroscopic antiferromagnetic or paramagnetic phases and are electronically isolated from one another by embedding them in quantum barriers, such as magnetic NiO6 octahedra locally surrounded by wide-gap MgO.
AI.result: Even when the local magnetic motifs are electronically isolated from each other, corresponding to vanishing long-range order, they exhibit an intrinsic band gap. The abstract does not provide quantitative gap values or other numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The origin of band gaps in antiferromagnetic or paramagnetic phases need not be long-range order or strong correlation; it can be understood within a mean-field-like band-structure approach with symmetry breaking.

title: Interaction between fluids and Helfrich membranes
summary: We propose a finite-element method to determine the dynamics of a fluid interacting with a membrane---a fluid layer equipped with a Helfrich elastic free energy [W. Helfrich, Z. Naturforschung C, 28, 693, (1973)]. Our analysis is based on a partitioned approach, where the state of the fluid, of the membrane, and of the mesh, are solved for at staggered steps. We show the predicting capabilities of the method by considering a macroscopic example of an elastomer membrane, which bulges as it interacts with air injected through a channel. We demonstrate that our method allows for describing large membrane deformations which are not accessible by perturbative methods. We discuss the limitations of our method, by characterizing its added-mass instability. Finally, we show how our analysis allows for understanding the physical mechanism of bulge formation, which is due to a combination of elastic stresses and membrane boundary conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a finite-element, partitioned, staggered scheme for fluid interaction with a Helfrich-elastic membrane, demonstrates large-deformation elastomer bulging under injected air, characterizes an added-mass instability, and explains bulge formation via elastic stresses and membrane boundary conditions.
AI.motivation: To determine the dynamics of a fluid interacting with a membrane governed by Helfrich elastic free energy and to describe large membrane deformations that perturbative methods cannot access.
AI.method: A finite-element method based on a partitioned approach is used, solving the fluid, membrane, and mesh states at staggered steps.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on a macroscopic elastomer membrane that bulges when air is injected through a channel; it captures large membrane deformations, its added-mass instability limitation is characterized, and bulge formation is explained as a combination of elastic stresses and membrane boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed partitioned finite-element approach can predict fluid–Helfrich-membrane dynamics, including large deformations, while its added-mass instability defines a limitation; the analysis provides physical insight into bulge formation. No quantitative performance metrics are provided in the abstract.

title: Breaking the Fixed-Substrate Limitation of Deep Learning Ellipsometry with Pseudo-Substrate Spectra
summary: A machine learning method, deep learning ellipsometry (DLE), enables direct and rapid estimation of the optical constants and structures of thin films from spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) spectra. However, conventional neural-network-based DLE models are restricted to the specific substrate used during training, and applying them to a different substrate requires ~100 h of retraining. Here, we propose a framework that overcomes this fixed-substrate limitation by introducing a two-input feature-wise linear modulation DLE (FiLM-DLE). In this model, the SE spectra of a thin-film structure are input together with those of the substrate measured before film deposition, which we term the pseudo-substrate spectra. Any substrate, including a multilayer stack, is thus represented solely by its measured SE response, analogous to the pseudo-dielectric function, so that no prior knowledge of the substrate structure is required. Trained on a virtual dataset of 165 million samples representing metal, glass, and SiO2/Si substrates with different SiO2 thicknesses, a single FiLM-DLE model, trained once, extracts thin-film optical constants and structures with high accuracy and shows strong applicability to substrates not included in the training datasets. Experimental validation on 47 thin-film samples across diverse substrates yielded sample-averaged mean absolute errors, relative to conventional manual analysis, of 0.047 for refractive index, 0.030 for extinction coefficient, and 1.52 nm for thickness, with each analysis completed in under 2 s. FiLM-DLE thus eliminates the need for a separate DLE model for each substrate and enables rapid, high-accuracy optical characterization of thin films on diverse substrates.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FiLM-DLE, a two-input deep-learning ellipsometry framework that uses measured pseudo-substrate spectra to remove the fixed-substrate limitation of conventional DLE, enabling one trained model to characterize thin films on diverse substrates rapidly and accurately.
AI.motivation: Conventional neural-network-based deep learning ellipsometry models are restricted to the substrate used during training, and adapting a model to a different substrate requires approximately 100 h of retraining. The authors aim to eliminate this need for separate substrate-specific models.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-input feature-wise linear modulation DLE (FiLM-DLE) model that inputs thin-film spectroscopic ellipsometry spectra together with pseudo-substrate spectra measured before film deposition. The substrate, including multilayer stacks, is represented solely by its measured ellipsometry response without prior structural knowledge. A single model was trained on a virtual dataset of 165 million samples covering metal, glass, and SiO2/Si substrates with varied SiO2 thicknesses.
AI.result: The single trained FiLM-DLE model extracted thin-film optical constants and structures with high accuracy and generalized to substrates not included in training. Experimental validation on 47 thin-film samples across diverse substrates gave sample-averaged mean absolute errors versus conventional manual analysis of 0.047 for refractive index, 0.030 for extinction coefficient, and 1.52 nm for thickness, with each analysis completed in under 2 s.
AI.conclusion: FiLM-DLE overcomes the fixed-substrate limitation of conventional DLE, eliminating the need for a separate model per substrate and enabling rapid, high-accuracy optical characterization of thin films on diverse substrates.

title: Exact environment checkpointing for memory-limited DMRG and TDVP
summary: Finite matrix-product-state sweep algorithms, such as the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP), store one environment tensor per site. At the bond dimensions needed for frustrated and two-dimensional systems this stack, rather than the state itself, exhausts the memory of the device. We adapt checkpointing to these sweeps: every $k$-th environment is kept, with $k\approx\sqrt{N}$ for $N$ sites, and the blocks in between are rebuilt when the sweep returns to them. The rebuild repeats the original contractions, so energies and states are reproduced bit for bit when the contractions are deterministic. Environment memory falls by 4.6-10x on cylinders of 96-384 sites. Bond-dimension searches with an implementation that rebuilds checkpoints at each half-sweep give gains of 1.77 for one level and 2.07 for two levels with eight contraction chunks on a single 141 GB GPU, using a 144-site triangular $J_1$-$J_2$ cylinder and stored baselines with matching chunking. Separate timings with checkpoints retained across half-sweeps give a one-level overhead of 6-15%, depending on the local eigensolver. At $D=1536$ the two-level schedule with eight chunks takes 1.42 times the sweep time of the equally chunked stored baseline, or 1.79 times that of the unchunked stored baseline. Simple models of the memory and the run time reproduce the measurements to within a few per cent. Unlike offloading, the method needs no host memory or disk, and the two can be combined. Implementations are provided for ITensorMPS.jl, TeNPy, MPSKit.jl and quimb.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces exact environment checkpointing for finite matrix-product-state sweep algorithms DMRG and TDVP, storing only every k-th environment tensor and rebuilding intermediate environments by repeating deterministic contractions. This substantially reduces environment memory, with modest runtime overhead, and is implemented in four tensor-network libraries.
AI.motivation: In finite DMRG and TDVP sweeps, one environment tensor is stored per site; for frustrated and two-dimensional systems at large bond dimensions, this environment stack rather than the state itself exhausts device memory. The authors seek a memory-reduction method that avoids requiring host memory or disk, as offloading does.
AI.method: They adapt checkpointing to finite MPS sweeps: keep every k-th environment, with k approximately sqrt(N) for N sites, and rebuild the intervening blocks when the sweep returns to them by repeating the original contractions. When contractions are deterministic, energies and states are reproduced bit for bit. Implementations are provided for ITensorMPS.jl, TeNPy, MPSKit.jl, and quimb, and the approach can be combined with offloading.
AI.result: Environment memory falls by 4.6-10x on cylinders of 96-384 sites. Bond-dimension searches on a 144-site triangular J1-J2 cylinder using a single 141 GB GPU and matching chunking show gains of 1.77 for one level and 2.07 for two levels with eight contraction chunks. With checkpoints retained across half-sweeps, one-level overhead is 6-15% depending on the local eigensolver. At D=1536, the two-level eight-chunk schedule takes 1.42 times the sweep time of the equally chunked stored baseline and 1.79 times that of the unchunked stored baseline. Simple memory and runtime models reproduce measurements within a few per cent.
AI.conclusion: Exact environment checkpointing reduces memory use in memory-limited DMRG and TDVP sweeps without needing host memory or disk, at the cost of modest recomputation overhead. It can be combined with offloading and is implemented across several tensor-network libraries.

title: Spatiotemporal beam stirring of femtosecond pulses in a multicore fiber driven by spectral decorrelation
summary: Multicore fibers (MCFs) are promising for ultrafast laser systems, but random coupling between their cores makes the output power distribution unstable. Previously, we observed spatiotemporal beam stirring of narrowband sub-nanosecond pulses in a 7-core fiber, where Kerr nonlinearity equalizes the core powers. Here, we study the propagation of 150-fs pulses at 1052 nm in the same fiber. As the fiber length increases up to 20 m, the output core powers become equalized with a spread $<7\%$, and the far-field speckle pattern transforms into a bell-shaped total beam. In contrast to the sub-nanosecond case, the effect does not depend on the input peak power (0.2--15 kW) and originates from the spectral decorrelation of the random coupling between the cores, whereas a narrowband CW source yields an unstable output with a $\sim 40\%$ spread. Coupled-mode simulations reproduce these results.

AI.tldr: Propagation of 150-fs, 1052-nm pulses in a 7-core multicore fiber equalizes output core powers and produces a bell-shaped far-field beam as fiber length reaches 20 m; the effect is independent of input peak power and attributed to spectral decorrelation of random inter-core coupling rather than Kerr nonlinearity.
AI.motivation: Multicore fibers are promising for ultrafast laser systems, but random coupling between cores causes unstable output power distribution. Prior work with narrowband sub-nanosecond pulses showed spatiotemporal beam stirring assisted by Kerr nonlinearity; this paper examines whether and how femtosecond pulses behave similarly.
AI.method: The authors study 150-fs pulses at 1052 nm propagating in the same 7-core fiber for lengths up to 20 m, measuring output core powers and far-field speckle patterns. They compare behavior across input peak powers of 0.2–15 kW and with a narrowband continuous-wave source, and use coupled-mode simulations to reproduce the results.
AI.result: With increasing fiber length up to 20 m, output core powers become equalized with a spread below 7%, and the far-field speckle pattern transforms into a bell-shaped total beam. Unlike the sub-nanosecond case, the effect does not depend on input peak power (0.2–15 kW). A narrowband CW source instead yields an unstable output with about 40% spread. Coupled-mode simulations reproduce these observations.
AI.conclusion: For femtosecond pulses, spatiotemporal beam stirring in the multicore fiber originates from spectral decorrelation of random coupling between cores, rather than Kerr-nonlinearity-driven power equalization. This mechanism enables stable equalized output and a bell-shaped beam for broadband ultrafast pulses.

title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; Supplementary Information included (49 figures, 11 tables). IANN is MIT-licensed. Code: https://github.com/changzhiai/IANN - Documentation: https://iann.readthedocs.io - Curated DFT databases: https://huggingface.co/datasets/changzhiai/dft-databases - Foundation models: https://huggingface.co/changzhiai/iann-foundation-models
summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. Additionally, IANN provides an agent interface to facilitate integration with autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: IANN is an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements seven equivariant interatomic graph neural networks (PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA) behind a single data object, trainer and deployment route, adds automatic distributed training, self-describing checkpoints usable as ASE calculators, ensembles or TorchScript models in LAMMPS, and releases PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million DFT structures.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning interatomic potentials reach near-DFT accuracy at a fraction of the cost, but each state-of-the-art architecture ships as a separate codebase with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing architectures on the same dataset or deploying a trained model in production therefore requires substantial re-engineering.
AI.method: IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network) is a unified PyTorch framework in which the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are computed for every architecture by a single analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the atomic-graph edge vectors, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from SLURM, PBS or MPI environments. Self-describing checkpoints serve as ASE calculators, as uncertainty-reporting ensembles, or as TorchScript models run in LAMMPS via bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference, and an agent interface supports integration with autonomous agents.
AI.result: The framework enables comparison of the seven architectures under identical conditions on a common dataset of millions of structures. PaiNN foundation models are released, trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. The same training script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation.
AI.conclusion: IANN consolidates fragmented equivariant MLIP implementations into one open-source, user-friendly framework with unified data handling, training, and deployment, thereby simplifying benchmarking across architectures and moving trained models into production simulation; the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy benchmarks for the individual architectures.

title: Lock-in phase evidence for the electro-optic effect of interfacial water on ITO electrodes
summary: Attribution to the Pockels effect of interfacial water, reported at interfaces between transparent electrodes and aqueous solutions, has relied on using an optical model to estimate the contribution of changes in the electrode's own carrier density to the electromodulation spectrum and subtracting this contribution. In this study, we test this attribution using the phase, without subtracting the electrode contribution with an optical model. Because the carrier response of the electrode follows charge modulation at several hundred hertz without delay, it has a common phase at all wavelengths apart from sign reversals of the response. However, the measured transmission modulation spectra at the interface between indium tin oxide (ITO) and 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ aqueous NaCl show a phase peak near 420 nm, where the ITO response becomes small. This peak cannot be explained solely by a step-like change due to sign reversal of the response. This peak appears even when the working-electrode potential, the modulation frequency, or the electrode is changed. Furthermore, this phase peak can be explained by a thin-film calculation assuming that a uniform refractive-index change on the electrolyte side contributes with a phase different from that of the electrode response. This result, an observation independent of the estimate of the electrode contribution, supports the attribution to the electro-optic effect of interfacial water.

AI.tldr: Lock-in phase measurements at ITO/aqueous NaCl interfaces reveal a phase peak near 420 nm that is inconsistent with electrode carrier modulation alone and is explained by a thin-film model with a distinct-phase uniform refractive-index change on the electrolyte side, supporting an electro-optic effect of interfacial water.
AI.motivation: Previous attribution of interfacial water's Pockels effect relied on an optical model to estimate and subtract the contribution of electrode carrier-density changes to the electromodulation spectrum. This study tests that attribution using phase information without subtracting the electrode contribution via an optical model.
AI.method: The authors measured transmission modulation spectra and their phase at the interface between indium tin oxide (ITO) and 0.1 mol L^-1 aqueous NaCl, without optical-model subtraction of the electrode contribution. They examined the phase while changing the working-electrode potential, modulation frequency, and electrode, and compared the observed phase peak with a thin-film calculation assuming a uniform refractive-index change on the electrolyte side with a phase different from that of the electrode response.
AI.result: The measured spectra show a phase peak near 420 nm, where the ITO response becomes small. This peak cannot be explained solely by a step-like change from sign reversal of the electrode response, appears even when the working-electrode potential, modulation frequency, or electrode is changed, and can be explained by the thin-film calculation assuming a uniform refractive-index change on the electrolyte side contributing with a phase different from that of the electrode response.
AI.conclusion: The phase-based observation, independent of estimates of the electrode contribution, supports attribution of the interfacial signal to the electro-optic effect of interfacial water.

title: Formulation of Brownian chain molecular dynamics and the path-resolved quasi-density operator
summary: Brownian chain molecular dynamics (BCMD) [M. Shiga, J. Comput. Chem. 43, 1864 (2022)] was introduced as a practical path-integral-based approach to approximate quantum vibrational dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems. Its equations of motion combine Newtonian dynamics of the centroid variables with overdamped Brownian dynamics of the non-centroid path variables. Here, we introduce a path-resolved quasi-density-operator (path-QDO) representation by extending the QDO construction underlying centroid molecular dynamics to the full discretized imaginary-time path. For two position-diagonal observables, this representation gives an exact expression for the Kubo-transformed correlation function in the fine-discretization limit, without requiring either observable to be linear. BCMD can be viewed as a phenomenological, time-homogeneous Markov approximation to the exact reduced propagation in these path variables, although its generator is not derived from the path-QDO formulation. We also formulate and validate a multiple-time-step algorithm that allows pseudo-Hamiltonian errors in the deterministic propagation to be controlled by separating the Brownian refresh interval from the inner integration time step. We test the path-QDO representation on one-dimensional models and present BCMD infrared spectra of q-TIP4P/F ice, ambient water, and hot water, comparing them with published results from other approximate quantum-dynamics methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a path-resolved quasi-density-operator (path-QDO) representation for Brownian chain molecular dynamics (BCMD), an approximation to quantum vibrational dynamics. It gives an exact Kubo-transformed correlation-function expression for two position-diagonal observables in the fine-discretization limit, interprets BCMD as a phenomenological time-homogeneous Markov approximation, validates a multiple-time-step integrator, and tests the approach on one-dimensional models and infrared spectra of q-TIP4P/F ice and water.
AI.motivation: BCMD was introduced as a practical path-integral-based method for approximating quantum vibrational dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems. The authors aim to extend the quasi-density-operator construction underlying centroid molecular dynamics from the centroid to the full discretized imaginary-time path, thereby providing a path-resolved representation and testing BCMD against other approximate quantum-dynamics methods.
AI.method: The authors formulate a path-resolved quasi-density-operator (path-QDO) representation by extending the QDO construction to the full discretized imaginary-time path. For two position-diagonal observables, they derive an exact expression for the Kubo-transformed correlation function in the fine-discretization limit without requiring either observable to be linear. They also formulate and validate a multiple-time-step algorithm that separates the Brownian refresh interval from the inner integration time step to control pseudo-Hamiltonian errors in deterministic propagation. The path-QDO representation is tested on one-dimensional models, and BCMD infrared spectra are computed for q-TIP4P/F ice, ambient water, and hot water and compared with published results from other approximate quantum-dynamics methods.
AI.result: The path-QDO representation yields an exact expression for the Kubo-transformed correlation function for two position-diagonal observables in the fine-discretization limit, without requiring either observable to be linear. BCMD is shown to be interpretable as a phenomenological, time-homogeneous Markov approximation to the exact reduced propagation in the path variables, although its generator is not derived from the path-QDO formulation. The multiple-time-step algorithm is formulated and validated, allowing pseudo-Hamiltonian errors in deterministic propagation to be controlled. The representation is tested on one-dimensional models, and BCMD infrared spectra are presented for q-TIP4P/F ice, ambient water, and hot water and compared with published results from other approximate quantum-dynamics methods; quantitative spectral agreement is not specified in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a path-QDO representation can be constructed for the full discretized imaginary-time path and provides an exact Kubo-transformed correlation-function expression for two position-diagonal observables in the fine-discretization limit. BCMD can be viewed as a phenomenological, time-homogeneous Markov approximation to the exact reduced path-variable propagation, though not derived from the path-QDO formulation. A validated multiple-time-step integration scheme is presented, and BCMD spectra for q-TIP4P/F ice and water are compared with published approximate quantum-dynamics results; the abstract does not provide a detailed quantitative conclusion about relative accuracy.

title: Telecom-band optical parametric oscillation in a passive silicon microring resonator at cryogenic temperatures
summary: At telecommunications wavelengths, free carriers generated by two-photon absorption limit optical parametric oscillation (OPO) in silicon. Here, we demonstrate telecom-band OPO in a passive silicon microring resonator without electrical carrier sweep-out, driven by a single continuous-wave (CW) pump at 4.5 K. We achieve an on-chip OPO onset power of 2.25 mW and a total conversion efficiency of 1.9% into all parametric sidebands at a pump power of 4.8 mW. Despite CW pumping, the parametric output emerges as a train of pulses synchronized with microsecond-scale self-pulsing. At higher pump powers, OPO emission is absent during intervals of sustained sub-GHz oscillations in the pump transmission, narrowing the temporal window for OPO. Furthermore, by adjusting the pump detuning, we observe OPO at temperatures up to 55 K. These results demonstrate that nonlinear cavity dynamics govern the temporal structure and operating conditions of cryogenic silicon OPOs, providing new insights into controlling the oscillation regimes and temporal characteristics of on-chip nonlinear light sources compatible with cryogenic quantum photonic circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates telecom-band optical parametric oscillation in a passive silicon microring resonator at cryogenic temperatures using a single continuous-wave pump, without electrical carrier sweep-out. It reports milliwatt-scale onset power, percent-level conversion efficiency, self-pulsing dynamics, and operation up to 55 K.
AI.motivation: At telecommunications wavelengths, two-photon-absorption-generated free carriers limit optical parametric oscillation in silicon. The authors aim to realize telecom-band OPO in a passive silicon microring resonator without electrical carrier sweep-out and to understand its cryogenic operating conditions and temporal dynamics.
AI.method: The authors use a passive silicon microring resonator pumped by a single continuous-wave laser at 4.5 K. They measure OPO onset power and conversion efficiency, characterize the temporal structure of the parametric output and pump transmission, examine behavior at higher pump powers, and vary the pump detuning to test OPO at temperatures up to 55 K.
AI.result: An on-chip OPO onset power of 2.25 mW and a total conversion efficiency of 1.9% into all parametric sidebands at a pump power of 4.8 mW are achieved. Despite CW pumping, the parametric output is a pulse train synchronized with microsecond-scale self-pulsing. At higher pump powers, OPO emission is absent during intervals of sustained sub-GHz pump-transmission oscillations, narrowing the OPO temporal window. With pump detuning, OPO is observed at temperatures up to 55 K.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear cavity dynamics govern the temporal structure and operating conditions of cryogenic silicon OPOs. The results provide insights into controlling oscillation regimes and temporal characteristics of on-chip nonlinear light sources compatible with cryogenic quantum photonic circuits.

title: Affordable Analytic Gradients for G0W0-BSE Excited States for Multiple GW Variants via Back-Propagation
summary: We derive, implement and validate analytic nuclear gradients for three variants of $GW$ self-energies---the contour-deformation (CD), the analytic continuation (AC), and the contour deformation with $W$-analytic-continuation (CD-WAC)---and for the Bethe--Salpeter equation (BSE) built on top of them. All gradients are expressed as contractions of a set of covectors connected to derivatives of primitive quantities in SCF calculations. The derivation of these covectors is a back-propagation procedure through the $GW$ and BSE equations. Central finite differences confirm the correctness of all implemented gradients. With the AC-$GW$-BSE gradient we optimize the excited-state geometries of carbon monoxide, a donor-acceptor dye labelled as DA1, and DMABN, a typical model system for twisted intramolecular charge-transfer phenomena (TICT), and have obtained results that successfully reproduce observations from experiments or high-level calculations. We also performed trajectory surface hopping (TSH) simulations of nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD) of DMABN using the SHARC NAMD package, showing the capacity of our method to simulate NAMD problems. We performed timing and memory scaling tests, demonstrating that the gradient calculations of both $GW$ and BSE scale asymptotically as $N^4$ for timing and $N^3$ for memory. All source codes used in the present work, including the REST program package and the modified SHARC NAMD package that supports REST as the quantum chemistry backend, are available on Gitee https://gitee.com/restgroup/rest and https://gitee.com/qirui-gao-2025/sharc

AI.tldr: The paper derives, implements, and validates analytic nuclear gradients for GW-BSE excited states using three GW self-energy variants and back-propagation, enabling excited-state geometry optimization and nonadiabatic molecular dynamics with favorable asymptotic scaling.
AI.motivation: Affordable analytic nuclear gradients are needed for GW-BSE excited states across multiple GW variants so that excited-state geometry optimization and nonadiabatic dynamics can be performed without relying on finite differences.
AI.method: The authors express all gradients as contractions of covectors obtained by back-propagation through the GW and BSE equations. They implement and validate gradients for contour-deformation GW, analytic-continuation GW, contour-deformation GW with W analytic continuation, and BSE built on these variants. Validation uses central finite differences. AC-GW-BSE gradients are used to optimize excited-state geometries of carbon monoxide, DA1, and DMABN, and trajectory surface hopping NAMD simulations of DMABN are performed with SHARC. Timing and memory scaling are also tested.
AI.result: Central finite differences confirm the correctness of all implemented gradients. AC-GW-BSE geometry optimizations reproduce experimental or high-level calculation observations for carbon monoxide, DA1, and DMABN. TSH NAMD simulations of DMABN demonstrate the method's capability for nonadiabatic dynamics. Gradient calculations for both GW and BSE scale asymptotically as N^4 in timing and N^3 in memory. Source codes, including REST and a modified SHARC package, are available.
AI.conclusion: Back-propagation provides a validated and affordable route to analytic nuclear gradients for multiple GW variants and BSE, supporting excited-state geometry optimization and NAMD simulations. The implementation is released as open-source software.

title: Polarization-Resilient Plasmonic Nanoantenna Arrays for Fiber-Coupled Terahertz Spectroscopy with Record-high Dynamic Range
summary: Achieving polarization-resilient optoelectronic responses while harnessing the strong light-matter interactions enabled by plasmonic nanostructures remains a fundamental challenge in ultrafast optoelectronics. Here, we demonstrate that the polarization sensitivity of plasmonic optoelectronic devices is governed not simply by optical absorption, but by its interplay with ultrafast photocarrier transport and local electric-field distributions, establishing a design principle for achieving polarization resilience without compromising optoelectronic efficiency. Through theoretical modeling and experimental validation, we demonstrate that this interplay enables plasmonic nanoantenna arrays to maintain highly efficient terahertz generation and detection across different optical polarization states, overcoming a longstanding limitation of plasmonic optoelectronics. Exploiting this principle, we introduce a high-power fiber-coupled terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) architecture that integrates polarization-resilient plasmonic nanoantenna arrays with hollow-core antiresonant fibers. By suppressing optical dispersion and nonlinearities during high-power femtosecond pulse delivery, this architecture unlocks the superior optoelectronic properties of GaAs-based photoconductors without sacrificing the flexibility and robustness of fiber coupling. The resulting system generates a record-high 2.1 mW of terahertz radiation and achieves a 145 dB peak dynamic range over 60 seconds, representing a 300-fold improvement over state-of-the-art fiber-coupled THz-TDS systems. This breakthrough opens new opportunities for probing weak light-matter interactions, characterizing strongly attenuating materials, and realizing high-throughput hyperspectral imaging and spatially distributed terahertz sensing beyond controlled laboratory environments.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a design principle for polarization-resilient plasmonic optoelectronics and uses it to build a high-power fiber-coupled terahertz time-domain spectroscopy system with record-high dynamic range.
AI.motivation: Polarization-sensitive optoelectronic responses remain a fundamental challenge for plasmonic devices, and fiber-coupled terahertz time-domain spectroscopy systems need higher terahertz power and dynamic range without losing fiber flexibility and robustness.
AI.method: The authors combine theoretical modeling and experimental validation to show that polarization sensitivity is governed by the interplay of optical absorption, ultrafast photocarrier transport, and local electric-field distributions. They design polarization-resilient plasmonic nanoantenna arrays and integrate them with hollow-core antiresonant fibers to suppress optical dispersion and nonlinearities during high-power femtosecond pulse delivery, enabling GaAs-based photoconductors in a fiber-coupled architecture.
AI.result: The system generates a record-high 2.1 mW of terahertz radiation and achieves a 145 dB peak dynamic range over 60 seconds, reported as a 300-fold improvement over state-of-the-art fiber-coupled terahertz time-domain spectroscopy systems.
AI.conclusion: The work overcomes a longstanding limitation of plasmonic optoelectronics and enables fiber-coupled terahertz spectroscopy with high power and dynamic range, opening opportunities for probing weak light-matter interactions, characterizing strongly attenuating materials, high-throughput hyperspectral imaging, and spatially distributed terahertz sensing beyond controlled laboratory environments.

title: Neural Surrogates for Tabulated Nuclear Equations of State in Core-Collapse Supernova Simulations
comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: Large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations rely on tabulated nuclear equations of state (EOSs), whose memory requirements can become a practical constraint in massively parallel calculations. We explore a compact alternative by replacing the tabulated thermodynamic mapping with a neural-network surrogate, using the Lattimer--Swesty EOS as a representative reference model. The surrogate directly predicts pressure, sound speed, and effective adiabatic index from $(\log ρ, \log e, Y_e)$ and accurately reconstructs the nonlinear thermodynamic structure of the EOS, including its behavior across phase-transition regions. It reproduces one-dimensional shock-tube solutions with hydrodynamic errors at the $\sim 10^{-3}$ level under different thermodynamic conditions and yields hydrostatic equilibrium configurations closely matching those obtained with the reference EOS. We find that smaller regression errors do not necessarily yield better hydrodynamic performance, demonstrating the importance of hydrodynamic validation in surrogate model selection. A compact network with only $\sim 10^4$ parameters retains this accuracy while reducing the memory required to store the EOS from $\sim 160$ MB to $\sim 100$ KB, corresponding to a reduction by a factor of $\sim 1500$. The surrogate also remains stable through collapse, bounce, shock formation, and post-bounce evolution in a one-dimensional adiabatic core-collapse calculation. These results demonstrate the potential of compact neural EOS surrogates for reducing memory requirements in large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a compact neural-network surrogate for tabulated nuclear equations of state used in core-collapse supernova simulations, replacing the thermodynamic lookup with direct predictions from (log ρ, log e, Y_e). Using the Lattimer–Swesty EOS as reference, the surrogate reproduces thermodynamic structure and hydrodynamic behavior while reducing EOS storage from about 160 MB to about 100 KB.
AI.motivation: Large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations depend on tabulated nuclear equations of state, and the memory required to store these tables can become a practical constraint in massively parallel calculations. The authors therefore explore a compact neural alternative.
AI.method: A neural-network surrogate replaces the tabulated thermodynamic mapping of the Lattimer–Swesty EOS. It predicts pressure, sound speed, and effective adiabatic index directly from (log ρ, log e, Y_e). The authors test thermodynamic reconstruction, one-dimensional shock-tube solutions, hydrostatic equilibrium configurations, and a one-dimensional adiabatic core-collapse calculation through collapse, bounce, shock formation, and post-bounce evolution.
AI.result: The surrogate accurately reconstructs the EOS nonlinear thermodynamic structure, including phase-transition regions. It reproduces one-dimensional shock-tube solutions with hydrodynamic errors at the ∼10^-3 level and yields hydrostatic equilibrium configurations closely matching the reference EOS. A compact network with only ∼10^4 parameters retains this accuracy while reducing EOS memory from ∼160 MB to ∼100 KB, a factor of ∼1500. The authors also find that smaller regression errors do not necessarily imply better hydrodynamic performance.
AI.conclusion: Compact neural EOS surrogates can substantially reduce memory requirements for large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations while remaining stable through key collapse and post-bounce stages. The results also show that hydrodynamic validation is important in surrogate model selection.

title: Broadband Absorption Bounds for Coated PEC Spheres: Curvature, Angular Momentum, and Localized Sources
summary: We investigate fundamental limits on broadband electromagnetic absorption by a material-coated perfectly electrically conducting (PEC) sphere. Exact reflection coefficients are derived for the transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) spherical modes. Their long-wavelength asymptotics, combined with causality and contour integration in the complex wavelength plane, yield sum rules relating the wavelength-integrated modal reflection to the static material parameters, coating thickness, curvature, and complex reflection zeros. For the dipolar modes ($n=1$), known passive spherical-wave sum rules establish analytically a material-dependent lower bound on the weighted logarithmic reflection integral. Extension to higher-order modes requires a nonnegativity condition on higher odd moments of the reflection zeros; we formulate this condition as a conjecture and provide extensive Monte-Carlo evidence for passive dispersive coatings. The resulting bounds establish a per-channel absorption--bandwidth tradeoff and reveal the spherical-harmonic order as a discrete transverse-wavenumber variable, recovering the familiar planar attenuation factor in the locally planar limit. Finally, we show how the modal bounds can be combined for a localized external source. For a radial electric dipole outside the sphere, the near-field excitation is decomposed into TM spherical channels, leading to a source-weighted broadband absorption bound. As the source approaches the surface, progressively higher angular momenta contribute, directly linking near-field spatial localization to the hierarchy of modal absorption constraints.
