AI.tldr: The paper derives broadband electromagnetic-absorption bounds for a material-coated PEC sphere using exact TE/TM modal reflection coefficients, long-wavelength asymptotics, causality, and complex-wavelength contour integration. It obtains sum rules and per-channel absorption-bandwidth tradeoffs, proves a material-dependent dipolar bound, conjectures a higher-mode nonnegativity condition supported by Monte Carlo evidence, and extends the modal bounds to a localized radial electric dipole source.
AI.motivation: The work aims to establish fundamental limits on broadband electromagnetic absorption by a coated perfectly electrically conducting sphere, including how curvature, angular momentum, material dispersion, coating thickness, and localized external illumination constrain absorption-bandwidth performance.
AI.method: Exact TE and TM spherical-mode reflection coefficients are derived. Their long-wavelength asymptotics are combined with causality and contour integration in the complex wavelength plane to obtain sum rules. For n=1 dipolar modes, passive spherical-wave sum rules yield an analytical material-dependent lower bound on a weighted logarithmic reflection integral. Higher-order modes require a nonnegativity condition on higher odd moments of the reflection zeros, formulated as a conjecture and tested with extensive Monte Carlo simulations for passive dispersive coatings. Modal bounds are then combined for a radial electric dipole outside the sphere by decomposing its near field into TM spherical channels.
AI.result: The analysis yields sum rules connecting wavelength-integrated modal reflection to static material parameters, coating thickness, curvature, and complex reflection zeros. A material-dependent lower bound is established analytically for the n=1 weighted logarithmic reflection integral. Conditional on the conjectured nonnegativity condition, higher-order modal bounds are obtained with Monte Carlo support. The bounds give a per-channel absorption-bandwidth tradeoff, identify spherical-harmonic order as a discrete transverse-wavenumber variable, and recover the planar attenuation factor in the locally planar limit. For a radial electric dipole, a source-weighted broadband absorption bound is derived; as the source approaches the surface, progressively higher angular momenta contribute, linking near-field spatial localization to the modal absorption hierarchy. No numerical bound values are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that coated PEC spherical absorbers are subject to modal, curvature-dependent broadband absorption constraints that can be expressed through sum rules and per-channel absorption-bandwidth tradeoffs. Dipolar bounds follow analytically, while higher-order bounds depend on a conjectured reflection-zero moment condition with Monte Carlo evidence. The framework also connects localized source proximity and near-field spatial localization to increasingly higher angular-momentum absorption channels.

title: Efficient simulation of the generalized Langevin equation using a basis of dynamically relevant histories for memory and noise
summary: The Generalized Langevin Equation (GLE) is a cornerstone for modeling non-Markovian dynamics, but its numerical solution remains challenging due to the history-dependent convolution and the need to generate colored noise with a prescribed correlation function. We introduce a forward construction that addresses both challenges within a single framework. We represent an arbitrary trajectory as sum of relevant and irrelevant parts, where relevant part can be decomposed into a small number of characteristic history patterns that make the main contribution to future dynamics. It allows to reduce numerical cost to \(O(d^2)\) for $d$ chosen patterns instead of full history. The same construction applies to colored noise generation, where the causal filter plays the role of the memory kernel. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the method for several representative kernels, including long-range kernels with power-law tails.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a forward construction for efficiently simulating the generalized Langevin equation by representing relevant trajectory histories with a small set of characteristic patterns and using the same framework for colored-noise generation.
AI.motivation: The generalized Langevin equation is central to modeling non-Markovian dynamics, but numerical solution is challenging because of the history-dependent convolution and the need to generate colored noise with a prescribed correlation function.
AI.method: The authors decompose an arbitrary trajectory into relevant and irrelevant parts, representing the relevant part as a small number of characteristic history patterns that dominate future dynamics. This reduces numerical cost to O(d^2) for d selected patterns instead of requiring the full history. The same construction is applied to colored-noise generation, with the causal filter acting as the memory kernel.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated to be accurate and efficient for several representative kernels, including long-range kernels with power-law tails. No quantitative performance or error values are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework addresses history-dependent convolution and colored-noise generation within a single construction and is concluded to provide accurate, efficient simulation for the tested memory kernels.

title: Optimization Framework for Full-Skyrmionic Polarimetry
summary: Optical skyrmionic beams hold considerable potential for applications in quantum information and weak-intensity detection. These applications require accurate measurements of full topological observables using imaging Stokes polarimetry, with measurement states optimized in advance to limit the effect of stochastic error sources. However, the optimization framework for general Stokes polarimetries is based on a linear reconstruction chain for Stokes vectors and cannot quantitatively evaluate the nonlinear reconstruction of topological observables. Here, we define full-skyrmionic polarimetry (FSP) and construct its optimization framework from the reconstruction chain for full topological observables. Based on existing polarization evaluating functions (PEF), we introduce topological evaluating functions (TEF) and develop a multi-stage FSP optimization methodology. Numerical results confirm that topological optimization can further improve the reconstruction of topological observables, even when the measurement states are already optimal for polarization. Increasing the redundant projection number also effectively suppresses the effects of all stochastic error sources, providing a low-cost methodology to improve the reconstruction of both polarization and topological observables. The FSP optimization framework can identify topologically optimal configurations for arbitrary FSP structures, providing a guideline for high-precision full-skyrmionic measurements at weak-intensity levels and potential skyrmion ellipsometry.

AI.tldr: The paper defines full-skyrmionic polarimetry and develops a multi-stage optimization framework for reconstructing full topological observables of optical skyrmionic beams, using topological evaluating functions and redundant projections to improve robustness against stochastic errors.
AI.motivation: Accurate full-topological-observable measurements via imaging Stokes polarimetry are needed for quantum information and weak-intensity detection, but existing optimization frameworks rely on linear Stokes-vector reconstruction and cannot quantitatively evaluate the nonlinear reconstruction of topological observables.
AI.method: The authors define full-skyrmionic polarimetry (FSP), construct an optimization framework based on the reconstruction chain for full topological observables, introduce topological evaluating functions (TEF) building on existing polarization evaluating functions (PEF), and develop a multi-stage FSP optimization methodology. They also examine increasing the redundant projection number and use numerical results to assess reconstruction performance.
AI.result: Numerical results show that topological optimization further improves reconstruction of topological observables even when measurement states are already optimal for polarization. Increasing the redundant projection number effectively suppresses all stochastic error sources, providing a low-cost way to improve reconstruction of both polarization and topological observables. The framework can identify topologically optimal configurations for arbitrary FSP structures.
AI.conclusion: The FSP optimization framework provides a guideline for high-precision full-skyrmionic measurements at weak-intensity levels and has potential for skyrmion ellipsometry. Experimental validation is not reported in the abstract.

title: Beyond global density in a stochastic sandpile: the role of spatial signatures in the predictability of extremes
summary: In self-organized critical systems the global load is a strong precursor of extreme events. In the two-dimensional Manna sandpile, grain density alone predicts extreme avalanches with an AUC of about 0.96. We ask whether density fully determines the system's readiness for an extreme event, that is, whether microstates with the same number of grains are equivalent. Because density is such a strong predictor, a method that sees the full microstate can score well just by counting grains. We therefore compare only states with an identical number of grains. Even then, both a parameter-free statistic and a convolutional network distinguish states that precede an extreme avalanche from typical ones, while shuffled controls do not. The signal is a load contrast between the center and the dissipative boundaries, carried by the two lowest symmetric cosine modes. Their normalized energy is a single variable that needs no training. Together with density it recovers most of the gain that a network trained on the full microstate achieves over density alone. Readiness for an extreme avalanche therefore depends both on the total load and on how that load is distributed relative to the boundaries.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether global grain density fully determines extreme-event readiness in the two-dimensional Manna sandpile. By comparing microstates with identical grain numbers, it finds that spatial load distribution relative to dissipative boundaries provides additional predictive information beyond density.
AI.motivation: Global load is a strong precursor of extreme avalanches in self-organized critical systems, with grain density alone achieving an AUC of about 0.96 in the 2D Manna sandpile. The authors ask whether density fully determines readiness for an extreme event, or whether microstates with the same number of grains can differ in their likelihood of preceding an extreme avalanche.
AI.method: Because full-microstate methods can score well simply by counting grains, the authors compare only states with an identical number of grains. They use a parameter-free statistic and a convolutional network to distinguish states preceding an extreme avalanche from typical states, with shuffled controls. They identify a center-to-boundary load contrast carried by the two lowest symmetric cosine modes, whose normalized energy requires no training, and combine it with density.
AI.result: Density alone predicts extreme avalanches with an AUC of about 0.96. Even at fixed grain number, both the parameter-free statistic and the convolutional network distinguish pre-extreme states from typical ones, while shuffled controls do not. The normalized energy of the two lowest symmetric cosine modes, together with density, recovers most of the gain that a network trained on the full microstate achieves over density alone.
AI.conclusion: Readiness for an extreme avalanche in the 2D Manna sandpile depends not only on total load but also on how that load is spatially distributed relative to the dissipative boundaries.

title: Multi-output neural network surrogate for double-pulse femtosecond optothermal control of thin silicon films on fused silica
summary: We introduce a multi-output feedforward neural network surrogate trained on a coupled multiple-reflection and two-temperature model to map double-pulse femtosecond laser excitation (1030 nm) of crystalline silicon films on fused silica across film thicknesses (50-500 nm) and inter-pulse delays (0-10ps). Trained via Levenberg-Marquardt optimization on 2000 physical simulations, the dual-hidden-layer network ([40,30] neurons) simultaneously predicts six strongly coupled optothermal observables, peak electron temperature, peak lattice temperature, peak carrier density, minimum and maximum absorptivity and minimum refractive index achieving coefficients of determination R2 larger than 0.9998 across all targets. Evaluating a dense 200 by 200 design grid in milliseconds resolves pronounced thin-film interference fringes and carrier-induced index modulation, identifying an optimal optothermal coupling regime at d=156 nm and Dt=4.572 ps. This unified machine-learning workflow eliminates computationally expensive multi-physics runtime bottlenecks for real-time laser processing control and inverse photonic thin-film design.

AI.tldr: A multi-output feedforward neural network surrogate is trained on coupled multiple-reflection and two-temperature simulations to predict six coupled optothermal observables for double-pulse femtosecond laser excitation of crystalline silicon films on fused silica, enabling rapid design-grid evaluation and identification of an optimal optothermal coupling regime.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to eliminate computationally expensive multi-physics runtime bottlenecks and support real-time laser processing control and inverse photonic thin-film design.
AI.method: A dual-hidden-layer feedforward neural network with [40,30] neurons was trained via Levenberg-Marquardt optimization on 2000 physical simulations from a coupled multiple-reflection and two-temperature model. It maps 1030 nm double-pulse femtosecond excitation across 50-500 nm film thicknesses and 0-10 ps inter-pulse delays and simultaneously predicts peak electron temperature, peak lattice temperature, peak carrier density, minimum and maximum absorptivity, and minimum refractive index.
AI.result: The surrogate achieved coefficients of determination R2 larger than 0.9998 for all six targets. Evaluating a dense 200 by 200 design grid in milliseconds resolved thin-film interference fringes and carrier-induced index modulation and identified an optimal optothermal coupling regime at d=156 nm and inter-pulse delay of 4.572 ps.
AI.conclusion: The unified machine-learning workflow provides a fast surrogate for coupled optothermal thin-film behavior, removing computationally expensive multi-physics runtime bottlenecks for real-time laser processing control and inverse photonic thin-film design.

title: Intrinsic memory limits resonant control of complex cardiac spiral waves
summary: Resonant forcing is known to induce controlled drift of phase-locked spiral waves in excitable media. Here, we show that intrinsic memory fundamentally alters this paradigm in complex meandering spirals typical of cardiac tissue, where phase-dependent responses to successive perturbations over the meander cycle interfere destructively to produce metastable quasi-stationarity or constructively to induce stable confinement. These dynamical insights motivate an improved low-energy multi-pulse feedback protocol that robustly drives spiral waves to termination through sustained directed drift.

AI.tldr: Intrinsic memory in complex meandering cardiac spiral waves limits resonant control: successive phase-dependent perturbations can interfere destructively to yield metastable quasi-stationarity or constructively to cause stable confinement. These insights motivate a low-energy multi-pulse feedback protocol that robustly terminates spirals via sustained directed drift.
AI.motivation: Resonant forcing is known to induce controlled drift of phase-locked spiral waves in excitable media, but this paradigm may not hold for complex meandering spirals typical of cardiac tissue. The paper aims to understand how intrinsic memory affects resonant control and to use these dynamics to improve spiral-wave termination.
AI.method: The abstract reports a dynamical analysis of phase-dependent responses to successive perturbations over the meander cycle and proposes an improved low-energy multi-pulse feedback protocol. Specific models, experimental preparations, and numerical or analytical methods are not provided.
AI.result: Intrinsic memory fundamentally alters resonant control: phase-dependent responses interfere destructively, producing metastable quasi-stationarity, or constructively, inducing stable confinement. The proposed multi-pulse feedback protocol robustly drives spiral waves to termination through sustained directed drift.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic memory imposes fundamental limits on resonant control of complex cardiac spiral waves, but understanding these memory-dependent interference effects enables a low-energy feedback strategy for robust spiral-wave termination.

title: Geometry-Derived Capacitance Dyadics with Floquet Sideband Correction for Anisotropic Periodic Patch Metasurfaces
summary: Homogenised sheet models describe periodic metallic patch layers using a scalar sheet capacitance, which is only valid when the effective response is isotropic. An isotropic response exists for unit cells with patch geometries that have rotational symmetry of order three or higher. Lower-symmetry unit cells with irregular or random geometries generically require a full 2 x 2 surface-capacitance dyadic. We present a framework that computes this dyadic directly from the arbitrary gap-connected patch geometry on a unit cell of a hexagonal lattice. The two-dimensional Bravais periodicity fixes the two independent macroscopic loading directions, the connectivity of the gap ensures a full-rank response for the geometries considered here, and the point-group symmetry of the patch constrains the form of the dyadic. A quasi-static boundary value problem on a single periodic cell then determines its independent entries. We use the surface-capacitance dyadic in the anisotropic surface- wave dispersion relation, which includes the leading spatially-dispersive first shell Floquet-sideband correction. For each new patch geometry, the dyadic and the first-shell correction are obtained from a single quasi-static cell problem and from the reconstructed boundary. So anisotropic surface- wave dispersion follows without a per-geometry full-wave eigenmode band sweep or sheet-tensor retrieval. We validate this geometry-to-dispersion chain against full-wave eigenmode simulations across six representative symmetry classes, showing that the correction captures band flattening near the Brillouin-zone boundary and improves agreement relative to the local dyadic model.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a full 2 x 2 surface-capacitance dyadic from arbitrary gap-connected patch geometry on a hexagonal unit cell and combines it with a first-shell Floquet-sideband correction to predict anisotropic surface-wave dispersion without per-geometry full-wave eigenmode band sweeps.
AI.motivation: Scalar sheet-capacitance homogenisation is valid only for isotropic responses, typically unit cells with rotational symmetry of order three or higher. Lower-symmetry irregular or random patch geometries generically require a full anisotropic surface-capacitance dyadic, motivating a geometry-derived approach that avoids repeated full-wave band sweeps or sheet-tensor retrieval.
AI.method: Two-dimensional Bravais periodicity fixes two independent macroscopic loading directions, gap connectivity ensures a full-rank response for the considered geometries, and patch point-group symmetry constrains the dyadic form. A quasi-static boundary value problem on a single periodic cell determines the independent entries. The dyadic is used in the anisotropic surface-wave dispersion relation with the leading spatially dispersive first-shell Floquet-sideband correction, obtained from one quasi-static cell problem and the reconstructed boundary.
AI.result: The geometry-to-dispersion chain was validated against full-wave eigenmode simulations across six representative symmetry classes. The Floquet-sideband correction captures band flattening near the Brillouin-zone boundary and improves agreement relative to the local dyadic model. Experimental validation is not reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables anisotropic surface-wave dispersion for periodic patch metasurfaces to be obtained directly from patch geometry using a single quasi-static cell calculation plus a first-shell Floquet correction, with improved accuracy over the local dyadic model. Broader applicability and experimental verification are not detailed in the abstract.

title: Dissipative many-body theory of electron-phonon-photon systems
summary: Optical cavities offer opportunities to control quantum materials, but radiative leakage and vibrational relaxation call for microscopic theories that treat interactions and dissipation on equal footing. We develop a Keldysh-Lindblad nonequilibrium Green's function framework for interacting electrons coupled to quantized photon and phonon fields. The formulation accommodates boson-number-nonconserving Hamiltonians and dissipative channels that combine electronic transitions with bosonic processes. We derive the mixed electron-boson diagrammatic expansion and the corresponding Kadanoff-Baym equations, retaining environmental noise, initial correlations, and interaction-induced memory. The equal-time equations govern the electronic density matrix and the bosonic covariance. As an illustration, we construct jump operators that preserve a semiconductor with filled valence bands and an empty photon field. Within a mean-field treatment, this state remains stationary although its two-time propagators exhibit dissipative broadening. The framework opens new avenues for studying correlated dynamics in lossy cavities and vibrational environments.

AI.tldr: Develops a Keldysh-Lindblad nonequilibrium Green's function theory for interacting electrons coupled to quantized photon and phonon fields, derives mixed diagrammatics and Kadanoff-Baym equations including dissipation and memory, and illustrates stationary semiconductor states with dissipative broadening.
AI.motivation: Optical cavities offer opportunities to control quantum materials, but radiative leakage and vibrational relaxation require microscopic theories that treat interactions and dissipation on equal footing.
AI.method: The paper develops a Keldysh-Lindblad nonequilibrium Green's function framework for interacting electrons coupled to quantized photon and phonon fields. It accommodates boson-number-nonconserving Hamiltonians and dissipative channels combining electronic transitions with bosonic processes, derives a mixed electron-boson diagrammatic expansion and Kadanoff-Baym equations, and obtains equal-time equations for the electronic density matrix and bosonic covariance. As an illustration, it constructs jump operators preserving a semiconductor with filled valence bands and an empty photon field within a mean-field treatment.
AI.result: The formulation retains environmental noise, initial correlations, and interaction-induced memory. In the illustrative mean-field treatment, the semiconductor state with filled valence bands and an empty photon field remains stationary, while its two-time propagators exhibit dissipative broadening. No quantitative or experimental results are reported.
AI.conclusion: The framework opens new avenues for studying correlated dynamics in lossy cavities and vibrational environments.

title: Predicting local electric field in Al$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$N p-i-n photodiodes using exciton Franz-Keldysh photocurrent spectroscopy
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table included. Submitted to Applied Physics Letters
summary: In AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes, reverse bias redshifts and broadens the sub-bandgap photocurrent responsivity through the eXciton Franz-Keldysh (XFK) effect, and this spectral line shape encodes the local electric field inside the device. Fitting the photocurrent spectra of two such photodiodes, with 5% and 40% Al, to an XFK absorption model at each bias yields the local voltage, $V_l$, a single parameter that sets the line shape and uniquely determines the electric-field profile inside the device. In both devices, $V_l$ varies linearly with the applied bias ($R^2 = 0.994$ and $0.998$) but changes far more slowly than the bias itself, revealing a strong local reduction of the electric field that points to non-uniform electrostatics. The slopes show that only 12.4% of the applied bias in the 5% Al device, and 45.8% in the 40% Al device, drops across the junction at the probed location. Extrapolated to zero bias, $V_l$ gives built-in voltages of 3.39 and 4.29 V, within 0.02 V of the 3.41 and 4.28 V obtained from technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulation, which validates the extracted local voltages at equilibrium. These results extend sub-bandgap photocurrent spectroscopy to AlGaN devices as an optical probe of local electrostatics, relevant to ultraviolet photodetectors and high-voltage electronics.

AI.tldr: Sub-bandgap photocurrent spectra of AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes are fitted with an exciton Franz-Keldysh model to extract a local voltage that determines the internal electric-field profile; the extracted voltages scale linearly with reverse bias, reveal strongly non-uniform electrostatics, and agree with TCAD built-in voltages.
AI.motivation: To develop sub-bandgap photocurrent spectroscopy as an optical probe of local electrostatics in AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes, with relevance to ultraviolet photodetectors and high-voltage electronics.
AI.method: Photocurrent responsivity spectra were measured under reverse bias for two AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes with 5% and 40% Al and fitted at each bias to an exciton Franz-Keldysh absorption model. The fit yields a local voltage, Vl, which sets the spectral line shape and uniquely determines the electric-field profile; zero-bias Vl values were compared with TCAD simulations.
AI.result: Reverse bias redshifted and broadened the sub-bandgap photocurrent through the exciton Franz-Keldysh effect. Vl varied linearly with applied bias (R^2 = 0.994 and 0.998) but far more slowly than the bias, with only 12.4% of the applied bias in the 5% Al device and 45.8% in the 40% Al device dropping across the junction at the probed location. Extrapolated zero-bias Vl gave built-in voltages of 3.39 and 4.29 V, within 0.02 V of the TCAD values of 3.41 and 4.28 V.
AI.conclusion: Exciton Franz-Keldysh photocurrent spectroscopy is extended to AlGaN devices as an optical probe of local electrostatics. The results indicate non-uniform electrostatics with a strong local reduction of the electric field and are relevant to ultraviolet photodetectors and high-voltage electronics.

title: Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction for Binary-Encoded Fourier Single-Pixel Imaging
summary: Digital micromirror devices enable high-speed Fourier single-pixel imaging (Fourier-SPI), but their binary modulation introduces quantization errors that degrade the reconstructed image quality. In particular, each binarized Fourier probe contains non-target Fourier components, thereby distorting the corresponding Fourier-domain measurement. This Letter presents a Fourier domain correction framework that characterizes these errors using the Fourier-domain response matrix of the decoded binary Fourier patterns. Accordingly, a response-matrix-based Fourier-SPI measurement model is established by partitioning the matrix into components associated with the sampled and unsampled frequencies, thereby decomposing the quantization error into sampled-frequency crosstalk and unsampled-frequency leakage. This model established a generalized correction framework, termed Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction (FCLC), alongside two simplified methods: Fourier Sampled-Frequency Crosstalk Correction (FSCC) and Fourier DC Crosstalk Correction (FDCC). FSCC is implemented via an inversion-free Richardson-type iteration, whereas FDCC admits a closed-form solution. Numerical simulations and experiments across multiple binary encoding strategies reveal that the proposed framework improves reconstruction fidelity without modifying the binary patterns or acquisition process.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Fourier-domain correction framework for binary-encoded Fourier single-pixel imaging that mitigates quantization errors from digital micromirror device binary modulation, improving reconstruction fidelity without changing the binary patterns or acquisition process.
AI.motivation: Digital micromirror devices enable high-speed Fourier single-pixel imaging, but their binary modulation causes quantization errors: each binarized Fourier probe contains non-target Fourier components that distort Fourier-domain measurements and degrade reconstructed image quality.
AI.method: The authors characterize these errors using the Fourier-domain response matrix of decoded binary Fourier patterns and establish a response-matrix-based Fourier-SPI measurement model. By partitioning the matrix into sampled- and unsampled-frequency components, they decompose quantization error into sampled-frequency crosstalk and unsampled-frequency leakage. They propose the generalized Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction framework, plus Fourier Sampled-Frequency Crosstalk Correction implemented by an inversion-free Richardson-type iteration and Fourier DC Crosstalk Correction with a closed-form solution.
AI.result: Numerical simulations and experiments across multiple binary encoding strategies show that the proposed framework improves reconstruction fidelity without modifying the binary patterns or the acquisition process. Specific quantitative performance gains are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Fourier-domain response-matrix modeling and crosstalk/leakage correction can mitigate quantization errors in binary-encoded Fourier single-pixel imaging while preserving the original binary encoding and acquisition workflow.

title: Femtosecond Free-Space Time-Frequency Transfer at km/s Relative Motion with Doppler Compensation
summary: A global optical clock network holds great promise for a wide range of applications, including international metrology--particularly the redefinition of the ``second''--as well as navigation, geoscience, and fundamental physics. Satellite-based high-precision time-frequency dissemination is essential for realizing such a network. Despite remarkable progress in ground-based free-space simulations over high-loss channels, the Doppler effect arising from satellite motion has remained an unsolved barrier. Here we demonstrate femtosecond two-way time-frequency transfer over a 113-km free-space link under simulated Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s. To overcome the Doppler barrier, we first reproduce satellite-like Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s on the ground by locking a frequency comb to a broadly tunable laser. We then correct the resulting disturbances with two complementary techniques: a dual-channel sampling architecture that compensates for optical dispersion and radio frequency (RF) nonlinearity while eliminating Nyquist dead zones, and an iterative interferogram reconstruction algorithm that removes Doppler-induced distortion. After correction, residual systematic errors are within $\pm10$ fs over the full 1.55 km/s range. Using simulated medium earth orbit (MEO) and geosynchronous orbit (GSO) satellite trajectories, we achieve fractional frequency instability of $3.9\times10^{-19}$ at 4,600 s and $3.6\times10^{-19}$ at 23,600 s, respectively. This extends the operational velocity range by nearly two orders of magnitude beyond previous free-space demonstrations, removing the last major technical barrier to a global femtosecond-precision satellite-based time-frequency link.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates femtosecond two-way free-space time-frequency transfer over a 113-km link under simulated satellite Doppler shifts up to 1.55 km/s, using a frequency-comb-based Doppler emulator and two correction techniques to achieve residual timing errors within ±10 fs and 10^-19-level fractional frequency instability for simulated MEO and GSO trajectories.
AI.motivation: A global optical clock network requires satellite-based high-precision time-frequency dissemination, but satellite motion introduces Doppler shifts that have remained a major barrier despite progress in ground-based free-space simulations over high-loss channels.
AI.method: The authors reproduce satellite-like Doppler shifts up to 1.55 km/s on the ground by locking a frequency comb to a broadly tunable laser, then apply a dual-channel sampling architecture to compensate optical dispersion and RF nonlinearity while eliminating Nyquist dead zones, together with an iterative interferogram reconstruction algorithm to remove Doppler-induced distortion.
AI.result: After correction, residual systematic errors are within ±10 fs across the full 1.55 km/s range. For simulated MEO and GSO satellite trajectories, fractional frequency instability reaches 3.9×10^-19 at 4,600 s and 3.6×10^-19 at 23,600 s, respectively, extending the operational velocity range by nearly two orders of magnitude beyond previous free-space demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: The approach removes a major technical barrier to a global femtosecond-precision satellite-based time-frequency link and supports future satellite time-frequency dissemination for metrology, navigation, geoscience, and fundamental physics.

title: Bringing coherent closer to compute: coherent-lite multidimensional on-chip interconnect beyond 100 terabits per second
summary: The continued scaling of artificial intelligence (AI) demands optical interconnects that deliver higher bandwidth density within stringent electrical-bandwidth and energy budgets. Coherent optics offers a route beyond the per-lane bandwidth constraints of intensity-modulation direct-detection links, yet its receiver complexity and power overhead have largely confined its use to longer reaches. Here we bring coherent optics closer to compute by demonstrating a coherent-lite multidimensional on-chip interconnect that combines wavelength- and mode-division multiplexing with self-homodyne detection. The architecture co-transmits the local oscillator (LO) and parallel data channels within a single silicon waveguide, using polarization-division routing to preserve LO purity and support high-order modulation. Based on this principle, we develop an inverse-designed dual-polarization mode multiplexer that provides over 37 dB inter-polarization isolation across the C band in an $8 \times 6~μ$m$^2$ footprint, enabling millimetre-scale on-chip multimode routing. Without power-intensive digital carrier recovery, the architecture delivers a single-wavelength line rate of 2 Tb s$^{-1}$ and scales to an aggregate line rate of 103.96 Tb s$^{-1}$ across four modes and 100 wavelengths, using formats up to 64-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM). These results extend on-chip coherent interconnects into the hundred-terabit-per-second regime, offering a scalable route to bandwidth-dense optical connectivity for next-generation computing systems.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a coherent-lite, multidimensional silicon-photonic on-chip interconnect that combines wavelength- and mode-division multiplexing with self-homodyne detection, achieving 2 Tb/s per wavelength and 103.96 Tb/s aggregate across four modes and 100 wavelengths.
AI.motivation: Artificial-intelligence scaling requires optical interconnects with higher bandwidth density under stringent electrical-bandwidth and energy constraints. Coherent optics can exceed per-lane limits of intensity-modulation direct-detection links, but receiver complexity and power overhead have restricted coherent use mainly to longer reaches.
AI.method: The authors use a coherent-lite multidimensional on-chip interconnect combining wavelength- and mode-division multiplexing with self-homodyne detection. The local oscillator and parallel data channels are co-transmitted in a single silicon waveguide, with polarization-division routing preserving local-oscillator purity and supporting high-order modulation. An inverse-designed dual-polarization mode multiplexer provides over 37 dB inter-polarization isolation across the C band in an 8 × 6 μm² footprint and enables millimetre-scale on-chip multimode routing without power-intensive digital carrier recovery.
AI.result: The architecture achieves a single-wavelength line rate of 2 Tb/s and an aggregate line rate of 103.96 Tb/s across four modes and 100 wavelengths, using modulation formats up to 64-ary quadrature amplitude modulation.
AI.conclusion: The results extend on-chip coherent interconnects into the hundred-terabit-per-second regime and offer a scalable route to bandwidth-dense optical connectivity for next-generation computing systems.

title: Spacer-Engineered Spectral Selectivity in Metal-Carbon Solar-Thermal Absorbers
summary: Spectrally selective solar-thermal absorbers must capture sunlight while limiting emission at operating temperatures where the Planck spectrum overlaps the solar band. We connect this trade-off to a controlled optical mechanism in a metal-carbon metasurface. A radiative-limit calculation using AM1.5D illumination identifies how cutoff wavelength, infrared absorptivity and concentration together constrain equilibrium temperature, while the metasurface calculations reveal the additional role of a sharp spectral transition. We then separate the dielectric gap from the absorbing carbon layer in a gold--carbon architecture. Frequency-domain fields and material-resolved dissipation show that the spacer controls the overlap of a gap-localised mode with carbon, extending the high-absorptivity band and sharpening its infrared roll-off. A thickness sweep demonstrates that the spectrum with the strongest visible absorption need not give the highest radiative-limit equilibrium temperature. Polar-angle- and polarisation-resolved calculations demonstrate the angular robustness of the proposed plasmonic metasurface and assess the extent to which normal-incidence spectra approximate hemispherical emission. The calculated high-temperature values are benchmarks for the fixed-geometry, fixed-optical-constant model, not operating temperature predictions for the gold structure. The study establishes spacer-controlled loss partitioning as a route to shaping solar-thermal spectra and distinguishes optical selectivity from materials durability and useful heat output.

AI.tldr: A computational study of a gold-carbon plasmonic metasurface shows that dielectric spacer thickness controls how a gap-localized mode overlaps the carbon absorber, thereby extending visible absorption and sharpening the infrared roll-off; however, the spectrum with the strongest visible absorption is not necessarily the one yielding the highest radiative-limit equilibrium temperature.
AI.motivation: Spectrally selective solar-thermal absorbers must absorb sunlight while suppressing infrared emission at operating temperatures where the Planck spectrum overlaps the solar band, so the paper aims to connect this radiative trade-off to a controlled optical mechanism in a metal-carbon metasurface.
AI.method: The authors use an AM1.5D radiative-limit calculation to relate cutoff wavelength, infrared absorptivity, and concentration to equilibrium temperature, and perform frequency-domain metasurface calculations for a gold-carbon architecture with a separated dielectric gap and absorbing carbon layer. They analyze fields and material-resolved dissipation, sweep spacer thickness, and calculate polar-angle- and polarization-resolved responses.
AI.result: The radiative-limit calculation shows how cutoff wavelength, infrared absorptivity, and concentration constrain equilibrium temperature, while metasurface calculations reveal the added role of a sharp spectral transition. Spacer-controlled overlap of a gap-localized mode with carbon extends the high-absorptivity band and sharpens the infrared roll-off. A thickness sweep shows that the strongest visible absorption does not necessarily give the highest radiative-limit equilibrium temperature. Angular and polarization calculations indicate angular robustness and assess how well normal-incidence spectra approximate hemispherical emission. The abstract does not report experimental fabrication or measured performance.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes spacer-controlled loss partitioning as a route for shaping solar-thermal spectra and distinguishes optical selectivity from materials durability and useful heat output. The calculated high-temperature values are benchmarks for the fixed-geometry, fixed-optical-constant model rather than operating-temperature predictions for the gold structure.

title: Universal Statistics of Random Waves in Multi-Port non-Hermitian Scattering Systems
summary: We study the statistical properties of wave transport of a fixed multi-port non-Hermitian scattering system through wavefront shaping to explore all possible coherent illumination conditions. This is a departure from traditional approaches utilizing cavity shaping to create an ensemble of systems with different detailed scattering arrangements that lead to uncorrelated field configurations. Using microwave measurements in the low channel-number limit, we empirically demonstrate universal statistics in the probability density functions (PDF) of reflectivity, transmissivity, and absorptivity, Fisher information and the difference between forward propagating and time reversed transmissivity. Because the PDFs depend only on the number of input channels and the eigenvalues of Hermitian operators, we demonstrate how cavity shaping can be used to manipulate these eigenvalues, even creating Diabolic Point degeneracies, giving us direct control over the shapes and bounds of transport phenomena PDFs. We further investigate the PDFs when the excitations are finite bandwidth pulses as opposed to monochromatic waves, and determine the behavior in the limits of two channels and many channels. Our results establish a new paradigm in statistical investigations and cavity shaping applications by focusing on outcomes arising from all possible excitations, rather than creating conditions for one specific wavefront that optimally achieves a desired purpose.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally and theoretically studies universal transport statistics in a fixed multi-port non-Hermitian scattering system by using wavefront shaping to explore all coherent illumination conditions, rather than cavity-shaping ensembles. Microwave measurements in the low-channel-number limit show universal probability density functions for reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, Fisher information, and forward-versus-time-reversed transmissivity differences, with shapes and bounds controlled by channel number and Hermitian-operator eigenvalues.
AI.motivation: Traditional statistical studies use cavity shaping to generate an ensemble of scattering systems with different detailed arrangements and uncorrelated field configurations. This work instead seeks a statistics based on all possible coherent excitations of a fixed multi-port non-Hermitian system, shifting focus from finding one optimal wavefront to characterizing outcomes across all possible excitations.
AI.method: The authors use wavefront shaping of a fixed multi-port non-Hermitian scattering system and microwave measurements in the low channel-number limit. They empirically obtain probability density functions of reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, Fisher information, and the difference between forward-propagating and time-reversed transmissivity. They also use cavity shaping to manipulate eigenvalues of Hermitian operators, including creating Diabolic Point degeneracies, and investigate finite-bandwidth pulse excitations as well as the two-channel and many-channel limits.
AI.result: The measured probability density functions exhibit universal statistics depending only on the number of input channels and the eigenvalues of Hermitian operators. Cavity shaping can manipulate these eigenvalues, even producing Diabolic Point degeneracies, thereby providing direct control over the shapes and bounds of transport-phenomenon PDFs. The PDF behavior is further determined for finite-bandwidth pulses versus monochromatic waves and in the two-channel and many-channel limits.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a new paradigm for statistical investigations and cavity-shaping applications by focusing on outcomes arising from all possible excitations of a fixed non-Hermitian scattering system, rather than creating conditions for a single wavefront that optimally achieves a desired purpose.

title: A database of optical and thermal-radiative behaviour of materials under solar radiation
summary: Solar-matter interactions are important in many scientific and engineering applications. Modeling them needs consistent optical and thermal-radiative properties over the full solar spectrum. Here we present SpaderOptics, a database for 21 materials: metals, oxides, semiconductors, polymers, ceramics, and carbon. It compiles wavelength-dependent refractive indices and extinction coefficients from the literature. Each literature source is kept separate, together with its original conditions. One physics-based calculation chain turns these data into reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, and emissivity for different incidence angles, slab thicknesses, and temperatures. Combined with the Air Mass Zero (AM0) solar spectrum, the properties give absorbed, reflected, and transmitted solar flux for concentrated sunlight. Equilibrium temperatures are given for both a theoretical lumped body and for a slab body, in which thermal conduction is considered. All data are limited to the solid state, up to a material-specific upper temperature limit. Currently, the database applies to extraterrestrial (AM0) sunlight only. A graphical App is also provided for exploring and visualizing the database.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SpaderOptics, a database of wavelength-dependent optical constants for 21 materials, converted through a physics-based calculation chain into angle-, thickness-, and temperature-dependent radiative properties and solar-flux/equilibrium-temperature results under AM0 sunlight, with a graphical exploration App.
AI.motivation: Solar–matter interactions are important across scientific and engineering applications, and modeling them requires consistent optical and thermal-radiative properties over the full solar spectrum.
AI.method: SpaderOptics compiles literature values of wavelength-dependent refractive indices and extinction coefficients for 21 materials spanning metals, oxides, semiconductors, polymers, ceramics, and carbon. Each literature source and its original conditions are retained separately. A physics-based calculation chain derives reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, and emissivity for different incidence angles, slab thicknesses, and temperatures. Combined with the AM0 solar spectrum, these properties yield absorbed, reflected, and transmitted solar flux for concentrated sunlight, as well as equilibrium temperatures for a theoretical lumped body and a slab body with thermal conduction. Data are restricted to the solid state up to material-specific upper temperature limits, and a graphical App supports exploration and visualization.
AI.result: The output is the SpaderOptics database for 21 materials plus a graphical App. It provides optical and thermal-radiative properties and solar-flux and equilibrium-temperature results; currently it applies only to extraterrestrial AM0 sunlight. The abstract does not report validation metrics or uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a consistent, source-traceable database and calculation framework for modeling optical and thermal-radiative behavior of solid materials under concentrated AM0 solar radiation, with current scope limited to extraterrestrial sunlight and material-specific solid-state temperature limits.

title: Deterministic nonlinear domain engineering algorithm with variable sub-coherence-length domains
summary: We present a new and improved deterministic algorithm that calculates the poling domains for the implementation of arbitrary phase-matching functions (PMF) in quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals for parametric down-conversion photon sources. In contrast to previous work, the algorithm presented here makes full use of the limits of the fabrication process, such as the minimum feature size and resolution of the lithographic process underpinning the poling procedure. This minimizes the tracking error to the target electric field and improves the accuracy in reaching the desired PMF. We give a tutorial on how to calculate the target function for arbitrary PMFs and run the algorithm. We also demonstrate the procedure on a relevant application in quantum sensing, where we use a quadratic phase on the PMF to implement a broadband photon spectrum while maintaining high nonlinearity across the crystal. The designed crystal is experimentally tested, and the result matches expectations.

AI.tldr: A deterministic algorithm is presented for designing poling domains that implement arbitrary phase-matching functions in quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals for parametric down-conversion photon sources. It exploits fabrication limits, is explained tutorial-style, and is demonstrated with a broadband quantum-sensing design whose experimental test matches expectations.
AI.motivation: Arbitrary phase-matching functions in quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals are needed for parametric down-conversion photon sources, but previous deterministic poling-domain algorithms did not fully exploit fabrication constraints, limiting accuracy in reaching the target electric field and desired phase-matching function.
AI.method: The paper introduces an improved deterministic algorithm that calculates poling domains for arbitrary phase-matching functions while incorporating fabrication limits such as minimum feature size and lithographic resolution. It provides a tutorial for calculating the target function for arbitrary phase-matching functions and running the algorithm, and applies a quadratic phase to the phase-matching function to design a broadband photon spectrum while maintaining high nonlinearity across the crystal.
AI.result: The designed crystal was experimentally tested and matched expectations. The abstract does not provide quantitative performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: The algorithm enables more accurate deterministic engineering of quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals by using fabrication-process limits, and the experimental demonstration supports its practical use for broadband photon sources in quantum sensing. Further quantitative comparisons are not provided in the abstract.

title: Reversal of dynamical backaction and cooling below the quantum backaction limit in Floquet-driven multimode optomechanical resonators
comment: 31 pages, 11 figures. Main text: 16 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Supplementary Information: 15 pages, 5 figures. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23734788
summary: Dynamical backaction describes how a driven cavity field responds with delay to mechanical motion, and can be used to cool that motion toward its quantum ground state or amplify it into self-oscillation. Control over this interaction underpins laser cooling, high-fidelity state preparation, quantum transduction, and phonon lasing. In conventional cavity optomechanics, both the sign and the magnitude of the optical damping are dictated by the laser detuning, and cooling is bounded by quantum backaction (QBA), the optomechanical analogue of the Doppler limit in cold atoms. We show, in theory and experiment, that dynamical backaction can be strongly enhanced in multimode optomechanical resonators driven by time-varying (Floquet) optical fields. A modulated drive couples a sideband-unresolved MHz mode to a sideband-resolved GHz mode through the shared cavity, replacing the QBA limit of the target mode by the occupancy of the auxiliary mode. Experimentally, we cool the MHz mode to $47 \pm 13$ phonons, about half its single-mode QBA limit and an order of magnitude below what single-tone backaction reaches at the same intracavity photon number. The character of the interaction can moreover be completely inverted at fixed laser detuning, turning cooling into amplification and vice versa, controlled solely by the modulation frequency. Floquet driving thus extends open-loop quantum control, which requires no measurement or feedback, to mechanical resonators outside the resolved-sideband regime.

AI.tldr: The paper shows theoretically and experimentally that Floquet-modulated optical driving in multimode optomechanical resonators enhances and can invert dynamical backaction, enabling cooling of a sideband-unresolved MHz mechanical mode below its single-mode quantum backaction limit.
AI.motivation: Conventional cavity optomechanics ties the sign and strength of optical damping to laser detuning, and cooling is bounded by the quantum backaction limit, analogous to the Doppler limit in cold atoms. The authors aim to overcome this constraint, particularly for mechanical modes outside the resolved-sideband regime.
AI.method: They use multimode optomechanical resonators driven by time-varying Floquet optical fields. A modulated drive couples a sideband-unresolved MHz mode to a sideband-resolved GHz mode through the shared cavity, replacing the target mode's quantum backaction limit with the occupancy of the auxiliary mode. Experiments test cooling and inversion of dynamical backaction at fixed laser detuning.
AI.result: The MHz mode is cooled to 47 ± 13 phonons, about half its single-mode quantum backaction limit and an order of magnitude below single-tone backaction at the same intracavity photon number. At fixed laser detuning, the interaction can also be completely inverted, switching cooling to amplification and vice versa solely via the modulation frequency.
AI.conclusion: Floquet driving extends open-loop quantum control, requiring no measurement or feedback, to mechanical resonators outside the resolved-sideband regime and enables control over dynamical backaction beyond conventional detuning constraints.

title: Unconventional Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect beyond Magnetization Scaling Driven by Pulse-Field-Induced Metamagnetism in Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$
summary: First-order phase transitions often proceed through metastable states and complicated phase coexistence, yet such nonequilibrium processes are obscured in bulk measurements. The magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) probes the local off-diagonal optical response, offering access to local magnetic dynamics beyond bulk measurements. Here, we investigate the magnetic-field-induced antiferromagnetic (AFM)-ferrimagnetic (FRM) transition in the polar insulator Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$ using pulsed-field MOKE measurements extended for the first time up to 60 T and down to 1.4 K. The MOKE response exhibits unexpected and huge nonmonotonic transient behavior across the metamagnetic phase transition. The MOKE behavior does not show any scaling with the bulk magnetization, pointing to an MOKE analogue of the unconventional anomalous Hall effect. This is a new class of off-diagonal response emerging exclusively at the boundary between competing magnetic orders. At low temperatures, MOKE profiles are highly reproducible in detail, whereas at elevated temperatures they depend strongly on magnetic-field history and pulse protocol, suggesting changes in the driving mechanism of the phase transition. We infer that the excess MOKE anomaly originates from AFM-FRM phase interfaces in real space. Our results, extending MOKE into the 60 T regime, establish pulsed-field magneto-optics as a novel probe capable of uncovering transient and hidden field-induced phenomena through unconventional off-diagonal optical responses.

AI.tldr: Pulsed-field magneto-optical Kerr effect measurements up to 60 T and down to 1.4 K reveal a huge nonmonotonic MOKE anomaly across the field-induced antiferromagnetic-ferrimagnetic transition in Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$ that does not scale with bulk magnetization, indicating an unconventional off-diagonal response linked to AFM-FRM phase interfaces.
AI.motivation: First-order phase transitions often involve metastable states and phase coexistence that are obscured in bulk measurements. The authors use MOKE, which probes the local off-diagonal optical response, to access local magnetic dynamics beyond bulk magnetization measurements.
AI.method: The authors performed pulsed-field magneto-optical Kerr effect measurements on the polar insulator Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$, extending MOKE for the first time up to 60 T and down to 1.4 K, while investigating the magnetic-field-induced antiferromagnetic-ferrimagnetic transition.
AI.result: The MOKE response shows unexpected, huge nonmonotonic transient behavior across the metamagnetic phase transition and does not scale with bulk magnetization, pointing to an MOKE analogue of the unconventional anomalous Hall effect. At low temperatures the MOKE profiles are highly reproducible in detail, whereas at elevated temperatures they depend strongly on magnetic-field history and pulse protocol. The excess MOKE anomaly is inferred to originate from AFM-FRM phase interfaces in real space.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes pulsed-field magneto-optics as a novel probe capable of uncovering transient and hidden field-induced phenomena through unconventional off-diagonal optical responses, and identifies a new class of off-diagonal response emerging at boundaries between competing magnetic orders.

title: Quantum geometric spectroscopy with Schrödinger cat states
summary: We propose a spectroscopic approach that reads out the quantum geometry of matter from the quantum decoherence of Schrödinger-cat light, in the same way that optical absorption reads out the energy structure of matter. For a cat-state probe comprising a superposition of two coherent states, the interbranch coherence of the outgoing light encodes the overlap between the matter states driven by the two branches. We show that, when the electromagnetic fields of the two branches differ only slightly, cat-branch decoherence is quantified by dynamical quantum geometry, which characterizes infinitesimal displacements on the matter-state manifold. For frequency-selective kitten probes of equilibrium matter, we further establish a partition law for the quantum geometric tensor between light and matter, enabling optical readout of matter quantum metric and Berry curvature through, for example, the brightening of a stellar zero in the outgoing Husimi function. For nonequilibrium matter in a pure state, short-pulse cat probes also provide a time-resolved witness of multipartite entanglement through the transient quantum metric, which can be extracted from homodyne measurements of the outgoing light. By turning cat-state decoherence, conventionally regarded as a loss of quantum information, into a carrier of information about matter, this approach establishes a spectroscopic principle that directly probes quantum-state geometry and fluctuations alongside conventional response-based spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: Proposes using the quantum decoherence of Schrödinger-cat light to spectroscopically read out the quantum geometry of matter, including the quantum metric, Berry curvature, and multipartite entanglement, via interbranch coherence and homodyne detection.
AI.motivation: Conventional spectroscopy reads the energy structure of matter through optical absorption. The authors aim to develop an analogous spectroscopy that directly accesses quantum-state geometry and fluctuations, turning cat-state decoherence from a loss of quantum information into a carrier of information about matter.
AI.method: A cat-state probe is formed from a superposition of two coherent states; its interbranch coherence encodes the overlap of matter states driven by the two branches. For small differences between the branch electromagnetic fields, cat-branch decoherence is quantified by dynamical quantum geometry. Frequency-selective kitten probes of equilibrium matter yield a partition law for the quantum geometric tensor between light and matter, enabling optical readout of the matter quantum metric and Berry curvature, for example through brightening of a stellar zero in the outgoing Husimi function. For nonequilibrium matter in a pure state, short-pulse cat probes provide a time-resolved witness of multipartite entanglement through the transient quantum metric extracted from homodyne measurements.
AI.result: The abstract reports a theoretical proposal establishing that cat-branch decoherence can be quantified by dynamical quantum geometry, that a light–matter partition law for the quantum geometric tensor enables readout of quantum metric and Berry curvature, and that short-pulse cat probes can witness multipartite entanglement in nonequilibrium pure states via homodyne measurements. No experimental data or quantitative performance results are provided.
AI.conclusion: The approach establishes a spectroscopic principle that directly probes quantum-state geometry and fluctuations alongside conventional response-based spectroscopy by converting Schrödinger-cat decoherence into information about matter.

title: Architectural Principles for Parameter-Efficient Unitary Transformations in Coherent Optical Neural Networks
summary: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. However, practical implementations are constrained by the number of tunable parameters due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. In such parameter-constrained settings, achieving high expressive power remains a central challenge. We identify two key architectural requirements for maintaining high expressive power under these constraints: (i) statistical uniformity in the implemented transformations and (ii) strong mixing capability per parameter, which enables rapid and unbiased redistribution of information across modes. To realize these requirements, we develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter--beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. Computational evaluations show that, particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks. We further quantify these design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error. The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture built from phase-shifter–beam-splitter pairs to implement parameter-efficient unitary transformations in coherent optical neural networks, improving performance under restricted tunable-parameter budgets compared with conventional Mach-Zehnder mesh architectures.
AI.motivation: Practical coherent optical neural networks are constrained by the number of tunable parameters because of fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. Maintaining high expressive power under such parameter constraints is a central challenge. The authors identify statistical uniformity of implemented transformations and strong mixing capability per parameter as key architectural requirements.
AI.method: The authors develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter–beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. They perform computational evaluations and quantify design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error in feedforward and recurrent networks.
AI.result: Particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks.
AI.conclusion: The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks and supports the identified architectural principles for maintaining expressive power under parameter constraints.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Passive and Active Radio-Frequency Photonic Imaging
summary: Radio-frequency (RF) photonics enables broadband, phase-coherent sensing beyond the reach of purely electronic architectures, yet at a given optical carrier power its sensitivity is bounded by the standard quantum limit of the optical readout. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that this limit can be surpassed in both passive and active RF imaging modalities by encoding RF signals onto a bright phase-squeezed optical carrier and recovering them via balanced homodyne detection, while the RF front end, illumination, and image reconstruction remain classical. A unified measurement model shows that phase squeezing reduces the variance of the additive readout noise by a single factor $g$, yielding peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) gains of up to $2G$, where $G\equiv10\log_{10}(1/g)$: between $G$ and $2G$ for deterministic targets in active imaging when the classical noise of the echoes is negligible against the readout noise, and set by the ratio of scene noise to readout noise in passive imaging. We validate the model in an experiment in the 5--20 MHz band, in which synthesized RF scenes are replayed through a physical squeezed-light receiver. With 3 dB of squeezing, the PSNR improves by about 6 dB, close to $2G$, in the readout-noise-dominated regime of both modalities, and the model predicts the measured gains without free parameters. These results identify where squeezed-light readout benefits RF-photonic imaging: wherever the optical readout noise, rather than the scene or the RF front end, dominates the image error.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates that phase-squeezed optical readout can surpass the standard quantum limit in passive and active radio-frequency photonic imaging, with a unified model validated in the 5–20 MHz band and about 6 dB PSNR improvement using 3 dB squeezing.
AI.motivation: Radio-frequency photonics provides broadband, phase-coherent sensing beyond purely electronic architectures, but at a given optical carrier power its sensitivity is bounded by the standard quantum limit of the optical readout.
AI.method: The authors encode RF signals onto a bright phase-squeezed optical carrier and recover them by balanced homodyne detection while keeping the RF front end, illumination, and image reconstruction classical. They develop a unified measurement model and validate it experimentally in the 5–20 MHz band by replaying synthesized RF scenes through a physical squeezed-light receiver.
AI.result: Phase squeezing reduces the variance of additive readout noise by a factor g, giving PSNR gains up to 2G, where G = 10 log10(1/g). With 3 dB of squeezing, PSNR improves by about 6 dB, close to 2G, in the readout-noise-dominated regime of both modalities, and the model predicts the measured gains without free parameters.
AI.conclusion: Squeezed-light readout benefits RF-photonic imaging specifically where optical readout noise, rather than scene noise or RF front-end noise, dominates the image error.

title: Record-proof optical communication enabled by a quantum receiver with lossless optical decryption
summary: We propose record-proof physical-layer encryption (PLE) based on quantum-optimal reception. Unlike conventional symmetric-key encryption algorithms, the proposed scheme prevents decryption of recorded signals even if the secret key is disclosed after transmission. Existing PLE schemes rely on practical limitations of the eavesdropper's receiver in pursuing record-proof security; ours instead exploits the noncommutativity of conjugate optical quadratures to give the legitimate receiver an intrinsic sensitivity advantage. A phase-controlled Kennedy receiver performs lossless optical decryption and near-optimal binary-state discrimination. We demonstrate record-proof security with a 3.0-dB channel-loss budget, showing that quantum receivers offer cryptographic functions beyond sensitivity enhancement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes record-proof physical-layer encryption using a phase-controlled Kennedy quantum receiver that exploits noncommuting optical quadratures for lossless optical decryption and near-optimal binary-state discrimination, demonstrating a 3.0-dB channel-loss budget.
AI.motivation: Conventional symmetric-key encryption and existing physical-layer encryption schemes may not prevent decryption of recorded signals if the secret key is later disclosed; prior record-proof approaches rely on practical limitations of the eavesdropper's receiver. The authors instead seek an intrinsic sensitivity advantage for the legitimate receiver based on quantum optics.
AI.method: The proposed scheme uses quantum-optimal reception and exploits the noncommutativity of conjugate optical quadratures. A phase-controlled Kennedy receiver performs lossless optical decryption and near-optimal binary-state discrimination. Specific modulation, key-rate, and implementation details are not provided in the abstract.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate record-proof security with a 3.0-dB channel-loss budget and show lossless optical decryption with near-optimal binary-state discrimination. The abstract does not report additional performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: Quantum receivers can provide cryptographic functions beyond sensitivity enhancement, enabling record-proof physical-layer encryption in optical communication.

title: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. Yet when early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmea- sured gap, so disagreement-guided search has no reason to look where the new phenomenon lies. When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI-driven discovery should target informative unmeasured regions rather than only testing where candidate models disagree, because disagreement-guided search can systematically miss narrow phenomena absent from early data.
AI.motivation: AI scientists often use a chain of hypotheses and select experiments where candidate models disagree most. However, when early observations miss a narrow feature, model selection can favor simple curves that agree across the unmeasured gap, leaving disagreement-guided search with no reason to probe the region containing the new phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials in which a narrow peak was omitted from the starting data. They compared discovery behavior, including model-disagreement-guided search, random search, and strategies that probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly.
AI.result: Both AI scientists sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. The agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly.
AI.conclusion: Asking the right question—probing informative unmeasured regions and following up anomalies—rather than testing only where current models disagree, is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

title: Porosification of the dielectric layer in alternating-current electroluminescence devices enables high-resolution tactile imaging
summary: Vision-based tactile sensing enables high-resolution contact perception, yet bulky optical architectures consume valuable space and constrain the functional design of dexterous robotic hands. Here we introduce a self-emissive tactile imaging strategy based on alternating-current electroluminescence (ACEL) devices, in which a compressible porous dielectric encodes contact pressure into spatial emission patterns without external illumination or discrete sensing pixels. We identify a nonlinear capacitance-dependent emission window that provides a basis for tunable pressure-to-light conversion. Pore-size engineering further suppresses local emission deficiencies, reducing spatial intensity variation by nearly ninefold and enabling faithful imaging of contact features down to 100 μm. The continuous electroluminescent interface also reproduces complex contact patterns without computational reconstruction of electrical fields. Direct lamination of the ACEL device onto a complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) image sensor is expected to enable compact contact imaging in an assembly less than 5 mm thick, substantially thinner than conventional vision-based tactile sensors. This approach could reduce the space required for high-resolution tactile imaging, offering greater design freedom for dexterous robotic hands.

AI.tldr: A self-emissive tactile-imaging strategy based on alternating-current electroluminescence (ACEL) devices uses a compressible porous dielectric to convert contact pressure into spatial emission patterns, enabling 100 μm feature imaging and a proposed CMOS-integrated assembly less than 5 mm thick.
AI.motivation: Vision-based tactile sensing provides high-resolution contact perception, but bulky optical architectures consume space and constrain the functional design of dexterous robotic hands. The paper aims to provide compact, high-resolution contact imaging without external illumination or discrete sensing pixels.
AI.method: The authors use ACEL devices with a compressible porous dielectric that encodes contact pressure into spatial emission patterns. They identify a nonlinear capacitance-dependent emission window for tunable pressure-to-light conversion and apply pore-size engineering to suppress local emission deficiencies. The continuous electroluminescent interface is used to reproduce contact patterns without computational reconstruction of electrical fields, and direct lamination onto a CMOS image sensor is proposed for compact contact imaging.
AI.result: The identified nonlinear capacitance-dependent emission window provides a basis for tunable pressure-to-light conversion. Pore-size engineering reduces spatial intensity variation by nearly ninefold and enables faithful imaging of contact features down to 100 μm. Complex contact patterns are reproduced without computational reconstruction of electrical fields. Direct lamination of the ACEL device onto a CMOS image sensor is expected to enable an assembly less than 5 mm thick, substantially thinner than conventional vision-based tactile sensors.
AI.conclusion: The approach could reduce the space required for high-resolution tactile imaging and offer greater design freedom for dexterous robotic hands.

title: Study of Randomness in Quantum Random Number Generator using Bayesian Neural Networks
summary: We propose a Bayesian neural network (BNN) framework to quantify the intrinsic (aleatoric) uncertainty in a continuous-variable quantum random number generator (CV-QRNG). This provides a direct data-driven measure of the QRNG's randomness generation. The BNN is trained on raw homodyne voltage time-series data from a fiber-coupled vacuum-fluctuation QRNG (VFQRNG). For each voltage data segment, the network predicts a Gaussian distribution (mean and variance) for the next sample, and the ensemble-averaged predicted variance is used as a diagnostic of entropy-related behavior under assumptions of our quantum source model. Thus, the predicted variance serves as a BNN model-based monitor of the randomness-generation process. We validate that the BNN metric increases with the local-oscillator (LO) power, consistent with theoretical min-entropy (extractable randomness). We also show the metric is sensitive to practical imperfections, coarse-graining (simulating limited analog-to-digital converter (ADC) sampling) or reducing ADC bit depth causes a clear drop in predicted aleatoric uncertainty, consistent with the source min-entropic model. These results establish the BNN-based metric as a complementary, physically motivated diagnostic tool for QRNG characterization. Unlike conventional tests (e.g. autocorrelation) that miss hardware issues like low ADC resolution, our method provides a direct real-time monitor of the VFRNG performance. Therefore, this metric is useful for real-time monitoring of CV-QRNG conditions, including drifts and other imperfections.

AI.tldr: The paper uses a Bayesian neural network trained on raw homodyne voltage time series from a fiber-coupled vacuum-fluctuation continuous-variable quantum random number generator to quantify aleatoric uncertainty as a real-time diagnostic of randomness generation.
AI.motivation: Conventional QRNG tests such as autocorrelation can miss practical hardware imperfections, so the authors seek a direct, data-driven, physically motivated monitor of randomness-generation behavior in a CV-QRNG.
AI.method: A BNN predicts a Gaussian distribution, mean and variance, for the next sample of each homodyne voltage segment from a fiber-coupled VFQRNG; the ensemble-averaged predicted variance is used as a diagnostic under the quantum source model and is compared with theoretical min-entropy and practical imperfections.
AI.result: The BNN metric increases with local-oscillator power, consistent with theoretical min-entropy, and drops under coarse-graining or reduced ADC bit depth, consistent with the source min-entropic model.
AI.conclusion: The BNN-based metric is established as a complementary, physically motivated diagnostic for QRNG characterization and is useful for real-time monitoring of CV-QRNG conditions, including drifts and other imperfections.

title: On-demand valley control in a WSe2/CrPS4 heterostructure via optically programmed magnetic order
summary: The ability to optically control the valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional semiconductors is critical for scalable valleytronics. While magnetic proximity effects can lift valley degeneracy, static interfaces lack the dynamic control needed for devices. Here, we demonstrate on-demand optical switching of valley symmetry breaking in a WSe2/CrPS4 heterostructure by exploiting light-tunable magnetic order. Using polarization- and time-resolved photoluminescence, we show that excitation below the ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) gap preserves an out-of-plane Néel vector in CrPS4, generating a net out-of-plane spin at the interface and enabling spin-polarized charge transfer. This yields a robust polarization gap in the WSe2 A-exciton decay dynamics without an external magnetic field. Excitation above the LMCT gap extinguishes the polarization gap, indicating a rotation of the Néel vector to in-plane. This reversible switching provides direct evidence of spin-polarized charge transfer. Furthermore, the same optical excitation enables optical control of the decay dynamics of the low-energy excitons (XLE) by ~42%, which is potentially attributed to the modification of interfacial couplings. Our work establishes a first unique multifunctional platform where magnetic symmetry, valley polarization, and exciton relaxation are integrated and dynamically controlled by light.

AI.tldr: The paper reports reversible, all-optical control of valley symmetry breaking and exciton relaxation in a WSe2/CrPS4 heterostructure by tuning CrPS4 magnetic order with below- versus above-LMCT-gap excitation.
AI.motivation: Scalable valleytronics requires dynamic optical control of the valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional semiconductors; magnetic proximity effects can lift valley degeneracy, but static interfaces lack the needed dynamic control for devices.
AI.method: The authors use polarization- and time-resolved photoluminescence to study a WSe2/CrPS4 heterostructure. Excitation below the ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) gap is used to preserve an out-of-plane Néel vector in CrPS4, generate a net out-of-plane interfacial spin, and enable spin-polarized charge transfer; excitation above the LMCT gap is used to drive the Néel vector in-plane.
AI.result: Below-gap excitation produces a robust polarization gap in WSe2 A-exciton decay dynamics without an external magnetic field, while above-gap excitation extinguishes this polarization gap, indicating reversible Néel-vector rotation and providing direct evidence of spin-polarized charge transfer. The same optical excitation also controls low-energy exciton (XLE) decay dynamics by approximately 42%, potentially through modified interfacial couplings.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes, according to the authors, a multifunctional platform integrating magnetic symmetry, valley polarization, and exciton relaxation under dynamic optical control.
